Now, therefore, we shall explain the duties based on custom and tradition (*sāmayācārika-dharma*). *Note: Variant readings from the edition by A. Chinnaswami (Kashi Sanskrit Series, No. 93, Benares 1932) are included in brackets, generally following the end of each *sūtra*. Differences in *sandhi* are disregarded, and obvious typographical errors have been corrected.* ĀpDhS 1.1.1.1: *athātaḥ sāmayācārikān dharmān vyākhyāsyāmaḥ* |
The consensus of those who know the Dharma is authoritative;
so too are the Vedas.
There are four castes: the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra.
Among them, each preceding one is superior by birth.

For those who are not Śūdras and whose actions are not defective, there is the right to initiation, Vedic study, the establishment of the sacred fires, and the performance of fruitful rites. Service is the duty of the Śūdra toward the other castes.
In each preceding caste, there is greater supreme bliss.
(8) Initiation for the sake of knowledge is a purificatory rite according to the revealed scripture.
(9) For the Brāhmaṇa states: "The Sāvitrī is recited from all the Vedas. (10)

"Indeed, he who initiates one who is ignorant, and he who is himself ignorant, enter from darkness into darkness; so says the Brāhmaṇa. (ĀpDhS 1.1.1.11) In that regard, [one should choose] a preparer who is distinguished by noble birth and learning. (ĀpDhS 1.1.1.12) And in him alone, who has reached the culmination of learning and ritual action and who does not deviate from the duties (dharma). (ĀpDhS 1.1.1.13)
He from whom one gathers (ācinoti) the dharmas is the teacher (ācārya). One should never bear malice toward him,
for he gives birth to one through knowledge.
That is the most excellent birth.
(17) The parents produce only the physical body.

(18) One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in the spring, a Rājanya in the summer, and a Vaiśya in the autumn; specifically, a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth year from conception, a Rājanya in the eleventh year from conception, and a Vaiśya in the twelfth year from conception. (19)
Now follow the optional rites (kāmyāni).

In the seventh year, one desiring spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa); in the eighth, one desiring long life; in the ninth, one desiring splendor (tejas); in the tenth, one desiring food; in the eleventh, one desiring sensory power (indriya); in the twelfth, one desiring cattle.

Until the sixteenth year for a Brāhmaṇa, until the twenty-second for a Kṣatriya, and until the twenty-fourth for a Vaiśya—provided he is capable of fulfilling the vows—we shall describe those [rites] which are to be performed.

If the time for the Sāvitrī has passed, he shall observe the student’s vow (brahmacarya) pertaining to the three Vedas for one season. Then follows the initiation (upanayana). Thereafter, he shall perform ritual ablutions in water for one year.
Now, one should be taught [the Veda].
Now, those whose father and grandfather have not been initiated are declared to be equal to killers of a Brahmin (*brahmahatya*). One should avoid their arrival, feeding them, and marriage with them.
For those who desire it, there is an expiation. Just as [the penance] for the first transgression lasts for one season, so does that for a year.
Then follows the initiation ceremony, and after that, the ritual touching of water.
Having counted the years according to each individual who has not yet been initiated,
he should perform the rite with the seven *pāvamānī* verses beginning with “*yad anti yac ca dūrake*,” with the *yajus-pavitra*, the *sāma-pavitra*, and the *āṅgirasa*;
or else, simply with the *vyāhṛtis*.

Now, one may be taught [the Veda]. Now, those for whom the initiation (*upanayana*) is not remembered back through the great-grandfather and so on are considered as belonging to the cremation ground (*śmaśāna*).

One should avoid their arrival, their eating together, and marriage with them. If they desire it, the penance (*prāyaścitta*) is that they should practice the student’s life (*brahmacarya*) according to the three Vedas for twelve years; then follows the initiation, and thereafter the touching of water with the *Pāvamānī* verses and others.

Now follows the instruction on the duties of a householder. There is no teaching of the Veda. Therefore, for one who desists from it, the purificatory rite is the same as that prescribed for the first transgression.
Thereafter, it is as in the case of the natural state. For one who has been initiated, there is residence as a student (brahmacārin) in the teacher’s household for forty-eight years.
[The penance is] one quarter less, or half, or three-quarters [of the standard].
It is at least twelve years. For a religious student (*brahmacārin*) who is seeking knowledge, there is no fasting imposed by another.
[= K 17, K 18: Now follows the rule for the religious student (brahmacarya).
ĀpDhS 1.1.2.19: He shall remain dependent on his teacher, except in cases that cause loss of caste. ĀpDhS 1.1.2.20: He shall act for the benefit of his guru and not oppose him with his speech.
21. He shall sleep on a low seat. 22. He shall not eat food that has been specially prepared for him.
23. Likewise, he shall avoid alkaline substances, salt, honey, and meat.
He shall not sleep during the day;
he shall not indulge in perfumes;
he shall not engage in sexual intercourse.
27. He should not boast of his own excellence. 28. He should not wash his limbs.
29. However, he may wash those parts that are smeared with impurity when the teacher is not looking on.
One should not bathe in water while boasting; if one should bathe, he should float like a staff.
One should have his hair matted, or wear a single lock of matted hair on the crown, and have the rest shaved.
A triple-stranded girdle made of Muñja grass, wound from left to right, is for a Brāhmaṇa, provided he has the means.
A bowstring is for the Kṣatriya;
or it may be made of muñja grass mixed with flax;
a thread of sheep’s wool is for the Vaiśya.
Some say it may be made of *sairī* or *tāmalī* wood.

A staff made of *pālāśa* wood is for a Brāhmaṇa; one grown from the trunk of a *nyagrodha* tree and pointing downward is for a Rājanya; one of *bādara* or *audumbara* wood is for a Vaiśya. Some teachers, however, prescribe a wooden staff without regard to caste. [The same applies to] the garment.
ĀpDhS 1.1.2.40: [The garments] are made of hemp, linen, or skins.
ĀpDhS 1.1.2.41: Some prescribe that the garment be dyed with a decoction.
ĀpDhS 1.1.3.1: That of a Kṣatriya is dyed madder-red.
The girdle of a Vaiśya is made of hemp.
The girdle of a Brāhmaṇa is made of the skin of a black antelope or of a deer;
if it is made of black antelope skin, he should not sit or lie on a seat or bed that has not been spread with grass.
The skin of the Ruru deer for a Kṣatriya; the skin of a goat for a Vaiśya;
and the wool of sheep, as well as blankets, for all castes.

Desiring the increase of spiritual power (*brahman*), he should wear only skins; desiring the increase of political power (*kṣatra*), only garments; desiring the increase of both, both. For so says the Brāhmaṇa. However, he should always wear a skin as his upper garment. He should not look at dancing.
He shall attend assemblies and social gatherings;
he shall not be habitually engaged in idle talk;
he shall be habitually reserved.
ĀpDhS 1.1.3.15: He shall not imitate the teacher's improper behaviors, nor perform his own independent actions.
ĀpDhS 1.1.3.16: He shall converse with women only as much as is necessary.
ĀpDhS 1.1.3.17–24: He should be gentle, tranquil, self-controlled, modest, firm in resolve, untiring, free from anger, and free from envy.

Bringing all his gains to his teacher, he should go on his alms-round in the evening and in the morning without reciting mantras; while begging, he should avoid those of bad character and those who are accursed.
A student who is composed, when women refuse him, takes away their sacrifice, their gift, their oblation, their offspring, their cattle, their Vedic splendor, and their food.
Therefore, one should not refuse a group of students (*brahmacārin*) who are wandering about; for even among them, there may be one who is such as this and observes such a vow—so says the Brāhmaṇa.
One should not seek alms by inference; rather, it is through what is seen or heard.
A Brāhmaṇa should beg with the word "bhavat" at the beginning.
A Kṣatriya [should address him] with "bhavanta-madhyam"; a Vaiśya with "bhavant-antam. Having collected that [wood] and placed it near, he should announce it to the teacher.
He should eat what is served by him.
If he is away from his teacher, he should eat what is served by the teacher’s family.
If he is away from them as well, he may eat what is served by other Śrotriyas.
35. He should not go about for his own sake.
36. Having eaten, he himself should wash the vessel. 37. And he should not leave any food residue.
If he is unable [to do so], he should bury it in the ground;
or he should cast it into the waters;
or he should entrust it to an Ārya.
Or [he may give it] to a Śūdra who stands between [himself and the fire].

(ĀpDhS 1.1.3.41) One who has gone abroad should eat after having offered [a portion] of his alms-food into the fire. (ĀpDhS 1.1.3.42) Alms-food is praised as being equivalent to an oblation; in that regard, the teacher serves as the deity. (ĀpDhS 1.1.3.43)
And [he should do so] for the sake of the *āhavanīya* fire (ĀpDhS 1.1.3.44). Having fed him (ĀpDhS 1.1.3.45),
he eats what remains as leavings (ĀpDhS 1.1.4.1).
That [offering] is indeed the remnant of the oblation (havirucchiṣṭa).
Whatever other substances he offers according to what is available, those are indeed the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
This is the sacrifice of the religious student (brahmacārin), which is perpetually extended.
Nor [should he give] to him [food containing] alkaline salt, honey, or meat; as it is said: "Just as [one avoids] alkaline salt, honey, and meat.
By this, other restrictive rules are explained.
For scripture is more authoritative than customary practice based on inference;
moreover, a cause for engagement is observed,
for pleasure is indeed perceived [as that cause].
One may eat the leavings of the father and of the eldest brother. If there is a lapse from dharma, [the food] must not be eaten. Every evening and morning, one should fetch a water-jar.
Having brought firewood from the forest together with his wife, he should place it below [the fire].
He should not go out to fetch firewood after sunset. Having kindled the fire and swept around it, he should add fuel in the evening and in the morning, according to the instruction.
Some say that the worship of the fire should take place only in the evening.
One should sweep around the kindled fire with the hand, not with a broom. Prior to this [point], however, one may act as one pleases.
One should not perform useless acts or sip water with the remainder of water used for the sacred fires.
One should not sip water that has been stirred by the hand or drawn up with only one hand.
And one should avoid sleep.
Now, day by day, he should protect his teacher through actions consistent with dharma and artha.
Having protected him, when going to sleep, he should say: "I have protected the protector of dharma.
If the teacher should transgress a rule either through negligence or intentionally, he should point it out to him in private.
If [the teacher] does not turn back, the student should himself undertake the duties or cause them to be performed.
Now, they say that he who rises first and goes to sleep last does not sleep at all.
For a religious student who has thus disciplined his self, all his duties—even those belonging to the householder—become fruitful and accomplished right here.
The word *tapas* refers to the observances (*niyama*).

(1.2.5.1) If one transgresses them, knowledge and ritual action flow away from this person, along with the sacred Veda (*brahman*) and his offspring. (1.2.5.2) It results in falling into a pit and is detrimental to longevity. (1.2.5.3)

Therefore, seers (ṛṣis) are not born among later generations due to the transgression of observances. However, some become "seers through sacred learning" (*śruta-ṛṣi*) upon rebirth by means of the remainder of the fruits of their actions, such as Śvetaketu.
Whatever even a concentrated Brahmin acquires from his teacher, the fruit thereof becomes for him exactly like that of sacred knowledge (*brahman*).

Furthermore, they teach that whatever one intends with the mind, speaks with speech, or perceives with the eye—whether one is forming a resolution, meditating, speaking, or looking—it becomes exactly so.
(ĀpDhS 1.2.5.8) The rites to be performed for the propitiation of the teacher consist of the *svastyayana* and the completion of the study.
(ĀpDhS 1.2.5.9) Apart from these, other duties of the religious student (*brahmacārin*) cease. (ĀpDhS 1.2.5.10)
The student who maintains his private Vedic study, who delights in dharma, who practices austerity, who is upright and gentle, succeeds.
Always rising during the latter part of the night, while standing before the teacher, he should offer the morning salutation, saying: "I am so-and-so, sir.
And this applies to others as well—those residing in the same village who are older—before the morning meal.

And upon returning from a journey, when meeting [others], a Brāhmaṇa desiring heaven and long life should salute by extending his right arm level with the ear; a Rājanya, level with the chest; a Vaiśya, level with the waist; and a Śūdra should salute with his hands joined in añjali at a low level.
And for those of the preceding castes, there shall be the dropping of the name, as well as the salutation and the return-salutation.
But when the sun has risen, having met the teacher, there shall be the clasping of his feet;
and this salutation shall always take place.
"Having performed the respectful salutation (*upasaṃgrahaṇa*), [one should address him as] 'Teacher' (*ācārya*)," so say some.

(ĀpDhS 1.2.5.20) With his right hand, having touched the teacher's right foot from below, he should grasp it including the toes. (ĀpDhS 1.2.5.21) Some say that both feet should be grasped by pressing them with both hands. (ĀpDhS 1.2.5.22)

23. Throughout the entire day, he should remain closely applied to his studies and uninterrupted in his recitation. 24. Likewise, he should do so during tasks for his teacher. 25. And even on days when study is forbidden, he should do so mentally.
He should study when summoned.
He should always cause his teacher to lie down at night, having washed and massaged his feet;
permitted by him, he may lie down himself.
And he should not stretch out his feet toward him.
Some say that there is no stretching out of the feet while one is on a couch.
Nor should he speak while lying down in the presence of the teacher.
When addressed, however, he should reply while remaining seated if the teacher is seated; if the teacher is standing, he should reply after rising.
He should follow one who is walking, and run after one who is running.
He should not sit down wearing shoes, nor with his head wrapped, nor with his hands tucked into his garments.
But one who is on a journey or engaged in ritual work may sit down [if he cannot stand]. If he does not sit down,
he should attend upon his teacher like a god— without gossiping, with a clear mind, and listening to his speech.

He should not have his hands under his armpits. He should study with the wind blowing from behind him, without supporting himself against anything with his hand, and without leaning on anything else. When wearing two garments, he should wear the sacrificial thread over the left shoulder (yajñopavītī).
But one who has only a single garment should have the sacred thread hanging below the navel;
facing [the teacher], he should face away from him;
not too close, nor too far.
ĀpDhS 1.2.6.22: [He should sit] as far as he can reach with his two arms while seated.
ĀpDhS 1.2.6.23: Not against the wind.
ĀpDhS 1.2.6.24–25: One who studies a single chapter should sit facing the right arm; many may sit according to the available space.

One should not sit while [the teacher] is standing, except when [sitting] is prescribed by the practice of yoga. One should not lie down while [the teacher] is sitting. And one should not perform an action while [the teacher] is desiring to act, provided that it is within one's power to do so.
And he should not clasp the feet of one who occupies his own station in his presence;
or he may address him by his lineage name (*gotra*).
Nor should he rise toward him, nor rise after him.
Even if he should be his teacher, [he should rise from his seat];
he should move away from his place and from his seat.
Some say that one should address even such a teacher as "my teacher" by using the name of his own pupil.

But toward one who, though not related to him as a teacher, is entitled to respect because of his conduct, he should behave as toward a teacher, even if that person is merely a junior student (*anvaksthānīya*). Having eaten in his presence, he should not rise without first offering the leftovers, nor should he rinse his mouth (*ācamet*). He should rise after addressing him with the words, "What shall I do? or he may rise silently.
He should rise either silently or [with a greeting].
He should not turn his back toward his teacher; rather, having circumambulated him from left to right, he should depart.
He should not look at a naked woman.
One should not smell plants or trees after cutting them. One should avoid sandals, an umbrella, and a vehicle.
One should not smile.
ĀpDhS 1.2.7.7: "If he should smile, he should smile with his mouth covered," for so says the Brāhmaṇa.
ĀpDhS 1.2.7.8: He should not kiss a woman with his mouth.
ĀpDhS 1.2.7.9: He should not desire her with his heart.
One should not touch water without a specific reason.
For the Brāhmaṇa says: "One who is menstruating, one with blood-stained teeth, and one who speaks the truth [should avoid touching water].
Regarding the knowledge he acquires from his teacher, those who belong to the lineage of that teacher are also his teachers in that respect.
ĀpDhS 1.2.7.13: When he sees others whom he should otherwise greet by clasping the feet, then these [others] should be greeted in that manner.
ĀpDhS 1.2.7.14: When several teachers are present and alms have been obtained, the alms belong to whichever teacher he is attending.
ĀpDhS 1.2.7.15–17: Upon returning home from his studies, he should give [the alms] to his mother; the mother should present them to her husband; the husband [should present them] to the teacher.
Or he may employ it for religious duties.

Having acquired as much learning as he is capable of, he should offer the Vedic teacher’s fee according to his ability and in accordance with the law. But if the teacher has fallen into distress, he should obtain it even from a fierce person or from a Śūdra.
ĀpDhS 1.2.7.21: Some say that it is always lawful to obtain the teacher’s requirements from a Śūdra or an Ugra.
ĀpDhS 1.2.7.22: And having given [the gift], he should not speak of it.
ĀpDhS 1.2.7.23: And having performed [the service], he should not remember it.

He should avoid self-praise and the disparagement of others. When commanded, he should do exactly that. And his livelihood may be obtained elsewhere than from the teacher, provided it does not involve transgressing the teacher's instructions.
Except for clasping the feet and eating the leftovers, one's conduct toward the teacher’s wife is the same as toward the teacher himself.
Likewise, this applies when he teaches him [the Veda] at his command,
and also toward a fellow student who is older.
ĀpDhS 1.2.7.30: The conduct toward the teacher’s son is the same as toward the teacher, with the exception of eating his leavings.
ĀpDhS 1.2.7.31: This same customary rule applies to these [persons] even for one who has returned home from studentship. ĀpDhS 1.2.8.1: As is the conduct of the religious student (brahmacārin).

ĀpDhS 1.2.8.2: Wearing garlands, having his face smeared, having his hair and beard anointed, being sprinkled or rubbed with unguents, wearing a turban or a head-wrap, wearing a tunic, sandals, or wooden shoes; ĀpDhS 1.2.8.3: One should not perform or cause these acts to be performed by him during the daily religious observances (*udācāra*); ĀpDhS 1.2.8.4: Nor during private activities (*svairikarma*).

ĀpDhS 1.2.8.5: Just as [one should avoid] cleaning the teeth, anointing, and scraping [the nails]. ĀpDhS 1.2.8.6: And the teacher should not mention the substances used for those acts when they have come into contact with himself.

ĀpDhS 1.2.8.7: But having bathed at the proper time according to the rule, he should not withhold [the food] that has been brought, whether he has been invited or has gone there of his own accord; so say some.
He should not sit on a seat that is higher, nor on one with many legs, nor on one that is supported on all sides.
He should not occupy a bed or a seat already used by another. When traveling on a road, he may mount a vehicle if so directed.
One should avoid [using] a gaming hall, a whetstone, a mat, and a bed.
One should not address the teacher with anything other than pleasant words unless one has been addressed first.
One should avoid poking at him, whispering in his ear, laughing at him, calling out to him, mentioning his name [in a disrespectful manner], and giving him commands.
In times of distress, he may make himself known for the sake of his livelihood.
Living together with his teacher, he should go to see him every morning and evening without being summoned.
And upon returning from a journey, he should see him on that very day.

ĀpDhS 1.2.8.19–20: When the teacher and the sub-teacher meet, the student should clasp the hands of the sub-teacher and desire to clasp the hands of the teacher; the other (the sub-teacher) should then refuse. ĀpDhS 1.2.8.21: And honor toward him [the sub-teacher] is suspended in the presence [of the teacher].
ĀpDhS 1.2.8.22: He should go frequently to the teacher’s household for the purpose of seeing him, bringing with him as much as he can afford, even down to items for cleaning the teeth.

[K adds: 8.23 One should not approach one's mother, father, teacher, the sacred fires, or the household with empty hands; nor should one approach a king unless one has studied the Veda. ĀpDhS 1.2.8.23: In that regard, this is the conduct toward the teacher. ĀpDhS 1.2.8.24: Desiring him as if he were his own son, and not concealing anything regarding all matters of dharma, the teacher should, being well-prepared, cause him to grasp the knowledge. [K = 25]
And one should not, except in times of distress, obstruct him from his own interests by interrupting his Vedic study.

(25) A student who fails to achieve proficiency while under the guidance of his teacher becomes, in effect, a non-student, even though he has placed himself under him. (26) Likewise, a teacher who neglects what has been revealed in the sacred tradition ceases to be a teacher. (27)
And he should constantly reproach him for his offenses.

(ĀpDhS 1.2.8.28) Frightening, fasting, touching water, and exclusion from sight are the punishments, applied according to the gravity of the offense, until desistance occurs. (ĀpDhS 1.2.8.29) When he has desisted and completed his period of studentship (*brahmacarya*), one should dismiss him with the words: "Be next in line to the other duties. (ĀpDhS 1.2.8.30)
Having performed the opening ceremony (*upākaraṇa*) on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, one shall not study during the first month at nightfall.
On the full moon day of Taiṣya, or under the asterism Rohiṇī, one should cease.
Some say [one should cease] after four and a half months.

ĀpDhS 1.3.9.4: One should avoid reciting [the Veda] at sacred fords (*nigama*). ĀpDhS 1.3.9.5: Or one may study after the ground has been smeared with a lump of cow dung from an ox (*ānaḍuha*). ĀpDhS 1.3.9.6: One must not study within the distance of a throw of a yoke-pin (*śamyā*) in every direction from a cremation ground (*śmaśāna*).
When a village or a field has been settled upon, there is no suspension of study.
However, while that [corpse] is still being recognized in that very place, one should not study.
A Śūdra and an outcast (patita) are like a cremation ground.
According to some, [the suspension of study occurs] when [a woman] is in the same house.

However, in the case of a Śūdra woman, there is a suspension of study only upon looking at her or being looked at by her. Likewise, there is a suspension upon sexual intercourse with any other woman who has transgressed her caste.

One who is about to study the Veda, desiring to converse with a woman in her courses, should first converse with a Brāhmaṇa and then converse with her. But having conversed with her, he must again converse with a Brāhmaṇa before he studies; thus there is the highest welfare for her offspring.
[There is no study] within a corpse;

[there is no study] within a *caṇḍāla*. But when corpses have been carried out, there is no study until they have crossed the boundary. [K: when they have gone out; var.: when they have been carried out]
And [he should do so] upon seeing [them] in the forest;
(17) and on that day, when outsiders have arrived in the village; (18) even if they are present [at other times]. (19)
During the period of twilight, when there is thunder, [the suspension lasts] for the night (ĀpDhS 1.3.9.20). During lightning, it lasts until one goes to sleep (ĀpDhS 1.3.9.21).

When lightning flashes at dawn, or for as long as one can discern a dark or reddish glow from the distance of a *śamyā*-throw, during that time the day, including the evening, is a period of non-study (anadhyāya) (ĀpDhS 1.3.9.22).
[One should study] during the small hours of the night when there is thunder;
some say [after] midnight;
and also when cattle are being penned.
ĀpDhS 1.3.9.26: And [one should not study] as long as those who are to be executed are being executed.
ĀpDhS 1.3.9.27: One should not study while mounted on the back of animals. ĀpDhS 1.3.9.28: [One should not study] for a day and a night on new-moon days.
And during the Cāturmāsya sacrifices;
the Vairamaṇa, the Aṣṭākya, and the Aupākaraṇa—these are three-day periods [of impurity] for teachers.
Likewise for kinsmen who are related by blood.

In the case of a mother, a father, or a teacher, the period of impurity lasts for twelve days. During those days, there is ritual bathing in water as prescribed by the rules; this continues for that same duration. Furthermore, for those who follow the deceased, there is the shaving of the hair.

"Those who have returned [from their teacher] should not have their hair shaved, except at the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*); so say some. Furthermore, there is a *Brāhmaṇa* passage: "This [head] is indeed empty and uncovered when it is shaven; that which is the top-knot (*śikhā*) is its covering. However, in the case of sacrificial sessions (*satras*), the shaving of the top-knot occurs because of a specific scriptural injunction.

Regarding the death of a teacher, some say [one should observe impurity] for three days and nights. Regarding the death of a learned Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*) who has not been dead for a full year, one day.
Regarding the death of a fellow student (*sabrahmacārin*), some say [the same].
Upon the arrival of one learned in the Veda (*śrotriya*), one who desires to learn, or one who is already studying, should study only after having obtained permission;
or he may teach him.
Furthermore, in the presence of his teacher, he should study only after saying, "Recite, sir! (*adhīhi bho*).
Or he may teach.
(16) One who desires to learn should clasp both [feet] of the teacher, both before and after the lesson.

The barking of dogs and donkeys, the howling of hyenas, the cries of the *ekasṛk* and the owl, all sounds of musical instruments, and the sounds of weeping, singing, and *sāman* chants [constitute times unfit for study].
(ĀpDhS 1.3.10.19) Furthermore, there is no study of the *sāmans* according to other recensions (*śākhā*).
(ĀpDhS 1.3.10.20) And in all cases involving vocal actions, [there is no study] where these [sounds] might mingle. (ĀpDhS 1.3.10.21)
ĀpDhS 1.3.10.22: Having vomited, [he should remain] until the end of sleep.
ĀpDhS 1.3.10.23: Or, having consumed clarified butter.
ĀpDhS 1.3.10.24: [This applies when one has a] foul odor.
One should not study sour food that has come into contact with oneself; nor after eating at night; nor while the hands are full of water.

Having eaten food prepared for a deceased person, there shall be no study for the entire day including the evening. (28) This applies until the food has been fully digested. (29) However, one may finish the meal with food that was not intended for a *śrāddha*. (30)
At the commencement of a *kāṇḍa*, one who has not had his mother present [should not eat];
at the conclusion of a *kāṇḍa*, one who has not had his father present [should not eat].
Some say that this also applies after eating at a sacrifice to deities who have human forms.
There is no suspension of study on account of stale rice, nor on account of raw meat.
Likewise, there is no suspension on account of herbs, trees, roots, and fruits.
On the day one begins a section (kāṇḍa) or performs the recitation of a section (anuvāka), one should not study that same section on that day.
And during the commencement and completion of the recitation of a *pārāyaṇa* of that particular Vedic knowledge;
when the wind makes a sound on the ground or there is a rustling of grass; when it rains or where streams of rain fall;
and at the boundary between a village and a forest.
And on a high road;
and having traveled abroad, that day is for the resumption of study;
and during activities performed at one's own will.

ĀpDhS 1.3.11.13: Just as in the case of washing the feet, massaging, and anointing the body; [K 11, 1: hands, 2: ointments]. ĀpDhS 1.3.11.14: For that duration of time, one should neither study nor teach. [K 12] ĀpDhS 1.3.11.15: During the two twilights. [K 13]
Likewise, one who has climbed a tree;

one who has immersed himself in water; and at night, one who is in an open space. (16+17+18 = K 14: Likewise, one who has climbed a tree, one who has immersed himself in water, and at night, one who is in an open space.)
And also during the day when [the sun] is obscured.
The recitation of the *anuvākas* is not prescribed during the months of Āṣāḍha and Vāsantika. Nor is it prescribed for the daily lesson (*nityapraśna*) except according to the rule.
The rule for that is as follows:
Having not yet eaten his morning meal, having gone to the edge of water, being self-restrained and pure, he should study in a clean place according to the lesson, reciting it aloud;
or, during a time when there is no formal lesson, he should study it mentally.

When lightning is imminent, during thunder, when there is a lack of ritual purity (*aprāyatya*), regarding the food of the deceased, and during mist, they prescribe a mental suspension of study (*mānasa*).
Some say this applies specifically to the eating of *śrāddha* food.
Where lightning, thunder, and rain occur together outside of the rainy season, there is a three-day suspension of study.
Some say that the suspension lasts as long as the earth remains flooded with water.
According to others, the suspension of these [studies] lasts for one or two days.

At the eclipse of the sun or moon, during an earthquake, when there is thunder in the waters, at the fall of a meteor, and during a fire-omen, there is a suspension lasting until the same time on the following day for all branches of learning.

In the case of clouds appearing out of season, a halo around the sun and moon, a rainbow, a mock-sun, or a fish-shaped apparition; and when there is a foul odor in the wind or during a mist—one should not study during all these times for as long as they persist. (ĀpDhS 1.3.11.31) When the wind has ceased, one may study for a moment. (ĀpDhS 1.3.11.32) If a female jackal howls, or if a one-legged bird cries out, one should not study until sleep. (ĀpDhS 1.3.11.33)

At night, one should not study in the forest, nor where there is no fire, nor where there is no gold. (ĀpDhS 1.3.11.34) One should not study that which has not been previously taught, nor the Vedic meters outside of their proper season. (ĀpDhS 1.3.11.35) And also at the time of twilight. (ĀpDhS 1.3.11.36)
37. This is prescribed for all times. [K 33] 38. Other matters have been stated above regarding assemblies. [K 34] 1. "Austerity and Vedic study," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

Regarding this, it is heard in scripture: "Whether he recites his daily study while standing, sitting, or lying down, he performs austerity; for the daily study of the Veda is indeed austerity. Furthermore, there is the *Vājasaneyi-Brāhmaṇa*: "This daily study of the Veda is indeed the sacrifice to Brahman. Its *vaṣaṭ*-calls are the thundering, the lightning, the crashing of thunder, and the blowing of the wind. Therefore, when it thunders, lightens, crashes with thunder, or when the wind blows, one should certainly recite; [this is] so that there may be no failure of the *vaṣaṭ*-calls."
In another recension, the sentence concludes as follows:

"Now, if wind should blow, or it should thunder, or lightning should flash, or a thunderclap should strike, he should recite a single Ṛg-verse, a single Yajus-formula, or a single Sāman, saying: 'Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Suvaḥ! Truth! Austerity! I offer this into faith! By this very means, his private Vedic study becomes properly undertaken. [K 1: *vā vāto* instead of *vāto vā*; K 2: *teno haiva* instead of *teno haiva*]

This being so, that which is not prohibited by the agreement of the Aryas [is valid]. For they teach the rules regarding study and non-study; that would be meaningless if one were to disregard the Vājasaneyi Brāhmaṇa. Indeed, the agreement of the Aryas has no discernible underlying cause.
Regarding sacred knowledge (*vidyā*), an interruption of study (*anadhyāya*) is prescribed; however, no such interruption applies to the application of mantras during ritual acts (*karmayoga*).

The injunctions declared in the Brāhmaṇas have their textual recensions lost; they are inferred from their actual performance. But where activity proceeds from the perception of pleasure, there is no scriptural authority (*śāstra*).
One who follows that [neglect] prepares himself for hell. Now, the rules have been stated for the Brāhmaṇas; their praise is that they are the "Great Sacrifices" and the "Great Sattras."
Every day, one should offer the *bhūtabali* and give gifts to humans according to one’s ability.

To the gods, an offering with the exclamation *svāhā* should be made using even wood; to the ancestors, an offering with the exclamation *svadhā* using even a vessel of water; and [one should perform] the private recitation of the Veda (*svādhyāya*).
Honor should be rendered to those of higher castes and to those who are older.
One who is joyful becomes arrogant; one who is arrogant transgresses the Dharma; indeed, upon the transgression of Dharma, there is hell.
There is no instruction for one who has returned home [from his teacher].
The syllable *Oṃ* is the gate to heaven; therefore, one about to study the Veda should begin with this.
And by engaging in other idle chatter, the Brahman departs through such worldly speech. In sacrifices, there are these and similar utterances of invocation.
And in the world, during rites for prosperity, there should be these very same types of sentences, such as "An auspicious day! Hail! Prosperity!"
One should not perform a *kṛcchra* penance without a formal agreement, except for the threefold proclamation and the threefold simultaneous recitation.
Hārīta says that one must proceed without hesitation until the Veda has been mastered;
there is no other way outside of the Veda.
One should clasp the feet of a teacher who has been formally appointed to teach for as long as the study lasts;
some say this should be done constantly toward one who is worthy [of such honor];
there is no other course of action.
But regarding the elders:
when there is a mutual application of the Veda among them, no further progress is possible;
they teach that "the Veda thus increases."

"When the marriage has been performed, one who desires further learning should live for two months every year in the teacher's household with a concentrated mind," says Śvetaketu; "for by this method, I acquired more learning than in the previous period.
This, however, is contradicted by the scriptures.
For when the establishment of the household has taken place, the obligatory duties are prescribed:
the Agnihotra sacrifice, guests,
and whatever else is similarly enjoined.
One should not refuse him when he urges one for the sake of study;
nor should one perceive any fault in him. If an invitation does not occur spontaneously, there is simply no proceeding with him.
Service toward one's mother and father is to be performed as toward a teacher. (K 5) Upon returning from his studies, all elders are to be saluted by clasping their feet.
(K 6) And also upon returning from a journey, when meeting them. (K 7)

Among brothers and sisters, one should perform the salutation by clasping the feet according to their seniority. (K 8) And there should be constant honor toward them, as prescribed by the teachings. (K 9) One should rise to meet and greet officiating priests, fathers-in-law, paternal uncles, and maternal uncles who are younger than oneself. (K 10)
Or he may clasp [the feet] silently.
(ĀpDhS 1.4.14.12) A ten-year-old is considered a city-friend (*paurasakhyam*); a five-year-old is a fellow-student (*cāraṇa*). One who is three years older than a *śrotriya* deserves a salutation.
(ĀpDhS 1.4.14.13) When a difference in age is known, one must salute the elder. (ĀpDhS 1.4.14.14)
One need not salute a teacher who has fallen into a precarious situation.
Or, having climbed up after him, one may salute him.
However, in all cases, one must rise before saluting.
One who is impure shall not be saluted. Likewise, one shall not salute someone who is impure. And one who is impure shall not return a greeting. [18+19+20 = K 17]
Women who are of equal age [are saluted by name].

(ĀpDhS 1.4.14.21) One should not salute while wearing shoes, with the head wrapped, or with the hands occupied. (ĀpDhS 1.4.14.22) Women, as well as Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, are addressed by their pronoun, not by name. (ĀpDhS 1.4.14.23)
Some say that one should behave toward one's mother and the wife of one's teacher in this same manner.

(ĀpDhS 1.4.14.24) Know that a ten-year-old Brahmin and a hundred-year-old Kṣatriya are father and son; of these two, the Brahmin is the father. (ĀpDhS 1.4.14.25) One should ask a person younger than oneself or a peer about their well-being. (ĀpDhS 1.4.14.26)
"Health" for a Kṣatriya; "no loss" for a Vaiśya; "freedom from disease" for a Śūdra.
One should not pass by a *śrotriya* without speaking to him;
nor should one pass by a woman in the forest.

During the attendance upon teachers, elders, and guests, during the fire-oblation, the recitation of prayers, eating, sipping water, and Vedic study, one should wear the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*).
Having sipped water from water that has reached the ground, one becomes pure. Or, one becomes pure if someone who is already pure causes him to sip water.
One should not sip water from the drops of rain.
Likewise, [one should not touch] water in a hole;
nor [water] that is hot without a reason;
and one who has an empty hand should, after raising it, sip water from a vessel.
When one has the capacity, one should not remain impure even for a moment, nor naked.
There is no purification for one who is in the water;
however, having emerged from it, one should sip water.

One should not place unsprinkled fuel into the fire. On a spread of grass where one is sitting, even if it is impure, one who is pure may consider himself pure provided he does not touch others who are impure. The same applies to grass and wood that have been buried.
Having sprinkled it with water, he may use the garment. If it has been defiled by a swelling [or a corpse], he should plunge into water with his clothes on.
Or, having washed that spot, touched it with fire, washed it again, and sipped water, he becomes pure.
One should not sit near the fire while impure.
Some say [one should not do so] even from a distance of one arrow-length.
Nor should one blow upon it.

And he should not place [the water-pot] on a bed. In a village that has abundant fuel and water, where the means of purification are under one's own control, there a Brāhmaṇa’s dwelling is in accordance with dharma.

Having voided urine or feces, having washed away the smears of urine and feces, the smears of food, the smears of impurity from eating, and those smears of semen, and having washed his feet and sipped water, he becomes pure.
Standing or bent forward, he should sip water;
sitting down, he should sip water three times with water that reaches his heart.
He should wipe his lips three times, or twice, according to some.
He should touch [the organs] once; some say twice.
Having sprinkled his left hand with his right hand, he should touch his feet, his head, and his sense organs—the eyes, the nostrils, and the ears—and then he should touch water.
But one who is about to eat, even if already pure, should sip water twice, wipe his mouth twice, and touch [the lips] once.
Having touched the two lips as far as the dark edge, he should sip water.
One does not become impure by the hairs of the beard as long as they remain inside the mouth, provided that he does not touch them with his hand.

ĀpDhS 1.5.16.12: Regarding those drops which are perceived falling from the mouth, sipping water (ācamana) is prescribed for them. ĀpDhS 1.5.16.13: Some say that one should not sip water for those [drops] that fall upon the ground. ĀpDhS 1.5.16.14: After dreaming, sneezing, smelling the breath from the nose, touching tears, touching blood, hair, fire, cows, a Brāhmaṇa, or a woman; after walking on a high road; after touching something impure; after touching an impure person; and after putting on the lower garment (nīvī)—one should touch water. [K 1: *kṣavadhau*; K 2: *śiṅghaṇikā* and variant *śṛṅghāṇikā*]
Or [he may offer] fresh dung, herbs, or earth.
Meat cut with a knife intended for killing is unfit to be eaten.
One should not bite off a portion of a cake with one's teeth.

In whose family one dies, food must not be eaten there during the ten-day period of impurity. Likewise, while the woman who has given birth has not yet arisen from her confinement, and while a corpse remains inside the house.
Food that has been defiled by one who is impure is not pure, yet it is not necessarily unfit for consumption.
However, food brought by an impure Śūdra is unfit for consumption.
And so too is any food in which there is a hair.
Or anything else that is impure;
that which has been touched by impure things;
or a worm that frequents impurity.
Or [the food is defiled by] the limb of a mouse;
or by what has been trodden upon with the foot;
or by a garment.
If it has been seen by a dog or by one who uses an earthenware vessel; or if it has been brought in by a garment;
or if it has been brought at night by a female slave.
Or while [he] is eating;
or where a Śūdra might touch [him];
or in the same row as those unworthy [to sit].
Or when people are eating, if one should rise and offer the leavings or sip water;
or when they should give food after having reviled it;
or [food] smelled by humans or by other impure things.
One should not eat on a boat,
nor likewise in a palace;
however, one may eat on ground that has been prepared.
One should eat from an earthen vessel that has not been consecrated by heating;
if it has been consecrated, only when it is burnt;
and a metal vessel is pure when it has been scrubbed.
A wooden vessel is [to be used] after being scraped clean.
At a sacrifice, one should act according to the traditional injunctions.
One should not eat food purchased from a market.

Likewise, among liquids, one should avoid meat, honey, and salt; however, one may use oil and clarified butter after placing them in water. Prepared food that has stood overnight is unfit for eating, drinking, or consuming, as is anything turned sour.

[One may eat] with the exception of molasses, parched grain, rice, *karambha*, *bharūja*, flour-meal, vegetables, meat, flour-cakes, preparations of milk, herbs, forest plants, roots, and fruits. [ĀpDhS 1.5.17.20] And sour gruel that has not been mixed with other substances. [ĀpDhS 1.5.17.21] All intoxicating liquors are forbidden to be drunk.
Likewise, the milk of a camel,

the milk of a female deer, the milk of a cow in heat, the milk of a cow that has recently calved, and the milk of a cow that miscarries [are forbidden]. Also, the milk of a cow within ten days of calving [is forbidden].
Likewise, [the consumption of] fermented liquids and plants;
(26) *karañja*, garlic, and *parārīkā*;
and whatever else they declare [to be forbidden].
"For food that has been sneered at is not to be eaten," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
[The meat of] single-hoofed animals, camels, gavayas, village pigs, śarabhas, and cows is forbidden.
The meat of milch-cows and oxen is edible.
"The ox-hide of a bull is pure," so says the Vājasaneyaka.
The cock is the chief among those that scatter their food; the water-fowl is the chief among those that peck.
Meat-eating carnivores;
the *haṃsa*, *bhāsa*, *cakravāka*, and *suparṇa* birds;
and [birds] excluding the *kruñca*, *krauñca*, *vārdhrāṇasa*, and *lakṣmaṇa*.

Among five-toed animals, those are edible with the exception of the monitor lizard, the tortoise, the porcupine, the hedgehog, the rhinoceros, the hare, and the stinking khara. (ĀpDhS 1.5.17.37) The *iṭa* fish is not to be eaten.
(ĀpDhS 1.5.17.38) [Not to be eaten are] the snake-headed, the soft-chested, the carnivorous, and others that are deformed, such as those having a human head. (ĀpDhS 1.5.17.39)
Honey, raw grain, a path, meat, land, roots and fruits, protection, pasture, a dwelling, and fodder for draft animals—these may be accepted from a person of fierce character.
Hārīta says that even these are not to be accepted if they have not been brought by a resident pupil.
Or, they may accept them while they are still raw.
Or [he may eat] cooked food that is tasteless.
They should not be well-fed.
Even when he himself has no means of subsistence, he may eat after giving gold or a beast.
One should not settle down permanently.
Having obtained a means of livelihood, one should cease [the practice].
One who has returned home from his teacher should not eat food belonging to the three castes beginning with the Kṣatriya.

ĀpDhS 1.6.18.10: By nature, the food of a Brāhmaṇa is to be eaten; it is not to be eaten only for a specific reason. [K: It is to be eaten without a specific reason. ĀpDhS 1.6.18.11: Where one performs an act that requires penance, [that food is] unfit to be eaten. ĀpDhS 1.6.18.12: Once the penance has been performed, his food may be eaten.

ĀpDhS 1.6.18.13: Some say that food may be eaten from all social classes who abide by their own respective duties, with the exception of a Śūdra. ĀpDhS 1.6.18.14: Even from such a Śūdra, however, one may eat if he has been brought [as food] for the sake of religious duty (*dharma*). ĀpDhS 1.6.18.15: Having given gold or a cow, one may eat; one should not settle there permanently, but having obtained a means of livelihood, one should desist.
The food of a corporation is unfit to be eaten; likewise, that which is offered by calling out to the public; and the food of all those who live by a craft.
Those who live by the sword;
those who [live by] the bow;
and physicians.
A usurer;
one who has been consecrated for sacrifice but has not yet purchased the King Soma;
[one who eats] only at the conclusion of the Agniṣomīya offering.
Or, when the omentum has been offered, the initiated person may eat.
Or, when that which is designated for the sake of the sacrifice has been set aside, they may eat from the remainder; for so says the Brāhmaṇa. A eunuch [is excluded].
One who carries out the commands of kings;
one who does not perform sacrifices with sacrificial oblations;
and a spy.
One who has renounced the world contrary to the prescribed rule; one who neglects the sacred fires;
one who avoids all [Vedic study]; a learned Śrotriya who has been expelled from his community; and the husband of a Śūdra woman.

One who is intoxicated, insane, bound, naked, one who has sat down in protest (pratyupaviṣṭa), and one who causes another to sit down in protest—[these are impure] for that duration of time. Who is one whose food may be eaten?
"One who desires it," says Kaṇva.
"It is meritorious," says Kautsa.
"Whoever may give it," says Vārṣyāyaṇi.
"If the impurity in a person is stationary, it must be experienced; but if it is mobile, one becomes free from fault through giving. [K: indeed]
Pure alms should be eaten by the Ekakuṇika, the Kāṇva, the Kutsa, and likewise the Puṣkarasādin.
The Vārṣyāyaṇīya [tradition] is endowed with everything. One who desires merit should eat [only what is obtained] from all [sources].

One should not eat even of that which is meritorious if it is not desired [by oneself]. One may eat whatever is offered from any source whatsoever. Hārīta says that this does not apply to food obtained through an improper assignment.

Now they cite two verses from the Purāṇas: "Prajāpati considered alms that are offered up, brought forward, and not previously announced as fit to be eaten even from one who has committed evil deeds. But his ancestors do not eat for fifteen years, nor does the fire carry his oblation, he who holds such [alms] in contempt."
The food of a physician, a hunter, a surgeon, a snarer, an unchaste woman, and a eunuch is not to be eaten.

Furthermore, they cite this: "The killer of an embryo transfers his guilt to the eater of his food; the innocent man incurs it by accusing another; and the thief who has escaped punishment transfers his guilt to the king by begging from him."
One should not practice religious duties by placing worldly aims at the forefront,

for such acts become fruitless with respect to spiritual elevation (*abhyudaya*). Just as when a mango tree is planted for the sake of its fruit, shade and fragrance arise as secondary benefits, so too when one practices righteousness, worldly aims arise as secondary consequences.
If they do not arise [in him], there is no loss of dharma.
He should be free from malice and difficult to deceive regarding the talk of deceivers, rogues, atheists, and children.
Dharma and adharma do not say, "We two are moving about. Neither gods, Gandharvas, nor ancestors declare, "This is dharma" or "This is adharma."
That which the noble ones praise when it is being performed is dharma; that which they censure is adharma.

One should adopt the conduct of those who are well-disciplined, aged, self-possessed, free from greed, and devoid of hypocrisy—conduct that is unanimously established among all peoples and shared by the noble ones.
In this way, one conquers both worlds.
Trade is not prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa.
In times of distress, however, he may engage in commerce, avoiding those goods that are forbidden as merchandise.

These forbidden items are: human beings, liquids, dyes, perfumes, food, hides, a cow that has recently calved, phlegm, water, young sprouts, fermenting grain, pepper and long pepper, grain, meat, weapons, and the hope of a meritorious deed.

One should especially not sell sesame seeds or rice among grains. Furthermore, the mutual exchange of these is not prescribed. Nor should there be an exchange of food for food, of humans for humans, of liquids for liquids, of fragrances for fragrances, or of knowledge for knowledge.
He should engage in trade with goods that have not been purchased [for resale]:
with *muñja* and *balbaja* grasses, roots and fruits,
and unprocessed grass and wood.
One should not settle down permanently [in such a way].
Having obtained a means of livelihood, one should desist.
No social interaction with outcasts is permitted.
Likewise [one becomes an outcast] by using the vessels of those who have fallen from their caste.
Now, the causes for falling [from caste]:

theft, false accusation, killing a human being, neglecting the Veda, destroying an embryo, sexual intercourse with the mother, the father, or other female relatives connected by birth—including their offspring—and sexual intercourse with a woman with whom one should not have intercourse, as well as the drinking of *surā* liquor.
Having approached the wife of a teacher, the female friend of a teacher, or other women who are the wives of others,
some say one does not fall [from his caste] for violating the bed of one who is not a guru. However, the constant practice of unrighteous acts [leads to such a fall].
Now, the causes of impurity:
sexual intercourse with Śūdra women by noble (Ārya) men;
and the eating of the meat of forbidden animals.
[The penance for consuming the excrement] of a dog, a human, domestic fowl, or pig, or of carnivorous animals;
(16) [the penance for] consuming the urine or feces of humans;
and (17) [the penance for] an Ārya consuming the leavings of a Śūdra or approaching one who has been excluded from the company of vessels.
Some say that even these [other acts] cause loss of caste.
Others than these are merely defective and cause impurity.
Having recognized a fault, one should not be the first to proclaim it to others regarding a fallen person; however, one should avoid him in religious duties.
One should practice spiritual disciplines that are consistent with reason and free from worldly pursuits.
There is nothing higher than the attainment of the Self.
In this regard, we shall cite verses concerning the attainment of the Self.

All living beings are indeed the city of Him who dwells in the secret cave, who is never slain and is free from blemish. Those who follow Him, who is immovable though His abode is moving, they become immortal.
Whatever is here in this world called an object of sense, the wise man, having shaken off all that, should follow Him who dwells in the secret cave.

"Having not found this [Self] within myself, practice what is beneficial and avoid what is harmful. Then, among others, I seek the station of the virtuous without expectation—[that] great body of splendor, the Lord established everywhere. "He who is eternal in all beings, wise, immortal, and firm; bodiless, soundless, formless, touchless, great and pure—he is everything, the supreme goal, he is indeed the equinox, he is the city of Vaiśravaṇa."

He who would practice this in every respect and always conduct himself toward him with devotion—he, being disciplined, who perceives that which is difficult to see and subtle, shall rejoice in the world.
Seeing all beings in the Self and contemplating them as such, the wise man should not be deluded; he who sees the Self everywhere indeed shines as Brahmā upon the back of the firmament.

He who is subtle, finer than a lotus fiber, pervading all and abiding; greater than the earth, firm, and abiding by encompassing all—he is the Supreme Lord (*parameṣṭhin*), distinct from the senses of this world, yet not other than the object of knowledge, and all-pervasive. From him all bodies originate; he is the root, eternal, and everlasting.
In this life, the eradication of faults has yoga as its root; having removed those things that burn living beings, the wise man attains security.
Now we shall set forth the faults that lead to the destruction of living beings:
anger, joy, wrath, greed, delusion, hypocrisy, malice, falsehood, gluttony, calumny, envy, lust, resentment, lack of self-control, and lack of yoga; their eradication is rooted in yoga.

Absence of anger, absence of exultation, absence of malice, absence of greed, absence of delusion, absence of hypocrisy, absence of treachery, speaking the truth, moderation in eating, absence of slander, absence of envy, sharing with others, renunciation, uprightness, gentleness, tranquility, self-control, non-opposition toward all beings, yoga, nobility, lack of cruelty, and contentment—these are the rules of conduct common to all stages of life (*āśrama*). By practicing these according to the prescribed rule, one becomes destined for all [auspicious] states.
Having killed a Kṣatriya, one should give a thousand cows as an expiation for the enmity; a hundred for a Vaiśya, and ten for a Śūdra.
And in every case, a bull is additionally required for the purpose of expiation.
And it is the same regarding women of these [classes].
Having killed a student of the Veda belonging to either of the two former classes, or one who has entered a sacrificial session, or a mere Brāhmaṇa, one is accused [of a mortal sin].
And [he must avoid] a woman who is pregnant without her condition being known, as well as a woman of the Ātreya lineage.
His atonement for this is as follows:

having built a hut in the forest, remaining silent, with the head of a corpse as his banner, and covering himself from below the navel to above the knees with a garment made of half-wool and half-hemp.
His path is between the two tracks. Having seen another [person], he should step aside.
He should enter the village with a broken, reddish earthenware bowl.
"Who will give alms to one who is accused?"—with these words, he should go to seven houses;
that is his means of subsistence.
If he obtains nothing, he shall fast.
And he shall tend the cows.
Their going out and coming in constitute his second purpose in the village.
Having practiced this for twelve years, he becomes perfected and attains fellowship with the virtuous.
Or, having built a hut on the path of a battle, he may dwell there desiring to win over Brāhmaṇas and cattle; once he has been thrice repulsed, or having won them back, he is released.
Or, having undergone the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of an Aśvamedha sacrifice, he is released. This same penance applies to one who, when duty and wealth come together, chooses wealth.

Having killed his teacher or a *śrotriya* who has completed his sacred studies, he shall perform this very penance until his final breath. In this world, there is no restoration for him; however, his stain is removed.
One who has violated the bed of his teacher shall cut off his penis together with the testicles, place them in his joined palms, and go toward the southern direction from which there is no return.
Or, having embraced a glowing iron image, he shall complete his penance. A drinker of *surā* shall drink *surā* while it is in contact with fire.
A thief, with disheveled hair, taking a wooden pestle upon his shoulder, shall go to the king and confess his deed; the king shall strike him with it, and release comes through death.
If permission is granted, the sin falls upon the one who grants it.
Alternatively, he may enter the fire, or undertake severe austerity;
or he may bring about the end of his life by gradually reducing his food intake.

Or, one may perform the *kṛcchra-saṃvatsara* penance. Furthermore, they cite this: "Having committed theft, having drunk liquor, or having approached the wife of a teacher—even if not having committed the murder of a Brahmin—one should eat moderately at the fourth meal-time and enter the water according to the ritual of the *savana*s. Alternating between standing and sitting, these [sinners] cast away evil after three years. (1 = K 10, 11: theft; 2 inserts: |; 3: *nundante*)

Having avoided the first caste, or having killed a member of the first caste, he should go to battle and stand his ground; there they may kill him. Alternatively, having caused his hair, skin, and flesh to be offered as an oblation, he should enter the fire. For killing a crow, a peacock, a peacock-of-the-forest, a ruddy goose, a swan, a crane, a frog, a mongoose, a *ḍerikā* mouse, or a horse, the penance is the same as for a Śūdra.
[One incurs the same penance] for killing a milch cow or a bull without a valid cause;
likewise for other living beings when they are engaged in carrying a burden.
Having reviled one who should not be reviled, or having spoken an untruth, one must subsist for three nights on food that is neither milk, nor pungent, nor salted.
For a Śūdra, there shall be fasting for seven nights;
and the same applies to women.
In cases where there is a charge of grievous sin, provided no life has been harmed, one limb of those [accused] shall be cut off.

Having committed an act of non-Aryan behavior, slander, or forbidden conduct; having consumed what is unfit to be eaten, drunk, or tasted; having discharged semen into a Śūdra woman or into a place other than the womb; or having intentionally performed a blameworthy act, whether intentionally or unintentionally—one should touch water with verses that do not contain the word *āpaḥ*, or with verses addressed to Varuṇa, or with other purificatory mantras, according to the repetition of the act.
One who has spilled his semen should sacrifice a donkey to Nirṛti with a *pākayajña*. A Śūdra should consume the sacrificial remains of that offering.
[This is] the expiation for studying incorrectly.

For one year, remaining devoted to the welfare of his teacher, he should restrain his speech, releasing it only during Vedic recitation; [he should likewise restrain his speech] toward the teacher, the teacher’s wife, and when going on alms-round.
The same applies to other sinful acts involving loss of caste, regarding which we shall state the subsequent [penances].
Or he may offer oblations to Desire and Anger with the formula, "Desire has done it; Anger has done it," or he should mutter this.

On a festival day (parvan), he should either eat sesame seeds or fast; then, on the following day, having touched water, he should repeat the Sāvitrī mantra a thousand times, either accompanied by breath-control (prāṇāyāma) or without breath-control.

On the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, having fasted while subsisting on sesame seeds, or on the following day, having touched the water of a great river, he should offer a thousand pieces of wood with the Sāvitrī verse, or recite it. Or he should perform sacrificial rites and sacrifices intended for purification.
Having eaten food that is unfit to be eaten, he should undergo the Naiṣpurīṣya penance.
That is attained in seven nights.
Or, one should touch water at both twilights during the winter and the cool season;
or, one should perform the twelve-night *kṛcchra* penance.

ĀpDhS 1.9.27.7: For three days one eats only what is not seasoned and does not eat during the day; then for three days each, one observes the vow of not begging for food; for three days one eats nothing at all—this is the rule for the twelve-night *kṛcchra* penance. ĀpDhS 1.9.27.8: One should practice this very same rite for a year; that is the *kṛcchra*-year penance. ĀpDhS 1.9.27.9: Now another [rule]: even after committing many acts that cause loss of caste, one becomes purified by having performed the penance through three recitations of the Veda while fasting.

ĀpDhS 1.9.27.10: Carrying an ignoble woman on his bed, giving out interest, drinking fermented liquors, and acting like a non-Brāhmaṇa after having been saluted—he should sit upon blades of grass with his back scorched by the sun. ĀpDhS 1.9.27.11: Whatever sin a Brāhmaṇa incurs in a single night by serving a man of black complexion, he destroys that sin in three years by eating only at every fourth mealtime and subsisting on water.
"Whoever regards the property of another as his own becomes a thief," so say Kautsa, Hārīta, Kaṇva, and Puṣkarasādi.
Vārṣyāyaṇi says that there are exceptions regarding the appropriation of certain things:
"The fodder for a yoke-animal and the food for a draft-animal do not prohibit [the taking] from their owners."
An excessive seizure [of property] becomes unsuccessful.
Hārīta says that in all cases it must be preceded by consent. One should not go to see an outcast teacher or a kinsman.
And he should not enjoy the pleasures derived from her.
If she happens to meet him by chance, he should pass by her silently after merely acknowledging her.
A mother undertakes many duties for the sake of her son; therefore, service toward her is obligatory even if she has fallen from her caste.
But there shall be no association with those who follow unrighteousness (ĀpDhS 1.10.28.10).

Having consented to enjoyments acquired through unrighteous means, and having declared, "Neither we nor unrighteousness," covering himself from below the navel to above the knees, touching water at the three times of day, eating food that is neither milk, nor pungent, nor salty, he shall not enter a house for twelve years (ĀpDhS 1.10.28.11).
Thereafter, success is attained (ĀpDhS 1.10.28.12).
Now, if there should be sexual intercourse with Āryas,

this same [penance] applies even to other acts causing loss of caste (*patanīya*). However, one who has violated the teacher’s bed (*gurutalpa*) shall enter a hollow metal image (*sūrmi*), set it ablaze at both ends, and burn himself therein.

"This is false," says Hārīta. For he who considers himself or another to be superior becomes one who is indeed accursed. By this very rule, he should perform penance until his final breath; there is no restoration for him in this world, but his taint is removed.

ĀpDhS 1.10.28.19: One who has abandoned his wife shall put on a donkey-skin with the hair turned outward and beg for alms from seven houses, saying, "Alms for one who has abandoned his wife. That shall be his mode of livelihood for six months. ĀpDhS 1.10.28.20:

But in the case of a woman who has transgressed against her husband, there is the practice of performing the *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights for that same duration of time. ĀpDhS 1.10.28.21: Now, a killer of an embryo (*bhrūṇahan*) shall put on either a dog-skin or a donkey-skin with the hair turned outward, and take a human skull for the purpose of covering himself.

Carrying a leg of a bedstead as his staff and announcing his occupation by saying, "Who will give alms to the slayer of a learned Brahmin? he should wander about. Having obtained sustenance for life in a village, he should take refuge in an empty house or at the root of a tree, thinking: "I have no association with noble men. By this very rule he should live until his final breath; for him there is no restoration to social standing in this world, but his taint is indeed removed.
He who kills unintentionally incurs the fruit of the offense; [if he kills] intentionally, the fruit is greater. The same applies to other actions involving offenses as well.
Likewise, [this applies] during meritorious rites.
Even for the sake of testing, a Brāhmaṇa must not take up a weapon.
For it is stated in the Purāṇa: "He who kills one who has attacked him for the purpose of violence—anger merely touches anger; there is no fault in that."

Now, those who have been accused of a grave sin may live together, intending to perform what is righteous. They may act as mutual sacrificers for one another, as mutual teachers, and marry among themselves.
Having produced sons, they should say: "O Brahmin, depart from us; for thus shall the noble ones among us attain their goal.
Moreover, one does not fall [from caste] so long as he retains his virility.
This is to be understood by this: for one who is deficient in a limb begets a son who possesses all limbs. "This is false," says Hārīta;
a woman has the same nature as a curd-vessel.

For when one churns impure milk that has been poured into a vessel for curd, no religious duty (*dharmakṛtya*) is performed by that means. Likewise, there is no contact with that which is impure once it has turned white (curdled). Malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) and curses (*anuvyāhāra*) cause impurity, but they do not entail loss of caste (*apatanīya*). Hārīta, however, says that they do entail loss of caste.

But for one whose conduct constitutes a cause for falling [from caste], the penance for acts that cause impurity consists of twelve months, twelve half-months, twelve periods of twelve days, twelve periods of seven days, twelve periods of three days, twelve days, seven days, three days, or one day—according to the repetition of the act.
Thus is the expiation for acts causing impurity, in proportion to the repetition of the deed.
"Some say that one bathes [i.e., completes the student's course] by means of knowledge;
others say likewise by means of a vow measured at forty-eight years; and still others say by means of both knowledge and the vow."
In all of these cases, his conduct is like that of a *snātaka*.
There is a distinction in the fruit of honor according to the distinction of concentration and the distinction of the sacred revelation.
Now follow the observances of a *snātaka*.
One should practice exiting and entering the village by the eastern side, or by the northern side. At both twilights, one should sit outside the village, remaining silent.
In case of a conflict between two rules, that which is based on direct Vedic revelation (*śruti*) is more authoritative.
One should avoid all dyed colors on one's garment; likewise, one should avoid that which is naturally black. One should wear a garment that does not shine brightly.

And one should not refuse [to perform a service] when one has the capacity to do so. One should avoid covering the head during the day while performing the acts of voiding urine or excrement, except for the purpose of protection.
However, one may cover the head while voiding urine or excrement on the ground, provided that something is placed as a barrier between the head and the earth.
One should avoid performing the acts of voiding urine or excrement in one's own shadow.
However, one may void urine in one's own shadow.
One should not perform the acts of voiding urine or excrement on a staircase, in a ploughed field, on a path, or in water.
Likewise, one should avoid performing the acts of spitting and sexual intercourse in water.
(K 22) One should avoid performing the acts of voiding urine and excrement while facing fire, the sun, water, a Brāhmaṇa, cows, or deities.
(K 23) For the purification after voiding urine and excrement, one should avoid using a stone, a clod of earth, or green plants and trees, by tearing them from above. (K 24)
One should not, within one's power, stretch out toward fire, water, a Brāhmaṇa, cattle, a deity, a door, or a crosswind.
Furthermore, they also cite this:
One should eat food facing the east; one should speak facing the south.
One should void urine facing north, and the washing of the feet facing west.

One should perform the acts of voiding urine and excrement at a distance from one’s dwelling, toward the southern direction or the south-western quarter. Furthermore, after sunset, one should avoid performing the acts of voiding urine and excrement outside the village or even at a distance from one’s dwelling. And one who is impure should not utter the names of the deities.
And [he should avoid touching] a man belonging to both classes of deities and to the king.
He should avoid touching a Brāhmaṇa or a cow with his foot. And he should not touch them with his hand unless there is a specific reason.

One should avoid speaking ill of cows, sacrificial fees, and virgins. One should not call a cow "stṛhatī" (or "spṛhatī"), nor should one speak of a cow that has been joined with its calf except for a specific reason.
One should not say of a non-cow, "It is a non-cow"; one should rather say, "It is a potential cow.
One should not say of what is auspicious, "It is auspicious"; one should rather say, "It is meritorious" or "It is excellent. And one should not walk over a rope to which a calf is tied.
One should not pass between the two *pleṅkha* beams.
One should not say, "This one is my rival. If he were to say, "This one is my rival," he would produce a hateful enemy. One should not point out a rainbow to another.
One should not look at [the sun] when it is falling [behind the horizon].

One should avoid looking at the sun when it is rising or setting. Because the sun protects living beings by day and the moon by night, one should desire greater protection for oneself on the night of the new moon (amāvāsyā) through self-restraint, celibacy, and proper conduct.
For on that night, the sun and the moon dwell together.
(ĀpDhS 1.11.31.20) He should not enter a village by a bypath. If he should enter, he should mutter this *ṛc*: "Homage to Rudra, the lord of the dwelling," or another verse addressed to Rudra.

(ĀpDhS 1.11.31.21) He should not give his leavings to one who is not a Brāhmaṇa. If he should give them, he should scrape off some of the food with his teeth, place it upon that person, and then give it. (ĀpDhS 1.11.31.22)

He should avoid anger and other defects that burn living beings. During the rainy season and autumn, he who is devoted to sacred study should avoid sexual intercourse. Having engaged in sexual union, he should not sleep with her for the entire night.
One should avoid teaching while lying down.
Nor should one teach on that bed upon which one lies down oneself.
One should not wear visible garlands or apply visible ointments.
32.6. He should always adorn himself for his wife during the night.
32.7. He should avoid immersing his head in water.
32.8. And he should not bathe after sunset.

He should avoid a seat made of *pālāśa* wood, sandals, and a wooden stick for cleansing the teeth; likewise, he should avoid praising his teacher in his presence by saying, "How well you have bathed," and so forth. He should remain awake until nightfall.
There is no study during the night, except for the instruction of disciples in the Dharma;
or one may do so mentally by oneself. After midnight, however, there is study.
Having risen after the latter part of the night, one should not go back to bed thinking, "It is a time unfit for study. One may, however, sleep on water or recite mentally.
He should not frequent low places or regions inhabited by those of low conduct; nor should he attend assemblies or social gatherings.
If he must go to a social gathering, he should circumambulate it clockwise and then depart.
He should avoid entering cities and should not answer questions posed to him. Moreover, they cite this example:

"The root and the tuft of the one who speaks ill are torn out; he destroys his offspring, his cattle, and his dwelling. O Dharmaprahrāda, Death, weeping so that the boy would not be harmed, answered the question."
He should avoid mounting a donkey vehicle, as well as ascending or descending uneven places. He should not cross a river by swimming with his arms, nor should he board a boat that is unsafe.

Cutting grass, crushing clods of earth, and spitting—these, as well as whatever else is censured, should not be done without a specific reason. Whatever else is censured, that too [should not be done].
1. From the time of taking the hand [in marriage], the vow of the two householders begins.
2. They shall eat at two times of the day.
3. And they shall not eat until they are fully satisfied with food.
On the festival days (parvan), there is fasting for both [husband and wife].
Fasting means eating at another time;
and it consists of being satisfied with food.
On this day, they two should eat whatever is dear to them;
they should sleep on the ground;
and they must abstain from sexual intercourse.
On the following day, there is the *sthālīpāka* (cooked rice offering). Its procedure is explained by the rules for the *pārvaṇa* sacrifice.
People prescribe this as an obligatory rite.
Wherever one intends to kindle the fire, there one should draw three lines each directed toward the east and the north, sprinkle them with water, and then kindle the fire.
Having poured out this water, one should set down another [vessel] to the north or to the east.
It is the constant vow of the two householders that the water-vessels should never be empty of water.

16. On the day [of the new moon], one should not sleep during the daytime. 17. And during the season, one should have sexual union with one's wife according to the vow. 18. Even during the intervening period, it is only with the wife.
And cohabitation occurs by the command of a Brāhmaṇa.
(ĀpDhS 2.1.1.19) There should be union while wearing only the woman’s garment. (ĀpDhS 2.1.1.20) And they shall sleep together for as long as the union lasts. (ĀpDhS 2.1.1.21) [K: sleeping together]
22. Then they separate.
23. There is the touching of water.
Or else, having washed off the smears and sipped water, there is the sprinkling of the limbs.
For all social classes (*varṇas*), there is supreme and immeasurable happiness in the performance of their own duties (*svadharma*).

Thereafter, upon returning [to a new birth], one obtains—by means of the remainder of the fruits of one's actions—birth, appearance, class, strength, intelligence, wisdom, wealth, and the performance of dharma. That [cycle] revolves like a wheel, bringing about happiness in both worlds.
Just as there is an increase in the fruit of medicinal plants and trees according to the specific nature of the seed and the treatment of the field,
so too is the increase in the fruit of sin described by this.

A Brahmin, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya who has been accused of theft is born in the next world, after a limited period in hell, as a Caṇḍāla if he was a Brahmin, a Paulkasa if he was a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiṇa if he was a Vaiśya.

By this [rule], others who have fallen away through actions that result in defects are born in wombs that result in defects, specifically in those wombs that cause the loss of caste (varṇa-paridhvaṃsa).
Just as there is a defect in touching, conversing with, or looking at a *caṇḍāla*, so too is there a penance for that.

For touching, the penance is immersion (*avagāhana*); for conversing, conversing with a Brāhmaṇa; and for looking, looking at the luminaries (the sun, etc.). [Note: For touching water, the penance is immersion.]
ĀpDhS 2.2.3.1: At the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, Aryas who are pure should be the preparers of the food.
ĀpDhS 2.2.3.2: Facing the food, one should avoid speaking, coughing, or sneezing.
ĀpDhS 2.2.3.3: Having touched one's hair, limbs, or clothing, one should touch water.
Or, Śūdras supervised by an Ārya may be the performers of the consecration rites. For them, the same rule regarding the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) applies.
In addition, there must be the shaving of the hair of the head, the beard, the body hair, and the nails every day.
And there shall be a touching of water together with the garment.

Or rather, they may sow [the seeds] only on the eighth days or on the new and full moon festivals. Having placed the prepared food out of sight over the fire, one should sprinkle it with water; that is called the "purification for the gods."
When the food is prepared, standing there, he should announce to the host, “It is ready.
The reply is, “May that be well-prepared; may the Virāj, the food, not fail me.
For the two householders, whatever offerings and oblations of edible food are performed are connected with heaven and prosperity.
ĀpDhS 2.2.3.13: When these mantras are employed, there shall be sleeping on the ground, celibacy, and avoidance of pungent and salty food for twelve days.
ĀpDhS 2.2.3.14: For the last [mantra], there is a fast for one night.
