ĀpDhS 2.2.3.15: Regarding the offerings, the consecration at each respective place consists of wiping with the hand, sprinkling water, placing [the offering], and finally pouring water around it.
In the *aupāsana* fire or the cooking fire, one should offer oblations with the hand, using each of the first six mantras one by one.
(ĀpDhS 2.2.3.17) The sprinkling of water around the fire occurs both before and after, as previously described.
(ĀpDhS 2.2.3.18) Likewise, for the *bali* offerings gathered in various locations, the sprinkling of water around the fire is performed once at the end.
ĀpDhS 2.2.3.19: When available, they should be performed with [the offering] mixed with broth.
ĀpDhS 2.2.3.20: To the west of the fire, [he performs the rites] with the seventh and eighth [formulas], ending toward the north.
ĀpDhS 2.2.3.21: In the vicinity of the water-vessel, [he performs the rite] with the ninth [formula].
In the middle of the house, he performs the offering with the tenth and eleventh [verses], ending toward the east.
In the north-eastern part of the house, he performs it with the four [verses] following [the tenth].
At the place of the bed, he performs it with the verse containing the word *kāma*.
ĀpDhS 2.2.4.2: On the threshold, with a verse containing a reference to the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).
ĀpDhS 2.2.4.3: On the covering board, with the following [verse]. ĀpDhS 2.2.4.4: On the seat of the Brahman priest, with the subsequent [verses].

To the south, he should perform the rite for the ancestors with the characteristic marks of the ancestors, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī) and with his hand turned downwards.
The rite for Rudra is to the north, as in the case of the other deities.
For these two, the sprinkling of water is performed separately because of the difference in their ritual requirements.
At night, with the last [verse], [he performs] the Vaihāyasa [offering].
He who, being undistracted, performs these [rites] constantly according to the instruction, attains heaven and prosperity.
And the first portion must be given away.
ĀpDhS 2.2.4.11: He should feed the guests first.
ĀpDhS 2.2.4.12: [He should feed] children, the elderly, those afflicted by disease, and women who are pregnant.
ĀpDhS 2.2.4.13: At the proper time, the two householders should not refuse one who comes seeking food.

In the absence [of these], earth, water, grass, or kind words—these indeed never fail in the house of a virtuous man. Those who behave in this manner attain infinite worlds. One should give a seat, water, and food to a Brāhmaṇa who is not studying; one should not rise up for him.
One should rise to greet a person who is worthy of being greeted. This applies to both a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya as well.
One should employ a Śūdra who has arrived as a guest in some work, and then give him food.
Or slaves may bring a Śūdra from the royal household and honor him like a guest.
(ĀpDhS 2.2.4.20) An upper garment must always be worn. (ĀpDhS 2.2.4.21) Or else, a cord alone may serve the purpose of the sacred thread (*upavīta*). (ĀpDhS 2.2.4.22)

ĀpDhS 2.2.4.23: Where food has been eaten, that place should be swept together, carried away, and sprinkled with water; having scraped off the residues from the vessels and mixing them with water, one should pour them out to the north in a clean spot for Rudra. In this way, the site becomes auspicious. ĀpDhS 2.2.4.24: However, it is recorded in tradition that a Brāhmaṇa may be an *ācārya*. ĀpDhS 2.2.4.25:
In times of distress, study may be undertaken by a Brāhmaṇa under a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya teacher.
26. And she follows behind him. 27. From that time forward, when they are traveling, the Brāhmaṇa alone should go in front.
1. Having performed the introductory rite (upākaraṇa) for all the sciences as well as for the Upaniṣads, there shall be no study on that day.
ĀpDhS 2.2.5.2: Having completed his studies, he may depart immediately.
ĀpDhS 2.2.5.3: If he is in haste, however, he may go at will after reciting the Veda while in the presence of his teacher; in this way, welfare is secured for both. ĀpDhS 2.2.5.4:

If the teacher should come upon him after he has returned home, the student should go out to meet him facing him, clasp his feet, and touch water without feeling any disgust; having placed him in front and seated him, he should honor him according to the instructions.
When a seat, a bed, food to be chewed, food to be eaten, or a garment is offered, he should behave with greater humility.
Standing, supporting the teacher with his left hand, he should cause him to sip water;
or he may do so for another person of equal status.
He should desire to imitate [the teacher's] standing, sitting, walking, and smiling.
When the teacher is nearby, he should avoid passing urine, excrement, or wind; speaking loudly; laughing; spitting; cleaning his teeth; cracking his knuckles; frowning; clapping; and spitting.
He should avoid touching or conversing with his wife or children in a manner that implies intimacy.
One should avoid contradicting the words of a teacher with one’s own words,
as well as those of superiors;
and one should also avoid censuring or reviling any living being.
And by means of knowledge, one should master the sciences.

(ĀpDhS 2.2.5.14) If one does not shine through a particular science, one should approach the teacher again and master it with disciplined effort. (ĀpDhS 2.2.5.15) The restrictive observances (*niyama*) of the teacher last from the commencement (*upākaraṇa*) until the conclusion (*utsarjana*) of the study. He should avoid cutting hair, eating meat, performing *śrāddha* rites, and sexual intercourse. (ĀpDhS 2.2.5.16)
Or he may take a wife for the sake of procreation.

He should be intent upon the transmission of knowledge to his disciples and upon the observances according to the traditional scriptures. Conducting himself in this manner, he secures the welfare of his ancestors, his descendants, and himself.
By mentally, verbally, and physically—through mind, speech, breath, sight, hearing, skin, genitals, and stomach—eschewing all discharges, he prepares himself for immortality.
ĀpDhS 2.3.6.1: When there is doubt regarding a person’s caste or conduct, one should kindle a fire for the sake of determining the dharma and inquire about his caste and conduct.

ĀpDhS 2.3.6.2: If he claims his integrity, saying, "Agni is the witness, Vāyu is the listener, and Āditya is the observer; he claims his integrity—may integrity be his, and let this man be false in his sin," one should proceed to instruct him.
ĀpDhS 2.3.6.3: An approaching guest comes like a blazing fire.
ĀpDhS 2.3.6.4: Having studied at least one branch of each of the Vedas in accordance with the dharma, one becomes a *śrotriya*.
ĀpDhS 2.3.6.5: One who approaches a householder engaged in his own duties, motivated by dharma and for no other purpose, is a guest (*atithi*).
ĀpDhS 2.3.6.6: Through the honoring of such a guest, there is peace and heaven.
Having approached him face-to-face and greeted him according to age, he should offer him a seat.
Some say that, within one's means, the seat should not have many legs.
He should wash his feet; some say that a Śūdra couple should do so.
ĀpDhS 2.3.6.10: One of the two should perform the consecration. ĀpDhS 2.3.6.11: He should cause water to be brought for him in an earthen vessel, according to some.
ĀpDhS 2.3.6.12: One who has not returned home from his teacher’s house should not cause water to be brought [for himself].
In this case, the rules regarding study and the conduct of life are also applicable.
Having greeted him with kind words, one should satisfy him with savory foods, edibles, and water, at least to the extent of the lowest requirement.
One should provide him with a dwelling, a bed above, a mattress, a pillow, a coverlet, and an ointment for the body.
Having summoned the preparer of the food, he should pour out rice or barley for that purpose.
He should look at the prepared foods, saying: "Is this more? Is this more? He should say only: "Take out more."
One should not eat the food of one who hates him, or of one who hates [others], nor of one who suspects him of a fault, or of one who has been suspected of a fault;
for it is known from scripture: "He indeed consumes the sin of that person."
This very sacrifice of the householder belongs to Prajāpati and is perpetually extended.
That fire which is for guests is the Āhavanīya; that which is in the household is the Gārhapatya; and that upon which food is cooked is the Anvāhāryapacana.
He who eats before the guest eats strength, nourishment, progeny, cattle, and the merit of sacrifices and charitable works—indeed, he eats the very essence of the house.

Food with a libation of milk is equal to the Agniṣṭoma; with clarified butter, it is equal to the Ukthya; with honey, it is equal to the Atirātra; and with meat, it is equal to the Dvādaśāha. By [giving] water, there is an increase of progeny and longevity.
It is known from tradition that dear and even non-dear guests cause one to go to the heavenly world.
When he gives [food] in the morning, at midday, and in the evening, these become the [three] Soma-pressings.

Whatever he performs, that indeed is the *udavasāna* (concluding rite). Whatever he soothes, that is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and the praise. Whatever he accomplishes, those are the *viṣṇukrama* strides.
"That which he approaches is the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath)," for so says the Brāhmaṇa.
If a king should arrive as a guest, one should cause him to receive a more distinguished honor than that accorded to oneself.

If a guest should arrive when the fire-sacrificer has established his sacred fires, the host should rise to meet him personally and say: "O Vrātya, where have you stayed? "O Vrātya, [here is] water. "O Vrātya, satisfy yourself.

Before the offering of the Agnihotra, he should mutter softly: "O Vrātya, may it be as your mind desires. "O Vrātya, may it be as your will desires. "O Vrātya, may it be as your pleasure desires. "O Vrātya, may it be as your wish desires."

If a guest should arrive when the fires have been taken out but before the oblations have been offered, he himself should rise to meet him and say, "O Vrātya, give me leave; I shall offer the oblation. Only when permitted by him should he offer the oblation. If he should offer it without being permitted, [the sage] declares a fault against the Brāhmaṇa.

It is known from tradition: "If one should lodge guests for one night, he conquers the earthly worlds; by a second night, the worlds of the intermediate space; by a third, the celestial worlds; by a fourth, the distant worlds; and by lodging them for an unlimited number of nights, he conquers unlimited worlds.

(ĀpDhS 2.3.7.16) If a guest who has not completed his Vedic studies should arrive claiming to be such, one should give him a seat, water, and food with the words, "I give this to a *śrotriya*"; in this way, it becomes complete for him. (ĀpDhS 2.3.7.17)
One should not rise up or descend from one's seat for a guest for whom one has already prepared a lodging, provided that he has been greeted first.
One should eat only what remains after the guests have been fed.
One should not consume flavorful foods in the house unless some portion remains for the guests.

One should not cook choice food for one's own sake alone. A person who has mastered the Vedas is worthy of the cow and the madhuparka offering; so too are the teacher, the officiating priest, the bath-graduate, or a king who is endowed with righteousness.
To the teacher, the officiating priest, the father-in-law, and the king—when they come for a visit after a year has passed—a cow and the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*) are offered.
The honey-mixture consists of curd mixed with honey, or milk mixed with honey.
Water is [offered] when there is no [other substance].

The Veda has six auxiliary limbs (Aṅgas). These are: phonology (Chandas), ritual science (Kalpa), grammar (Vyākaraṇa), astronomy (Jyotiṣa), etymology (Nirukta), and phonetics (Śīkṣā), as well as metrics (Chandoviciti).

However, the term "Veda" applies to the collection of rites that have words and meanings as their basis, upon the completion of the traditional recitation (Samāmnāya). In that regard, the aforementioned number [of six] is contradicted.
"But it is the consensus of those who know the principles of logic that there is no separate designation for the subsidiaries apart from the primary acts.
"Having neglected a guest, if one remembers this after having begun to eat, he should stop eating from that point and fast."
On the following day, having gratified them according to his inclination, he should complete the journey. (He should go) as far as a vehicle [is available] for one who possesses a vehicle;
or as far as the other may permit him.
In the event of uncertainty regarding the boundary, he should desist.
At the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, he should make all [beings] sharers, down to dogs and Caṇḍālas;
however, some say that one should not give to those who are unworthy.
One who has been initiated should avoid the leavings of women and of one who is uninitiated. All gifts should be preceded by water.
In the sacrificial ritual, it should be according to the revealed scripture.

A distribution of food is ordained for those who are permanent dependents, provided it does not cause hardship for them. One may, at will, deprive oneself, one's wife, or one's son of food, but never a slave or a laborer.
Furthermore, one should ensure that one’s own deprivation of food is such that it does not render one incapable of performing one’s duties.

Moreover, they also cite this: "Eight mouthfuls are the meal for a sage (*muni*), sixteen for a forest-dweller, thirty-two for a householder, and an unlimited amount for a student (*brahmacārin*). The fire-maintainer (*āhitāgni*), the ox, and the student—these three achieve success only while eating; there is no success for them through fasting."
The occasions for begging are: the teacher, marriage, a sacrifice, the desire of one's parents to support themselves, and the breaking of a vow by an Arhat.

In these cases, having considered the qualities [of the recipient], one should give according to one's ability. However, begging for the sake of gratifying the senses is not an occasion; one should not heed that.

Āpastamba Dharmasūtra 2.5.10.4: The specific duties of a Brāhmaṇa are studying, teaching, sacrificing, officiating at sacrifices, giving gifts, receiving gifts, inheriting, and gleaning ears of grain or picking up single grains. [K 5; *śiloñchaḥ*] Āpastamba Dharmasūtra 2.5.10.5: And anything else that has not been claimed as one's own. [K 6] Āpastamba Dharmasūtra 2.5.10.6: These same duties apply to a Kṣatriya, with the exception of teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and receiving gifts, and with the addition of wielding the rod of punishment and engaging in battle. [K 7]
The duties of a Vaiśya are like those of a Kṣatriya, with the exception of punishment and warfare; they additionally include agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade.

(K 8) One should not appoint as a sacrificial priest one who has not studied the Vedas, nor one who haggles over his fee. (9, māṇam) One who has not studied the Vedas is unworthy of officiating at sacrifices. (K 10)

In battle, one should act according to the means prescribed by those experts in its application. (K 11) The noble ones declare that killing is forbidden for those who have laid down their weapons, those with disheveled hair, those with palms joined in supplication, and those who have turned their backs.

(K 12) For those who, despite having mastered the scriptures, deviate from them due to weakness of the senses, the teacher should prescribe penance according to the specific act, as has been stated. (K 13)
If they should transgress the sacred law, he should bring them before the king. The king should bring them before the domestic priest who is skilled in dharma and artha.
He [the priest] should appoint Brahmins [to investigate the case].

ĀpDhS 2.5.10.16: According to the degree of their strength, he should cause them to wither away through restrictive observances, except for execution and slavery. ĀpDhS 2.5.11.1: For the other castes, the king, having considered their actions, should inflict punishment until the loss of life.
ĀpDhS 2.5.11.2: And he should not inflict punishment when there is doubt.
Having thoroughly investigated the matter after it has been sifted through divine inquiries, the king should proceed to inflict punishment.
A king who conducts himself in this manner conquers both worlds. The path belongs to the king, except when he encounters a Brāhmaṇa.
When they meet, the way must be yielded to a Brāhmaṇa alone.
The way must be yielded by everyone to one in a vehicle, to one burdened with a load, to one who is ill, and to a woman.
And the way must be yielded by those of lower castes to those of higher castes.
ĀpDhS 2.5.11.9: To those who are uncultured, fallen, intoxicated, or insane, food must be given by all [members of the community] for the sake of their own well-being.

ĀpDhS 2.5.11.10: Through the practice of righteousness, a lower caste attains each successive higher caste during the transformation of birth. ĀpDhS 2.5.11.11: Through the practice of unrighteousness, a higher caste descends to each successive lower caste during the transformation of birth.
If one’s wife is endowed with both virtue and offspring, he should not take another.

If there is a deficiency in either of these, another may be taken before the establishment of the sacred fires. For once the fire has been established, she becomes connected with those rites of which this [wife] is an integral part.

One should not give one’s daughter to a man of the same *gotra*. Nor to one who is related to her mother through [maternal] kinship. In the *brāhma* form of marriage, having ascertained the family, character, learning, and health [of the groom], one should bestow the daughter upon him for the sake of offspring and joint religious duties, after adorning her according to one's ability. [The bride should be endowed with auspicious marks.]
In the *ārṣa* form, a pair of cattle should be given to the father of the daughter.
In the *daiva* form, one should bestow her upon the officiating priest during the course of a sacrifice.
When they unite with each other out of mutual desire, that is the *gāndharva* form.
If one should carry off the girl after giving away wealth according to one's ability, that is the Āsura form. If one should carry her off after deceiving the father-in-law, that is the Rākṣasa form.
Among these, the first three are commendable; each preceding one is superior to the next.
ĀpDhS 2.5.12.4: As the marriage is contracted, so do the offspring become.
ĀpDhS 2.5.12.5: One should not step upon anything that has been touched by the hand of a Brāhmaṇa unless it has been sprinkled with water.
ĀpDhS 2.5.12.6–7: One should not pass between the fire and a Brāhmaṇa, nor between several Brāhmaṇas.
Or, having obtained permission, he may pass by.
He should not hold fire and water simultaneously.
And he should avoid the bringing together of various fires.
One should not circumambulate the fire being brought toward one's face until it has been established on the ground. One should not join one's hands behind one's back.

While sleeping, or having fallen asleep at sunset, or while still hungry, one should remain seated and silent for the night. When morning has dawned, having touched water, one may release the vow of silence.
Having fallen asleep while the sun was rising, or having failed to eat, he should remain standing during the day with his speech controlled.
Some say that he should restrain his breath until he is exhausted,
or if he has seen an evil dream.
Or when one desires to accomplish a specific purpose;
or upon the transgression of another rule;
or when there is doubt regarding the fault or the result—[in these cases], that [act] should not be performed.
Thus it is with regard to the permitted and forbidden days for Vedic study. One should not speak as if one were an eyewitness when there is doubt.

Among those who have studied after sunset, those who have studied at sunrise, those with deformed nails, those with black teeth, an elder brother whose younger brother marries first, a younger brother who marries before his elder, an elder brother whose younger brother maintains a sacred fire, a younger brother who maintains a sacred fire before his elder, an elder brother whose younger brother performs the *pariṣṭa* rite, and a younger brother who performs the *parivitta* rite—among these, for each successive one, the penance for the act of impurity is increasingly more severe.
And some say that after performing those penances, the mark [of the offense] should be removed.
For one who approaches a wife of equal caste who was previously ordained by scripture according to the proper season, their sons have a connection through their ritual duties;

there is also an undivided inheritance for both. There is fault in sexual intercourse with a woman who has not been previously married, with one who has not undergone the sacramental rites, or with one of a different caste.
Even in that case, the son belongs to the one who committed the fault; for the Brāhmaṇa says, "The son belongs to the progenitor.
Furthermore, they cite this example: "O Progenitor, it is only now that I am jealous of women, not before; when [the gods] declared in the abode of Yama that the son belongs to the progenitor."
"The seed-bearer leads the son away after death to the abode of Yama; therefore, fearing the seed of another, they guard their wives."
"Guard this thread with vigilance; let no one sow seeds of another in your field. In the world beyond, the son belongs to the progenitor; the sower makes this thread in vain. (ĀpDhS 2.6.13.6c)
A transgression of the law and acts of violence were observed among the ancients.
Due to their extraordinary spiritual power, no sin accrued to them. One who imitates them without having scrutinized that [matter] perishes.

There is no such thing as the giving away or the purchase of a child. Regarding marriage, it is heard in the sacred tradition that the giving of a gift to one who has a daughter is optional; however, for the sake of dharma, it is prescribed that one hundred cows plus an extra chariot (*adhiratha*) should be given to the father of the daughter.
To say that this should be done "in vain" (or falsely) is incorrect. In this context, the term "purchase" is merely figurative praise; the relationship is based on dharma.
Having satisfied the eldest son with a single share of the property,

he should divide the inheritance among his sons while he is still living, making equal shares, excluding one who is impotent, insane, or an outcast. In the absence of sons, the inheritance goes to the nearest *sapiṇḍa* relative.

In the absence of that [heir], the teacher shall take it; in the absence of the teacher, the pupil, having taken it, shall employ it for the sake of those purposes or for religious duties. Or the daughter may do so. In the absence of all these, the king shall take the inheritance.
"Some say that the eldest is the heir.
"In a specific region, gold, black cows, and black land belong to the eldest.
"The chariot and the household utensils in the house belong to the father."
"Some say that the ornaments and the paternal property belong to the wife.
This is contradicted by the sacred scriptures.
It is heard in the Veda without qualification: "Manu divided his inheritance among his sons."
Moreover, it is heard in a single passage: "Therefore, they exclude the eldest son from his share of the wealth.

Furthermore, those who know the principles of logic say that this is a constant restatement (*nityānuvāda*) and not an injunction (*vidhi*), just as: "Therefore, goats and sheep move together among cattle"; "Therefore, the mouth of a *snātaka* seems to resound with the *repha* sound"; and "Therefore, the goat and the learned *śrotriya* are most desirous of women.
For all those who are endowed with merit (*dharma*) are entitled to shares.
But even the eldest brother shall deprive of his share one who acquires property through unrighteous means. There exists no partition between husband and wife;
from the time of taking the hand, they are joint in ritual duties.
Likewise regarding the fruits of merit;
and regarding the acquisition of property;
for they do not teach that there is theft when giving occurs on account of a specific occasion during the absence of the master.
By this, the customs of regions and families are explained.

For those related to the mother through consanguinity and for those related to the father up to the seventh person, or as far as the relationship is known—if they have died, one must perform the ritual touching of water (udakopasparśana), excepting fetuses that have not reached one year of age. Among these, however, the same rule applies only to the mother and the father.
And those who take [the body];
(5) when his wife has died or when a supreme guru has passed away, there shall be fasting for as long as the period lasts;
(6) they should assume the appearance of those who are ill.

Having disheveled their hair and scattered dust over themselves, wearing a single garment, they face south and immerse themselves once; having emerged, they sit down. This is done three times. (K 7) [K 1: *opyaikavāsaso*; 2: *upamajjya*; 3: omits *|*; 4: adds K 8:
*evaṃ triḥ*] Having poured out water based on that [immersion], they return to the village without looking back and do what women tell them to do.
Regarding other [types of death], some teachers teach this very same procedure.
One should feed those who are pure and learned in the sacred formulas (*mantra*) at all ritual acts.

One bestows gifts by means of the place, the time, purity, and a worthy recipient. That food which is not prepared in one’s own fire and of which no portion is first offered [to the gods] must not be eaten.
There is no offering of alkaline substances or salt. Likewise, there is no [offering] of inferior things or of what has been mixed.
For the offering of non-sacrificial food, one should push aside the hot ashes toward the north and offer it therein; thus it becomes both offered and unoffered in the fire.
A woman shall not offer the oblation; nor one who has not been initiated. Until the ceremony of the first feeding with solid food, fetuses do not become impure.
"Until one year has passed," say some. "As long as they do not recognize the directions," say others.
"Until the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*)," say yet others.
For in this matter, the qualification [to study] is established by the scriptures;
that is the finality,
and it is also recorded in the Smṛtis.

In ancient times, gods and humans existed together in this world. Then, by means of their ritual acts (*karman*), the gods ascended to heaven, while humans were left behind. Those among them who undertake such acts become united with the gods and Brahman in that other world. Now, Manu has proclaimed this rite under the name of *śrāddha*, for the sake of the ultimate welfare of progeny. In this rite, the ancestors are the deities, while the Brāhmaṇas serve the purpose of the *āhavanīya* fire.
It should be performed month by month. (K 3) The afternoon of the dark fortnight is superior. (K 4) Likewise, the later days of the dark fortnight are preferable. (K 5)

In all the days of the dark fortnight, when the rite is performed, one gratifies the ancestors; however, due to the performer’s restriction regarding the specific time, there is a distinction in the fruit.
When it is performed on the first day, offspring consisting mostly of females is born. On the second day, thieves are born.
In the third [generation], [the descendants] possess Vedic splendor (*brahmavarcas*).
In the fourth, they possess small livestock.
In the fifth, they have male offspring; they have many children, and none among them dies childless.
In the sixth year, he is habituated to traveling and to playing with dice.
In the seventh year, there is success in agriculture.
In the eighth year, there is prosperity.
In the ninth [year], one-eyed animals;
in the tenth, success in legal proceedings;
in the eleventh, black iron, tin, and lead.
In the twelfth [year], one possesses cattle.
(K 18) In the thirteenth, one has many sons, many friends, and handsome offspring; however, they die young. (K 19) In the fourteenth, there is success in weaponry. (K 20)
On the fifteenth day, there is nourishment. (K 21) In that regard, the substances are sesame, beans, rice, barley, water, roots, and fruits.
(K 22) However, when the food is oily, the gratification of the ancestors is more intense and lasts for a longer period. (K 23)
Likewise, [there is satisfaction] with wealth acquired in accordance with dharma and bestowed upon a worthy recipient.
(25) Satisfaction for one year is obtained through the gift of cow’s products. (26) Greater than that is the satisfaction obtained through the gift of buffalo’s products. (27)
By this, the purity of the meat of domestic and wild animals is explained.
(ĀpDhS 2.7.16.28) [ = K 27] On a bed spread with rhinoceros hide, one obtains an infinite duration of time through the meat of the rhinoceros.
(ĀpDhS 2.7.17.1) Likewise, through the meat of the *śatabali* fish. (ĀpDhS 2.7.17.2)
And also that of the *vārdhrāṇasa* [or *vārghrāṇasa*].
Being self-restrained and serene-minded, having invited them, he should feed Brāhmaṇas who know the Veda, provided they are not related by birth, lineage, mantra, or being a pupil.
However, if others lack good qualities, even a uterine brother who is superior should be fed.
By this, the rules for students (*antevāsins*) are explained.

Furthermore, they cite this example: "The *saṃbhojanī* is called the 'demon’s alms'; it goes neither to the ancestors nor to the gods. Here on earth it wanders, its merit exhausted, like a cow that has lost her calf wandering from one stall to another.
"She who eats together here causes the family to perish from house to house."
Among those of equal qualities, one who is advanced in age is more venerable; so too is one who is destitute of wealth if he desires [hospitality].
On the previous day, there is the announcement;
on the following day, the second [announcement].
The third invitation is [the same].
Some teachers prescribe that the *śrāddha* should be performed three times;
as the first, so the second and the third.

In all rites, having taken portions from all [the food], he should eat of the remainder a quantity no less than a mouthful, as prescribed. According to the northern custom, however, water-vessels are brought into the hands of those who are seated.
He addresses them, saying, "Let it be served; let it be offered in the fire."
"Let it be lifted up at will; let it be offered into the fire at will"—when thus permitted, one may lift it up and offer it.
They avoid the sight of the *śrāddha* by dogs and those who have been excluded from the community.

A leper, one afflicted with skin disease, one who has approached the bed of another's wife, the son of a soldier, and one born of a Śūdra woman by a Brāhmaṇa—these, while eating at a *śrāddha*, become defilers of the row.

One who has mastered the *Trimadhu*, the *Trisuparṇa*, and the *Trināciketa*; one who knows the *Caturmedha* and the *Pañcāgni*; one who chants the *Jyeṣṭhasāman*; one who has studied the Veda; one who is well-versed (*anūcāna*) in the scriptures; and the son of such a person—these, being learned in the Vedas (*śrotriyas*), become purifiers of the assembly when eating at a *śrāddha*.
And one should not perform a *śrāddha* at night. Furthermore, once it has begun, there shall be no eating until its completion.
Except during an eclipse of the moon.
One should avoid molasses, churned buttermilk, oil-cake, honey, and meat; black grain, the food of a Śūdra, and whatever else is considered unfit to be eaten;
that which is not fit for an oblation, falsehood, anger, and that by which one might provoke anger—one desiring memory, fame, intelligence, heaven, and prosperity, should avoid these twelve things.

Covering the area from below the navel to above the knees, touching water at the three times of the day, subsisting on food not cooked over fire, avoiding the shade, and alternating between standing and sitting, he shall observe this vow for one year. They say that this is equivalent to forty-eight years. [ĀpDhS 2.8.18.5] There is a daily *śrāddha* offering. [ĀpDhS 2.8.18.6] Outside the village, the pure ones prepare it in a pure place.
In that regard, there are new articles:
(K 8) those by which the food is prepared and those upon which it is eaten; (K 9) and he should give those to those who have eaten. (K 10)
He should feed those who have mastered the Vedas.
He must not give the remains of his food to one who does not possess those qualities. This he should do for a year.
Of these, the highest [penance] should be performed with iron and a goat. One should also cause a concealed place of measurement to be made. In its northern half, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas.

"They see both: the Brahmins eating and the ancestors in the *māna*," so they teach. (ĀpDhS 2.8.18.16) From this point onward, the rite may be performed or not performed as desired. (ĀpDhS 2.8.18.17) For by means of the *śrāddha*, the ancestors experience satisfaction. (ĀpDhS 2.8.18.18)
One who desires prosperity should perform [the rite] under the asterism Tiṣya.

Having had white mustard seeds ground into powder, he should wash his hands and feet with them, rinse his mouth and his ears, and then, sitting where the wind does not blow strongly, he should eat facing south, remaining silent on a goat skin; this is the primary rule. However, they teach that eating while facing such a direction is detrimental to longevity for one’s mother.
A cup made of udumbara wood with a golden base is prescribed for the Praśāstṛ.
It must not be used by anyone else;
he should hold it only as long as it takes to swallow a mouthful.
Without spilling [the water],
he should not discard it;
or rather, he may discard it.
He should swallow the entire morsel together with the thumb. He should not make a sound with his mouth,
nor should he shake his hand.
Having sipped water, he should hold his hands above until they become wet.
Then he should touch fire.
And during the day he should not eat anything other than roots and fruits.
One should avoid those [foods] that are designated as *sthālīpāka* offerings.
He should eat wearing his sacred thread over the left shoulder and covered with an upper garment. However, at the obligatory (*naiyyamika*) *śrāddha*, he should provide food that contains oil.

Clarified butter and meat constitute the primary rule. In their absence, oil and vegetables may be used. On the day of the Maghā asterism, one should feed the Brahmins with clarified butter in accordance with the ritual for the Śrāddha.
ĀpDhS 2.8.20.1: At the monthly *śrāddha*, one should employ a *droṇa* measure of sesame seeds by whatever means one is able.
ĀpDhS 2.8.20.2: One should feed those who possess the required qualities, and they should not give the remnants of the food to anyone lacking those qualities.

ĀpDhS 2.8.20.3: During the northern course of the sun (*udagayana*), on any day during the waxing moon (*āpūryamāṇapakṣa*), having fasted for at least one night under the asterism Tiṣya, one desiring prosperity should cook a *sthālīpāka* offering, sacrifice to Mahārāja, feed a Brāhmaṇa with that [food] mixed with clarified butter, and have him recite words for the attainment of prosperity.
In this manner, day by day, until the next Tiṣya constellation; two [verses] on the second day; three on the third day.
In this manner, by adding [one day] for each year,
he prospers with great nourishment.
From the very beginning, there is fasting.

One should avoid eating food from which the vital energy has been extracted (such as that from which the best portions have been removed). One should avoid standing on ashes or chaff. One should avoid washing one foot with the other and standing upon it.
20.13 And swinging the feet;
20.14 and placing one shank upon the knee;
20.15 and scratching with the nails.
And [the making of] cracks without cause;
and whatever else they declare [to be forbidden];
and [the use of] a yoke-halter in matters connected with dharma and in the acquisition of property.
And he should deliver [the goods] at a proper crossing; 20. he should be the driver when there is no proper crossing, provided there is no danger;
21. and he should gather together the people.
And he shall enjoy those pleasures that are not opposed to dharma;
in this way, he conquers both worlds.
There are four stages of life (*āśrama*): that of the householder, that of the teacher’s family, that of the silent sage, and that of the forest-dweller.
By conducting oneself with undistracted attention in all of these according to the instructions, one attains security.
For all of them, residence in the teacher’s family beginning from the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) is common.
For all [students], there is no release from the pursuit of knowledge.
Having understood the ritual actions, he may undertake whatever he desires.

Just as there is a rule for one seeking knowledge, by that very same rule a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārin) shall remain until the end, even unto the casting off of his body in the teacher’s household.
Now, concerning the wandering mendicant (*parivrāja*):
from this very state, he goes forth as a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*).
Regarding him, they teach [the following].

The sage should be without fire, without a fixed dwelling, without shelter, and without protection; abandoning all speech except for the private recitation of the Veda (*svādhyāya*), and obtaining sustenance for life within a village, he should wander without concern for this world or the next. For him, a discarded garment is prescribed. Some say there should be complete liberation from all possessions.
Abandoning truth and falsehood, pleasure and pain, these Vedas, and this world as well as the next, one should seek the Self. The attainment of security is achieved through awakened intellect;
that [attainment] is contradicted by the scriptures.
If, upon awakening, one attains security, one would not experience suffering even in this very life.
By this, the subsequent [stage] is explained.
Now, the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*).
From this very state, one who has observed the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) goes forth as a wandering mendicant (*pravrajati*).
To him they teach: "He should maintain a single fire, be homeless, without shelter, and without refuge, a sage (*muni*) who abandons even his Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya*) and speech.
For him, clothing made of materials from the forest is prescribed.
Then he should live subsisting on roots, fruits, leaves, and grasses;
finally, he should subsist on things that have fallen of their own accord.
Then he should take refuge in water, air, and space.
Among these, each subsequent stage of union is superior in terms of its fruit.
Alternatively, some teachers prescribe the sequence specifically for the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*):
having completed his studies, taken a wife, and established the sacred fires, he undertakes those ritual acts that are prescribed, beginning with the *soma* sacrifices as the lowest limit.

Having built a house, he shall dwell outside the village together with his wife, his offspring, and the sacred fires; or he may live alone. He shall subsist by means of gleaning ears of corn or picking up individual grains.
And from that point forward, he should not accept gifts.
Having been consecrated, he should offer oblations.
He should descend slowly into the water, striking it gently, and touch the water while facing the sun. [K 1: he should enter the water; K 2: facing]
ĀpDhS 2.9.22.14: This is the rule for touching water in all cases.
ĀpDhS 2.9.22.15: Regarding his implements, they prescribe that he should have them in pairs—specifically, those for cooking and eating, and the axe, hatchet, and sickle.
ĀpDhS 2.9.22.16: Taking one from each pair and giving away the others, he should depart for the forest.
From this point forward, his fire-oblation, livelihood, invitation to guests, and clothing shall consist only of forest products.
In those rituals where there are sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) or boiled grains (*caru*), these should be performed.
And everything, including the private recitation of the Veda (*svādhyāya*), shall be done in a low voice.
One should not cause the forest to be heard [by shouting].
A shelter for the sake of the fire [is permitted].
One may [recite] in the open air by oneself.
He should use a bed or seat that is not spread with a coverlet. When new grain has been obtained, he should permit the consumption of old grain.
Or, desiring a greater discipline, he should fetch his daily sustenance every day with a vessel, both morning and evening.
Then, subsisting on roots, fruits, leaves, and grasses, he should practice; finally, he should resort to water, air, and space. Of these, each subsequent stage is superior in its result.
Regarding this, they cite two ancient verses:

"Those eighty-eight thousand seers who desired offspring took the path to the south of Aryaman and reached the cremation grounds. Those eighty-eight thousand seers who did not desire offspring take the path to the north of Aryaman; indeed, they attain immortality. Thus is the praise of those who maintain their vital energy (*ūrdhvaretas*).
Moreover, there are also those whose intentions are fulfilled:
namely, rain, the granting of offspring, vision from afar, swiftness like thought, and whatever else is of a similar nature.
Therefore, because they are based on sacred revelation and because their fruits are perceptible, some declare these stages of life to be superior.

But for those who are advanced in the three Vedas, the firm conviction is that "the Vedas are the authority. Regarding this, they consider any practice that contradicts what is heard in the Vedas—concerning rice, barley, animals, clarified butter, milk, sacrificial vessels, and the wife—to be without authority, on the grounds that it must be performed loudly or softly as prescribed.
As for what is called the "cremation ground," this is ordained as a purificatory rite for the person at the conclusion of various rituals.
Beyond that, an eternal fruit is heard of in the Vedas, designated by the term "heaven."
Furthermore, the sacred tradition (āmnāya) declares his immortality through progeny: "In thy offspring thou art born again; that, O mortal, is thy immortality.
Moreover, this very same person is perceived separately as having grown forth; and a similarity is observed, though the physical body itself is indeed different.

Engaged in the duties prescribed by the learned, they increase the fame and the heavenly merit of their ancestors in the life hereafter. In this same way, each subsequent generation increases the merit of those preceding them. Until the dissolution of all beings, they remain victors in heaven; at the time of re-creation, they become the seeds [of future existence], according to the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa*.

Moreover, there is also the word of Prajāpati: "The threefold knowledge, the life of studentship, procreation, faith, austerity, sacrifice, and the giving of gifts—those who perform these, with them indeed we are; he who praises anything else becomes dust and perishes."
Among them, only those who have committed evil perish, like the leaf of a tree; they do not harm others.
In this world, no connection with actions exists for him, nor, likewise, in the next world, with the fruits of actions.
This is to be understood by means of this [analogy].
"This is the creation of Prajāpati and the seers.
Among them, those who have performed meritorious deeds are perceived as having supreme, radiant natures.

However, by means of a portion of their karma or through austerity, someone might—with a physical body—conquer a finite world and achieve the fulfillment of their intentions; yet that does not constitute the superiority of the stages of life (āśramas).
The general and specific duties of all the social classes have been explained. Now we shall describe those of the king specifically.
He should cause a dwelling and a city to be measured out with the door facing south.
His residence should be within the inner city.

To its east is the residence; that they call the place of invitation. To the south of the city is the assembly hall, with doors opening to the south and the north, so that both the exterior and the interior are visible.
In all [these buildings], the sacred fires must be maintained perpetually.

The worship of the sacred fire is constant, just as in the case of a householder. He should provide lodging for guests who are at least as learned as one well-versed in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) in his dwelling. According to their merits, he should provide them with dwellings, beds, food, and drink.
He shall not live at the expense of his teachers or dependents.
In his domain, no one shall perish from hunger, disease, cold, or heat, whether due to a lack of resources or through intentional neglect.
In the middle of the assembly hall, having raised up a place for gambling and sprinkled it with water, he shall set down an even number of Vibhītaka dice according to their purpose.

Āryas should be pure and devoted to truth; they should be gamblers [only for sport]. The taking up of weapons, dancing, singing, and instrumental music shall not be found except among those dependent upon the king.
The king is a provider of security in whose realm there is no fear of thieves, whether in the village or in the forest.
By giving land and wealth to Brahmins according to their merit, without causing hardship to his dependents, a king conquers infinite worlds.

If a king who is intent on recovering the property of Brahmins is slain while fighting, they say of him: "He is a sacrifice whose sacrificial post is his own self and whose sacrificial fee is infinite.
By this, other heroes are also explained: those who, fighting for a righteous purpose, abandon their bodies.

In villages and cities, he should appoint noble, pure, and truthful men for the protection of the subjects. Their attendants should likewise possess those same qualities. A city extending for one *yojana* in every direction must be protected from thieves.
A *krośa* from the villages [is the distance for which they are responsible]. (ĀpDhS 2.10.26.7) There, whatever is stolen, they must restore that;
he shall cause the lawful toll to be paid. (ĀpDhS 2.10.26.8–9)
An unlearned Śrotriya;
women of all castes;
and boys before the appearance of their secondary sexual characteristics.
And those who dwell for the sake of learning;
and those ascetics who are devoted to dharma;
and a Śūdra who washes their feet.
Those who are blind, mute, deaf, diseased, or outcasts, as well as those who have become useless through the possession of wealth;
and a young man who, though not acting with premeditation, enters another's wife's quarters or addresses a maiden [improperly], shall be restrained by a verbal reprimand.
But if the act is intentional and the offender is of wicked intent, he shall be punished.
When sexual intercourse has occurred, his penis shall be cut off along with the testicles.
In the case of a virgin, however, he shall be stripped of his own property and banished.
Now, regarding a servant of the king:
from this point forward, she must be protected from sexual intercourse;
however, when a means for her purification has been found, he shall deliver her back to her masters.
27.1 When [the penance] has been performed, the connection with dharma is as before.
27.2 One should not point out a woman who stands in the place of a *sagotra* relative to others. 27.3 For they teach that a woman is given away for the sake of the family (*kula*).
That [practice] has been misinterpreted due to the weakness of the senses.
For the superiority of the hand is indeed not distinct [from that of the foot].
Indeed, upon the transgression of that [rule], both [the giver and the receiver] go to hell.
For a greater spiritual prosperity results from undertaking the observances than from offspring produced by such an undertaking. An Ārya man shall not procreate upon a Śūdra woman;
a Śūdra man shall be put to death for procreating upon an Ārya woman.
And he should cause his wife to fast.
They teach that for a single sexual union with a woman of the same caste who has previously belonged to another man, one quarter of the penance falls upon him;
likewise, for each repetition, a quarter falls away.
In the fourth [offense], everything [is forfeited]. For a Śūdra who reviles an Ārya who is righteous, the tongue shall be cut off.
For one who makes himself equal [to an Ārya] in speech, on the road, on the bed, or on the seat, there shall be a flogging with a rod.

In cases of killing a person, theft, or seizing land, one who has committed such acts should be put to death after having surrendered his own property. However, in these cases, the punishment for a Brāhmaṇa shall be the blinding of the eyes.
Alternatively, he may be bound in secret for violating the rules or for other offenses.
Until the completion [of the study]; if it is not completed, he is to be expelled.
The teacher, the officiating priest, the graduate, and the king may provide protection, except in the case of one deserving death.
If, after a field has been taken up for cultivation, there is a failure of fruit due to a lack of effort, that field shall be confiscated from whoever was prosperous [and failed to work it].
For a plowman who lacks oxen, or for a herdsman, if they abandon their work, there shall be a flogging with a rod. Likewise for a herdsman;
and his cattle shall be impounded.
Having left the pen, he should cause the cattle of those who eat during the day to emaciate, but he should not let them perish.
(28.5) If, after having penned the cattle, they die or are lost, he should restore them to their owners.
(28.6) If he sees cattle that have been let loose in the forest through negligence, he should bring them back to the village and restore them to their owners. (28.7)
If he does so again through negligence, he shall be confined for one night; thereafter, he shall not be watched over.
One who, being ignorant, takes another's property—whether firewood, water, roots, flowers, fruits, perfumes, food, or vegetables—is to be restrained by a verbal reprimand.
For one who knows better, there shall be the confiscation of his clothing.

One who takes food while his life is in danger is not subject to punishment even if he acts out of desire. (K 13) When the occasion for punishment has arisen, if the king fails to inflict it, the sin touches him.
(K 14) The instigator, the one who consents, and the doer are sharers in the fruits—whether heaven or hell—of their actions. (K 15)
29.2 Whoever undertakes more labor receives a corresponding distinction in the fruit.
29.3 The husband and wife are the masters of the wealth. 29.4 Others [may use it] with their permission.

In a legal dispute, those who are endowed with learning and noble birth, who are aged, wise, and unerring in matters of dharma [shall decide]. In case of doubt, having deliberated by means of signs or through divine ordeal, on an auspicious day in the morning, when the fire has been kindled at the edge of water in the presence of the king, and after both sides have been made to declare their case, the chief witness, with the consent of all, shall state the truth in response to the question.
In the case of untruth, the king shall inflict punishment;
furthermore, there is hell for him in the life hereafter.
In the case of truth, there is heaven and the praise of all beings.
That which is knowledge regarding women and Śūdras is the completion [of study].

They teach that this is the supplement of the Atharvaveda. The fulfillment of dharma is traditionally declared to be through the recitation; however, it is completed by the performance of the ritual acts.

In this regard, the defining characteristic is as follows: one should adopt the conduct that is unanimously agreed upon in all regions by the noble ones who are well-disciplined, aged, self-possessed, free from greed, and devoid of hypocrisy; one should emulate their way of life. In this manner, one conquers both worlds.
Some say that one should learn the remaining points of dharma from women and from members of all social classes. Others say this.
And thus the Āpastambīya Dharmasūtra is completed.

The Veda is the root of Dharma;
(1.2) so too are the Smṛti and the conduct of those who know it;
(1.3) transgression of Dharma and violence are observed even among the great.
But not when the purpose is perceptible.
(GDhS-A 1.1.4) Due to the weakness of what follows. (GDhS-A 1.1.5) When there is a conflict between two rules of equal strength, there is an option. (GDhS-A 1.1.4–5)
The initiation (*upanayana*) of a Brāhmaṇa takes place in the eighth year; in the ninth or fifth year, it is performed for the sake of a desired result. The count of years begins from conception.
That is his second birth.
Because of that, he is the teacher (ācārya).
And because of the recitation of the Veda.
For the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya, [the time for initiation] is the eleventh and twelfth years respectively.
For a Brāhmaṇa, the Sāvitrī [initiation] does not lapse until the sixteenth year;
for a Rājanya, it does not lapse until the twenty-second year.
GDhS-A 1.1.14b | GDhS-St 1.14: For a Vaiśya, [the girdle] is made of two-fold [grass].
GDhS-A 1.1.15 / GDhS-St 1.15: The girdles are made of muñja grass, a bowstring, and a cord of murvā fiber, respectively.
GDhS-A 1.1.16 / GDhS-St 1.16: The skins are those of the black antelope, the ruru deer, and the goat, respectively.
1.17. For all [students], the garments are made of hemp, linen, bark, or the skin of the kutapa goat. 1.18. And [the garment] may be cotton, provided it is unadorned.
1.19. Some [teachers] say that it may also be dyed saffron-colored.

GDhS-A 1,1.20a | GDhS-St 1.20: That of a Brāhmaṇa is made of wood. GDhS-A 1,1.20b | GDhS-St 1.21: Those of the other two [castes] are madder-red and yellow, respectively. GDhS-A 1,1.21 / GDhS-St 1.22: The staffs of a Brāhmaṇa are made of Bilva or Palāśa wood.
In the case of the remaining [sacrificial posts], they are made of *aśvattha* or *pailava* wood. Or rather, any wood fit for sacrifice may be used for all of them.
They should be unblemished, curved like a sacrificial post (*yūpa*), and provided with bark.
The measurements [of the staffs] are equal to the height of the head, the forehead, or the tip of the nose.
They may have shaven heads, matted hair, or a single tuft of matted hair.
One who has food in his hand or is impure from eating should sip water for purification without setting the object down.
GDhS-A 1,1.28 / GDhS-St 1.29: The purification of metallic, earthenware, wooden, and woollen objects is by means of scrubbing, burning, scraping, and washing.
GDhS-A 1,1.29 / GDhS-St 1.30: Stones, gems, shells, and pearls are purified like metallic objects. (Variant: "mother-of-pearl" for "shells").
Bone and earth are treated like wood; the ground is also treated like a sowing-place;
ropes, split bamboo, and leather are treated like cloth.

GDhS-A 1.1.33 / GDhS-St 1.34: Or there may be the discarding of those [substances] that are excessively defiled. GDhS-A 1.1.34 / GDhS-St 1.35: Facing either the east or the north, one should begin the purification.

GDhS-A 1.1.35 / GDhS-St 1.36: Sitting on a clean spot, having placed the right arm between the knees, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (yajñopavītī), having washed the hands up to the wrists, and remaining silent while touching the heart, one should sip water three or four times.
He wipes [the mouth] twice;
he should also sprinkle water on his feet.
One should touch the apertures of the head;
one should also place [the water] upon the crown of the head.
This should be done again after sleeping, eating, and sneezing.

GDhS-A 1.1.41 / GDhS-St 1.38: Regarding food particles stuck between the teeth, [one becomes pure] as with the teeth themselves, except when they are touched by the tongue. GDhS-A 1.1.42 / GDhS-St 1.39: Some say [this applies] until they fall out. GDhS-A 1.1.43 / GDhS-St 1.40: One should know that regarding those that have fallen out, it is like saliva; one becomes pure simply by swallowing them.

GDhS-A 1,1.46 / GDhS-St 1.41: Drops [of water] do not make one impure by leaving a residue, unless they fall upon a limb. GDhS-A 1,1.45 / GDhS-St 1.42: Purification from an impure substance consists in the removal of its stain and odor. GDhS-A 1,1.46 / GDhS-St 1.43: That [removal] should first be done with water and then with earth.
And [one becomes impure] upon contact with urine, feces, oil, exudations, food, or sexual intercourse;
and in whatever case the sacred tradition (āmnāya) may prescribe [impurity].
GDhS-A 1,1.49a | GDhS-St 1.46: Having grasped the left hand [of the teacher] with his own hand, excluding the thumb, he should address the teacher, saying, "Recite, sir!
(āmantrayet).
GDhS-A 1,1.49b | GDhS-St 1.47: Thereupon, there is the touching of the eyes, the mind, and the vital breaths with *darbha* grass.
There, with the mind fixed on the eye,
one should touch the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) with *darbha* grass;
[then] there should be three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), each consisting of fifteen *mātrās*.
51. And he should sit on [grass] with the tips pointing eastward. 52. The five *vyāhṛtis*, preceded by *oṃ* and ending with *satya*.
53. In the morning, he shall perform the clasping of the teacher’s feet. 54.
And at the beginning and end of the recitation of the Veda, [he shall do so].
55. Having been permitted, the disciple shall sit down to the south, facing east, or facing north.
56. And the recitation of the Sāvitrī [is required] at the beginning when undertaking the Veda. 57. The syllable *oṃ* [is used] even elsewhere.
GDhS-A 1,1.59 / GDhS-St 1.58: If [the teacher] goes inside [the house], there must be a renewed initiation (*punar-upasada*).
GDhS-A 1,1.60 / GDhS-St 1.59: In the case of dogs, mongooses, snakes, frogs, or cats [entering the sacrificial fire], there shall be a three-day fast and a stay away from home (*vipravāsa*).
GDhS-A 1,1.61 / GDhS-St 1.60: For others, there shall be breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) and the consumption of clarified butter (ghṛtaprāśana).
GDhS-A 1,1.62 / GDhS-St 1.61: And likewise for studying [the Veda] in a cremation ground.
Before initiation, there is freedom of action, freedom of speech, and freedom of consumption.
{VAR_St: one who acts, speaks, and eats according to his own will} / From what is not offered in sacrifice;
/ A student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*).
He disposes of his urine and feces as they arise. For him, no rule for ritual sipping (ācamana) exists.
GDhS-A 1,2.6 / GDhS-St 2.2b: Except for wiping, sprinkling with water, and washing;
GDhS-A 1,2.7 / GDhS-St 2.3: there is no impurity resulting from touching that [corpse];
GDhS-A 1,2.8 / GDhS-St 2.4: however, one should not appoint such a person to perform the fire-oblation or the offering of the bali.
GDhS-A 1,2.9 / GDhS-St 2.5: He shall not pronounce the Veda, except when offering the *svadhā* libation.
GDhS-A 1,2.10 / GDhS-St 2.6: The rules of restraint begin with the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*). GDhS-A 1,2.11 / GDhS-St 2.7: Studenthood (*brahmacarya*) has been described.
Tending the sacred fires, gathering fuel, and begging for alms; speaking the truth;
and performing ritual ablutions with water.
Some [teachers] prescribe the gift of a cow and other rites;
(GDhS 1.2.15) And [they prescribe] being outside during the twilight prayers.
(GDhS 1.2.16) He should stand during the morning prayer and sit during the evening prayer, remaining silent while the light is still visible, or until the stars appear. (GDhS 1.2.17)
He shall not look at the sun.

He shall avoid honey, meat, perfumes, garlands, sleeping during the day, anointing the body, vehicles, shoes, umbrellas, lust, anger, greed, delusion, singing, playing musical instruments, bathing for pleasure, cleaning the teeth, exhilaration, dancing, singing, slander, and fear.
In the presence of the teacher, one must not cover the neck, wear a girdle around the thighs, lean against a support,
or stretch out the feet; nor should one spit, laugh, yawn, crack the knuckles, or stretch the limbs.
Beholding or touching a woman when there is suspicion of sexual intercourse;
gambling, associating with the low-born, taking what is not given, and violence;
and the names of one's teacher, his son, and a consecrated person.
GDhS-A 1,2.25a | GDhS-St 2.19: Their speech should be pure (or, according to the variant: their speech should be sweet). GDhS-A 1,2.25b | GDhS-St 2.20: A Brāhmaṇa must always avoid intoxicants.
He should sleep and sit on the ground, rise before [his teacher] and go to rest after him; he should restrain his speech, arms, and belly;
and he should mention the name and lineage of his teacher with respect.
GDhS-A 1,2.29 / GDhS-St 2.24: When one who is superior has been honored, the same [rules apply].

GDhS-A 1,2.30 / GDhS-St 2.25: One should respond [to a command] after leaving one's bed, seat, or standing place. GDhS-A 1,2.31 / GDhS-St 2.26: One should approach [the teacher] when called, even if not seen by him.
While sitting on a lower seat or remaining seated, one should rise upon seeing the teacher when he is passing by or when he sits down;
one should follow him as he walks away.
Having announced and declared his ritual action, he is one who studies when summoned (āhūtādhyāyī). (GDhS-A 1.2.34 / GDhS-St 2.28b; GDhS-A 1.2.35 / GDhS-St 2.29)
He should be intent on what is pleasing and beneficial [to his teacher]. The same applies toward the teacher’s wife and sons.
However, he must not eat the leftovers of their food, nor bathe them, nor adorn them, nor wash their feet, nor massage them, nor clasp their feet.
GDhS-A 1,2.39 / GDhS-St 2.33: Having returned from a journey, one should perform the respectful salutation (*upasaṅgrahaṇa*) to the wives of one's gurus.
GDhS-A 1,2.40 / GDhS-St 2.34: Some teachers say this is not required for young wives who have reached marriageable age.
GDhS-A 1,2.41 / GDhS-St 2.35: One should go about begging alms from people of all castes, with the exception of those accused of crimes and those who have fallen from their caste.
The word *bhavat* should be employed at the beginning, middle, and end [of the request for alms], according to the order of the social classes (*varṇa*).
When it is not possible [to obtain food] from teachers, kinsmen, or gurus, one may seek it elsewhere.
Among these, one should avoid each preceding one more than the following. Having informed the teacher and being permitted by him, one may eat.

GDhS-A 1,2.46 / GDhS-St 2.40: In his absence, [the offering is made] to his wife, his son, or a fellow student. GDhS-A 1,2.47 / GDhS-St 2.41: Restraining his speech, being satisfied, and not being greedy, he should offer water.
The instruction of a pupil is to be carried out without corporal punishment. In case of incapacity [to restrain him], [the teacher may use] thin cords made of rope or split bamboo.
GDhS-A 1,2.50 / GDhS-St 2.44: One who strikes with something other than [the prescribed means] shall be punished by the king.

GDhS-A 1,2.51 / GDhS-St 2.45: He should observe the life of a religious student (*brahmacarya*) for twelve years for each Veda. GDhS-A 1,2.52 / GDhS-St 2.46: Or he may do so for twelve years for all the Vedas together.

Or [the period of studentship] may last until the completion of the Vedic study. At the end of his studies, the teacher should be invited with a gift. Or, having performed the ritual, he may bathe with the teacher's permission.
The teacher is the most excellent among gurus;
some say it is the mother.
Regarding this,
some authorities state that there is an option concerning the stages of life (āśrama).
The student, the householder, the mendicant, and the forest-dweller.
Of these, the householder is the source, because the others do not produce offspring.
Regarding this, that which has been stated for the student [is as follows].
Dependence upon the teacher lasts until the end [of life].
After completing the duties for the guru, one should recite prayers. In the absence of the guru, one should follow the conduct toward his offspring.
{VAR_St: -apatye vṛttiḥ} GDhS-A 1,3.7b | GDhS-St 3.8: In their absence, [he may seek support] from an aged fellow-student or from the sacred fire.
GDhS-A 1,3.8 / GDhS-St 3.9: Conducting himself in this manner and having conquered his senses, he attains the world of Brahman.
And this applies to the subsequent [sections] as well, provided it is not in conflict with them. Or:
"and this applies to the others as well, provided it is not in conflict."
A mendicant should not accumulate possessions; he should remain chaste; and he should maintain a steady discipline during the rainy season.
One who seeks alms should go to the village. He should wander at the end of the day, before others have returned. He should refrain from expressing a desire for specific food.
Restrained in speech, sight, and action;
he shall wear a garment only for the purpose of covering his private parts.
According to some, [a garment] that has been discarded should be washed before being used again. One should not take for use any part of plants or trees that has not been detached [from the source].
One should not stay in a village for a second night during the non-seasonal period.
He should either be shaven-headed or wear a topknot. He should avoid the destruction of seeds.
For he should be impartial toward all beings, whether in regard to injury or favor.
He should not undertake [new] undertakings. A forest-dweller (vaikhānasa) shall dwell in the forest, subsisting on roots and fruits, devoted to austerity,
having established the *śrāvaṇaka* fire.
He should eat food that is not rustic;
he should worship the gods, the ancestors, men, beings, and the sages.
He should be hospitable to all guests, with the exception of those who are prohibited. He may also consume the meat of a boar.
He shall not stand upon ground ploughed by a plow. He shall not enter a village.
He shall have matted hair and wear garments of bark or animal skins.
One should not eat [the food of another] for more than a year.
However, the teachers maintain that there is only one stage of life (āśrama), because the householder’s state is explicitly prescribed. It is the householder’s state.
Of the householder's state, of the householder's state.

GDhS-A 1,4.1 / GDhS-St 4.1: A householder should marry a wife who is of equal status, not previously married to another, and younger than himself. GDhS-A 1,4.2 / GDhS-St 4.2: Marriage is with those who do not share the same *pravara* (ancestral lineage). GDhS-A 1,4.3a / GDhS-St 4.3: [This applies] beyond the seventh degree on the father’s side among paternal kinsmen.
And from the seed-giver [the impurity lasts for ten days]. From the maternal relatives up to the fifth degree.
For a *brāhma* marriage, he should give [the girl], having clothed and adorned her, to one who is endowed with learning, good conduct, kinship, and character.
In the *prājāpatya* rite, the formula for the union is: "Let dharma be practiced together.
In the *ārṣa* rite, one should give a pair of cattle to the bridegroom.
The *daiva* rite consists of giving [the girl] to the officiating priest within the sacrificial enclosure after having adorned her.
The Gāndharva [form of marriage] is the union of two who desire each other of their own accord. The Āsura [form of marriage] is the honoring of women with wealth.
The Rākṣasa [form] results from taking her by force;
the Paiśāca [form] results from approaching her while she is unconscious.
GDhS-A 1,4.12 / GDhS-St 4.14: The first four [classes] are lawful.
GDhS-A 1,4.13 / GDhS-St 4.15: Some say there are six.

GDhS-A 1,4.14 / GDhS-St 4.16: From women of the same caste, those born of women one degree lower, two degrees lower, and three degrees lower are known as the Savarṇa, Ambaṣṭha, Ugra, Niṣāda, Dauṣmanta, and Pāraśava respectively.
But the *pratiloma* [offspring] are the Sūta, Māgadha, Āyogava, Kṣattṛ, Vaidehaka,
and Caṇḍāla.
A Brāhmaṇa woman bears sons from men of the [other] castes in the direct order of classes: a Brāhmaṇa, a Sūta, a Māgadha, and a Caṇḍāla.
(GDhS 1.4.16) From those same [men], a Kṣatriya woman bears an Ūrdhvāvasiktha, a Kṣatriya, a Dhīvara, and a Pulkasa.
(GDhS 1.4.17a) From those same [men], a Vaiśya woman bears a Bhṛjjakaṇṭha, a Māhiṣya, a Vaiśya, and a Vaideha. (GDhS 1.4.17b)

GDhS-A 1.4.17c | GDhS-St 4.21: Some say that the Pāraśava, Yavana, Karaṇa, and Śūdra are [all] simply Śūdras. GDhS-A 1.4.18a | GDhS-St 4.22: The transition to another caste occurs through advancement or degradation in the seventh generation.
GDhS-A 1,4.18b | GDhS-St 4.23: Or on the fifth [day], according to the teachers.
{VAR_St: saptamena; pañcamenācāryāḥ} GDhS-A 1,4.19 / GDhS-St 4.24:
And for those born from a different species.
But those born in the reverse order (pratiloma) are devoid of dharma;
and so too is [the son] born of a Śūdra woman.
But from a Śūdra woman of a different caste, he has the livelihood of an outcast (patita). From one of the lowest caste, he is the most sinful.
Virtuous sons purify [their ancestors] for three generations from the *ārṣa* marriage; ten generations from the *daiva* marriage.
GDhS-A 1,4.26b | GDhS-St 4.32: Ten [generations] from the son of a Prājāpatī wife.
GDhS-A 1,4.27 / GDhS-St 4.33: A son of a Brāhmī wife [sanctifies] ten ancestors, ten descendants, and himself; he is a true son of a Brāhmī wife.
{VAR_St: ten descendants}
He should approach his wife during her season.
GDhS-A 1,5.2 / GDhS-St 5.2: Or rather, he may do so in all cases, except for what is forbidden.
GDhS-A 1,5.3 / GDhS-St 5.3: He shall worship the gods, the ancestors, men, beings, and the sages.
GDhS-A 1,5.4 / GDhS-St 5.4: He shall constantly engage in the private recitation of the Veda.
GDhS-A 1,5.5a | GDhS-St 5.5: And the offering of water to the ancestors.
GDhS-A 1,5.5b | GDhS-St 5.6: Other [rites] according to one's ability.
GDhS-A 1,5.6 / GDhS-St 5.7: The fire is either that of the wife or that of the inheritance.
In that [fire] are performed the domestic rites (gṛhyakarmāṇi).
These consist of the sacrifices to the gods, the ancestors, and men, as well as the private recitation of the Veda (svādhyāya) and the offering of oblations (balikarma).

The oblations are offered to Agni in Agni, to Dhanvantari, to the Viśvedevas, to Prajāpati, and to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. And offerings are made to the deities of the quarters, each to their respective domain.
At the doors, [he offers] to the Maruts (or, according to another version, to the Mahāntas).
Having entered, [he offers] to the household deities.
To Brahmán, in the center; to the Waters, at the water-pot; [to Vāyu], according to GDhS-A 1,5.14a; to Ākāśa, in the intermediate space, according to GDhS-St 5.16.
The bali offering is to be cast out.
At night, [the offering] is for those who roam at night.
After having caused the benediction (svasti) to be recited, the giving of alms follows, preceded by water.
The same applies to righteous acts of giving.
(GDhS-A 1,5.17 / GDhS-St 5.19) The rewards for giving to a non-Brahmin, a Brahmin, a learned Śrotriya, and one who has mastered the Vedas are respectively equal, double, a thousandfold, and infinite.

(GDhS-A 1,5.18 / GDhS-St 5.20) Outside the sacrificial ground, there shall be a distribution of goods to those who have come for the sake of their teacher, for the sake of a dwelling, for medicine, for the sake of livelihood, those whose resources are exhausted, those about to sacrifice, those engaged in Vedic study, those on a journey, and those who have won a universal victory. (GDhS-A 1,5.19 / GDhS-St 5.21)
When they beg, cooked food is to be given to those other than [the aforementioned unworthy persons].
Even after having promised, one should not give to one who is joined with unrighteousness.
The words of one who is angry, joyful, terrified, afflicted, greedy, childish, aged, dull-witted, intoxicated, or insane, though false, do not constitute a mortal sin.
One should feed first the guest, the child, the sick, the pregnant woman, the newly married daughter living in her father’s house, and the elderly; these are to be fed before the others.
And the act of cooking must be announced to the teacher, the father, and friends.
The madhuparka is offered upon the arrival of a sacrificial priest (*ṛtvij*), a teacher (*ācārya*), a father-in-law (*śvaśura*), a paternal uncle (*pitṛvya*), or a maternal uncle (*mātula*).
It is offered again after a year has passed.
It is also offered prior to a sacrifice or a wedding.
And [one should offer] to a king and to a *śrotriya*.
To one who is not a *śrotriya*, [one should offer] only a seat and water.
But for a *śrotriya*, one should provide water for the feet (*pādya*), the guest-water (*arghya*), and various kinds of food.
Or [the gift] may be constant, distinguished by refinement.
Food should be given from the midst [of the meal] to one who is not learned but is of virtuous conduct. In the opposite case, grass, water, and ground [should be given].
But in the opposite case:
"A welcome [is offered] at the very end," and "There is also honor and excessive hospitality."
5.34/38: Bedding, seating, dwellings, following behind, and attendance are the same toward equals and superiors.
5.35/39: Even to a lesser degree, [these duties apply] toward one who is inferior.

GDhS-A 1,5.36 / GDhS-St 5.40: A guest who does not belong to the same village, who stays for only one night, and who waits under a tree until the sun appears [is entitled to hospitality]. GDhS-A 1,5.37 / GDhS-St 5.41: There shall be inquiries regarding his welfare, health, and freedom from disease.
GDhS-A 1,5.38 / GDhS-St 5.42: For a Śūdra, only the last [of these questions] applies.
A non-Brāhmaṇa is not a guest for a Brāhmaṇa, except when he is included at a sacrifice. (Or: except when he is included at a non-sacrificial rite.)
But the meal for the Kṣatriya [should be served] after the Brāhmaṇas.
The others [should be fed] together with the servants out of compassion; [this is] for the sake of compassion.
In a gathering,
one should perform the clasping of the feet every day.
But upon returning from a journey abroad,
[he should perform the *abhivādana*] toward his mother, father, their relatives, his ancestors, his teachers of knowledge, and their teachers;
and when meeting another person, [he should do so] toward that other person.
In a gathering of those who do not know [one's name], one should offer a salutation by pronouncing one's own name, saying, "I am so-and-so.
Regarding the union of a woman and a man, some maintain that there is no fixed rule for the person offering the salutation.
One should not, when not away from home, [greet] women who are not one's mother, paternal aunt, wife, or sister.
One should not perform the formal salutation (*upasaṃgrahaṇa*) for the wives of brothers or sisters. [Some versions read "and fathers-in-law."]
One must rise to greet and salute officiating priests, fathers-in-law, paternal uncles, and maternal uncles who are younger than oneself; [but not those who are older].
Likewise, any other person who is senior—such as a village headman who is at least eighty years old—even if he is a Śūdra, is to be saluted like one's own son.
Even a lower Ārya [must not be addressed by name] by a Śūdra;
he should avoid pronouncing his name.
The servant of a king shall address him as "Ajapa" (O Reciter).
A companion born on the same day shall address him as "Bho Bhavan" (O Sir). A fellow citizen ten years his senior shall address him as "Paura" (Citizen).
GDhS-A 1,6.15b | GDhS-St 6.16: One who maintains the five fires is supported by a fifth part [of the king's revenue].
GDhS-A 1,6.15c | GDhS-St 6.17: A Śrotriya who is a wandering bard (cāraṇa) is supported by a third part.
GDhS-A 1,6.16 / GDhS-St 6.18: Those who perform the duties of Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas but are devoid of Vedic learning [are supported by a fourth part].
And one who has been consecrated [for a sacrifice] is [to be honored] prior to the purchase [of the Soma].
Wealth, kinship, occupation, birth, learning, and age are grounds for respect, each subsequent one being stronger than the preceding. But sacred learning is the most weighty of all.
GDhS-A 1,6.20a | GDhS-St 6.22: Because dharma has its root in that [the Veda].
GDhS-A 1,6.20b | GDhS-St 6.23: And because of the revealed scripture (śruti).

GDhS-A 1,6.21 / GDhS-St 6.24: One should yield the right of way to those with a vehicle, to one who is in his tenth decade of life, to one who is worthy of protection, to a bride, to a snātaka, and to a king.
But by a king, [it should be given] to a *śrotriya*, to a *śrotriya*.
[GDhS-A 1,7 = GDhS-St VII]
GDhS-A 1,7.1 / GDhS-St 7.1: In times of distress, it is permissible for a Brāhmaṇa to acquire knowledge from one who is not a Brāhmaṇa.
GDhS-A 1,7.2 / GDhS-St 7.2: Following him and serving him are required. GDhS-A 1,7.3 / GDhS-St 7.3: Once the study is completed, the Brāhmaṇa becomes his teacher.

Sacrificing for others, teaching, and receiving gifts are [the means of livelihood] for all [classes]. Among these, each preceding one is more venerable than the following. In the absence of those, the occupation of a Kṣatriya [is permitted].
In the absence of that [the occupation of a Kṣatriya], he may follow the livelihood of a Vaiśya. His merchandise is as follows: [GDhS 1.7.8].
Scented substances, flavors, prepared food, sesame, salt, linen, and skins;
dyed and washed garments. (GDhS 1.7.9–10)
Milk and its derivatives [are pure].
Roots, fruits, flowers, herbs, honey, meat, grass, water, and road-levies are pure.
And domestic animals are pure except when associated with injury.

1.7.14: A man, a ram, a maiden, and a cow that has miscarried are [always] [fit for sacrifice]. 1.7.15: According to some, the earth, rice, barley, goats, sheep, horses, bulls, milch-cows, and oxen are also [fit for sacrifice].
1.7.16: But there is a restriction.
GDhS-A 1,7.17 / GDhS-St 7.17: [The bartering] of liquids is [permitted] for liquids.
GDhS-A 1,7.18 / GDhS-St 7.18: And [the bartering] of animals [is permitted for animals]. GDhS-A 1,7.19 / GDhS-St 7.19: But not [the bartering] of salt or prepared food.
And [the same applies] to sesame seeds.
(GDhS-A 1,7.20 / GDhS-St 7.20) But with an equal amount of raw grain, one may exchange for cooked food when there is immediate need.
(GDhS-A 1,7.21 / GDhS-St 7.21) In case of inability, one may subsist in every way provided it is not by means of Śūdra wealth. (GDhS-A 1,7.22 / GDhS-St 7.22)
Some, however, permit even that [eating of forbidden food] when there is a danger to life;
but there is a restriction regarding the mixing of castes and the consumption of forbidden food.
In a life-threatening danger, even a Brāhmaṇa may take up arms;
a Rājanya may perform the duties of a Vaiśya.
In this world, two are firm in their observance of vows: the king and the learned Brāhmaṇa.
Of these two [fire and water], the life of the fourfold human race— consisting of those with internal consciousness who move, fly, and crawl— is dependent.
