Their duty (*dharma*) consists of procreation, protection, and the avoidance of intermixture.
He alone is one who has heard much;
he is a knower of the world, the Vedas, and the Vedāṅgas.
One who is proficient in the dialogues (vākovākya), the Itihāsas, and the Purāṇas;
one who depends on them and subsists according to them;
one who has been consecrated by the forty sacraments (saṃskāras).
He should be devoted to three duties;
or, he may be devoted to six.
GDhS-A 1,8.11 / GDhS-St 8.11: One who is well-trained in the rules of conventional conduct; GDhS-A 1,8.12 / GDhS-St 8.12: Such a person may not be avoided by the king for six [reasons];
GDhS-A 1,8.13 / GDhS-St 8.13: namely, he is one who is not to be killed, nor to be bound, nor to be fined, nor to be banished, nor to be censured, nor to be avoided.

GDhS-A 1,8.14 / GDhS-St 8.14: Conception, the rite for a male child, the parting of the hair, the birth ceremony, the naming ceremony, the first feeding of solid food, the tonsure, and the initiation.
GDhS-A 1,8.15 / GDhS-St 8.15: The four Vedic vows.
GDhS-A 1,8.16 / GDhS-St 8.16a: The ceremonial bath and union with a wife who practices the dharma together.

The performance of the five sacrifices is for the sake of the gods, ancestors, humans, spirits, and Brahmins. And [the performance] of these [five sacrifices is also required]. The Aṣṭakā, the Pārvaṇa-śrāddha, the Śrāvaṇī, the Āgrahāyaṇī, the Caitrī, and the Āśvayujī—these are the seven forms of the cooked-sacrifice (pākayajña).

The establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), the fire-oblation (*agnihotra*), the new- and full-moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), the first-fruits offering (*āgrayaṇa*), the four-monthly sacrifices (*cāturmāsya*), the independent animal sacrifice (*nirūḍhapaśubandha*), and the *sautrāmaṇī*: these are the seven forms of the *haviryajña*.
The *agniṣṭoma*, the *atyagniṣṭoma*, the *ukthya*, the *ṣoḍaśin*, the *vājapeya*, the *atirātra*, and the *aptoryāma*: these are the seven forms of the *soma* sacrifice.
Thus, these are the forty sacraments.
Now follow the eight qualities of the self:
compassion toward all living beings, patience, freedom from envy, purity, lack of fatigue, auspiciousness, generosity, and lack of possessiveness.

He who possesses these forty sacraments but lacks the eight qualities of the self does not attain union with Brahman nor residence in the same world as Brahman. But he who possesses even a portion of these sacraments together with the eight qualities of the self, indeed attains both union with Brahman and residence in the same world as Brahman.
Having bathed according to the prescribed rule and having taken a wife, he who practices the duties of a householder as they have been described should observe these following vows.
The *snātaka* [is as follows]:
He should always be pure, fragrant, and habituated to bathing.
If he has the means, he should not wear worn-out or dirty clothes. He should not wear clothing that is dyed red, ostentatious, or previously worn by another.

One should not wear a garland or sandals [while studying]. If one is unable [to bathe], one may study after washing [the feet]. One should not study while the beard is grown, except for a specific reason.

One should not hold fire and water simultaneously. One should not drink from one's cupped hands. One should not perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) while standing with water drawn up [in a vessel].

One should not [eat] food offered by a Śūdra, an impure person, or with only one hand. Nor should one discharge urine, feces, or impurities while facing the wind, fire, a Brāhmaṇa, the sun, water, deities, or cows.

One should not stretch out one's feet toward these deities. One should not remove urine or feces with leaves, clods of earth, or stones. One should not stand upon ashes, hair, nail-clippings, chaff, potsherds, or other impure things.
One should not converse with barbarians (mlecchas), the impure, or those who are unrighteous. Having conversed [with them], one should meditate mentally upon those who perform meritorious deeds.
Or he may converse with a Brāhmaṇa. He should say of a non-cow, "It is a cow"; and of what is not auspicious, "It is auspicious."
GDhS-A 1,9.22 / GDhS-St 9.21: "A skull" [is called] *bhagāla*.
GDhS-A 1,9.23 / GDhS-St 9.22: "The jeweled bow" (*maṇidhanus*) is the rainbow.
GDhS-A 1,9.24 / GDhS-St 9.23: One should not point out to another a cow suckling her calf.
And he should not prevent her [from approaching].
Having engaged in sexual union, he should not delay regarding purification. Nor should he recite his Vedic lesson on that same bed.
Having studied during the latter part of the night, he should not go back to sleep again.
He should not take pleasure with a woman who is unchaste.
Not with a woman in her menses;
nor should he embrace her;
nor a maiden.

GDhS-A 1,9.32 / GDhS-St 9.33: He shall avoid blowing on the fire with his mouth, speaking in a quarrelsome manner, wearing perfumes and garlands [for their own sake], scraping [his nails], eating together with his wife, looking at himself while applying collyrium, entering by a side door, washing his feet with the soles upwards, eating while seated on a bench, crossing a river by swimming with his arms, climbing or descending trees or uneven places, and exerting himself to the limit of his breath.
{VAR_St:
ca} GDhS-A 1,9.33 / GDhS-St 9.33: He shall not board a boat whose safety is doubtful.
GDhS-A 1,9.34 / GDhS-St 9.34: One should protect oneself from all sides. GDhS-A 1,9.35 / GDhS-St 9.35: One should not walk about during the day with one's head covered.
GDhS-A 1,9.36 / GDhS-St 9.36: [One may do so] having covered it at night.
And [one should not void] urine or excrement;
nor upon the ground without having covered it.
Nor from a human dwelling (GDhS-A 1,9.39 / GDhS-St 9.39).
Nor on ashes, on cow-dung, on ploughed land, in shade, on a path, or in a place desired by others (GDhS-A 1,9.40 / GDhS-St 9.40).
One should void both urine and feces during the day facing the north (GDhS-A 1,9.41 / GDhS-St 9.41).
And during the two twilights;
at night, facing south.
One should avoid a seat made of *pālāśa* wood, as well as sandals and a tooth-stick. Furthermore, one should avoid performing sitting, salutation, or prostration while wearing shoes.
One should not let the forenoon, midday, or afternoon pass fruitlessly; one should devote them to dharma, artha, and kāma according to one's ability.
Among these, however, one should be preeminent in dharma.

One should not look at another man’s wife while she is naked. One should not drag a seat with one's foot. One should not engage in the restlessness of the genitals, the stomach, the hands, the feet, speech, or the eyes.
GDhS-A 1,9.51 / GDhS-St 9.51: One should not, without cause, perform cutting, splitting, scraping, crushing, or tearing.
GDhS-A 1,9.52 / GDhS-St 9.52: One should not walk over a rope of calf-tethers. GDhS-A 1,9.53 / GDhS-St 9.53: One should not be a "house-to-house" beggar.
One should not go to a sacrifice unless invited;
however, one may go at will merely to see it.
One should not eat sacrificial food from one's lap.
One should not eat food brought by a servant at night.
One should not eat extracted fats, dregs of boiled rice, oil-cakes, freshly churned butter, and other such items whose vital essence has been removed.
Every evening and morning, one should eat food that has been honored, without finding fault with it. One should never sleep naked at night.
Or he may bathe [as a snātaka].
And he should practice that which those who are self-possessed, aged, well-disciplined, free from guile, greed, and delusion, and learned in the Vedas, declare.
For the sake of security and prosperity, he should seek refuge in the Lord.
One should not [speak ill] of anyone other than the gods, one's teacher, and righteous persons.

One should strive to dwell in a residence that has an abundant supply of firewood, water, fodder, *kuśa* grass, and garlands; where people exit easily; which is populated by noble persons; which is free from laziness; and which is governed by righteous men.
One should circumambulate clockwise auspicious objects, things that bring good fortune, temples, and crossroads.
Alternatively,
as a rule for times of distress, one may observe that entire conduct mentally,
[even] at crossroads and the like.
One whose nature is truth;
one who follows the conduct of the noble;
one who teaches the learned.
He should be disciplined in purity; he should be devoted to the sacred revelation (Śruti);
he should always be non-violent, gentle, firm in his resolve, and characterized by self-restraint and generosity.
A Snātaka who conducts himself in this manner, desiring to liberate his parents and his ancestors and descendants from evil, never falls from the world of Brahman; he never falls.
GDhS-A 2,1.1 / GDhS-St 10.1:
For the twice-born, study, sacrifice, and giving are [the duties]. GDhS-A 2,1.2 / GDhS-St 10.2:
For the Brāhmaṇa, teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and receiving gifts are additional [duties].
GDhS-A 2,1.3 / GDhS-St 10.3: But there is a restriction regarding the former [occupations].

GDhS-A 2,1.4 / GDhS-St 10.4: In the case of restrictions concerning the teacher, kinsmen, friends, elders, wealth, and learning, the gift of the Veda is permitted even other than as previously stated.
GDhS-A 2,1.5 / GDhS-St 10.5: Or agriculture and trade may be practiced, provided they are not performed by oneself.
And usury [is permitted].
For the king, the protection of all beings is an additional duty.
2.1.8 / 10.8: The infliction of just punishment.
2.1.9 / 10.9: He shall support Vedic scholars who are Brāhmaṇas.
2.1.10 / 10.10: And those Brāhmaṇas who are lacking in energy.
And those who do not perform the duties of a Brahmin;
and those who are merely students (upakurvāṇa).
And there is yoga for the sake of victory (GDhS-A 2.1.13);
especially so in times of danger (GDhS-A 2.1.14);
and the practice consists of the chariot and the bow (GDhS-A 2.1.15).
In battle, there is staying [in one's place] and not retreating. For there is no fault in causing injury in combat,

except in the case of those who are horsemen, charioteers, those with weapons raised, those with palms joined in supplication, those with disheveled hair, those with their backs turned, those who are seated, those standing on high ground, those mounted on trees, messengers, cows, Brahmins, and those who proclaim [a truce].
If a Kṣatriya should live by another [profession], he may subsist by that [other] occupation. The victor shall receive the wealth acquired in battle.
But the vehicle belongs to the king.
And there is a preferential share [for the eldest] even when the property was not acquired separately.
But the king shall distribute the remainder as is appropriate. The tribute to be given by farmers to the king is one-tenth, one-eighth, or one-sixth [of the produce].
GDhS-A 2,1.25 / GDhS-St 10.25: Some [teachers] maintain that for cattle and gold, the share is one-fiftieth.
GDhS-A 2,1.26 / GDhS-St 10.26: For merchandise, the toll (śulka) is one-twentieth.
GDhS-A 2,1.27 / GDhS-St 10.27: For roots, fruits, flowers, medicinal herbs, honey, meat, grass, and fuel, the share is one-sixth.
Because it is his duty to protect them;
therefore, he should be constantly devoted to them.
GDhS-A 2,1.30 / GDhS-St 10.30: One may subsist by means of a surplus.
GDhS-A 2,1.31 / GDhS-St 10.31: Artisans shall perform one day’s work every month. GDhS-A 2,1.32 / GDhS-St 10.32: By this, those who subsist by their own labor are explained.
And those who live by boats and carts;
one should give them food.
Merchandise may be returned by merchants at a reduced price. Having found lost property that has no owner, they shall announce it to the king.
GDhS-A 2,1.37 / GDhS-St 10.37: Having been publicly proclaimed, he shall be protected by the king for one year.
GDhS-A 2,1.38 / GDhS-St 10.38: After that period, one-fourth of the property belongs to the finder and the remainder to the king.
GDhS-A 2,1.39 / GDhS-St 10.39: Ownership arises through inheritance, purchase, partition, seizure, or finding.
For a Brāhmaṇa, what is obtained is additional;
for a Kṣatriya, what is conquered;
for a Vaiśya and a Śūdra, what is earned through labor.
The discovery of a hidden treasure belongs to the king;
however, it belongs to a learned Brāhmaṇa.

GDhS-A 2,1.45 / GDhS-St 10.45: Some say that even a non-Brāhmaṇa who reports [the thief] shall receive a sixth part. GDhS-A 2,1.46 / GDhS-St 10.46: Having recovered what was stolen by thieves, he should restore it to its proper place.
Or he may pay it from his own treasury.
The property of a minor must be protected until he reaches legal majority,
or until his formal initiation (samāvartana).
GDhS-A 2,1.50 / GDhS-St 10.49: For the Vaiśya, there are additional [duties], namely agriculture, trade, animal husbandry, and moneylending.
GDhS-A 2,1.51 / GDhS-St 10.50: The Śūdra is the fourth caste; he has but one birth.
GDhS-A 2,1.52 / GDhS-St 10.51: For him also, truthfulness, freedom from anger, and purity [are required].
GDhS-A 2,1.53 / GDhS-St 10.52: Some say that for the purpose of sipping water (ācamana), one should merely wash the hands and feet.
{VAR_St: thus some say}.
GDhS-A 2,1.54 / GDhS-St 10.53: [This applies to] the Śrāddha rite.
55. Supporting one's dependents. 56. Devotion to one's own wife. 57. And service to those who are superior.
From them he should seek his livelihood.
Among them, he should serve each preceding one more than the following.
Worn-out sandals, umbrellas, garments, brooms, and so forth;
eating the remnants of another's meal.
And [he may live by] the practice of a craft (GDhS-A 2.1.62 / GDhS-St 10.60).
And he who takes refuge with an Ārya must support him, even if he himself is impoverished (GDhS-A 2.1.63 / GDhS-St 10.61).
{VAR_St: āśrayīta}
And by that, the latter [is also established].
His accumulation [of wealth] should be for that purpose.
For him, the mantra of salutation is permitted.
GDhS-A 2,1.67 / GDhS-St 10.65: Some say that one should perform the *pākayajña* sacrifices oneself.
GDhS-A 2,1.68 / GDhS-St 10.66: And all [members of the family] should serve each other in ascending order [of seniority].
GDhS-A 2,1.69 / GDhS-St 10.67: In the case of an interchange between an Ārya and a non-Ārya, there is equality of the ritual act.
Equanimity.
GDhS-A 2,2.1 / GDhS-St 11.1: The king has authority over all, with the exception of a Brāhmaṇa.
GDhS-A 2,2.2 / GDhS-St 11.2: He should be one who acts rightly and speaks rightly.
He should be well-trained in the three Vedas or in the science of inquiry (ānvīkṣikī).
He should be pure, have his senses under control, and be endowed with virtuous associates and skillful means.
He should be impartial toward his subjects; he should act for their welfare. (Or: he should act for their welfare and [be impartial].)

While he is seated above, others besides the Brāhmaṇas should sit below him; they too should hold him in high regard. He shall protect the social classes (varṇas) and the stages of life (āśramas) in accordance with justice.
And he should establish those who have strayed in their own duty;
for thus one becomes a sharer in the merit of dharma.
And he should appoint a Brahmin as his domestic priest— one endowed with learning, noble lineage, eloquence, beauty, age, and good character;
one who is upright in conduct and ascetic.
Impelled by that [Brahman], he should perform his duties;
for it is known from scripture: "The Kṣatriya, when impelled by Brahman, prospers and does not falter."
And whatever those who contemplate divine portents and omens might declare, he should pay heed to that;
for some maintain that even one's acquisition and preservation of property (*yogakṣema*) depend upon them.

He should perform rites for prosperity—connected with pacification, auspicious days, benedictions, longevity, and blessings—as well as rites for causing enmity, subjugation, malevolent magic, and the ruin of enemies, in the domestic fire (*śālāgni*).
GDhS-A 2.2.18 / GDhS-St 11.18: The other [texts] belong to the officiating priests (ṛtvij), as has been stated.
GDhS-A 2.2.19 / GDhS-St 11.19: And his sphere of activity consists of the Veda, the Dharmaśāstras, the auxiliary sciences (aṅga), the Upavedas, and the Purāṇa.

The laws of regions, castes, and families, when not in conflict with the sacred scriptures (*āmnāya*), are authoritative. Farmers, merchants, cattle-herders, usurers, and artisans are [governed by] their respective classes.
GDhS-A 2,2.22 / GDhS-St 11.22: Having extracted the matters from those [sources] according to their respective authority, there is the establishment of dharma.
GDhS-A 2,2.23 / GDhS-St 11.23: Reasoning is the means for attaining [an understanding of] logic.
GDhS-A 2,2.24 / GDhS-St 11.24: Having inferred by means of that, one should lead [the matter] to its proper place.
In case of a conflict, having brought [the matter] back from those who are learned in the three Vedas and are elders, he should reach a final decision;
for in this way his supreme welfare (*niḥśreyasa*) comes about. It is known from scripture: "Brahman, when joined with Kṣatra, sustains the gods, the ancestors, and human beings."
They say that "daṇḍa" (punishment) is so called because of its power to subdue (*damana*); therefore, one should subdue those who are unsubdued by it.

The members of the social classes (*varṇa*) and stages of life (*āśrama*), being devoted to their respective duties, after death experience the fruits of their actions; thereafter, by the remainder [of their merit], they are born with distinguished country, caste, family, form, lifespan, learning, splendor, wealth, happiness, and intelligence.
The castes and stages of life attain [their respective states] according to their own duty, sacred learning, and conduct;
they undergo rebirth.
Those who act contrary to this perish in all directions.
The instruction of the teacher and punishment protect them. Therefore, the king and the teacher are beyond reproach; they are beyond reproach.
GDhS-A 2,3.1 / GDhS-St 12.1:
A Śūdra who, having intended to harm or having struck members of the twice-born with verbal or physical violence, shall have that limb by which he caused the injury cut off.

{VAR_St: Having deceived or having struck [the victim], he shall be released from the limb [he used].} GDhS-A 2,3.2 / GDhS-St 12.2: For violating an Arya woman, there shall be the excision of the organ and the confiscation of his property.
{VAR_St: and the confiscation of all his property.}
If he is a protector [of the Veda], the punishment is death. Furthermore, if he listens to the Veda, his ears are to be filled with molten tin and lac. If he recites it, his tongue is to be cut off.

GDhS-A 2,3.4c | GDhS-St 12.6: [The punishment] for retaining [a deposit] is the destruction of the body. GDhS-A 2,3.5 / GDhS-St 12.7: One who seeks to obtain [an advantage] in sitting, lying down, speech, or on the road shall be fined.
GDhS-A 2,3.6 / GDhS-St 12.8: A Kṣatriya [shall pay] one hundred [paṇas] for insulting a Brāhmaṇa.
GDhS-St 12.9: In cases of physical assault, the fine is double.

GDhS-A 2,3.7 / GDhS-St 12.10: A Vaiśya [assaulting a Kṣatriya] shall pay one and a half [times the standard fine]. GDhS-A 2,3.8 / GDhS-St 12.11: But a Brāhmaṇa [assaulting a Kṣatriya] shall pay fifty [paṇas].
Half of that [period] for a Vaiśya (GDhS-A 2,3.9 / GDhS-St 12.12);
nothing at all for a Śūdra (GDhS-A 2,3.10 / GDhS-St 12.13);
and for a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya, it is as for a Brāhmaṇa and a Rājanya (GDhS-A 2,3.11 / GDhS-St 12.14).

The guilt of theft for a Śūdra is eightfold. For the other castes, the fines increase twofold respectively for each successive class. If one who is learned transgresses, the punishment is more severe.
GDhS-A 2,3.15 / GDhS-St 12.18: For taking fruits, green vegetables, grain, or pot-herbs, the fine is five *kṛṣṇalas* if the amount is small.
GDhS-A 2,3.16 / GDhS-St 12.19: When an animal is harmed, the fault lies with its owner.

But if that [field] is under the charge of a keeper, [the fine is as follows]: on a path or in an unenclosed field, the responsibility lies with both the keeper and the owner of the field. For damage to a cow, the fine is five *māṣas*.
For a camel or a donkey, six [days];
for a horse or a buffalo, ten.
GDhS-A 2,3.22 / GDhS-St 12.25: For goats and sheep, [the fine] is two [paṇas] each.
GDhS-A 2,3.23 / GDhS-St 12.26: In the case of the total destruction [of the herd], the fine is one śada.
GDhS-A 2,3.24 / GDhS-St 12.27: For failing to perform prescribed duties and for practicing what is forbidden, there shall always be the forfeiture of one's own clothes and food, beyond that.

GDhS-A 2,3.25 / GDhS-St 12.28: For the sake of cows or the sacred fire, one may take grass, herbs, and the flowers of shrubs and trees as if they were one's own; likewise, one may take the fruits of plants that are not enclosed by a fence.
GDhS-A 2,3.26 / GDhS-St 12.29: Interest on a loan is lawful at the rate of five *māṣas* per month for every twenty [units of principal].
GDhS-A 2,3.27 / GDhS-St 12.30: Some say that [the interest] shall not exceed one year's amount.

GDhS-A 2,3.28 / GDhS-St 12.31: If it remains for a long time, there is a doubling of the principal through the application [of interest]. GDhS-A 2,3.29 / GDhS-St 12.32: A pledge that is being used does not increase [in value through interest].
[Interest] on what is intended to be given and on what is withheld;
[interest] accruing by the wheel and by the time;
and [interest] stipulated, bodily, by a pledge, and by the enjoyment of collateral.

Interest on loans shall not exceed fivefold on cattle, wool, hair, fields, and vehicles. Property belonging to one who is neither an idiot nor a minor, if enjoyed by others for ten years while the owner is present, belongs to the possessor.
One should not [speak] with a learned Vedic scholar,
an ascetic, or royal officers. One should not excessively enjoy cattle, land, or women.
Those who inherit the estate shall discharge the debt. Surety-money, trade-duties, tolls, liquor, gambling debts, and fines shall not devolve upon the sons.

GDhS-A 2,3.39 / GDhS-St 12.42: A treasure-trove, a pledge, a borrowed item, a purchase, or a deposit that has been lost—all these are not to be blamed [on the owner], provided the loss was due to the fault of the person [in possession]. GDhS-A 2,3.40 / GDhS-St 12.43: A thief, with disheveled hair and carrying a pestle, shall go to the king confessing his deed.
He is purified by execution or release. The king who does not execute the offender becomes guilty of sin. There shall be no corporal punishment for a Brāhmaṇa.
Exclusion from ritual acts, public proclamation of the offense, banishment, and branding are the punishments.
If he does not engage in [the prescribed penance], he must perform an expiation (prāyaścitta).

A minister who acts intentionally is equal to a thief. (GDhS-A 2.3.46 / GDhS-St 12.49) The recipient [of a gift] is also [equal to a thief] if the gift is joined with unrighteousness. (GDhS-A 2.3.47 / GDhS-St 12.50) The application of punishment depends on the knowledge of the person's capacity, the nature of the offense, and the circumstances. (GDhS-A 2.3.48 / GDhS-St 12.51)
Or rather, there is permission [to eat such food], because of the statement of an assembly of those learned in the Veda; because of the statement of an assembly of those learned in the Veda.
[GDhS-A 2,4 = GDhS-St XIII]
GDhS-A 2,4.1 / GDhS-St 13.1: In the event of a dispute, the determination of the truth is based on witnesses.
GDhS-A 2,4.2 / GDhS-St 13.2: There should be many witnesses who are blameless in their own duties, trustworthy to kings, and free from affection or enmity toward either party.

Even Śūdras [may be questioned]. However, a Brāhmaṇa, if he is not bound [by the court] and has not been summoned, shall not be detained for giving testimony at the word of a non-Brāhmaṇa. Those who are not assembled [in court] and have not been questioned shall not speak [as witnesses].
If they fail to speak or speak otherwise than the truth, they shall be at fault. (GDhS-A 2.4.6 / GDhS-St 13.6)
Heaven results from speaking the truth; in the opposite case, hell.
Even those who are not bound [by a formal oath] must speak [the truth].
There is no binding [oath] for the sake of causing pain.
And [there is guilt] in the case of what is spoken by one who is negligent.
There is guilt for the witnesses, the members of the court, and the king when there is an injury to the administration of justice.

GDhS-A 2,4.12 / GDhS-St 13.12: Some say that the act of truth is accomplished by means of an oath. GDhS-A 2,4.13 / GDhS-St 13.13: That [oath] should take place in the assembly of gods, kings, or Brahmins, but for those who are not Brahmins.
GDhS-A 2,4.14 / GDhS-St 13.14: A witness who speaks falsely regarding small cattle destroys ten.
For [stealing] a cow, a horse, a human being, or land, the fines increase tenfold respectively; or, in the case of land, the fine is the entire property.
GDhS-A 2,4.17 / GDhS-St 13.17: In the case of stealing, there is hell.
GDhS-A 2,4.18 / GDhS-St 13.18: [The same applies] to water as to land.
GDhS-A 2,4.19 / GDhS-St 13.19: And the same applies to sexual intercourse.
Regarding honey and clarified butter, [the rule] is like that for animals (GDhS-A 2,4.20 / GDhS-St 13.20).
Regarding clothing, gold, grain, and the Veda, [the rule] is like that for cows (GDhS-A 2,4.21 / GDhS-St 13.21).
Regarding vehicles, [the rule] is like that for horses (GDhS-A 2,4.22 / GDhS-St 13.22).
GDhS-A 2,4.23 / GDhS-St 13.23: A witness who speaks falsely should be censured and punished.
GDhS-A 2,4.24 / GDhS-St 13.24: There is no fault in speaking untruth if one's livelihood depends upon it.
GDhS-A 2,4.25 / GDhS-St 13.25: But not if it is for the sake of a livelihood from one who is more wicked.
The king, or a judge, or a Brāhmaṇa learned in the scriptures [shall preside]. He shall approach the judge. If there is no immediate perception [of the truth], he shall wait for one year.
In the case of a cow, a bull, or a woman engaged in procreation, one must act with haste.
And likewise in cases of emergency.
For a judge, speaking the truth is more important than all other duties; speaking the truth is [the highest duty].
Impurity on account of a death (śāva-āśauca) lasts for ten nights for the sapinda relatives, except for those who are officiating priests, those initiated for a sacrifice, and students.
For a Kṣatriya, it is eleven nights;
for a Vaiśya, twelve nights;
some say half a month.

For a Śūdra, it is one month. (GDhS-A 2,5.5 / GDhS-St 14.6) If another [impurity] should occur within that period, they shall be purified by the remainder of the first period. (GDhS-A 2,5.6 / GDhS-St 14.7) If it occurs when only one night remains, purification is achieved through two nights.

At dawn, [one should recite] with three [verses]. For those killed by cattle or Brahmins, [the recitation should be done] immediately after the event. And also for those killed through the wrath of a king.
In battle;
[and] for those who desire [death] by means of fasting, starvation, weapons, fire, poison, water, hanging, or falling [from a precipice],
there is a cessation of the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) in the seventh or the fifth generation.
The same applies at birth. That [impurity] belongs to the mother and the father; or it belongs to the mother alone.
In the case of a miscarriage, the period of impurity lasts for as many nights as there were months of pregnancy;
or it may last for three days.
Furthermore, if one hears of the birth after the tenth day has passed, the impurity lasts for a "bird-day" (two days with the intervening night).
[One day of impurity] for a kinsman by birth who is not a *sapiṇḍa*, and for a fellow student;
(GDhS-A 2,5.19 / GDhS-St 14.21) [one day] for a fellow celibate student (*sabrahmacārin*);
(GDhS-A 2,5.20 / GDhS-St 14.22) and likewise for a *śrotriya* who has arrived [at one's house].
GDhS-A 2,5.21 / GDhS-St 14.23: Upon touching a corpse, if it was done intentionally, the period of impurity lasts ten nights.

GDhS-A 2,5.22 / GDhS-St 14.24: The [periods of impurity] for Vaiśyas and Śūdras have already been stated. GDhS-A 2,5.23 / GDhS-St 14.25: Or [the impurity lasts] as long as the flow of menses continues.
And for the two preceding [cases], [the same applies].
Or [one may observe] three days.
And the same [rule applies] toward the teacher, his son, a woman, a sacrificer, and a pupil.
If a person of a lower caste should touch one of a higher caste, or if one of a higher caste should touch one of a lower caste, the period of impurity in that case is as prescribed for a corpse.

One becomes pure by bathing with one's clothes on after touching an outcaste (patita), a Caṇḍāla, a woman who has recently given birth (sūtikā), a menstruating woman (udakyā), a corpse, or anyone who has touched them, or by touching those who have touched such persons.
And [impurity is incurred] by following a corpse;
likewise, [by following] a dog.
Some say that one should [offer food] whenever [the child] dies.
Water-offerings for one whose tonsure has been performed should be made by the sapindas.
{VAR_St: for one whose hair-lock has been formed}
And [the same applies] to their wives (GDhS-A 2,5.33 / GDhS-St 14.35).
According to some, [this applies only] to those who have been given away in marriage (GDhS-A 2,5.34 / GDhS-St 14.36).
All [of them] must sleep on the ground, sit on the ground, and remain celibate (GDhS-A 2,5.35 / GDhS-St 14.37).
They shall not perform purification rites. They shall not eat meat until the formal offering has been made. The water-libation ceremony is performed on the first, third, seventh, and ninth days.
And there is the discarding of garments;
however, for those of the lowest castes, this occurs at the end.
The impurity resulting from the birth of teeth and so forth belongs to both the mother and the father.
For infants, for those residing in a foreign land, for renunciants, and for non-sapiṇḍas, purification occurs immediately.
And [one may go] for kings because of the obstruction of their duties;
and for a Brāhmaṇa, for the sake of not interrupting his private Vedic study.
Now follows the Śrāddha rite.
On the new moon day, one should offer [the śrāddha] to the ancestors;
or on the days beginning with the fifth of the waning fortnight.

GDhS-A 2,6.4 / GDhS-St 15.4: Or [he may give] everything according to his faith. GDhS-A 2,6.5 / GDhS-St 15.5: Or, when the substance, the place, and the Brāhmaṇas are present, there is no restriction regarding the time.
{VAR_St: vākālaniyamaḥ}
One should enhance the excellence of the food through the application of qualities and purificatory rites according to one's ability.
One should feed an odd number of guests, at least nine.
Or according to one's ability.
Or [he should invite] those learned in the Vedas who are endowed with eloquence, beauty, age, and good character.
Giving to the young is the first preference.
Some say [the son] should act like a father.
And he should not perform the duties of a friend for him. In the absence of a son, the *sapiṇḍas*, the mother’s *sapiṇḍas*, and the pupils shall offer [the funeral cakes].

GDhS-A 2,6.14a | GDhS-St 15.14: In their absence, the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) and the teacher (*ācārya*). GDhS-St 15.15: By offerings of sesame, beans, rice, barley, and water, the ancestors are satisfied for one month; by the flesh of fish, deer, *ruru* antelope, rabbit, tortoise, boar, and sheep, for years; by cow’s milk, milk, and milk-rice (*pāyasa*), for twelve years; and by the flesh of the *vārdhrīṇasa* (an old bull), the *kālaśāka* vegetable, goat, red goat, and rhinoceros, mixed with honey, they are satisfied eternally.

One should not feed a thief, a eunuch, an outcast, an atheist, one who lives like an atheist, a slayer of a hero, the husband of a younger sister whose elder sister is unmarried, one who officiates at sacrifices for women, a village priest, a shepherd, one who has abandoned the sacred fires, a drunkard, a rogue, a false witness, a juggler, and a paramour. (GDhS 2.6.15–16) / A paramour [is also forbidden]. (GDhS 2.6.17a)
And [the son belongs] to him to whom he belongs.

(GDhS-A 2,6.17 / GDhS-St 15.17b) One should avoid those who eat from a *kuṇḍa* (an illegitimate vessel), those who sell *soma*, arsonists, poisoners, those who have violated their vow of chastity (*avakīrṇin*), those employed by a group (*gaṇa*), those who approach forbidden women, those who are harmful, the elder brother whose younger brother marries first (*parivitti*), the younger brother who marries before his elder (*parivettṛ*), the one for whom the *agnihotra* is maintained by another (*paryāhita*), the one who maintains the fire for another (*paryādhātṛ*), those who have abandoned themselves, those with deformed nails, those with black teeth, those with white leprosy, those born of a remarried woman (*paunarbhava*), gamblers, those defeated in a wager, servants, counterfeiters, the husband of a *śūdra* woman, those who have renounced their caste duties (*nirākṛti*), those suffering from consumption (*kilāsin*), usurers, merchants, those who live by manual crafts, and those habitually addicted to gambling, instrumental music, clapping, dancing, and singing. (GDhS-A 2,6.18 / GDhS-St 15.18)
Those who have been divided from their father against his will. (GDhS-A 2.6.19 / GDhS-St 15.19) [Variant:
*cākāmena*]
Some [teachers] say that one may feed pupils and those of the same lineage (sagotra).
One should feed more than three [such persons],
provided they possess virtuous qualities.
One who performs a *śrāddha* on the same day as having sexual intercourse with a *śūdra* woman causes his ancestors to dwell for a month in her excrement.
Therefore,
he should remain celibate on that day.
Food seen by a dog, a *caṇḍāla*, or an outcast becomes defiled. Therefore, one should give it in an enclosed place.
Or he may scatter sesame seeds;
or one who purifies the company at a meal (paṅktipāvana) may pacify it.

One who purifies the company at a meal is: one who knows the six auxiliary sciences (ṣaḍaṅga), one who chants the Jyeṣṭhasāmans, one who has performed the three Nāciketa fires, one who knows the three Madhu sections, one who knows the Trisuparṇa, one who maintains the five sacred fires, a graduate (snātaka), one who knows the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas, one who knows the Dharma, and one who is descended from a lineage where the gift of a daughter in marriage was made to a worthy suitor.
The same applies to the *havir* offerings.
At a *śrāddha*, one should feed each of those beginning with the weak (*durbāla*).
And likewise in the case of a *śrāddha* where food has not been prepared; [some say] only in a *śrāddha*, others [say] in both cases.
Having performed the *upākaraṇa* ceremony at the beginning of the month of Śrāvaṇa, or on the full moon day of Proṣṭhapada, one should study the Vedic hymns (*chandas*) during the rainy season.
For four and a half months, or for five months during the southern course of the sun;
as a religious student with his hair unshorn, he shall not eat meat;
or this rule may last for two months.
One should not study when the wind carries dust during the day; nor at night when it is audible to the ear;
nor when there is the sound of a lute, a kettledrum, a clay drum, or a cry of distress.
[One should stop reciting] when there is the simultaneous howling of dogs, jackals,
and donkeys; and when there is a red rainbow, Indra’s bow, or mist.
And when clouds appear outside the rainy season;
when one has urinated or evacuated;
at night; and in the waters of the twilight prayers.
And while it is raining;
according to some, [he may study] when there is a continuous stream of raindrops.
[One should not study] while serving the teacher (GDhS-A 2,7.15 / GDhS-St 16.15);
nor during the appearance of celestial lights (GDhS-A 2,7.16 / GDhS-St 16.16);
nor when frightened, while standing in a vehicle, while lying down, or with feet raised (GDhS-A 2,7.17 / GDhS-St 16.17).

[One becomes impure] in the vicinity of a cremation ground, the edge of a village, a great road, or during a period of ritual impurity (GDhS-A 2,7.18); in the presence of a foul odor, a corpse inside [the house], one whose name should not be proclaimed during the day, a Cāṇḍāla, or a Śūdra (GDhS-A 2,7.19);
and when there is eructation after having eaten (GDhS-A 2,7.20).
As long as the sound of the *Ṛgveda*, the *Yajurveda*, or the *Sāmaveda* is heard [the impurity lasts].
A thunderclap, an earthquake, an eclipse by Rāhu, and a meteor are causes for immediate purification (*ākālika*).
So too are thunder, rain, and lightning, provided that the sacred fires have been kindled.
During the rainy season, [one should study] by day; during the other seasons, by night. When there is lightning, one should not study until the latter part of the night has passed.
GDhS-A 2,7.26 / GDhS-St 16.26: When [the rains] have begun for one-third [of the season] or more, [the suspension of study lasts] for the whole [period].
GDhS-A 2,7.27 / GDhS-St 16.27: According to some, [study is suspended] when a meteor and lightning appear together.
GDhS-A 2,7.28 / GDhS-St 16.28: [Study is suspended] during the afternoon thunder.
Even at nightfall;
(29) the entire night until midnight; (30) and during the day as long as there is still light. (31)

And when the king residing in one's territory has died; (2,7.32) and when one has returned from a journey together with another [relative]; (2,7.33) and for a day and a night after a crowded occasion, after a fire has been kindled, upon the completion of a Veda-recitation, after vomiting, at a Śrāddha, and after eating at a human sacrifice (Manuṣyayajña). (2,7.34)
And on the new moon day;
or for two days;
[the full moon days of] Kārttikī, Phālgunī, and Āṣāḍhī.
There are three Aṣṭakās, each lasting for three nights. Some [hold that] it is only the last one. Or rather, [the observance lasts] on both sides of the Vārṣika [Aṣṭakā].
GDhS-A 2,7.41 / GDhS-St 16.41: [The suspension of study lasts] for all [three] when there is a conjunction of rain, lightning, and thunder. GDhS-A 2,7.42 / GDhS-St 16.42: [Also when it is] raining.
After a meal during a festival;
for one who has studied [the Veda], for four muhūrtas at night;
some say this is constant in a city.

Even mental [impurity] occurs when one is impure. (GDhS-A 2.7.46 / GDhS-St 16.46) For those who have performed a *śrāddha*, [the impurity lasts] until the same time [the next day]. (GDhS-A 2.7.47 / GDhS-St 16.47) This applies even when there is contact with one who has not yet performed a *śrāddha* involving cooked food. (GDhS-A 2.7.48 / GDhS-St 16.48)
And those [rules] which they prescribe for each specific branch of knowledge.
GDhS-A 2.8.1 / GDhS-St 17.1:
A Brāhmaṇa shall eat the food of twice-born men who are praised for their own respective duties.
And he may accept [these things].

Fuel, water, fodder, roots, fruits, honey, [an offer of] protection from fear, a bed, a seat, a dwelling, a vehicle, milk, curd, a jar, a *śapharī* fish, *priyaṅgu* grain, a garland, a path, and vegetables are not to be refused by anyone.
Even when supporting one's ancestors, gods, teachers, or dependents, other things may be accepted.

And if there is no other means of livelihood [except] from a Śūdra: (GDhS-A 2.8.5 / GDhS-St 17.5). Those who tend cattle, those who till fields, those who act as family associates, and those who serve as attendants—[their food] may be eaten. (GDhS-A 2.8.6 / GDhS-St 17.6).

And a merchant who is not an artisan [is always unfit]. (GDhS-A 2.8.7 / GDhS-St 17.7) [Food] is always unfit to be eaten [if it comes from such a person]. (GDhS-A 2.8.8 / GDhS-St 17.8) [Food] into which hair or insects have fallen [is unfit to be eaten]. (GDhS-A 2.8.9 / GDhS-St 17.9)
That which has been defiled by the foot of a menstruating woman or by a black bird;
that which has been looked upon by a killer of an embryo (bhrūṇahan).
[GDhS-St 17.12; see GDhS-A 2.8.13] GDhS-A 2.8.12 / GDhS-St 17.13:
That which is defiled by its state of being.
GDhS-A 2.8.13 / GDhS-St 17.12: That which has been smelled by a cow.
GDhS-A 2,8.14 / GDhS-St 17.14: Sour gruel that is not mixed with curd.
GDhS-A 2,8.15 / GDhS-St 17.15: That which has been cooked again.
GDhS-A 2,8.16 / GDhS-St 17.16: Stale food, except for vegetables, condiments, oils, meat, and honey.

[One should avoid the food] of those who have abandoned their vows, of unchaste women, of those accused of crimes, of those of unknown origin, of staff-bearers (officials), of carpenters, of misers, of jailers, of physicians, of hunters, of those who live by arrows, of those who eat the leavings of others, and of those who hate social groups.
[This applies] to those unworthy of the company at a meal, starting from Durvāsas.
[Food] defiled by being left over, by the sipping of water, or by rising [from one's seat] is unfit for consumption.
Regarding those of equal or unequal status, [the guest] should behave with equanimity or inequality based on the degree of honor shown.
And [the milk] of one who has not been honored.
And the milk of a cow within ten days of calving during the period of birth-impurity. And [the milk] of goats and buffaloes.
GDhS-A 2,8.24 / GDhS-St 17.24: The milk of sheep, camels, and one-hoofed animals is always unfit for drinking.
GDhS-A 2,8.25 / GDhS-St 17.25: And [the milk] of a cow that is flowing excessively, of one that miscarries, and of one in heat.
GDhS-A 2,8.26 / GDhS-St 17.26: And [the milk] of a cow whose calf has died.
And five-toed animals, except for the porcupine, the hare, the śvāvidh, the iguana, the rhinoceros, and the tortoise;
(2,8.27) those with teeth in both jaws, those with forelocks, those without body hair, those with uncloven hooves, the kalaviṅka, the plava, the cakravāka, and the haṃsa;
(2,8.28) the crow, the kaṅka, the vulture, the hawk, water-birds, those with red feet or red beaks, and the domestic cock and pig. (2,8.29)
And [the meat of] a milch-cow and a bull;
and [the meat of] animals whose teeth have not yet fallen out, those that have perished, and meat not intended for sacrifice.
Sprouts,
garlic, onions, and exudations [are forbidden], as are *kimpāku* fruits.
Red birds that tear at wood are not to be eaten.
Woodpeckers,
cranes, herons, madgus, tiṭṭibhas, māndhālas, and nocturnal prowlers are not to be eaten.
Those that peck with their beaks, those that scratch with their claws, and web-footed birds are edible, with the exception of the *balāka*, the parrot, the *māndhālā*, and nocturnal creatures.
Fish that are not prepared [with spices] may be eaten. Those that must be killed for the sake of dharma may also be eaten.
One should consume fish killed by predators, or those whose defects have not been seen, after sprinkling them with water, provided they are approved by word. One should consume them.
[Those that are] not praised...
[GDhS-A 2,9 = GDhS-St XVIII]
In matters of dharma, a woman is not independent.
She must not transgress against her husband. She should be restrained in speech, sight, and action.
A man without a wife who desires offspring may take a brother’s widow. Once authorized by her husband, she shall not let the fertile season pass.
She may obtain offspring from those related through funeral offerings (*piṇḍa*), *gotra*, or *ṛṣi*, or even from one related solely through the womb.
GDhS-A 2,9.7 / GDhS-St 18.7: Some say [the son belongs] not to the husband, but to the progenitor.
GDhS-A 2,9.8 / GDhS-St 18.8: Not a second [marriage] beyond that [is permitted].
GDhS-A 2,9.9 / GDhS-St 18.9: The offspring belongs to the progenitor.
GDhS-A 2,9.10 / GDhS-St 18.10: According to agreement, [the ownership] belongs to the other.
GDhS-A 2,9.11 / GDhS-St 18.11: And while he is alive, [the ownership] remains with the owner of the field.
GDhS-A 2,9.12 / GDhS-St 18.12: From another [man], it belongs to him.
GDhS-A 2,9.13 / GDhS-St 18.13: Or from two [men].
GDhS-A 2,9.14 / GDhS-St 18.14: But because of protection, it belongs to the husband alone.
If he is heard from, she must go to him;
{if the husband is lost, there is a six-year period of fasting while he is heard from}.
But if he has gone forth as a wandering ascetic, there is a cessation of the marriage due to the impossibility of union.

GDhS-A 2,9.17 / GDhS-St 18.17: For a Brāhmaṇa, [the period of waiting] in connection with [receiving] knowledge is twelve years. GDhS-A 2,9.18 / GDhS-St 18.18: And likewise for a younger brother toward an elder brother regarding marriage or the taking of the sacred fires. GDhS-A 2,9.19 / GDhS-St 18.19: Some say it is six years.

After three menstrual periods have passed, a maiden may unite herself with one who is blameless, having discarded her paternal ornaments. The giving [of the bride] takes place before the first period.
GDhS-A 2,9.22 / GDhS-St 18.22: He who does not give [the gift] is at fault.
GDhS-A 2,9.23 / GDhS-St 18.23: Some say [he is at fault] prior to the handing over of the garment.
{VAR_St: vāsaḥ}
GDhS-A 2,9.24 / GDhS-St 18.24: One may take property from a Śūdra for the purpose of accomplishing a marriage or for the sake of maintaining religious duties.
GDhS-A 2,9.25 / GDhS-St 18.25: Even in other cases, one may take from a Śūdra who possesses many cattle but is deficient in performing his duties.
GDhS-A 2,9.26 / GDhS-St 18.26: [One may take] from a Śūdra who owns a hundred cows but has not maintained the sacred fires.
And [one should not eat] from one who possesses a thousand cows but does not drink Soma (GDhS-A 2,9.27). And [one should not eat] until the seventh meal without having accumulated [food for guests],
even if they are those whose rites have not been neglected (GDhS-A 2,9.28–29).
If questioned by the king, he shall declare [the truth]. For the king must support him if he is endowed with learning and good character.
If there is an obstruction to the administration of dharma, there is guilt in failing to report it.
The fault of non-performance; the fault is indeed a fault.
GDhS-A 3.1.1 / GDhS-St 19.1: The duties of the social classes (*varṇadharma*) and the duties of the stages of life (*āśramadharma*) have been declared.

GDhS-A 3.1.2 / GDhS-St 19.2: Now, indeed, this person becomes tainted by blameworthy action (*yāpya-karman*), such as: officiating at sacrifices for those for whom one should not officiate, eating what should not be eaten, speaking what should not be spoken, failing to perform prescribed duties, and indulging in forbidden acts.
Regarding this, they deliberate: "Should one perform an expiation, or should one not? They say: "One should not perform it," for "an action is never exhausted."
"One should perform [the rite]"—this is another view.
It is known from tradition: "Having sacrificed with the *punaḥstoma*, they return to the *savana*.
And: "Having sacrificed with the *vrātyastomas*..."
"He who performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice overcomes all evil, he overcomes even the murder of a Brahmin" (GDhS-A 3.1.9 / GDhS-St 19.9).
And: "One should cause him who is being falsely accused to perform the Agniṣṭut sacrifice" (GDhS-A 3.1.10 / GDhS-St 19.10).
GDhS-A 3.1.11 / GDhS-St 19.11: The means of expiation for that [sin] are recitation (*japa*), austerity (*tapas*), burnt offerings (*homa*), fasting (*upavāsa*), and giving gifts (*dāna*).

GDhS-A 3.1.12 / GDhS-St 19.12: The *Upaniṣads*, the *Vedānta*, the *Saṃhitās* among all the Vedic meters, the *Madhu* hymns, the *Aghamarṣaṇa*, the *Atharvaśiras*, the *Rudras*, the *Puruṣasūkta*, the *Rājana* and *Raivata* Sāmans, the *Bṛhat* and *Rathantara*, the *Puruṣagati*, the *Mahānāmnīs*, the *Mahāvairāja*, the *Mahādivākīrtya*, any one of the *Jyeṣṭhasāmans*, the *Bahiṣpavamāna*, the *Kūṣmāṇḍas*, the *Pāvamānīs*, and the *Sāvitrī*—these are the *Pāvamānī* (purificatory) texts.
GDhS-A 3.1.13 / GDhS-St 19.13: A milk-vow, eating vegetables, eating fruits, [eating] a handful of barley-gruel, consuming gold, consuming clarified butter, and drinking soma—these are purifying.
{VAR_St: prasṛtiyāvako}
GDhS-A 3.1.14 / GDhS-St 19.14: All mountains, all rivers, sacred lakes, holy fords, dwellings of sages, cow-pens, and sacred enclosures are [sacred] places.
GDhS-A 3.1.15 / GDhS-St 19.15: Celibacy, speaking the truth, touching water at the [three] libations, wearing wet clothes, sleeping on the ground, and fasting are forms of austerity.
Gold, a cow, a garment, a horse, land, sesame seeds, clarified butter, and food—these are the things to be given.
A year, six months, four, three, two, or one [month]; twenty-four days, twelve days, six days, three days, or a day and night—these are the durations of time.
{VAR_St: three, two, or one} GDhS-A 3.1.18 / GDhS-St 19.18:
These very [penances] shall be performed optionally when no specific instruction is given.
GDhS-A 3.1.19 / GDhS-St 19.19: For heavy sins, the penances are heavy; for light sins, they are light.
The Kṛcchra, the Atikṛcchra, and the Cāndrāyaṇa constitute the universal expiation (sarvaprāyaścitta).

GDhS-A 3,2.1 / GDhS-St 20.1: One should abandon a father who is a regicide, a priest for Śūdras, one who sacrifices for the sake of a Śūdra, a corrupter of the Vedas, a killer of an embryo, or one who dwells with outcastes (antyāvasāyin) or with a woman of the lowest caste.

Having assembled his teachers of sacred knowledge and his blood relations, they shall perform all the funeral rites for him, beginning with the water libations (GDhS-A 3,2.2). They shall also overturn his water-vessel (GDhS-A 3,2.3).

A slave or a laborer, having brought a vessel for impure substances from a refuse heap and having filled it from the water-jar of a female slave, shall turn toward the south and overturn it while pronouncing the name [of the deceased], saying: "I make so-and-so waterless. (GDhS-A 3.2.4 / GDhS-St 20.4) Everyone, wearing their sacred threads over the right shoulder and with their topknots loosened, shall touch that [vessel]. (GDhS-A 3.2.5 / GDhS-St 20.5)
3.2.6 / 20.6: Those who are teachers of knowledge and those related by birth should look upon [the student].
3.2.7 / 20.7: Having touched water, they enter the village.
3.2.8 / 20.8: From this point forward, having conversed with him, he should remain for one night reciting the Sāvitrī, if [the conversation] was preceded by ignorance.
And if it was done intentionally,
the impurity lasts for three nights.
But he who is purified by a penance—once he is purified, they should fill a vessel made of gold from a most holy pool or from flowing rivers and have him touch those waters.

Then they should give that vessel to him; having accepted it, he should recite: "Peaceful is the sky, peaceful is the earth, peaceful and auspicious is the intermediate space; I take that which is the radiant light."
GDhS-A 3,2.12a | GDhS-St 20.12: With these *yajus* verses, the *pāvamānī* verses, the *taratsamandī* verses, and the *kūṣmāṇḍa* verses, one should offer clarified butter into the fire.
GDhS-A 3,2.12b | GDhS-St 20.13a: One should give gold to a Brāhmaṇa. GDhS-A 3,2.13 / GDhS-St 20.13b: Or a cow.
And [the same applies] to the teacher (ācārya).
But he for whom the penance ends with death shall become pure upon dying.
In his case, they should perform all the funeral rites, beginning with the water libation.
This very same rite of peace-water (śāntyudaka) applies to all minor offenses (upapātaka).
GDhS-A 3,3.1 / GDhS-St 21.1:

An outcaste (patita) is one who has killed a Brahmin, drunk liquor, violated the bed of his Guru, or has committed an offense against his mother, father, or those related by birth; a thief; an atheist; one who habitually performs censurable acts; one who abandons those who are not outcastes; and one who is abandoned by those who are not outcastes.

And those who associate with such as these— namely, a killer of a Brahmin, a drinker of spirituous liquor, and one who has broken the bonds of kinship— as well as those who associate with them, shall undergo this for one year.
GDhS-A 3,3.4 / GDhS-St 21.4: Falling away from the duties of the twice-born is degradation (patana).
GDhS-A 3,3.5 / GDhS-St 21.5: Likewise, there is failure to attain [the higher worlds] hereafter.
Some [teachers] say that this is hell.
Regarding the three first [offenses],
Manu says they are not to be specified.
GDhS-A 3,3.8 / GDhS-St 21.8: Some say that a woman does not fall [from her caste] by having intercourse with one who is not a Guru’s bed (*agurutalpa*).
GDhS-A 3,3.9 / GDhS-St 21.9: A woman falls [from her caste] by killing an embryo (*bhrūṇahanī*) and by serving a man of a lower caste.
Giving false testimony,
malicious talebearing that reaches the king, and making a false accusation against one's teacher are equal to mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*).

GDhS-A 3,3.11 / GDhS-St 21.11: Among those unworthy of the company at meals (*apāṅktya*), up to the "one with weak eyes" (*durbāla*), the killing of a cow, the killing of a Brāhmaṇa, performing [the sacrifice] for that [purpose], and being an *avakīrṇin* (one who has broken his vow of celibacy) or one whose *sāvitrī* has lapsed—these constitute minor offenses (*upapātaka*).

GDhS-A 3,3.12 / GDhS-St 21.12: If one teaches [the Veda] out of ignorance, or if one serves an officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) or a teacher (*ācārya*) who has committed a cause for loss of caste (*patanīya*), they are to be abandoned.
GDhS-A 3.3.13 / GDhS-St 21.13: Except for the case of relinquishing [the gift], he falls [from his caste].
GDhS-A 3.3.14 / GDhS-St 21.14: And some say that the one who accepts it also falls.
GDhS-A 3,3.15 / GDhS-St 21.15: There is never a lack of maintenance for one's mother and father. GDhS-A 3,3.16 / GDhS-St 21.16: But they shall not share in the inheritance.
GDhS-A 3,3.17 / GDhS-St 21.17: The guilt is as great as that incurred by falsely accusing a Brāhmaṇa.
Twice [the penance is performed] for one who is innocent.
And [it is performed twice] for one capable of rescuing [a person] from harm by a weak person, if he does not do so.
Threatening a Brahmin while in a state of anger results in the loss of heaven for a hundred years;
in the case of striking him, the loss is for a thousand years.
Upon seeing blood, he should plunge into it as far as necessary and collect dust from that spot.
[GDhS-A 3,4 = GDhS-St XXII] GDhS-A 3,4.1 / GDhS-St 22.1:
Expiation. GDhS-A 3,4.2 / GDhS-St 22.2:
The killer of a Brahmin shall cast himself three times into the fire while his body is still dripping with blood.
Or he may become a target for those bearing weapons in battle.
Or, carrying a skull-topped staff and a begging bowl in his hand, he shall enter a village for alms for twelve years as a celibate student (*brahmacārī*), proclaiming his deed.
He must step aside from the path upon seeing an Ārya.

GDhS-A 3,4.6 / GDhS-St 22.6: By alternating between standing and sitting and touching water at the [three] libations, he becomes pure. GDhS-A 3,4.7 / GDhS-St 22.7: Or, if he recovers his life-breath for the sake of that [purpose], he is purified for a Brāhmaṇa. GDhS-A 3,4.8 / GDhS-St 22.8: When his wealth has diminished, he is purified after having performed at least three sacrifices.
Or at the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of an Aśvamedha sacrifice;

If a worm should arise from the occurrence of pus and blood at the opening of a wound on a Brāhmaṇa’s body,
what expiation (prāyaścitta) should there be?
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with *kuśa* grass—
one who has been bitten by a worm becomes pure by bathing and drinking these for three days.
One who has been defiled by a dog should immerse himself in water along with his clothes.
Or, having washed that spot, touched it with fire, washed it again, and having washed his feet and sipped water, he becomes pure.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"A Brahmin who has been bitten by a dog, having gone to a river that flows to the ocean,
becomes pure after performing one hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) and consuming clarified butter."
"Or by bathing with water from the horns of cows mixed with gold and silver, or with nine new jars [of water], one becomes pure immediately. Thus it is said.
Domestic animals are not to be eaten.
And carnivorous birds [are forbidden].
Likewise, [the meat of] a cock and a pig.
Except for goats and sheep.
The porcupine, the iguana, the hare, the hedgehog, the tortoise, and the rhinoceros—these five five-toed animals are edible, with the exception of the rhinoceros.
Likewise, the five cloven-hoofed animals—the ṛśya, hariṇa, pṛṣata, mahiṣa, and varāha—are permitted, with the exception of the kuluṅga.
Among birds, five types of scratchers (viṣkira) are permitted—the partridge, the pigeon, the grey partridge, the vārdhrāṇasa crane, and the peacock—excluding the vāraṇa and the avāraṇa.
The fish are the Sahasradaṃṣṭra, Cilicima, Varmi, Bṛhacchiras, Maśaka, Rohita, and Rājīva.
The milk of a cow that has not passed ten days since calving, nor of one in heat, is unfit for drinking.
And [the same applies] in the case of two cows, one whose calf has died and one whose calf is living.
Woolen cloth, camel’s milk, and the milk of one-hoofed animals are not to be drunk.
For drinking water that is unfit to be drunk, one must perform the Kṛcchra penance, except in the case of cow's milk.
In the case of cow-products, however, there shall be a fast for three nights.
This excludes stale vegetables, vegetable broth, meat, clarified butter, parched grain boiled in milk, molasses, curd, honey, and flour-meal.
Likewise, fermented liquids and molasses that have not yet solidified [are forbidden].

Having performed the opening ceremony (*upākaraṇa*) on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa or Āṣāḍha, they should perform the concluding ceremony (*utsarga*) on the full moon day of Taiṣya or Māgha. They should perform the concluding ceremony.
The gods delight in a pure sacrifice.
For the gods desire purity and are themselves pure.
Regarding this, he recites:

"O Maruts, pure is the oblation for you who are pure; I present the pure sacrifice to the pure ones. By the *ṛta*, those who observe the *ṛta* have come—the pure-born, the pure, the purifiers. (RV 7.56.12)
Among garments, that which is unwashed is pure.
Therefore, whatever is connected with a sacrifice, all of that one should perform using unwashed garments.
The wife, the sacrificer, and the officiating priests shall put on garments that have been washed, aired, and unworn.
Thus [the procedure applies] from the commencement onwards.
The same applies to long Soma sacrifices and sacrificial sessions (sattras).
And according to the traditional recitation.

Just as in the case of the *iṣṭis*, animal sacrifices, and *soma* rites performed for malevolent purposes (*abhicāra*), the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) should proceed wearing red turbans and red garments; and [the rule applies] to the *citravāsas* and *citrāsaṅga* rites, as well as the *ṛṣabha* and *kapāla* rites.
At the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādhāna), the garments should be made of linen; in their absence, they may be made of cotton or wool.
For those [objects] defiled by urine, feces, blood, semen, and so forth, purification is by means of earth and water through washing.
The rules regarding linen, silk, and bark garments are the same as those for clothing.
The rules regarding black antelope skins are the same as those for bark garments.
One should not wear a garment that has been put on over another, nor one that has been stepped upon, nor an upper garment that has not been washed.
One should not employ for the gods water that has been stirred up or that has been used by humans.
In the case of solid ground, the purification consists of smearing it with cow-dung.
The plowing of a porous field.
Having taken pure material from a moist [place], it serves as a covering.
The earth is purified by four means: by the treading upon it by cows, by digging, by burning, and by being rained upon.
And from the fifth smearing and the sixth time-period.
Grass placed on unprepared ground is purified by washing.
For items that have been defiled out of sight, sprinkling with water is required.
The same applies to small fuel-sticks.
In the case of contact with large pieces of wood, one should wash [the hands] and not dry them.
But for many [objects], sprinkling is prescribed.
For wooden vessels that have come into contact with food remnants, the purification is by scraping.
For those things defiled by contact with food-leavings or scrapings, there shall be scraping off.
The discarding of [food] defiled by urine, feces, blood, semen, and so forth, shall take place.
This is so except where there is a specific injunction to the contrary.

BDhS 1.6.13.30: Just as in these cases—the Agnihotra, the remnant of the *gharma*, the *dadhigharma*, the *kuṇḍapāyinya* sacrifice, the *utsarginām ayana*, the *dākṣāyaṇayajña*, the *caiḍādadha*, the *catuścakra*, and the *brahmaudanās*—in all of these, there is cleansing with water using *darbha* grass. BDhS 1.6.13.31: In all instances of consuming *soma*, the cleansing is performed on the *mārjālīya* mound with water alone.
The discarding of [objects] defiled by urine, feces, blood, semen, and so forth, is prescribed.
Earthenware vessels that have come into contact with food remnants should be submerged in water.
Those [objects] defiled by contact with food-leavings or stains must be burned again.
The discarding of those [objects] defiled by urine, feces, blood, semen, and so forth, is prescribed.
For metallic vessels that have been scrubbed as previously described, the purification is by washing.
The materials for wiping are cow dung, earth, and ashes.
In the case of vessels defiled by urine, feces, blood, semen, and so forth, they must be remade.
Or else, one should remain immersed in cow urine for seven nights, or likewise in a great river.
The same applies to objects made of stone.
The cleaning of alābu, bilva, and vināḍa vessels is performed with cow hair.
For enclosures made of reeds, bamboo, *śara* grass, and *kuśa* grass, purification is by means of cow-dung and water; that is, they are to be washed.
If rice grains are defiled, they should be washed and dried.
But for many [items], there is sprinkling with water.
The discarding of the rice grains.
The same applies to prepared sacrificial oblations.

In the case of large objects defiled by dogs, crows, and the like, one should remove that portion [of the object] and the food from the person; then, with the anuvāka beginning "pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ," there is sprinkling [of water].
In the case of honey, water, and products of milk, there is no need for purification when they are transferred from one vessel to another vessel.
In this same manner, one should place oil and clarified butter into water touched by food-leavings and then use them.
If impure matter is placed in the fire, one should consign the fire into oneself, churn out a new fire, and perform the Pavamāneṣṭi sacrifice.

In cases of differences regarding purity, place, mantras, repetition, purpose, substances, preparation, and time, each preceding factor takes precedence over the following. Each preceding factor takes precedence.
The sacrificial ground is characterized by movement from left to right.
Likewise, there is liberation.
In rites for the ancestors, the order is reversed.
One should wash that which has been struck by a foot.
Having touched a limb, or having touched water from a vessel, he should touch water again.

The same applies to acts of cutting, splitting, digging, throwing away, and to rites dedicated to the ancestors (pitrya), the rākṣasas, the nairṛtas, the raudras, and those intended for malevolent magic (abhicāraṇīya).
One should not protect oneself with any part of the sacrifice accompanied by a mantra.
The internal components are the constituent parts of the sacrifice.
The officiating priests are outsiders.
The wife and the sacrificer are the two most closely related to the officiating priests.

From the limbs of the sacrifice comes the clarified butter; from the clarified butter, the sacrificial oblations; from the oblations, the animal victim; from the animal victim, Soma; and from Soma, the fires.
The officiating priests shall not turn back from the sacrificial ground according to their respective duties.
If he faces the east, he should turn around toward his right shoulder.
Facing west, he [should perform] the left [hand].
The space between the *cātvāla* and the *utkara* is the *tīrtha* of the sacrifice.
In the absence of a *catvāla* pit, the *āhavanīya* fire and the *utkara* heap [are established].
Then the performers—the sacrificer and his wife—should enter [the sacrificial hall].
When the [funeral rite] has not been completed.
And when the sacrifice has concluded, the movement [of the priests] takes place from the region of the *utkara* heap.
One should not place upon the fire a piece of wood or a fuel-stick that has not been sprinkled with water, nor one that has not been brought forward, nor one that is damp.
The Brahman and the sacrificer enter by the front of the Āhavanīya fire.
"Behind the Āhavanīya fire," say some.
To the south of the Āhavanīya fire is the station of the Brahman; behind that is the station of the sacrificer.
The northern buttock [of the altar] is to the north of the Hotṛ's [station].
The utkara is the [place] of the Āgnīdhra.
Behind the Gārhapatya fire is the place for the wife.
At each of those times, he spreads darbha grass at that very moment.
And for each individual, a vessel of water should be kept ready for the purpose of sipping (ācamana).
One who has undertaken the vow should be consecrated.
One should not speak of another's sin, nor become angry, nor weep; one should not look at urine or feces.
Having seen something impure, he mutters: "The mind is unbound, the eye is poor; the sun is the best of lights. O consecration, do not abandon me."
Now, if it rains upon him, he should recite: "O flowing waters, bestow strength; bestow vigor; bestow power; do not destroy my consecration, nor my ascetic heat.
The four castes are the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra.
Among them, according to the sequence of the castes, a Brāhmaṇa may have four wives.
Three for a Kṣatriya.
For a Vaiśya, there are two.
A single [sacrificial cord] for a Śūdra.
Among those [wives], sons born of women of the same caste or of the next lower caste are of the same caste as their fathers.
From women one degree or two degrees lower [than the father], [the sons] are Ambaṣṭhas, Ugras, and Niṣādas.
From women in the reverse order of castes are born the Āyogava, Māgadha, Vaiṇa, Kṣattṛ, Pulkasa, Kukkuṭa, Vaidehaka, and Caṇḍāla.
From an Ambaṣṭha man and a woman of the first caste is born a Śvapāka.
From an Ugra, on the second day, a Vaiṇa is born.
From a Niṣāda and a woman of the third caste, a Pulkasa is born.
In the case of the opposite, it is a cock.
A son born of a Niṣāda father and a Niṣāda mother by one up to the fifth generation removes the status of a Śūdra.
One should initiate him; one should cause him to sacrifice in his sixth year.

The seventh is one whose seed is unaltered; these names—*samabīja* (of equal seed) and *sama* (equal)—fall in sequence upon them. One should initiate that sixth [son], and one should cause him to sacrifice; thus the seventh becomes unaltered. Those whom a man, not observing his vows, begets through similarity among the three castes—the wise call those fallen from the *sāvitrī* "vratyas."
The wise call these *vrātyas*.
The Rathakāra, Ambaṣṭha, Sūta, Ugra, Māgadha, Āyogava, Vaiṇa, Kṣattṛ, Pulkasa, Kukkuṭa, Vaidehaka, Caṇḍāla, Śvapāka, and others [are such].
Among them, those born from women of the same caste as their fathers are of the same caste.
From a Brāhmaṇa father and a Kṣatriya mother is born a Brāhmaṇa; from a Vaiśya mother, an Ambaṣṭha; and from a Śūdra mother, a Niṣāda.
"Some say he is a *pāraśava*."
From a Kṣatriya on a Vaiśya woman is born a Kṣatriya; on a Śūdra woman, an Ugra.
From a Vaiśya and a Śūdra woman is born a Rathakāra.
From a Śūdra, on a Vaiśya woman, a Māgadha is born; on a Kṣatriya woman, a Kṣattṛ; and on a Brāhmaṇa woman, a Caṇḍāla.
From a Vaiśya on a Kṣatriya woman is born an Āyogava; on a Brāhmaṇa woman, a Vaidehaka. From a Kṣatriya on a Brāhmaṇa woman is born a Sūta.
In that case, when there is a union with the two highest castes, the Ambaṣṭha is born as an *anuloma*.
(BDhS 1.9.17.9) The Kṣattṛ and the Vaidehaka are born as *pratiloma*. (BDhS 1.9.17.10)
One born from an Ugra father and a Kṣatriya mother is a Śvapāka.
From a Vaidehaka and an Ambaṣṭhā woman is born a Vaiṇa.
From a Niṣāda and a Śūdra woman is born a Pulkasa.
From a Śūdra, on a Niṣādī woman, a cock is born.
The wise call those born from the intermixture of castes *vrātyas*; the wise call them *vrātyas*.
The king, who receives a sixth part [of the produce], shall protect his subjects.

Brahman indeed deposited his own majesty among the Brāhmaṇas—endowed with the acts of studying, teaching, sacrificing, officiating at sacrifices, giving, and receiving—for the protection of the Vedas.
In the *kṣatra*, strength is joined with study, sacrifice, giving, weapons, the treasury, and the protection of beings for the prosperity of the *kṣatra*.
For a Vaiśya, [the livelihood] consists of activities connected with study, officiating at sacrifices, giving gifts, agriculture, trade, and cattle-rearing, for the sake of increasing his wealth.
Among Śūdras, [the duty] of the former [castes] is service.
"For they were created from the foot," so it is said.
He should appoint as domestic priest one who is capable of bearing the burden in every respect.
One should abide by his instruction.
In battle, he shall not retreat.
One should not strike with weapons that have ear-holes, nor with those smeared with poison.
One should not fight with those who are frightened, intoxicated, insane, or deranged; nor with those whose armor is missing; nor with women, children, the elderly, or Brahmins.
Except in the case of an assailant.
Moreover, they also cite this:

"If one kills an assailant who has come as an aggressor, even though he be a teacher born of a noble family, one does not become a killer of an embryo (*bhrūṇahan*); rather, it is the fury that meets the fury. Thus [it is said].
The maritime toll shall consist of ten paṇas for every hundred [of value], after deducting one excellent piece of merchandise.
In the case of others as well, one should determine a lawful share in accordance with their relative worth, provided it does not cause injury.
After having guarded for one year property whose owner is missing, the king shall take it from a non-Brāhmaṇa.
A Brāhmaṇa is indeed not to be killed for any offense whatsoever.

In the case of a Brāhmaṇa who has committed the murder of a Brāhmaṇa, sexual intercourse with the wife of a Guru, theft of gold, or the drinking of liquor, he shall be branded on the forehead with heated iron with the marks of a female pudendum, a vulva, a jackal, or a tavern-sign, and then banished from the realm.
In the case of killing a Brāhmaṇa, the punishment for Kṣatriyas and others is death and the confiscation of all their property.
In the case of killing those who are equal or inferior to them, he should prescribe appropriate punishments according to their respective strength.
Upon killing a Kṣatriya, one should release a thousand cows with an additional bull to the king for the purpose of avenging the enmity.
For a Vaiśya, one hundred cows; for a Śūdra, ten cows, and in this case, an additional bull.
The killing of a woman and the killing of a cow are explained by the [penance for] the killing of a Śūdra, except in the case of killing an Ātreyī woman, or a milch-cow, or a bull.
In the case of killing a cow or a bull, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance at the end [of the period].
The killing of an Ātreyī woman is explained by the [penance for] the killing of a Kṣatriya.

For killing a swan, a crane, a peacock, a ruddy goose, a peacock-pheasant, a crow, an owl, a frog, a *ḍiḍḍika*, a *ḍerikā*, a dog, a mongoose, a mongoose-cat, or others of this kind, one shall undergo the same penance as for a Śūdra.
For the sake of maintaining social order, a witness should give testimony exactly as it was seen or heard.
One quarter of the unrighteousness goes to the perpetrator; one quarter reaches the witness;
one quarter reaches all the members of the court; and one quarter reaches the king.
The king becomes free from sin, and the members of the court are likewise released;
the guilt falls upon the perpetrator where the one deserving of blame is indeed censured.
And having thus designated a witness, the discerning judge should question him with diligence.
"On the night you were born and on the night you shall die—
whatever good deed you have performed in the interval between these two,
all that shall go to the king if you speak falsely."

A witness who speaks falsely regarding testimony destroys three generations of fathers and three generations of grandfathers, as well as seven others— both those already born and those yet to be born.
In a lie for the sake of gold, one kills three ancestors;
in a lie regarding small cattle, one kills five; in a lie regarding a cow, one kills ten.
A witness who speaks falsely regarding a horse kills a hundred; he kills a thousand by speaking falsely regarding a man;
by speaking falsely regarding land, a witness kills everything.
Members of the four castes who have sons may serve as witnesses, except for those who are Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*), kings, renunciants, eunuchs, and those deficient in human faculties.
In the Smṛti, the understanding is primarily based on tradition.
Otherwise than this, one incurs the guilt of being a murderer of a king.
"One should drink boiled milk for twelve nights, or one should offer oblations with the *kūśmāṇḍa* verses; or one should offer oblations with the *kūśmāṇḍa* verses."
There are eight forms of marriage.
Having ascertained his learning and character, [the gift] is given to a student who requests it; that is the *brāhma* [gift].
Having clothed and adorned her, [he says]: "Let her practice dharma together with you. This is the Prājāpatya rite.
Having offered the first oblation of parched grain (*lājāhuti*), and having given a pair of cattle to the bridegroom, that is the *ārṣa* form. BDhS 1.11.20.5:
When the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) are being led forth within the sacrificial enclosure (*antarvedi*) to the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), that is the *daiva* form.

The Āsura [form] consists of winning over [the bride] with wealth. The Gāndharva [form] is the mutual union of one who desires her with her who desires him. The Rākṣasa [form] results from abduction by force.
One should approach a woman while she is asleep, intoxicated, or mentally deranged; this is the Paiśāca rite.
Of these, the first four belong to the Brāhmaṇa; among them, each preceding one is superior to the following.
Among the subsequent ones, each succeeding one is more sinful than the preceding.
In this regard as well, the sixth and seventh [stages] follow the duties of the Kṣatriya, because the Kṣatriya depends upon them.
For Vaiśyas and Śūdras, [the fasts] are on the fifth and eighth days.
For Vaiśyas and Śūdras have wives who are not restricted [to a single husband].
Because they are authorized for cultivation and service.
Some praise even the Gāndharva form of marriage, because it is accompanied by mutual affection in all cases.
It is known from tradition that as the marriage is contracted, so do the offspring become.

Moreover, they cite this: "It is known that the son of a Brāhmaṇī wife sanctifies ten ancestors, ten descendants, and himself—ten on the father's side through the *ārṣa* rite, ten on the mother's side through the *daiva* rite, and ten on both sides through the *prājāpatya* rite. Furthermore, the capacity to master the Veda belongs only to such sons.
A woman who is purchased for wealth is not ordained as a wife; she is neither for the rites to the gods nor for the rites to the ancestors. Kāśyapa declared her to be a slave.
Those who, deluded by greed, bestow their own daughter for a bride-price are sellers of themselves; they are sinful and perpetrators of a great crime.
They fall into a terrible hell and destroy their lineage down to the seventh generation;
furthermore, all matters concerning going and coming are regulated by the toll.

On the full moon day, the eighth day of the lunar fortnight, the new moon day, during a fire-omen, an earthquake, at a cremation ground, upon the death of a local ruler or a learned *śrotriya*, and when traveling to a place of pilgrimage, there shall be no study for a day and a night.

In the case of a foul odor in the wind, during mist, and amidst the sounds of dancing, singing, instrumental music, weeping, or the chanting of Sāmans, [one should remain impure] for that duration of time.
When there is a simultaneous occurrence of thunder, rain, and lightning, there shall be a suspension of study for three days, except during the rainy season.
Even during the rainy season, one should avoid it except for the rain itself, and during the day and night, one should observe that specific time.
And on the day of receiving a gift from or eating at a funeral rite for the ancestors, one must remain impure for the remainder of that day.
At meals, [he should eat] until full digestion.
For the Brāhmaṇa has his hand as his mouth.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"What is eaten and what is accepted as a gift are indistinguishable," so says the Śruti.
When the father has passed away, the impurity lasts for three nights.

There are indeed two kinds of semen for a learned Brāhmaṇa of good repute: one is above the navel, and the other is below it. That which is above the navel—by means of that he procreates when he initiates Brāhmaṇas, when he teaches them, when he officiates at their sacrifices, and when he performs what is righteous. All these constitute his offspring. Now, that which is below the navel—by means of that his own biological (aurasī) offspring is produced. Therefore, they do not say of a learned man of good repute who has no biological offspring, "He is childless."
Therefore, the Brahmin is said to have two names, two faces, two seed-sources, and two births.
And upon hearing or seeing a Śūdra who is unworthy of receiving gifts, one must remain [silent] for that same duration of time.
One should not study at night when jackals howl, until one falls asleep.
And one should not study during the day and night, at the two twilights, or on the days of the lunar phases.
He should not eat meat, nor should he approach a woman.
For it is known that on the days of the lunar changes (parvan), the Rākṣasas and Piśācas become prone to transgression.
On account of other portents and calamities, there shall be a suspension of study for a day and a night, except when the mind is otherwise engaged.
Even in the case of mental [birth or death], there is a suspension of study upon birth and death.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"The eighth day destroys the teacher; the fourteenth day destroys the pupil;
the fifteenth day destroys knowledge. Therefore, one should avoid [studying] on these festival days (*parvan*)."
Therefore, one should avoid [sexual intercourse] on the festival days (parvan).
Now, therefore, follow the rules for expiation.
A killer of an embryo [shall perform penance] for twelve years.

Carrying a skull-bowl and a staff topped with a skull, clothed in the skin of a donkey, and making his dwelling in the forest, he should construct a hut in a cremation ground using a corpse's head as a banner; therein he shall reside.
