Wandering for alms at seven houses while proclaiming his own deed, he shall sustain his life by that means; if he obtains nothing, he shall fast.
He should sacrifice with the Aśvamedha, the Gosava, or the Agniṣṭut.
Or he may purify himself at the final purificatory bath of a horse sacrifice.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"By killing a Brāhmaṇa unintentionally, one becomes defiled according to the law;
for that which is not preceded by intent, the seers declare an expiation."
For one who kills intentionally, no atonement is found.
"Having threatened [to strike], one should perform the Kṛcchra penance; in the case of actually striking, the Atikṛcchra.
Upon the flow of blood, one should perform both the Kṛcchra and the Cāndrāyaṇa.
Therefore, one should never threaten, nor should one cause blood to flow. Thus it is said.
For a Kṣatriya, it is nine years.
A Vaiśya has three [wives].
For a Śūdra, [the period of impurity lasts] one year.
And [the same applies] to a woman.
The Ātreyī woman is treated like a Brāhmaṇa woman.
One who has violated the bed of his guru shall lie upon a heated iron bed.
Or he may embrace a glowing iron image.

Alternatively, having cut off the male organ together with the testicles and placed it in his joined palms, he should walk toward the intermediate direction between the south and the west until he collapses.
A thief, having disheveled his hair and taken a club made of *saidhraka* wood upon his shoulder, should go to the king saying, "Kill me with this. With that [club], the king should strike him.
Moreover, they cite this example:
"Taking a club upon his shoulder, a thief should go to the king, saying:
'O King, mindful of the duty of a Kṣatriya, punish me with this.'"
"Whether he is punished or released, the thief is freed from his guilt;
but by failing to punish him, the king incurs the guilt of the thief. Thus [it is said].
Having drunk *surā*, one should burn the body with hot [liquor].
If one drinks [forbidden liquor] unintentionally, one should perform a quarter-kṛcchra penance for one year and undergo a second initiation.
And there is no lapse regarding the shaving of the head, the vows, or the observances, because these have already been performed previously.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"Having unintentionally drunk *vāruṇī* liquor, or having consumed urine or feces,
a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya deserves to undergo the rite of re-initiation (*punaḥsaṃskāra*)."
But he who drinks water that has stood overnight in a vessel used for keeping *surā* should subsist for six days on milk boiled with *śaṅkhapuṣpī*.
If one should die while being directed by his teacher, the teacher shall perform three *kṛcchra* penances.
This same [penance] applies to one who has not been consecrated.
For a religious student (brahmacārin), the performance of funeral rites for anyone other than his mother, father, or teacher results in the suspension of his vow.
If he should fall ill, he may at will consume all the remnants of his teacher's food for the purpose of medicine.
He may treat with whatever [remedy] he desires.
When he becomes ill, he should rise and worship the sun with this verse: "The swan dwelling in purity...
(RV 4.40.5). Having emitted semen during the day, he should drink water reaching his heart three times with the *retasyā* verses.
A student who approaches a woman is an *avakīrṇin*.
He should sacrifice a donkey as the animal victim.
The animal victim and the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) belong to Nirṛti; they have either the Rakṣases or Yama as their deity.
It is known from scripture that the portion for the sacrificer (prāśitra) is taken from the penis, and that they proceed with the ritual using the portions (avadāna) in the water.

Alternatively, on the night of the new moon, having kindled the fire and performed the ritual service pertaining to the wood-oblation (*dārvihomika*), he offers two oblations of clarified butter: "O Kāma, I am an outcast; I am an outcast. To Kāma, svāhā! O Kāma, I have been deceived; I have been deceived. To Kāma, svāhā! [K: *dārvihomikīṃ*]

Having offered the oblation, with hands joined in reverence, he should address the fire from a slightly oblique direction: "May the Maruts sprinkle me; may Indra sprinkle me; may Bṛhaspati sprinkle me; may this Agni sprinkle me with long life and with strength; make me long-lived."

BDhS 2.1.1.36: Then his kinsmen, in an assembly, should pour out a vessel of water [for him], saying, "I, so-and-so, am of such-and-such a condition. After he has performed the penance, having begun with water, milk, ghee, honey, and salt, the Brāhmaṇas should say to him, "Has the penance been performed by you? He replies, "Om. They should then perform for him the *savanīya* rite which completes the penance. BDhS 2.1.1.37: If he should unknowingly approach a woman of the same lineage (*sagotrā*), he should support her like a mother.

BDhS 2.1.1.38: If she has given birth, he shall perform a quarter of a *kṛcchra* penance for one year and offer oblations with these two verses: "Whatever deficiency has occurred in my self," and "Agni has given sight again. BDhS 2.1.1.39ab: The younger brother who marries before his elder, the elder brother so superseded, and the woman who marries him— BDhS 2.1.1.39cd: All of them go to hell, along with the giver of the bride and the officiating priest as the fifth.

"The elder brother who has married before his younger brother, the younger brother who marries before his elder, the one who gives [the girl] in marriage [in such a case], and also the officiating priest—these are purified by a twelve-night *kṛcchra* penance; a woman is purified in three nights. Thus it is said.
Now, the acts causing loss of caste (patanīya).
2.1.2.2 Traveling by sea.
The misappropriation of a Brahmin’s property that has been entrusted to one's care.
Falsehood regarding land.
Dealing in all kinds of merchandise.
Service to Śūdras.
Born from a Śūdra woman.
And [the same applies to] being the offspring of that [person].

Having performed any one of these [penances], they should eat at the fourth meal-time with moderation and enter the water according to the ritual for the *savanas*. By alternating between standing and sitting, they destroy that evil in three years.

"The sin that a Brāhmaṇa incurs by associating with one of black complexion for a single night, he destroys that sin in three years by eating only at every fourth mealtime and subsisting on water. Thus it is said.
Now, the minor offenses (upapātaka).

BDhS 2.1.2.13: Having approached a woman who should not be approached, the wife of a teacher, the female friend of a teacher, one who has lost her caste, or an outcast; practicing medicine, officiating at sacrifices for a village, living by the stage, being a teacher of acting, tending cows and buffaloes, and whatever else is of this nature, as well as defiling a maiden.
But their means of subsistence shall be the conduct of an outcast for two years.
Now, those things which cause impurity.

Gambling, malevolent magic, the practice of gleaning for one who has not established the sacred fires, the practice of begging by a student who has returned home, his continued residence in the teacher's house beyond four months, teaching him [after that period], and the pointing out of constellations [for divination].

The expiation for these [offenses] consists of twelve months, twelve half-months, twelve periods of twelve days, twelve periods of six days, twelve periods of three days, twelve days, six days, three days, one day and night, or one day, according to the repetition of the act.

Now, those who have fallen [from their caste], having come together, should practice the duties of those who sacrifice for one another, teach one another, and intermarry with one another. Having produced sons, they should say to them: "Depart from us; through you alone shall you attain the status of the Āryas."
Moreover, one does not fall [from caste] as long as the senses remain intact.
BDhS 2.1.2.20: This is to be understood by this: even one who is deficient in a limb may produce a son who possesses all limbs. [K: For he indeed produces one who possesses all limbs.
BDhS 2.1.2.21: Hārīta says that this is false.
Women are like a vessel for curdled milk. For when one churns impure milk that has been poured into a vessel for curdled milk, the cultured do not employ that [curd] for religious rites.
In this way, there is no contact with that impure semen which is produced.
For those born from impure semen, if they so desire, there is an expiation.
The third part of the offenses causing loss of caste applies to women; their [penance] is one-third.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"If one performs with sesame seeds any act other than eating, anointing, or giving, he becomes a worm in a dog's excrement and sinks down along with his ancestors. Thus it is said.
He who sells sesame seeds sells his ancestors; he who sells rice grains sells his vital breaths; and he who, for the sake of profit, gives away his daughter in marriage, sells his shares of merit.
BDhS 2.1.2.28 Grass and wood that have not been processed may be sold. [K: grass and wood] BDhS 2.1.2.29–29ab Furthermore, they also cite:
"Animals with only one row of teeth, and stone extracted from salt-mines..."
"O Brāhmaṇa, this is your merchandise: a thread dyed with safflower. Thus [it is said].
Or, excluding the most grievous sins, one should pour clarified butter over a tawny, reddish-brown cow with thick hair, scatter black sesame seeds upon her, and give her to a learned Brahmin.
Or, one may perform the Kūśmāṇḍa rites for twelve days.
"By this, one is released from whatever sin has been committed prior to the killing of a learned Brahmin."
If one falsely accuses another of a mortal sin (pātaka), one must perform a kṛcchra penance.
BDhS 2.1.2.34: That curse falls upon the one who utters it.
BDhS 2.1.2.35: One becomes an outcast by associating with an outcast for a year through officiating at sacrifices, teaching, or marriage, but not through sharing a vehicle, a seat, or food.
The penance for consuming impure substances is the *naiṣpurīṣya* fast; that is accomplished by seven nights.
Water, milk, and ghee—each for three days respectively, consumed while hot—constitute the *satapta-kṛcchra*.

BDhS 2.1.2.38: Eating only in the morning for three days, likewise in the evening for three days, eating only what is unasked for three days, and fasting for the final three days—this is the *kṛcchra* penance. [K: Eating in the evening for three days, eating only what is unasked for another three days, and not eating at all for the final three days is the *parāka*. BDhS 2.1.2.39: Eating in the morning for one four-night period, in the evening for another, eating only what is unasked for another, and fasting for the final four nights—these three four-night periods constitute the *kṛcchra* penance for women, children, and the elderly.
He should eat as much as he might take up in a single mouthful; as before, this is the *atikṛcchra*.
Subsisting on water is the third; that is the Kṛcchrātikṛcchra penance.
In the Kṛcchra penance, there is bathing in water at the three periods of the day.
Sleeping on the ground.
Wearing a single garment and shaving the hair of the head, the beard, the body hair, and the nails.
This same [rite] applies to a woman as well, with the exception of shaving the hair; with the exception of shaving the hair.

BDhS 2.2.3.1ab: One who constantly uses water for purification, who constantly wears the sacred thread, who constantly studies the Veda, and who avoids the food of a *vṛṣala*; BDhS 2.2.3.1cd: and who approaches his wife during her season and offers oblations according to the rule—that Brāhmaṇa does not fall from the world of Brahman.
"The Vedic scripture states: 'Manu divided his inheritance among his sons.'"
All [the shares] are equal, because there is no distinction among them.
Or the eldest may extract the best portion or the most excellent form.
"Therefore, they exclude the eldest son from his share of the wealth," so says the Śruti.
Or the eldest may set aside one [share] from among ten.
The others shall divide the property equally.
The division of the inheritance takes place with the father's consent while the father is still living.
Among the four castes, cows, horses, goats, and sheep constitute the senior share.
In the case of a combination of sons born of women of different castes, one should divide the inheritance into ten parts and distribute them in order as four, three, two, and one.
But when a legitimate son of the body (aurasa) has been born, those of equal caste (savarṇa) shall receive a third share.
Between the son of a wife of equal caste and the son of a wife of the next lower caste, if the son of the next lower caste is virtuous, he shall take the share of the eldest.
For one who possesses good qualities becomes the supporter of the others.
One should know that the son begotten by oneself upon a wife of equal caste who has undergone the sacraments is the *aurasa* (legitimate) son.
Furthermore, they cite this:
"From limb after limb you are born; from the heart you are produced."
"Thou art indeed the self named 'son'; live for a hundred autumns! [K omits].
Regarding the daughter: one born of a daughter who has been formally accepted is a *putrikāputra* (son of an appointed daughter), while any other is a *dauhitra* (daughter's son).
Furthermore, they also cite this:
"The son of an appointed daughter (putrikā) should designate his mother at the first rice-ball offering, his father at the second, and his paternal grandfather at the third. Thus [it is said].

He who is begotten on a wife whose husband is dead, or who is impotent or diseased, with the consent of another, is a *kṣetraja* (son of the soil). He has two fathers and belongs to two gotras; he is an heir to the funeral offerings (*svadhā*) and the inheritance of both.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"For one who has two fathers, there should be the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍas) for both; and with each rice-ball, the names of both should be mentioned.
There should thus be three rice-balls for six ancestors; by acting in this way, one does not go astray."
One who is given by both parents or by either one, and is accepted for the sake of offspring, is a *datta* (given son).
One whom she herself makes her own, being of similar status and with mutual desire, is a *kṛtrima* (adopted) son.
22. One born in secret in the house and discovered at the end is the *gūḍhaja* (secret-born). 23.
One who is abandoned by both parents or by either one, and is then taken up for the sake of offspring, is the *apaviddha* (cast-off).
24. He who is born of a woman whom one has approached without her being consecrated for marriage and without her having been given away in marriage is a *kānīna* (a maiden-born son).
25. He who is born of a woman who is married while she is already pregnant—whether that pregnancy was known or unknown—is a *sahoḍha* (a son received with the bride).
One who is purchased from the hands of his mother and father, or from either one of them, and is taken for the sake of offspring, is a "bought" (krīta) son.
If a woman, having abandoned a eunuch or one who has fallen from his caste, takes another husband, the son born of her as a remarried woman (paunarbhavī) is called a paunarbhava.
One who, being deprived of both mother and father, gives himself away is a self-given son (svayaṃdatta).
One born from a Śūdra woman by a man of the foremost of the twice-born castes is a Niṣāda.
From lust, the Pāraśava is born; these are the sons.
Moreover, they cite this: "The son of the body (*aurasa*),

the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*), the son born of the wife (*kṣetraja*), the son given (*datta*), the son made (*kṛtrima*), the son born in secret (*gūḍhaja*), and the son cast off (*apaviddha*)— these are declared to be the sharers of the inheritance."

The son of an unmarried girl (*kānīna*), the son received with a pregnant bride (*sahoḍha*), the purchased son (*krīta*), the son of a remarried woman (*paunarbhava*), the self-given son (*svayaṃdatta*), and the *niṣāda*— these they declare to be sharers of the family name (*gotra*).
"Of these, the first alone [is the one to be performed]," says Aupajaṅghani.
"O progenitor of women, I am envious now, but not before;
for in the abode of Yama, they declared that one is the son of him who begot him."
"The progenitor of the seed leads the son away after death to the abode of Yama;
therefore, fearing the seed of another, they guard their own wives. "Be vigilant and protect this lineage; let not the seed of another be sown in your field."
"In the life hereafter, the son belongs to the progenitor; the one who knows this in vain weaves this thread.
(BDhS 2.2.3.35cd) Until they reach the age of legal capacity, their shares, along with the interest thereon, shall be deposited under secure custody. (BDhS 2.2.3.36)
They shall support those who have passed beyond legal capacity with food and clothing.
And those who are blind, mentally dull, eunuchs, addicted to vices, diseased, and so forth.
Those who do not perform their duties.
Except for those born of outcasts.
There is no social interaction with those who have fallen [from their caste].
But even if his mother has fallen [from her caste], he should support her without speaking to her.
The daughters shall receive their mother’s ornaments, whether they were passed down through tradition or otherwise.
BDhS 2.2.3.44: No independence exists for a woman. BDhS 2.2.3.45-1: Now they also cite this: BDhS 2.2.3.45-2ab: The father protects her in childhood; the husband protects her in youth.
"But in old age, a son shall not allow a woman independence.
Thus [it is said]. For the Śruti declares: "Women are considered to be devoid of sensory power and without inheritance."
Striving for the welfare of their husband, they shall conquer the heavenly world.
In the event of a transgression, the Kṛcchra penance is prescribed.
And for killing a Śūdra, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
In the case of those born in the reverse order from Vaiśyas and others, one should perform the Kṛcchra, Atikṛcchra, and other such penances.
For men of the Brahmin and other castes, the period of studentship (brahmacarya) shall last for one year.
One should burn a Śūdra with a fire of straw.
Moreover, they also cite this:
For a non-Brāhmaṇa, corporal punishment shall be the penalty for adultery.
For all social classes alike, one's wife is more worthy of protection than one's wealth.
But there is no execution for those who are performers' wives, nor for those on the stage;
for they cause men to consort with these women, even when they are well-guarded.
Women are an incomparable means of purification; they are never defiled.
For month after month, their menstrual flow carries away their sins.

Soma gave them purity; Gandharva, eloquent speech; and Agni, the capacity to consume all things; therefore, women are free from blemish. One should abandon a woman who bears no offspring by the tenth year, and one who bears only daughters by the twelfth year.
One whose children have died [should wait] for fifteen years, but one who speaks unpleasantly [may be superseded] immediately.
For one year, the widow of the deceased shall avoid honey, meat, fermented liquors, and salt; she shall sleep on the ground.
"Six months," says Maudgalya.
From this point forward, a woman without a son may, with the permission of her elders, procreate a son through her husband’s brother.
Moreover, they also cite this:

"A barren cow, one that has already produced offspring, one that is without menses, and one whose progeny has ceased—such a cow should not be employed against her will, for no fruit is found in her. Thus it is said.

A maternal uncle’s sister, a father’s sister, a sister, a sister’s daughter, a daughter-in-law, a maternal uncle’s wife, and a friend’s wife—these are women who must not be approached for sexual intercourse.
For approaching women who should not be approached, the penance is the Kṛcchrātikṛcchra and the Cāndrāyaṇa.
By this, sexual intercourse with a Caṇḍāla woman is explained.
Moreover, they quote this:

"A Brāhmaṇa who has approached a Caṇḍālī woman, or having eaten [with her], or having accepted a gift from her—such a Vipra falls through ignorance; but through knowledge, he would attain equality [with her]."

"Having unintentionally approached the wife of a father, a teacher, or a king, one becomes a violator of the Guru’s bed; for that, the atonement previously mentioned applies. (BDhS 2.2.4.15) "If he is unable [to subsist] by teaching, officiating at sacrifices, or receiving gifts, he may live according to the duty of a Kṣatriya, because it is the next best alternative. (BDhS 2.2.4.16)
"Not so," says Gautama; "for the duty of the Kṣatriya is exceedingly fierce for a Brāhmaṇa."
Moreover, they also cite this:
"For the sake of a cow, for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa, or even in the event of a confusion of castes,
a Brāhmaṇa and a Vaiśya may take up arms out of regard for dharma."
The mode of life of a Vaiśya should be practiced [by the Kṣatriya] because it is the one immediately following his own.
Before the morning meal, he should be a laborer.
[He should perform the rite] with two goats whose nostrils are unperforated and which have their testicles intact, not prodding them with a goad and repeatedly encouraging them by shouting aloud.
The fire begins with the wife; in that fire, the performance of the rites takes place prior to the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya).

BDhS 2.2.4.23: From the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya) onwards, these [rites] become perpetual: namely, the establishment of the fires, the Agnihotra, the New and Full Moon sacrifices, the Āgrayaṇa, the animal sacrifice at the solstices (the summer and winter solstices), the Cāturmāsya sacrifices at the beginning of each season, the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ offering, and the Jyotiṣṭoma in the spring; in this way, one reaches security.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"Neither by one habituated to sleeping during the day, nor by one who eats all kinds of food,
can it be possible to go to heaven— much less so for one who has fallen after having ascended."
One should avoid wretchedness, deceit, and crookedness.
Furthermore, in this regard, they cite a verse from the dialogue between Uśanas and Vṛṣaparvan’s two daughters:
“You are indeed the daughter of one who praises, begs, and accepts;
but I am the son of one who is praised, gives, and does not accept.”
"For one who gives and for one who does not accept," so it is said.
BDhS 2.3.5.1: Ascetic practice consists of immersion in water.
BDhS 2.3.5.2: Having gratified the deities, one should perform the libation for the ancestors.
He pours out water at the edge of the water's flow with the verse, "Carrying strength...
(BDhS 2.3.5.3). Furthermore, they also cite:
"In flowing waters that are not obstructed, the three twice-born castes [may perform their rites]" (BDhS 2.3.5.4-2ab).
Having risen in the morning, they should perform the libations to the gods, the sages, and the ancestors.
When the waters are obstructed, they should not perform them; in that case, the builder of the embankment is entitled to a share of the merit.
"Therefore, one should avoid embankments and wells made by others."
Moreover, they also cite this:
"Or, having drawn out three lumps of earth, one should perform [the rite] in times of distress, but not always;
however, when [water] is obstructed, one should likewise take three lumps of earth from a well and three jars of water."

BDhS 2.3.5.8: Having accepted what is forbidden to be accepted, or having failed to sacrifice for one for whom one ought not to sacrifice, or having eaten the food of one whose food should not be eaten, one should mutter the *taratsamandīya* verse.
BDhS 2.3.5.9–1: Furthermore, they also cite this:
BDhS 2.3.5.9–2ab: Those who cause confusion among gurus, and those who cause confusion among disciples;
"Those whose food is mixed with mantras wait upon long darkness. Thus [it is said].
Now follow the observances of the Snātaka.

In the evening and in the morning, having offered the Vaiśvadeva oblation with whatever food is fit for consumption, he should honor arriving Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras according to his ability.
If he is unable to provide for many, he should give to one who possesses good qualities.
Or he who may have arrived first;
if a Śūdra has arrived, one should employ him in labor.
Or one should give the first portion to a learned Brahmin (śrotriya).
A distribution of food is ordained for those who are permanent dependents, provided it does not cause hardship for them. However, one must never eat without having first given [food] to them.
Furthermore, in this regard, they cite two verses from the *Anngīta*:

"He who, out of delusion, eats prepared food without first having given it to the ancestors, the gods, his servants, guests, and his circle of friends—he eats poison; I devour him, for I am his death."
Having offered the *agnihotra* oblation and performed the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice, he who— having honored his guests and his dependents,
being contented, pure, and full of faith— eats what remains, for him I become nectar (*amṛta*), and he nourishes me.

BDhS 2.3.5.19: A distribution of goods according to one's ability should be made to those who are not merely Brāhmaṇas by birth but are learned in the Vedas and have mastered them—specifically when they are seeking alms outside the sacrificial altar for the sake of their teacher, for a dwelling, for medicine, for sustenance, when they are impoverished, when they are about to perform a sacrifice, when they are engaged in Vedic study, when they are traveling on a journey, or when they are performing the Vaiśvajit sacrifice.
In the case of the others, cooked food [is offered].

Having thoroughly washed his hands and feet and sipped water, he should take the food brought to him in a clean, enclosed place; then, having cast away desire, anger, malice, greed, and delusion, he should eat with all his fingers, making no sound.
One should not discard the remnants of the rice balls into the vessel.
If one consumes food mixed with meat, fish, or sesame seeds, one should touch water and then touch fire.
And one should bathe after the sun has set.
One should avoid a seat made of *pālāśa* wood, sandals, and a tooth-stick made of *pālāśa* wood.
One should not eat food held in the lap.
One should not eat while seated on a chair.
He should carry a bamboo staff and two golden earrings.
One should avoid washing one foot with the other and stepping upon it.
One should not wear a garland outside [the garment].
One should not look at the sun at either sunrise or sunset.
One should not announce "the rainbow" to another person.
If he should say "maṇidhanus," one should simply say "maṇidhanus."
One should not pass between the Indra-kīla and the crossbar at the city gate.
One should not pass between the two swing-boards (pleṅkha).
And one should not walk over a rope tied to a calf's neck.
One should not step upon ashes, bones, hair, husks, potsherds, or water used for ritual bathing.
One should not tell another that a cow is suckling.
One should not say "non-cow" of a cow that does not give milk.
If he should say, "A cow that will become [one]," he should simply say, "A cow that will become."
One should not utter words that are sour, harsh, or rough.
One should not travel alone on a road.
Not with outcasts, nor with a woman, nor with a Śūdra.
One should not go out at evening.
One should not bathe naked.
One should not bathe at night.
One should not cross a river by swimming with one's arms.
One should not look into a well.
One should not look into a pit.
One should not sit down in such a place where another would make one rise up.
Way must be yielded to a Brāhmaṇa, to a cow, to a king, to one who is sightless,
to an elderly person, to one afflicted by heat, to a pregnant woman, and to one who is weak.

A righteous man should strive to dwell in a village that has an abundance of firewood, water, fodder, fuel, *kuśa* grass, and garlands; one from which people easily exit, which is crowded with wealthy folk, prosperous with industrious people, abounding in noble persons, and not accessible to barbarians (*dasyu*).
If a Brāhmaṇa who is the husband of a Śūdra woman dwells for twelve years in a village where the only water is from a well, he incurs the same status as a Śūdra.
With his body covered by the dust of the city, and with his eyes and face filled with that same dust,
even one who dwells in the city with a well-restrained self will not attain perfection— such a thing is impossible.
The dust raised by chariots, horses, elephants, grain, and cows is auspicious;
however, the dust of a broom, dogs, goats, sheep, donkeys, and clothing is inauspicious.
One should honor those who are worthy of honor.
A seer, a learned man, a distinguished king, a maternal uncle, a father-in-law, and an officiating priest—
these are declared by the scriptures to be worthy of the *arghya* offering, according to the specific divisions of time.
"Sages, learned men, and kings who have arrived at the commencement of a rite are [honored as] excellent officiating priests;
likewise, a maternal uncle and a father-in-law are to be honored whenever they visit within the course of a year. Thus it is said.
In the fire-sanctuary, in the midst of cows, in the presence of Brahmins,
during Vedic study, and while eating, one should expose the right arm.
An upper garment must be worn during these five activities:
during Vedic study, the voiding of excrement, giving gifts, eating, and sipping water for purification.

Offering oblations, eating, giving, presenting offerings, and receiving gifts—these acts, as well as the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), should not be performed with the knees outside [the hands]. This is the traditional rule.
"Beings are supported by food; 'Food is life,' so says the Śruti.
Therefore, food must be given, for food is the supreme oblation."
"Sin is pacified by the oblation; the oblation is pacified by food;
food attains peace through the sacrificial fee—such is the Vedic revelation. "It attains peace—such is our revelation," so it is said.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the rule for the worship of the twilight (saṃdhyopāsana).

Having gone to a sacred bathing place (tīrtha), whether he is impure and has bathed or pure and has not bathed, he should wash his feet and hands, sip water (ācamana), and sprinkle himself with water scented with fragrant substances, with verses containing the word *abliṅga*, with those addressed to Varuṇa, with the golden-hued verses (*hiraṇyavarṇāḥ*), with the *pāvamānī* verses, with the *vyāhṛtis*, and with other purificatory formulas; thus he becomes pure.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"Immersion in water is prescribed as the ritual bath for all social classes;
however, for the twice-born, sprinkling with water accompanied by mantras is specifically distinguished. Thus it is said.
And at the commencement of all ritual acts, before the time for the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*), one becomes pure by sprinkling oneself with this very collection of purifiers.
Moreover, they also cite this: "Seated upon *darbha* grass, holding *darbha* grass, with his hands moistened with water and facing westward, he should repeat the *Sāvitrī* one thousand times."
Or alternatively, one may perform it a hundred times with each breath-control (prāṇāyāma).
Or, mentally, ten times, with the *praṇava* at both ends and accompanied by the seven *vyāhṛtis*.
And when exhausted by three breath-restraints, he should [recite] the "Heart of Brahman."
With two verses addressed to Varuṇa—namely, "This my prayer, O Varuṇa" and "That I implore of thee"—he worships the night.
In the same manner, in the morning, he stands facing the east.
With two verses addressed to Mitra—namely, "Of Mitra, the supporter of the people" and "Mitra impels the people"—he worships the day. With these two [verses].
One may begin even the first [part] of the day that is preceded by the night, and complete it once the sun has risen.
Having commenced before sunset, one may even perform the evening rite after it has become very late.
And by the perfection of the two twilights, there is the continuity of day and night.
Moreover, there are two verses sung by Prajāpati on this subject:
"Those Brahmins who do not perform the twilight worship of the morning that has not yet arrived, nor of the evening that has not yet passed— how can they be considered true Brahmins?"
"Those Brahmins who do not constantly perform the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā) in the evening and the morning—let a righteous king, at his will, employ them in the labor of Śūdras. Thus it is said.
In that regard, if one fails at evening, there shall be a fast for the night; if one fails at dawn, there shall be a fast for the day.
One obtains the fruit of standing and sitting.
Moreover, they also cite this:
Whatever sin has been committed by the organ of generation, or whatever has been done by the feet;
or whatever has been done by the arms, or even by the mind, or by speech.
Having performed the evening twilight worship, one is thereby released from that [debt].
And he is joined with the night as well, and Varuṇa does not seize him.
In this very manner, having performed the morning worship, one is liberated from the evil committed during the night.
He is united with the day, Mitra protects him, and the Sun leads him to the heavenly world.

In this very manner, worshipping day by day at the junctions of day and night, purified by the Veda, become one with the Veda, and following the sacred teaching, the Brāhmaṇa conquers the world of Brahman; so it is known. He conquers the world of Brahman; so it is known.
Then, having washed his hands and taken hold of his water-pot and a lump of earth, he goes to a bathing place and washes his feet three times and himself three times.
Now, some indeed say: "One must not enter a cemetery, water, a temple, a cow-pen, or a place where Brahmins are, without having washed one's feet."
Then he approaches the water:
"I take refuge in Varuṇa, whose horns are of gold;
grant me a ford, as I entreat you, [for the removal] of that which has been eaten by me of the unrighteous, and of the acceptance of gifts from the wicked."

"Whatever evil has been done by me through thought, word, or deed—may Indra, Varuṇa, Bṛhaspati, and Savitṛ purify that again and again. Then, with joined palms, he takes water, saying: "May the waters and plants be friendly to us."
He sprinkles that water toward the direction in which he has an enemy, saying: "May ill-fated enemies befall him who hates us and whom we hate."

BDhS 2.5.8.6 Then, having touched water, he turns the water three times clockwise, saying: "Whatever in the waters is cruel, whatever is impure, whatever is unpeaceful—let that depart. BDhS 2.5.8.7 Having submerged himself in the water and emerged.
For one who is in water, there is no purification, nor the washing of clothes, nor the ritual touching of water.
If they are besieged, he worships with this: "Homage to Agni accompanied by the waters; homage to Indra; homage to Varuṇa; homage to Vāruṇī; homage to the waters."
Having emerged from the water and sipped water, one who has already sipped should sip again, reciting:

"May the waters purify the earth; may the purified earth purify me. May Brahmaṇaspati purify; may the purified Veda purify me. "Whatever is impure from remnants, whatever is unfit to be eaten, or whatever evil deed I have committed—may the waters purify all that in me, and the acceptance of gifts from the wicked, svāhā!"

Having made two strainers, he purifies himself with water using the three verses beginning with "O Waters, you are indeed sources of bliss," the four verses beginning with "Golden-colored, pure, purifying," and the verse beginning with "Pavamāna, [you who dwell] in the light."

Having purified himself with this Anuvāka, having gone into the water, having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) with the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn, having emerged and wrung out his garment, having put on unwashed, undamaged garments that have been washed and aired, and having sipped water, he should sit upon Darbha grass, holding Darbha blades, facing the east, and repeat the Sāvitrī one thousand times, or one hundred times, or an unlimited number of times, at least ten times.
Then he worships the sun with these [verses]: "Up from the darkness," "Up that one," "The bright," "That eye established by the gods," and "He who has risen."
Moreover, they also cite this: "The *praṇava*, the *vyāhṛtis*, and the *sāvitrī*—these five constitute the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*), which purify the Brāhmaṇa from sin day after day."
Purified by these five Brahmayajñas, he thereafter satiates the deities.

Om! Agni, Prajāpati, Soma, Rudra, Aditi, Bṛhaspati, and the Sarpas—these deities of the eastern doors, together with the constellations, the planets, the days and nights, and the muhūrtas, I gratify. Om! And I gratify the Vasus.

Om! I satiate the deities of the southern gates—Pitṛs, Aryaman, Bhaga, Savitṛ, Tvaṣṭṛ, Vāyu, Indra, and Agni—together with the constellations, the planets, the days and nights, and the muhūrtas. Om! And I satiate the Rudras. Om!

I satiate the deities of the western gates—Mitra, Indra, the Great Pitṛs, the Waters, the Viśvedevas, Brahmā, and Viṣṇu—together with the constellations, the planets, the days and nights, and the muhūrtas. Om! And I satiate the Ādityas.

Oṃ, I satiate the Vasus, Varuṇa, Aja Ekapād, Ahirbudhnya, Pūṣan, the two Aśvins, and Yama—these deities who have gates facing north, together with the constellations, the planets, the days and nights, and the muhūrtas. Oṃ, I satiate the Viśvedevas. Oṃ, and I satiate the Sādhyas.

Om, I satiate Brahmā. Om, I satiate Prajāpati. Om, I satiate the Four-faced One. Om, I satiate Parameṣṭhin. Om, I satiate Hiraṇyagarbha. Om, I satiate Svayaṃbhu. Om, I satiate the attendants of Brahmā. Om, I satiate the female attendants of Brahmā. Om, I satiate Agni. Om, I satiate Vāyu. Om, I satiate Varuṇa. Om, I satiate Sūrya.

Oṃ, I satisfy the Moon. Oṃ, I satisfy the Constellations. [K adds: I satisfy the Luminaries. Oṃ, I satisfy Sadyojāta. Oṃ, I satisfy the Puruṣa of Bhūḥ. Oṃ, I satisfy the Puruṣa of Bhuvaḥ. Oṃ, I satisfy the Puruṣa of Suvaḥ. Oṃ, I satisfy the Puruṣa of Bhūr-bhuvaḥ-suvaḥ. Oṃ, I satisfy Bhūḥ. Oṃ, I satisfy Bhuvaḥ. Oṃ, I satisfy Suvaḥ. Oṃ, I satisfy Mahas. Oṃ, I satisfy Janaḥ. Oṃ, I satisfy Tapaḥ. Oṃ, I satisfy Satya.

Om, I satiate the god Bhava. Om, I satiate the god Śarva. Om, I satiate the god Īśāna. Om, I satiate the god Paśupati. Om, I satiate the god Rudra. Om, I satiate the god Ugra. Om, I satiate the god Bhīma. Om, I satiate the god Mahān.

Om, I satiate the wife of the god Bhava. Om, I satiate the wife of the god Śarva. Om, I satiate the wife of the god Īśāna. Om, I satiate the wife of the god Paśupati. Om, I satiate the wife of the god Rudra. Om, I satiate the wife of the god Ugra. Om, I satiate the wife of the god Bhīma. Om, I satiate the wife of the god Mahat.

Om, I satiate the son of the god Bhava. Om, I satiate the son of the god Śarva. Om, I satiate the son of the god Īśāna. Om, I satiate the son of the god Paśupati. Om, I satiate the son of the god Rudra. Om, I satiate the son of the god Ugra. Om, I satiate the son of the god Bhīma. Om, I satiate the son of the god Mahat. Om, I satiate the Rudras. Om, I satiate the attendants of Rudra. Om, I satiate the female attendants of Rudra.

Om, I satiate Vighna. Om, I satiate Vināyaka. Om, I satiate Vīra. Om, I satiate Sthūla. Om, I satiate Varada. Om, I satiate Hastimukha. Om, I satiate Vakratuṇḍa. Om, I satiate Ekadanta. Om, I satiate Lambodara. [K: I satiate Gaṇapati. Om, I satiate the male attendants of Vighna. Om, I satiate the female attendants of Vighna as well.

Om, I satiate Sanatkumāra. Om, I satiate Skanda. Om, I satiate Indra. Om, I satiate Ṣaṣṭhī. Om, I satiate Ṣaṇmukha. Om, I satiate Jayanta. Om, I satiate Viśākha. Om, I satiate Mahāsena. Om, I satiate Subrahmaṇya. Om, I satiate the attendants of Skanda. Om, I satiate the female attendants of Skanda.
Om, I satiate Āditya. Om, I satiate Soma. Om, I satiate Aṅgāraka. Om, I satiate Budha. Om, I satiate Bṛhaspati. Om, I satiate Śukra. Om, I satiate Śanaiścara. Om, I satiate Rāhu. Om, I satiate Ketu.

Om, I satiate Keśava. Om, I satiate Nārāyaṇa. Om, I satiate Mādhava. Om, I satiate Govinda. Om, I satiate Viṣṇu. Om, I satiate Madhusūdana. Om, I satiate Trivikrama. Om, I satiate Vāmana. Om, I satiate Śrīdhara. Om, I satiate Hṛṣīkeśa. Om, I satiate Padmanābha. Om, I satiate Dāmodara. Om, I satiate the Goddess Śrī.

Oṃ, I satiate the goddess Sarasvatī. Oṃ, I satiate Puṣṭi. Oṃ, I satiate Tuṣṭi. Oṃ, I satiate Garuḍa. Oṃ, I satiate the attendants of Viṣṇu. Oṃ, I satiate the female attendants of Viṣṇu as well. [K: the goddess Puṣṭi... the goddess Tuṣṭi... Vainateya]

Om, I satiate Yama. Om, I satiate Yamarāja. Om, I satiate Dharma. Om, I satiate Dharmarāja. Om, I satiate Kāla. Om, I satiate Nīla. Om, I satiate Mṛtyu. Om, I satiate Vaivasvata. Om, I satiate Citra. Om, I satiate Citragupta. Om, I satiate Audumbara. [K adds: I satiate Vaivasvata. Om, I satiate the attendants of Vaivasvata. Om, I satiate the female attendants of Vaivasvata as well.

*Oṃ*, I satiate the gods of the earth. *Oṃ*, I satiate Kāśyapa. *Oṃ*, I satiate the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). *Oṃ*, I satiate Knowledge (*vidyā*). I satiate Jyeṣṭhā. *Oṃ*, I satiate Dhanvantari. *Oṃ*, I satiate the attendants (*pārṣada*) of Dhanvantari. *Oṃ*, I satiate the female attendants (*pārṣadī*) of Dhanvantari as well.
[K: I satiate Bharadvāja; I satiate Gautama; I satiate Atri; I satiate Āṅgirasa; I satiate Knowledge; I satiate Durgā; I satiate Jyeṣṭhā... (omits: "thus")]
Now, [the rule] for one who wears the sacred thread around the neck (nivītī).

Om, I satiate the Ṛṣis. Om, I satiate the Great Ṛṣis. Om, I satiate the Supreme Ṛṣis. Om, I satiate the Brahman-Ṛṣis. Om, I satiate the Divine Ṛṣis. Om, I satiate the Royal Ṛṣis. Om, I satiate the Learned Ṛṣis. Om, I satiate the Birth-Ṛṣis. Om, I satiate the Austerity-Ṛṣis. Om, I satiate the Truth-Ṛṣis. Om, I satiate the Seven Ṛṣis. Om, I satiate the Section-Ṛṣis. Om, I satiate the Female Ṛṣis.

Oṃ, I satisfy the wives of the ṛṣis. Oṃ, I satisfy the sons of the ṛṣis. Oṃ, I satisfy the grandsons of the ṛṣis. Oṃ, I satisfy Kāṇva Baudhāyana. Oṃ, I satisfy Āpastamba, the author of the Sūtras. Oṃ, I satisfy Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin. Oṃ, I satisfy Yājñavalkya, the Vājasaneyin. Oṃ, I satisfy Āśvalāyana Śaunaka. Oṃ, I satisfy Vyāsa. Oṃ, I satisfy Vasiṣṭha.

Om, I satiate the Praṇava. Om, I satiate the Vyāhṛtis. Om, I satiate Sāvitrī. Om, I satiate Gāyatrī. Om, I satiate the Metres (Chandas). Om, I satiate the Ṛgveda. Om, I satiate the Yajurveda. Om, I satiate the Sāmaveda. Om, I satiate the Atharvaveda. Om, I satiate the Atharvāṅgirases. Om, I satiate the Itihāsas and Purāṇas. Om, I satiate all the Vedas.
Oṃ, I satiate all the classes of gods. Oṃ, I satiate all beings. [K: I satiate the Atharvāṅgirasas...]

Then, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī): Om, I satiate the fathers with *svadhā* and reverence. Om, I satiate the grandfathers with *svadhā* and reverence. Om, I satiate the great-grandfathers with *svadhā* and reverence. Om, I satiate the mothers with *svadhā* and reverence. Om, I satiate the grandmothers with *svadhā* and reverence. Om, I satiate the great-grandmothers with *svadhā* and reverence. Om, I satiate the maternal grandfathers with *svadhā* and reverence. Om, I satiate the maternal grandfathers' fathers with *svadhā* and reverence.

Oṃ, I satiate the great-grandmothers of my mother with *svadhā* and salutation. Oṃ, I satiate the maternal grandmothers with *svadhā* and salutation. Oṃ, I satiate the paternal grandmothers of my mother with *svadhā* and salutation. Oṃ, I satiate the great-grandmothers of my mother with *svadhā* and salutation.

Om, I satiate the teachers with *svadhā* and obeisance. Om, I satiate the wives of the teachers with *svadhā* and obeisance. Om, I satiate the preceptors with *svadhā* and obeisance. Om, I satiate the wives of the preceptors with *svadhā* and obeisance. Om, I satiate friends with *svadhā* and obeisance. Om, I satiate the wives of friends with *svadhā* and obeisance. Om, I satiate kinsmen with *svadhā* and obeisance. Om, I satiate the wives of kinsmen with *svadhā* and obeisance. Om, I satiate counselors with *svadhā* and obeisance.
Om, I satiate the wives of the ministers with *svadhā* and homage. Om, I satiate all [ancestors] with *svadhā* and homage. Om, I satiate all [female ancestors] with *svadhā* and homage.
He pours out water at every sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*).
"Carrying strength, immortality, clarified butter, milk, sweet drink, and flowing liquor—you are the *svadhā* offerings; satisfy my ancestors! Be satisfied, be satisfied, be satisfied! BDhS 2.5.10.4.
One should not perform rites dedicated to the gods while wearing only a single garment or while one's clothes are wet.
"And those connected with the ancestors," so say some; "and those connected with the ancestors," so say some.

Now, these are the five great sacrifices; they indeed are the great sacrificial sessions (mahāsattras): the sacrifice to the gods, the sacrifice to the ancestors, the sacrifice to the spirits, the sacrifice to men, and the sacrifice to Brahman.
Day by day, one should offer oblations with the word "svāhā" until fuel sticks are exhausted; in this way, one completes this sacrifice to the gods.
Day by day, he should offer the *svadhā* oblation, at least with a vessel of water; in this way, he fulfills the requirement of the ancestral sacrifice (*pitṛyajña*).
Day after day, one should pay homage [to the elements] up to the flowers; thus one completes this sacrifice to the beings (bhūtayajña).
Day by day he should give food to Brahmins, even down to roots, fruits, and vegetables; in this way, he fulfills this sacrifice to men (manuṣyayajña).
Day by day he should perform the private recitation of the Veda up to the syllable *oṃ*; in this way, he completes this sacrifice to Brahman.

The private recitation of the Veda (*svādhyāya*) is indeed the sacrifice to Brahman. Of this very sacrifice to Brahman, speech is the *juhū* ladle, the mind is the *upabhṛt*, the eye is the *dhruvā*, intelligence is the *sruva* spoon, truth is the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*), and the heavenly world is the conclusion. Indeed, as great a world as one wins by giving away this earth filled with wealth, so great a world does he win—and even more than that, an inexhaustible one—who, knowing this, studies his private recitation; he conquers repeated death.

"Therefore, the Veda should be studied," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Furthermore, they also cite this: "Well-anointed, well-fed, and lying on a comfortable bed, whatever sacrifice one studies, by that very sacrifice it becomes as if performed for him."
Regarding this very dharma, some say that it has a fourfold division because it is not directly perceived; those who say there are four [stages of life] are proponents of ritual action (karmavāda).

[This applies] to the sacrifices performed with offerings (iṣṭi), those involving animal victims (pāśuka), those related to Soma (saumika), and the wood-offerings (dārvihoma). Regarding this, the following verse declares: "The four paths leading to the gods, which extend between heaven and earth—"
"O all you gods, grant him here among us who brings about for them freedom from decay and freedom from defeat. Thus [it is said].
The student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and the wandering mendicant.
A student of sacred knowledge shall serve his teacher until death.
The forest-dweller (vānaprastha) follows the conduct prescribed by the Vaikhānasa scriptures.

The Vaikhānasa, dwelling in the forest, subsisting on roots and fruits, devoted to austerity, performing ablutions at the three daily libations, having established the *śrāmaṇaka* fire, eating no village food, and worshipping gods, ancestors, spirits, men, and ṛṣis, shall provide hospitality to all guests; he may consume even meat that is not forbidden, provided it is obtained by purchase. He must not stand upon land tilled by the plough, nor enter a village. Wearing his hair in braids and clothed in rags or skins, he shall not eat more than once a year.
A wandering mendicant (parivrājaka), having abandoned his kinsmen and remaining without possessions, should go forth according to the prescribed rule;
having gone to the forest...
He should have only a tuft of hair on his head and be otherwise shaven.
He should possess only a loincloth for clothing. During the rainy season, he should stay in one place.
Wearing saffron-colored garments.
He should beg for alms when the pestle has been laid aside, when the embers have been extinguished, and when the exchange of bowls has ceased.
One who does not bear malice toward living beings through the restraints of speech, mind, and action.
One should carry a purifier for the sake of purification.
When performing water-related rites, one should do so with water that has been drawn up and strained.
Having cast aside Vedic rites, saying, "We shall cling to the middle state, being cut off from both sides," they [live].
But the teachers maintain that there is only one stage of life, because the others do not result in procreation.
Regarding this, they cite an example: "There was indeed an Asura named Kapila, the son of Prahlāda. Competing with the gods, he created these divisions. A wise man should not respect them."
"Because they are not seen. Regarding the phrase "those four," this is a statement concerning ritual action (*karmavāda*), referring to the *iṣṭi*, *paśu*, *saumika*, and *dārvihoma* sacrifices.
Regarding this, the following verse is recited:

"This is the eternal greatness of a Brāhmaṇa: he does not increase by action, nor does he become less. His very self is the knower of the path; having known that, he is not tainted by evil action. (BDhS 2.10.17.7)
He should say:

"By that splendor kindled by which the sun shines, through a son, a father becomes possessed of a father in his various wombs. One who does not know the Veda does not perceive that Great One, the Self who experiences all, in the hereafter. [K: in the hereafter]

"Those who move neither hither nor thither, who are not true Brahmins and do not offer the Soma sacrifice—they, having resorted to evil speech, weave a web like that of a spider, leading to lack of progeny. Thus it is said.

"O Agni, through offspring may I attain immortality. Indeed, when being born, a Brāhmaṇa is born burdened with three debts: he owes the sages the debt of studentship (*brahmacarya*), the gods the debt of sacrifice (*yajña*), and the ancestors the debt of progeny (*prajā*). Thus, there are innumerable statements concerning the connection with these debts. The triple knowledge, studentship, procreation, faith, austerity, sacrifice, and the giving of gifts—these are the seven kinds of wealth. Those who possess these are wealthy; those who lack them are poor. One should not honor a learned man who is without wealth, nor should one despise an ignorant man who possesses wealth. For knowledge is indeed the highest wealth. Even though a learned man may be destitute, one should honor him alone, for he is the best among men. Just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf, so sin does not cling to a learned man. Just as fire consumes dry grass, so does knowledge consume all evil deeds. Even if he is young in years, if he is endowed with learning and virtue, he is a "grandfather" (*pitāmaha*) and should be honored by the younger. Even if he is old in years, if he is devoid of learning and virtue, he is merely an "old man" (*vṛddha*) and should be avoided by the younger. As long as a learned man dwells in the house of another, he should be honored as if he were a guest; he should be fed before the household members and after the guests have been served. One should not eat food that has not been offered to a learned man. Whatever is given to a learned man becomes inexhaustible; whatever is given to an ignorant man reaches the ancestors alone. Therefore, one should give to a learned man, for he is the vessel for the offering. One should not give to an ignorant man, for it is like pouring an oblation into ashes. Just as a fire, when fanned by the wind, blazes up, so does knowledge, when imparted to a worthy recipient, increase. But just as water poured into a leaky jar does not remain, so does knowledge, when taught to an unworthy person, slip away. Therefore, one should examine a student carefully before initiating him, just as one examines a horse before mounting it. One should initiate a student who is pure, self-controlled, and free from defects. Having initiated him, one should instruct him in the Veda according to his capacity. One should not cause fatigue to a student, nor should one neglect his studies. One should always provide him with food, clothing, and a seat. One should never strike a student with the hand or with a stick, except to correct a physical defect. A teacher who imparts the Veda is a father; he who explains its meaning is a grandfather. Both should be honored with the same reverence as one's own parents. One should not dwell in the house of a teacher who is angry, nor in one who is lustful, nor in one who is greedy, nor in one who is negligent in his duties. One should live in the house of a teacher who is tranquil, self-restrained, and devoted to the sacred law. By living thus, a student attains long life and fame, and his merit increases daily. Having completed his studentship and having paid his debt to the teacher, he should marry a wife of equal caste who is endowed with auspicious marks. He should avoid a woman who is sickly, of low birth, or lacking in character. He should marry one who is not a *sapinda* relative and who has not been previously married to another. Having taken a wife, he should establish a household and perform the five great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*) daily. These are: the sacrifice to the Brahman (*brahmayajña*), the sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛyajña*), the sacrifice to the gods (*devayajña*), the sacrifice to all beings (*bhūtayajña*), and the sacrifice to men (*nṛyajña*). One should offer these sacrifices at the proper times, using the prescribed materials and methods. By performing these, a householder maintains the world and attains eternal bliss. One should not omit these sacrifices even for a single day; if they are omitted, the householder falls from his status. One should feed guests before one's own family, and should treat them with hospitality according to their merit. One should not refuse a guest who comes at the proper time, even if one has nothing to offer. One should offer food to a guest whether he is a friend or a stranger. One should not eat anything that has not first been shared with others. One should always speak the truth, and should speak what is pleasant. One should not speak what is true but unpleasant, nor what is pleasant but false. One should practice non-violence toward all living beings, both mobile and immobile. One should not steal, nor should one associate with thieves. One should be content with one's own property and should not covet the wealth of others. One should control one's senses and mind, and should be patient and self-restrained. One should be generous and compassionate, and should always seek the welfare of others. By following this path, a householder fulfills his duties and attains the highest state.
"Those who perform these [acts], we are with them; becoming dust, he perishes while praising something else.
Thus [it is said]. "He perishes while praising something else"—[K omits: he perishes while praising something else].
Now, we shall explain the oblations to the vital breaths (*prāṇāhuti*) of the *śālīna* and *yāyāvara* who sacrifice to the Self (*ātmayājin*).

At the conclusion of all necessary duties, having sat down facing the east in a place that has been swept and smeared with cow-dung, and having performed the ritual salutation (*upasthāna*) with the words "Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvar oṃ" as that [food] is being brought, he should restrain his speech.

Having sprinkled water clockwise around the food that has been set down with the *mahāvyāhṛtis*, and not releasing it with his left hand, he first drinks water with the formula, "Thou art the under-layer for immortality. Then, with the food, he offers the oblations to the vital breaths (*prāṇa-āhutis*): "Seated in the out-breath (*prāṇa*), I offer immortality; may thou enter me auspiciously, so that there be no burning. *Svāhā* to the out-breath! "Seated in the in-breath (*apāna*), I offer immortality; may thou enter me auspiciously, so that there be no burning. *Svāhā* to the in-breath! "Seated in the diffused breath (*vyāna*), I offer immortality..."

"May Śiva enter me for the sake of non-burning! Svāhā to the vyāna! Seated in the udāna, I offer the oblation of immortality. May Śiva enter me for the sake of non-burning! Svāhā to the udāna! Seated in the samāna, I offer the oblation of immortality. May Śiva enter me for the sake of non-burning! Svāhā to the samāna! Having offered these five oblations of food to the vital breaths (prāṇa), he should thereafter consume his meal in silence while meditating on Prajāpati with his mind; he must not utter speech in the interval.
BDhS 2.7.12.5: If he should utter speech in the interval, he should mutter "bhūr bhuvaḥ suvar oṃ" and then eat again. BDhS 2.7.12.6:

Upon seeing skin, hair, nails, insects, or mouse-droppings, he should remove that morsel from the spot, sprinkle it with water, scatter ashes over it, sprinkle it again with water, and then consume it after it has been verbally consecrated as pure.
Moreover, they also cite this:

"Seated, facing the east, with speech controlled, one should eat food without disparaging it; without letting [the food] fall, and with the mind fixed on that [act], having eaten, one should touch fire. Thus [it is said].
One should not bite with the teeth any food that requires chewing, such as cakes, bulbs, roots, fruits, or meat. One should not eat until completely satiated.

With the mantra, "Thou art the covering of immortality," having drunk water from above and sipped water for purification, he touches the region of his heart with the mantra: "Thou art the knot of the vital breaths; enter me as the pacifying Rudra; swell with this food."
Having sipped water again, he pours out the remainder from his hands onto the big toe of his right foot, [reciting]:
"A person the size of a thumb dwells within the thumb;
the Lord of the entire world, the Master, the consumer of all, is pleased. (BDhS 2.7.12.11-2ab, 3cd)

With hands raised, he should perform the consecration of the oblation (*hutānumantraṇa*): "Entering into faith (*śraddhā*) and the out-breath (*prāṇa*), the immortal oblation has been offered. Satisfy the out-breath with food. Entering into faith and the in-breath (*apāna*), the immortal oblation has been offered. Satisfy the out-breath with food. Entering into faith and the diffused breath (*vyāna*), the immortal oblation has been offered. Satisfy the out-breath with food. Entering into faith and the upward breath (*udāna*), the immortal oblation has been offered. Satisfy the out-breath with food. Entering into faith and the equalizing breath (*samāna*), the immortal oblation has been offered."
"O Prāṇa, swell with food"—with these five [verses].
"May my self in Brahman be for immortality."
And one should unite the self with the syllable.
Among those who perform all types of sacrifices, the one who sacrifices to the Self is distinguished as superior.
Moreover, they also cite this:
For just as cotton from the *iṣīkā* reed, when cast into fire, is set ablaze,
even so all the sins of one who sacrifices to the Self are consumed by fire.
"He who eats alone becomes the sole possessor of sin; the thoughtless man obtains food in vain. (BDhS 2.7.13.2)
In this very manner, he should offer oblations every day, both evening and morning.
Or, in the evening, with water.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"First, one should feed the guests; immediately thereafter, those who are pregnant;
likewise the children, the elderly, the indigent, and especially the sick."
But he who eats before giving to these [ancestors, gods, and guests] according to the rule—eating while remaining unaware—he does not eat; rather, he is eaten.

"Restraining his speech, he should eat the remains of the food after serving the ancestors, the deities, his dependents, as well as his mother, father, and teacher; thus is the dharma ordained. (BDhS 2.7.13.6)
Moreover, they also cite this:
"An ascetic (*muni*) should eat eight morsels; one living in the forest (*āraṇyavāsin*) sixteen;
a householder (*gṛhastha*) thirty-two; and for a student (*brahmacārin*), there is no limit."
"The one who has maintained the sacred fires, the ox, and the student—these three succeed only while eating;
there is no success for them while fasting. Thus it is said.
Whether he be a householder or a student, whoever practices austerity while fasting becomes an *avakīrṇin* through the neglect of the *prāṇāgnihotra*.
Except in the case of a penance; regarding a penance, the rule is exactly that.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"Between the morning meal and likewise the evening meal,
he who never eats at all is one who is perpetually fasting."
"But when eating is obstructed, one should mutter the mantras of the Prāṇāgnihotra;
and just as one would mutter the mantras of the Tretāgnihotra when the sacrificial materials are unavailable. Thus it is said.
Acting in this manner, one is fit for becoming Brahman; "one is fit for becoming Brahman. The ancestral rite (pitrya) bestows long life, leads to heaven, brings fame, and provides nourishment.

One who knows the *trimadhu*, one who knows the *triṇāciketa*, one who knows the *trisuparṇa*, one who maintains the five fires, one who knows the six auxiliary sciences (*ṣaḍaṅga*), one who knows the *śīrṣaka*, one who knows the *jyeṣṭhasāman*, and a *snātaka*—these are the purifiers of the assembly (*paṅktipāvana*).
In the absence of that, one who knows the secret [teachings].
"The Rig-verses, the Yajus-formulas, and the Sāman-chants—this is the greatness of the Śrāddha. Therefore, one who knows this should feed even a sapinda relative."

One should cause him to hear, slowly and with focused intent, the *sāmans* that destroy demons, the *yajus* formulas containing the word *svadhā*, the honey-verses (*madhvṛc*), and the purificatory texts (*pavitra*).

On the previous day, or indeed early in the morning, he should invite an odd number—at least three—of those who are pure, learned in the Vedas, possessed of good conduct, not related by birth, lineage, or mantra, and conversant with the sacred texts; having invited them, he seats them on seats prepared with *darbha* grass, facing either eastward or northward.

Then, having caused them to receive water mixed with sesame seeds and having adorned them with perfumes and garlands, he says, "I shall offer in the fire. Being permitted, he kindles the fire, strews grass around it, performs the *agnimukha* rite, and offers three oblations of food alone, saying: "To Soma, who is drunk by the ancestors, *svadhā*, homage, *svāhā*. To Yama, accompanied by the Aṅgirases and the ancestors, *svadhā*, homage, *svāhā*. To Agni Kavyavāhana, the maker of good offerings, *svadhā*, homage, *svāhā*. [K: having performed [the rites] with clarified butter alone].
Having sprinkled the food with the remainder of that [clarified butter], he should offer these same three oblations of the food [or, according to K: three oblations].
He should give a ball of food to birds.
"For it is known from sacred tradition that the ancestors move about in the likeness of birds."
Then he touches the other [parts] with his hand together with the thumb.

"O you who are equal to the earth, Agni is your witness; the *ṛc* verses are your greatness for the non-neglect of what has been given. The earth is your vessel, the sky is the lid; I offer you into the mouth of Brahman. I offer you into the out-breath and in-breath of the learned Brāhmaṇas. You are imperishable; may you not perish among the ancestors there in yonder world. [K: equal to the earth].

"Vāyu is the listener for you who are equal to the intermediate space; the Yajus-formulas are your greatness for the non-neglect of what has been given. The earth is your vessel, the sky is the lid; I offer you into the mouth of Brahman; I offer you into the out-breath and in-breath of the learned Brāhmaṇas. You are imperishable; may you not perish among my grandfathers there in that world."

"May the sun be the witness of that which is equal to heaven; may the *sāmans* be the illuminators of those [offerings]; may there be no negligence regarding what has been given. The earth is your vessel, the sky is the lid; I offer you into the mouth of the *brahman*. I offer you into the out-breath and in-breath of the learned *brāhmaṇas*. You are imperishable; may you not perish for my great-grandfathers in yonder world, in that world.
Now, indeed, it is said: "BDhS 2.8.15.1" [The text continues: "Now, indeed, it comes to pass..."
One should sprinkle that food with the remnants from the oblation into the fire;
for that which is offered without the thumb does not indeed gratify the ancestors.
When food is offered to the ancestors, released from both hands,
the evil-minded Asuras wait for that interval;
the Yātudhānas and Piśācas plunder that sacrificial offering.
For by the gift of sesame seeds, those who are without heirs [attain heaven], and likewise the Asuras through the power of anger.
Whatever recitations, burnt offerings, or acceptances of gifts one performs while wearing saffron-colored robes—

that oblation, whether among offerings to the gods (*havya*) or offerings to the ancestors (*kavya*), does not reach the deities. And whatever is given without the thumb, or whatever is accepted in that same manner, [is likewise ineffective].
"And he who sips water while standing does not prosper by that act. Thus it is said.
In all cases, water is offered at the beginning and at the end.
From the point of victory onwards, according to the prescribed rule.
The remainder has been explained in the section on the Aṣṭakā oblation.
At a rite for the gods, one should feed two; at a rite for the ancestors, three; or one at each of the two.
Even if he is very wealthy, he should not be overly attached to a large company.
Hospitality, the proper place and time, purity, and the excellence of the Brahmins—these five are destroyed by prolixity; therefore, one should avoid it.
"His ancestors are in front, his grandfathers on the left, and his great-grandfathers on the right; behind him are those who seek the funeral cakes. Thus it is said.
The instruction for one desiring offspring.
"The designation is based on the cause of procreation," said the two Aśvins.
Endowed with long life and austerity, devoted to the private recitation of the Veda and sacrifice,
and having conquered his senses, he should diligently procreate offspring within his own respective caste (or lineage).
From birth, a Brāhmaṇa enters into a bond of debt with three [obligations]. By discharging them, he becomes self-possessed and liberated from doubt regarding dharma.
Having honored the seers through the private recitation of the Vedas, Indra with the Soma sacrifice,
and his ancestors of old with offspring, he rejoices in heaven, freed from debt.
"Through a son one conquers the worlds; through a grandson one attains immortality;
and through a great-grandson, one ascends to the very heavens. Thus it is said.

And it is declared in the Veda: "A Brāhmaṇa, being born, is born with three debts—to the sages through studentship, to the gods through sacrifice, and to the ancestors through progeny. Thus the Veda shows this connection with debts.
By procreating a virtuous son, one delivers oneself.
A man who obtains a virtuous son delivers seven descendants, seven ancestors, and six others, himself being the seventh, from sin and fear.
Therefore, having produced a lineage of offspring, one attains the fruit.
Therefore, one should exert effort to produce offspring.
Through the application of medicinal herbs and mantras.
The instruction regarding that [duty] is taught by means of a similarity in verbal expression.
"Because it bears fruit for all social classes. [Regarding the phrase] "because it bears fruit":
[Deutero-Baudhāyana] BDhS 2.10.17.1: Now, therefore, we shall explain the rule for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*).
"Because of this very [reason], he departs as a wandering mendicant while still observing the vow of celibacy; so say some."
Now, [the rules] for those of the Śālīna and Yāyāvara classes who are childless.
Or, being destitute, he may establish his offspring in their own duty, or [he may go forth].
After seventy years, they prescribe renunciation.
Or [the time for study] is at the cessation of the duties of a forest-dweller.

"This is the eternal greatness of a Brāhmaṇa: he does not increase by action, nor does he become smaller. His very self is the knower of the path; having known that, he is not tainted by evil action. Thus [it is said]. (BDhS 2.6.11.30) "He leads one to non-rebirth; therefore, he is eternal. (BDhS 2.10.17.8)
Because it causes him to go to greatness, it is called "mahimā" (greatness).
Having had his hair, beard, body hair, and nails shaved off, he prepares [the following items].
The staffs, the sling, the water-strainer, the water-pot, and the bowl.
Having taken these—clarified butter, milk, and curd—to the edge of the village or the boundary of the village, or to the fire-sanctuary, he should consume this threefold mixture and fast.
Or water.

"Oṃ bhūḥ, I enter the Sāvitrī: *tat savitur vareṇyam*. Oṃ bhuvaḥ, I enter the Sāvitrī: *bhargo devasya dhīmahi*. Oṃ suvaḥ, I enter the Sāvitrī: *dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt*. Thus, [he recites] by quarters, then by half-verses, and then both in its entirety and separately.
"Having led himself from one stage of life (āśrama) to another stage of life, he becomes purified by Brahman"—so it is known.
Furthermore, they also cite:
"Having gone from one stage of life to another stage of life, having offered oblations, and having conquered his senses..."
"Exhausted by begging and making offerings, he subsequently becomes a mendicant. Thus it is said.
This very mendicant leads to infinity.

Before sunset, having kindled the *gārhapatya* fire, brought the *anvāhāryapacana* fire, and drawn out the flaming *āhavanīya* fire, he melts clarified butter over the *gārhapatya*, purifies it, takes four portions into the *sruva* ladle, and offers a full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) into the *āhavanīya* which has a fuel-stick placed upon it, saying: "Oṃ svāhā!"
"This is known as the Brahmānvādhāna."

Then, when the evening *agnihotra* has been offered, having spread grass-blades to the north of the *gārhapatya* fire and placed the vessels upon them in pairs with their openings facing downward, and having spread *darbha* grass in the *brahmāyatana* to the south of the *āhavanīya* fire and placed a black antelope skin over it, he remains awake for that night.

A Brāhmaṇa who, knowing this, fasts on the night of Brahmā, consigns his sacred fires within himself, and dies, overcomes all evil; he overcomes even the murder of a Brāhmaṇa. Then, rising during the *muhūrta* of Brahmā, he performs the morning *agnihotra* at the very proper time.
Then, having strewn the *pṛṣṭhyā* line and having carried forward the waters, he offers a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara. That well-known sacrifice is concluded.

He throws the *agnihotra* vessels—those not made of clay and not made of stone—into the *āhavanīya* fire, with the mantra: "May you two be of one mind for us. He throws the two kindling sticks (*araṇī*) into the *gārhapatya* fire with the mantra: "May you two be of one mind for us."
He internalizes the fires within himself. With the mantra, "O Agni, that body of yours which is fit for sacrifice," he smells each of the fires three times.

Then, standing within the sacrificial altar (antarvedi), having recited three times in a low voice—"Om, Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Suvaḥ; it has been renounced by me, it has been renounced by me, it has been renounced by me"—he recites it three times aloud.
"For the gods are indeed three-truthed," so it is known from scripture.
Saying, "Fearlessness to all beings from me," he pours out a full handful of water.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"The sage who wanders about after having granted freedom from fear to all beings—no fear arises for him from any being, even in this world. Thus it is said.
He remains silent.
With the words, "O friend, protect me," he takes up the staff.
With the words, "That which is on the further shore of the darkness," he grasps the sling.
With the mantra, "By that purifier with which the gods... he takes up the water-purifier.
With the mantra, "By which the gods rose upward through the light," he takes up the water-pot.
He takes up the vessel with the seven vyāhṛtis.

Having taken up his staff, sling, water-strainer, water-pot, and bowl, he goes to where there is water; having bathed, sipped water, and purified himself with the *surabhimatī*, *ābliṅga*, *vāruṇī*, *hiraṇyavarṇā*, and *pāvamānī* verses, he enters the water and performs sixteen breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) while reciting the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn. Having emerged, wrung out his garment, put on another clean garment, and sipped water, he recites: "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ."

Taking up the water-strainer, he offers libations: "Oṃ bhūḥ, I offer libation; Oṃ bhuvaḥ, I offer libation; Oṃ suvaḥ, I offer libation; Oṃ mahaḥ, I offer libation; Oṃ janaḥ, I offer libation; Oṃ tapaḥ, I offer libation; Oṃ satyam, I offer libation."
Having offered a handful of water to the ancestors as one does for the gods, he says: “Oṃ bhūḥ svadhā; Oṃ bhuvaḥ svadhā; Oṃ suvaḥ svadhā; Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ suvar mahar namaḥ.
Then, with the two verses beginning “ud u tyam” and “citram,” he worships the sun.

"Om" is Brahman. Indeed, he who shines yonder is the light; he who shines yonder is the Veda; he who shines yonder is that which is to be known. Thus, he satisfies his own self; he pays homage to his own self. The self is Brahman; the self is the light. One should repeat the Sāvitrī one thousand times, or a hundred times, or an unlimited number of times.

BDhS 2.10.17.42: Reciting "oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ suvar," he takes up water and a water-purifier (*pavitra*) and draws water. BDhS 2.10.17.43: From this point forward, he shall not sip water that has not been drawn out, nor that which is unstrained, nor that which is unpurified. BDhS 2.10.17.44: And from this point forward, he shall not wear white clothing.
He may carry either a single staff or three staffs.
Now, these observances come into being: non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, and the avoidance of sexual intercourse; as well as renunciation. Thus indeed.
There are exactly five secondary vows: freedom from anger, service to the teacher, vigilance, purity, and purity of food.
Now follows the practice of begging for alms: he should seek alms from Brāhmaṇas who follow the *śālīna* and *yāyāvara* modes of life, after the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice has been completed.
One should cause [the guest] to pronounce the word "bhavat" first.
He should wait for the duration of a cow-milking.

Then, having returned from the practice of begging for alms, he should wash his hands and feet in a clean place and offer them before the sun with the hymns "ud u tyam" and "citram. He offers them to Brahman with the hymn "brahma jajñānam."

It is known from scripture: "From the time of the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*) onwards, the fires belong to the sacrificer alone. His *prāṇa* is the *gārhapatya*, his *apāna* is the *anvāhāryapacana*, his *vyāna* is the *āhavanīya*, and his *udāna* and *samāna* are the *sabhya* and *āvasathya*. These five fires are situated within the self; he offers into the self itself."
This very sacrifice to the Self, centered in the Self and established in the Self, leads the Self to security; so it is known.
Having first distributed [the food] to living beings with compassion, he should touch the remainder with water and eat it like medicinal herbs.

Having consumed [the food] and sipped water, he worships the sun with the *jyotiṣmatī* verse, "Out of the darkness we have risen... (RV 7.89.2), after having murmured, "May speech be in my mouth; may breath be in my nostrils.
He should eat only as much food as is necessary for the maintenance of life—food that is unasked for, not prepared in anticipation, and obtained by chance. Thus it is said.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"An ascetic (*muni*) should eat eight morsels; one living in the forest (*āraṇyavāsin*) sixteen;
a householder (*gṛhastha*) thirty-two; and for a student (*brahmacārin*), there is no limit."

"Alms may be sought from members of all castes, or a single meal from twice-born men; or alternatively, alms may be sought from members of all castes, but never a single meal from twice-born men alone. Thus it is said.
Now, regarding that which the teachers declare to be the Upaniṣad, they cite this:

for one who is engaged in the observances of standing, silence, the hero’s posture (*vīrāsana*), bathing at the three libations (*savana*), and touching water, as well as the vows of the fourth, sixth, and eighth parts of the day, there is the practice of subsisting on grain-particles, oil-cakes, barley-gruel, curd, and milk.

In that regard, being engaged in silence, he should converse only as much as necessary with those learned in the three Vedas, with teachers, with sages, or with others belonging to the various stages of life who are deeply versed in scripture—keeping his teeth joined to his teeth, facing inward, and not conversing with women. It is known from tradition that there must be no lapse in this practice. (BDhS 2.10.18.16) He should employ one of the following: standing, silence, or the hero’s posture (*vīrāsana*). He should not bring these three together simultaneously. (BDhS 2.10.18.17)
It is known from tradition that wherever one has gone, one should observe the vows to such an extent that there is no lapse of them even in times of distress.

For one who is engaged in the vows at the fourth, sixth, and eighth meal-times, characterized by standing, silence, the vīrāsana posture, ritual bathing at the *savana* periods, and touching water; these eight do not destroy the vow: water, roots, ghee, milk, sacrificial oblation (*havis*), the desire of a Brāhmaṇa, the word of a teacher, and medicine.
He should mutter the mantras of the Agnihotra sacrifice in the evening and in the morning.
Having performed the evening twilight worship with the *vāruṇī* verses and the morning twilight worship with the *maitrī* verses;
the sage should be without fire, without a fixed dwelling, without shelter, and without a refuge.
Seeking alms for the sake of sustenance, he should enter the village; otherwise, he should restrain his speech for the sake of Vedic study. Thus it is said.

And it is known from scripture: "The *ṛc*s are limited, the *sāmans* are limited, and the *yajus* formulas are limited; but of this *brahman*, there is no end. One should announce that to the one who responds; that is the response (*pratigara*)."
