In this very manner, until the liberation from the body, he remains a tree-root dweller and a renouncer of the Vedas.
The Veda is a tree; its root is the *praṇava*. The Veda has the *praṇava* as its essence.
"Prajāpati said: 'Meditating upon the *praṇava*, one who possesses the *praṇava* becomes fit for union with Brahman.
One should wash the vessel of Brahman with the seven *vyāhṛtis*; one should wash it."
Now, concerning those who desire to follow the dharma of the *śālīna*, *yāyāvara*, and *cakracara* [householders], who subsist by means of nine modes of livelihood:
Because they proceed by means of those [duties], it is called their "livelihood" (vṛtti).
Because it takes its refuge in the house (śālā), it is called *śālīna*.
The state of being a Yāyāvara arises from the fact that one proceeds by means of an excellent mode of livelihood.
Because they move in succession, they are called "wheel-moving" (cakracara).
We shall explain them in detail.

The six *nivartanī*, the *kauddālī*, the *dhruvā*, the *saṃprakṣālanī*, the *samūhā*, the *phālanī*, the *śiloñchā*, the *kāpotā*, and the *siddhecchā*—these are the nine. BDhS 3.1.8: Or there is yet another tenth mode of livelihood among these. BDhS 3.1.9: Up to the ninth mode of livelihood.
Having had his hair, beard, body hair, and nails shaved, he prepares [the following items].
BDhS 3.1.11: A black antelope skin, a water-pot, a staff, a shoulder-pack, and a woolen garment (*kutapa*).
BDhS 3.1.12: Having performed the *traidhātavīya* sacrifice, he shall set out, or having performed the *vaiśvānarī* sacrifice.

BDhS 3.1.13: Then, in the morning when the sun has risen, having kindled the fires according to the sūtra, having melted the clarified butter over the *gārhapatya* fire and purified it, having heated and wiped the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, and having taken four portions of butter into the *sruk*, he offers the oblation to Vāstoṣpati in the *āhavanīya* fire. BDhS 3.1.14: Having recited the invitatory verse (*puronuvākyā*), "O Vāstoṣpati, recognize us," he offers the oblation with the offering verse (*yājyā*), "O Vāstoṣpati, with a propitious dwelling..."
"Some say that all [these acts] apply only to one who has established the sacred fires."
"According to some, he is a Yāyāvara."
Having departed, he stays at the edge of a village or at the boundary of a village; there he builds a hut or a monastery, or enters one already built.
BDhS 3.1.18: One should employ the black antelope skin and other items that have been prepared for their respective purposes according to the specific requirement each serves.

BDhS 3.1.19: The maintenance of the sacred fires is well known; the performance of the New and Full Moon sacrifices is well known; the regular practice of the five great sacrifices is well known; and the offering of the plants that have grown is seen as a well-established practice.
Having prepared them with the formula, "I offer what is pleasing to the Viśvedevas," or silently, he cooks them.
For him, teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and accepting gifts are discontinued, as are other sacrificial rites.
And it is observed that the sacrificial food (haviṣya) is also suitable for the commencement of a vow.
BDhS 3.1.23: That is to say, [food] mixed with clarified butter, mixed with curd, not pungent, not salty, without meat, and not stale.
BDhS 3.1.24: He observes celibacy, or he approaches his wife during her season.
At every change of the moon, one should have the hair of the head, the beard, the body hair, and the nails shaved, as well as perform the rules for purification.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"Two kinds of purity are heard of, which have been practiced by the cultured (śiṣṭas):
external purity, which is free from stains and odors; and internal purity, which is non-injurious."
"The limbs are purified by water; the intellect is purified by knowledge;
the inner self (bhūtātman) is purified by non-violence; and the mind is purified by truth. Thus it is said.
Regarding this which has been stated: "the sixfold turning back."
He makes exactly six turnings that are free from defects; he either sets aside a portion for the owner or takes it with permission.
BDhS 3.2.3: Before his morning meal, he should be a plowman, not piercing [the animals'] nostrils or their testicles, and prodding them repeatedly with a goad while encouraging them.
BDhS 3.2.4: By this method, he performs six turns; thus it is called the "six-turn" (*ṣaṇṇivartanī*) cultivation.

BDhS 3.2.5: Regarding the "hoe-cultivation" (*kauddālī*): near a body of water, he digs with a hoe, a plowshare, or a sharp piece of wood; he sows seeds and produces bulbs, roots, fruits, vegetables, and medicinal herbs.
One who works with a spade is called a *kauddālī*.

Moving with the *dhruvā* formula, he wraps his head with a white cloth, saying: "For prosperity, I wrap your head. He takes up a black antelope skin with the formula: "You are Vedic luster; for Vedic luster, you," and a strainer with formulas that do not contain the word *bhūti*. He takes up a water-pot with the formula: "You are strength; for strength, you. He takes up a carrying-pole with the formula: "You are grain; for nourishment, you. He takes up a staff with the formula: "Friend, protect me."
Then, having gone outside and muttered the *vyāhṛtis*, he mutters the consecration of the quarters:
"May the earth, the intermediate space, the sky, the stars, and the quarters;
may Agni, Vāyu, and Sūrya—may these deities protect me on the path. Thus.
Having recited the *mānastokīya* hymn and entered the village, he presents himself at every door of the houses along with his pack-load; this is what they call "making oneself visible."
When one occupation fails after another, because one subsists permanently by that very [occupation], it is proclaimed as "dhruvā" (the permanent).

"Saṃprakṣālanī" means the throwing away of herbs that have grown. There is no setting aside or hoarding; rather, having thoroughly washed the vessels, one turns them upside down—thus it is called "saṃprakṣālanī."

Regarding the term *samūhā*: wherever medicinal plants are found—in unobstructed places, on paths, in fields, or in open spaces—one gathers them by means of gathering (*samūhanyā*) and subsists upon them; thus she is called *samūhā*.

BDhS 3.2.13: "Phālanī" means non-injury; this is what is being stated here. She desires husked rice grains or seeds from virtuous people. Because she "cultivates" (phālayati) [them], she is called *phālanī*. [K: *Pālanī*... because she protects (*pālayati*), she is *pālanī*. BDhS 3.2.14: "Śiloñcha. In places where grain is not forbidden—on paths, in fields, or in open spaces wherever herbs are found—she gathers a single ear of grain (*kaṇiśa*) from each place and subsists on gleanings (*śila*) from time to time. Thus, she is called *śiloñcha*. [K: *Śiloñcha*... thus, she is *śiloñcha*.]

Regarding the *kāpotī* [gleaning]: in unobstructed places, on paths, in fields, or in any open space where herbs are found, one gathers a single herb at each spot with the fingers by means of pinching; because it is done like a pigeon (*kapota*), it is called *kāpotī*.

"Desiring what is prepared" (siddhecchā): one who, exhausted by his means of livelihood, or due to old age or the depletion of the bodily humors, desires food that has already been prepared by others; thus he is "one desiring what is prepared."

BDhS 3.2.17: For him, there is the internal mental transference (of the fires) into himself; his conduct is like that of a renunciant (*saṃnyāsin*), with the exception of the sacred grass ring (*pavitraka*) and the saffron-colored garment (*kāṣāya-vāsa*).

BDhS 3.2.18: Or else, he subsists on forest-grown grains (*vānyā*), such as trees, shrubs, creepers, medicinal herbs, and grasses, including *śyāmāka*, wild sesame (*jartila*), and so forth. Because he subsists by means of these forest-grown items, it is called "subsisting on forest-grown grains" (*vānyā*). BDhS 3.2.19-1: Now they also cite this example:
Moving about together with wild animals, dwelling with them alone,
and a mode of life identical to theirs— this is the manifest characteristic of heaven.
"The characteristic of heaven is perceptible. (BDhS 3.2.19–3) [BDhS 3.2.19 = BDhS 3.3.22].
Now, there are two types of forest-dwellers (vānaprastha). (BDhS 3.3.1) [K: of the forest-dweller, there are two types].
Those who cook and those who do not cook.

Among them, those who cook for themselves are of five kinds: those who live entirely in the forest, those who remove the husks from grain, those who eat roots and tubers, those who eat fruits, and those who eat vegetables.
In that regard, those known as the *sarvāraṇyaka* are of two kinds, as they resort to two types of forest-dwelling: the *indrāvasikta* and the *retovasikta*.

In that case, having brought creepers, shrubs, climbing plants, and trees known as *indrāvasiktā*, and having cooked them, he performs the morning and evening *agnihotra* oblations; then, having given portions to guests and those observing vows, the rest is for those who eat the remnants.

Regarding those [animals] called "impregnated by semen" (*retovasikta*), having brought meat killed by a tiger, a wolf, a hawk, or any other such predator, and having cooked it, one should offer the morning and evening *agnihotra* oblations, give portions to ascetics, guests, and those observing vows, and then the rest shall be eaten as remnants.

Those who subsist on grain that has been dehusked, having brought rice-grains excluding those with husks and having cooked them, perform the Agnihotra sacrifice morning and evening, give [the food] to ascetics, guests, and those observing vows, and then consume the remainder as their meal.
The same rule applies even to those who subsist on bulbs, roots, fruits, and vegetables.
There are exactly five types of those who do not cook for themselves: the unmajjaka, the pravṛttāśin, the mukhenādāyin, the toyāhāra, and the vāyubhakṣa.
In that regard, those called "emerging" (unmajjakas) are [those who emerge from the water] except for those made of iron or stone.
Those who eat what has been set forth, taking it with their hands.
Those who eat with their mouths, they eat with their mouths.
Subsisting on water means subsisting solely on water.
They subsist on air and remain without food.
Thus, ten initiations (*dīkṣā*) are prescribed for the Vaikhānasas.
He who, having undertaken his own scripture, maintains discipline, silence, and vigilance—
the Vaikhānasas are purified by being without food.
The acceptance of the sacred scriptures is mandatory for all members of the Brahman and Vaikhānasa orders.
He should not harm gadflies or mosquitoes; he should be like the Himalayas, a true ascetic, established in the forest, contented, and fond of bark garments, skins, and water.
A forest-dweller, devoted to austerity, should first honor guests who arrive at his hermitage at the proper time,
as well as the gods, Brahmins, and the sacred fires.
A life of hardship that cannot be taken away, common to beasts and birds,
procured from people on that very day, and consisting of astringent and bitter foods.
Having adopted this auspicious mode of life, which is avoided by the wicked,
and having taken refuge in dwelling in the forest, a Brāhmaṇa does not come to grief.
Moving about together with wild animals, dwelling together with them alone,
and a mode of life identical to theirs— this is the manifest characteristic of heaven.
"The characteristic of heaven is perceptible.
Now, if a religious student (*brahmacārin*) should act as if contrary to his vow, or eat meat, or have sexual intercourse with a woman—even in all cases of distress.

BDhS 3.4.2: Having kindled the fire within the inner chamber and strewn grass around it, and having performed the rites beginning with the oblation to Agni, he then offers the following oblations of clarified butter: "By desire was it done; desire performs [the act]; to desire indeed belongs all this—svāhā! To him who causes me to do it, svāhā! By the mind was it done; the mind performs [the act]; to the mind indeed belongs all this—svāhā! To him who causes me to do it, svāhā! By passion (rajas) was it done; passion performs [the act]; to passion indeed belongs all this—svāhā! To him who causes me to do it, svāhā!"

"Darkness performs what is done by darkness; all this belongs to darkness alone—to him who makes me do it, *svāhā*. Evil performs what is done by evil; all this belongs to evil alone—to him who makes me do it, *svāhā*. Wrath performs what is done by wrath; all this belongs to wrath alone—to him who makes me do it, *svāhā*. {cf. BDhS 2.8.14.7} BDhS 3.4.3:
From the *jaya* offering onwards, the rite is established until the granting of the boon of cows.
Having covered himself behind the fire with a black antelope skin, with the neck pointing eastward and the hair facing upward, he dwells there.

When the dawn has broken, having drawn himself away from the rear part [of the sacrificial ground], gone to a bathing place, and bathed according to the established rule, he stands within the water and performs sixteen breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) while reciting the *aghamaṣaṇa* hymn; then, having performed the established ritual of worshiping the sun, he goes to the house of his teacher.
One should understand this to be just like the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) at the end of a horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*).
BDhS 3.5.1 Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual procedure for the Aghamarṣaṇa, which is the most purifying of purifiers.

Having gone to a sacred bathing place (tīrtha), bathed, and dressed in clean garments, he should prepare a level space on the edge of the water; then, with a garment moistened once and with his hand filled once, facing the sun, he should recite the Aghamarṣaṇa as a private Vedic study (svādhyāya).
One hundred [repetitions] in the morning, one hundred at midday, one hundred in the afternoon, or an unlimited number.
When the stars have risen, he should consume a handful of barley-gruel.

One is released from minor offenses (upapātaka) committed intentionally or unintentionally after seven nights, except for the killing of an embryo, violating the teacher’s bed, stealing gold, and drinking liquor, which require twelve nights.
By a twenty-one-night rite, one crosses over even those [sins] and conquers them as well.

"Baudhāyana says that [one who performs this] crosses over everything, conquers everything, obtains the fruit of all sacrifices, becomes as one who has bathed in all sacred fords, becomes one who has fulfilled his vows in all the Vedas, becomes known by all the gods, purifies the lineage up to the sixth degree, and his rites become successful."
BDhS 3.6.1: Now, if one should consider oneself as heavy with the weight of deeds committed by oneself, one should cook a handful of barley-gruel for one's own sake when the stars have risen.
One should not offer an oblation into the fire from that [food].
And there is no offering of the bali-oblation here.
One should recite the mantra over the uncooked food, while it is being cooked, and once it is cooked.

BDhS 3.6.5-1ab: "You are barley; you are the king of grains; you belong to Varuṇa and are mixed with honey. BDhS 3.6.5-1cd: You are the cleanser of all sins; you are remembered by the seers as a means of purification."
Barley is ghee, barley is honey, barley is water, barley is nectar;

may they purify all the evil that has been committed by me through misdeeds. Whatever was done with speech, whatever deed was performed, or whatever was ill-conceived with the mind—[may they purify it].
O barley grains, purify for me all ill fortune and misfortune (kālakarṇī).
O barley grains, purify for me everything that has been brushed aside by dogs or pigs, that which is defiled by the leavings of crows, and the failure to serve one's mother and father.
"O barley grains, purify for me all that is joined with mortal sins, the terrible offenses against the king, the conduct of children and the aged, and every unrighteousness.
[Purify] the theft of gold, the violation of vows, and the officiating at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice."

"May all barley purify for me the censure of Brahmins! May the barley purify for me the food of a group, the food of a courtesan, the food of a Śūdra, the food from a funeral rite or a period of birth/impurity, the food of a thief, and all food from a recent funeral rite! Thus it is said.

While the food is being cooked, he should perform protection rites with the following: "Homage to Rudra, the lord of beings! May the sky be peaceful! and with this *anuvāka*, "Make your strength wide like a net," as well as the five sections beginning with "The gods who sit in front, led by Agni, slayers of demons," and the two verses beginning with "Mā nas toke" and "Brahmā devānām.
When the food is cooked, he should eat it quickly, having poured it into a vessel while remaining pure.

"O gods born of the mind, yoked by the mind, highly skillful, with Dakṣa as father—may they protect us, may they favor us; homage to them, svāhā to them!"—thus one should offer the oblation into oneself.
One who desires intelligence [should fast] for three nights.
Having drunk [it] for six nights, an evildoer becomes pure.

Having drunk [the kṣīrodaka] for seven nights, one purifies even the killing of a learned Brahmin (bhrūṇahatyā), sexual intercourse with the teacher’s wife, the theft of gold, and the drinking of liquor.
By drinking it for eleven nights, one expiates even the sin committed by one's ancestors.

"Or else, having drunk barley-gruel made from grains that have emerged from a cow for twenty-one nights, one beholds the hosts, beholds the lord of the hosts, beholds knowledge, and beholds the lord of knowledge—so says the venerable Baudhāyana."
BDhS 3.7.1: One who considers himself impure should offer oblations with the Kūṣmāṇḍa mantras.
BDhS 3.7.2: Just as a thief, just as a killer of an embryo, so indeed does he become who sheds semen in a place other than the womb.
"By this, one is released from whatever sin prior to the killing of an embryo."
Having emitted semen in a place other than the womb, except during sleep, one who is free from taint or desires purification [should perform penance].
On either the new moon day or the full moon day, having had his hair, beard, body hair, and nails shaved, he undertakes the vow according to the rule for a student.
For one year, or one month, or twenty-four days, or twelve nights, or six, or three.
He shall not eat meat, he shall not approach a woman, he shall not sit on a high seat, and he shall loathe falsehood.
Subsisting on milk is the first rule; or, consuming barley-gruel, he should perform the twelve-night kṛcchra penance or beg for alms.
In the case of such persons, a Kṣatriya should offer gruel (yavāgū), and a Vaiśya should offer curd-mixture (āmikṣā).

In the forenoon, having established the fire according to the ritual rules for the *pākayajña* and having strewn grass around it, he performs the rites beginning with the oblation to Agni (*agnimukha*), and then offers oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) with these three sections (*anuvāka*): "Whatever offense against the gods we have committed," "When not gambling, whatever debt I have incurred," and "Bestowing life upon you from every side. He should offer the clarified butter verse by verse.

He offers four oblations with the wooden spoon (*sruva*), reciting: "siṃhe vyāghra uta yā pṛdākau" (RV 8.48.5–8). Having offered the four "returning" oblations (*abhyāvartinī*) with the verses "agne 'bhyāvartin," "agne aṅgiraḥ," "punar ūrjā," and "saha rayyā," he stands in the world of the sacrificer with fuel-sticks in hand and worships with the twelve-verse hymn beginning, "vaiśvānarāya prati vedayāmaḥ.
[BDhS 3.7.13] "Whatever sin has ever been committed by me through mind or speech... (RV 6.51.7).
"Be gracious to me from all that; for you know it as it truly is, svāhā! Having placed a fuel-stick on the fire, he gives a boon.
From the *jaya* oblation onwards, the ritual is established until the giving of the cow and the boon.
Only one person shall attend to the fire.

Now, regarding the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*): "Whatever offense against the gods we have committed, whatever debt I incurred while not gambling—bestowing long life upon you from every side," with these words, he offers full oblations (*pūrṇāhuti*).

Having offered the Agnihotra and being about to begin it, he should offer with the Daśahotr formula; having offered the New and Full Moon sacrifices and being about to begin them, he should offer with the Caturhotr formula; having offered the Cāturmāsya sacrifices and being about to begin them, he should offer with the Pañcahotr formula; having offered at the animal sacrifice (Paśubandha), he should offer with the Ṣaḍḍhotr formula; having offered at the Soma sacrifice, he should offer with the Saptahotr formula.
And it is known from scripture: "One should offer oblations with these at the beginning of ritual acts; purified, one attains the worlds of the gods"—so says the Brāhmaṇa. So says the Brāhmaṇa.
BDhS 3.8.1: Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual procedure for the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
BDhS 3.8.2: One should fast on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight.
Having had his hair, beard, body hair, and nails shaved, or else having merely shaved his beard and wearing unwashed clothes, he should enter the dwelling while speaking the truth.
In that [case], his fire, once established, may be produced either by churning the two kindling woods or by other means.
A celibate student, a friend, or one who prepares the ritual instructions should be present.
BDhS 3.8.6: And the sacrificial food fit for oblation is that which is to be taken up for the vow.
BDhS 3.8.7: Having kindled the fire and strewn grass around it, and having performed the rites beginning with the offering to Agni, he makes an oblation from the uncooked food.

BDhS 3.8.8: "To Agni belongs the lunar day; to the Nakṣatra together with its presiding deity [belongs the second]; on this [occasion] one says, 'The cow has lowed'—[this refers to] the fifth [day], which belongs to the Moon; the sixth to Heaven and Earth; the seventh to Day and Night; the eighth to Rudra; the ninth to Sūrya; the tenth to Varuṇa; the eleventh to Indra; and the twelfth to the Viśvedevas."
Now they recite other [verses]: "And from the quarters together with their deities, and from the broad intermediate space together with its deity."

Having offered the oblation for Svistakrt with the verse, "Being born, he becomes ever new," he then draws out this remnant of the sacrificial food into a bronze vessel or a cup, pours over it condiments made from sacrificial grains, and eats fifteen morsels in their natural state.

"Recite 'To Prāṇa, svāhā! for the first; 'To Apāna, svāhā! for the second; 'To Vyāna, svāhā! for the third; 'To Udāna, svāhā! for the fourth; and 'To Samāna, svāhā! for the fifth. When there are four [verses], the first two are recited with two [syllables] each; when there are three, the first two are recited with two [syllables] each; when there are two, the first is recited with three [syllables] and the latter with two; and the single [verse] is recited with all [the syllables]."

"O Nigrābhyās," he says. Having drunk water, he then offers oblations of clarified butter: "May my prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna be purified; may I become light, stainless, and free from evil, svāhā! Speech and mind! Head and hands! Skin, hide, and flesh! Sound, touch, form, earth, water, and fire!

May my self consisting of food, the self consisting of vital breath, the self consisting of mind, the self consisting of consciousness, and the self consisting of bliss be purified; may I become light..."

"May I become free from passion and free from evil, svāhā!"—with these seven sections [K: namely, the sections beginning with "consisting of food" and "consisting of vital breath"], the rite is completed starting from the *jaya* oblation up to the granting of the boon of a cow.
He worships the sun with verses addressed to Sūrya and the moon with verses addressed to Candra.
Reciting "O Agni, do thou keep watch well," he murmurs while lying down to sleep.
"O Agni, you are the guardian of vows," [he says] upon waking.
One should not converse with women or Śūdras, nor should one look at urine or excrement.

Having seen something impure, he mutters: "The mind is unbound, the eye is poor; the Sun is the best of luminaries; O consecration, do not forsake me. [K adds: Now, if it rains upon him, he says: "Wetting [the earth], bestow strength. BDhS 3.8.19:
On the first day of the latter fortnight, he takes fourteen mouthfuls.
In this manner, by decreasing by one [meal] each day, [one reaches] the new moon day.
On the new moon day, no morsel of food is prescribed.
Now, on the first day of the bright fortnight, there is one [offering]; on the second, two.
In this manner, by increasing by one [day] each time, [the sequence continues] until the full moon day.
On the full moon day, he offers the cooked oblation (sthālīpāka) to Agni, to whichever lunar day (tithi) it may fall, and to the constellations (nakṣatras) together with their presiding deities.
Having offered oblations to the constellations preceding Śroṇā and Abhijit, along with their presiding deities, one should give a cow to the Brāhmaṇas.
This same Cāndrāyaṇa rite is called "ant-like" (pipīlikāmadhya) when performed in the regular order, and "barley-shaped" (yavamadhya) when performed in the reverse order.
Having performed either one of these, the perpetrator of sin becomes purified from all mortal sins (pātaka).
"For the sake of each desire, this is to be brought forth"—so they say.
Whatever desire one may long for, that one obtains by means of this [rite].

By this means, the sages purified themselves and performed their ancient rites. This [rite] is auspicious, meritorious, conducive to obtaining sons and grandsons, favorable for cattle, bestowing long life, leading to heaven, bringing fame, and fulfilling all desires.
One attains the splendor of the stars and union with, or residence in the same world as, the sun and the moon—he who studies this, he who studies this.
BDhS 3.9.1 Now, therefore, we shall explain the rule for the recitation of the Veda while fasting (anaśnat-pārāyaṇa).
He should wear clean garments or garments made of bark.
He should desire sacrificial food, water, or fruits.

Having gone out from the village toward the east or the north, having smeared a square sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) the size of a cow-hide with cow-dung, having sprinkled it with water, having drawn the lines, and having sprinkled it again with water, he should kindle the fire, strew grass around it, and offer oblations to these deities: "To Agni, svāhā! To Prajāpati, svāhā! To Soma, svāhā! [K]

"Oṃ *somāya svāhā*, *prajāpataye svāhā*, to the Viśvedevas, to the Self-Existent One, to the *Ṛg* verses, to the *Yajus* formulas, to the *Sāman* chants, to the *Atharvan* hymns, to Faith, to Wisdom, to Intelligence, to Prosperity, to Modesty, to Savitṛ, to Sāvitrī, to the Lord of the Assembly, and to Anumati. [K adds: He should recite this and not pause in the middle. BDhS 3.9.5: Having offered these oblations, he should begin the Veda and study it continuously.
BDhS 3.9.6: He should not speak in the interval, nor should he pause in the interval.
BDhS 3.9.7: Now, if he should speak in between, or if he should pause in between, he should restrain his breath three times and begin precisely from the point where he left off. BDhS 3.9.8:
In the event of a lack of inspiration, he should study for as long as it takes him not to know [the passage]; when he knows it—whether by way of the *ṛc*, the *yajus*, or the *sāman*— BDhS 3.9.9:
he should then study that *brāhmaṇa*, that *chāndasa*, and that *daivata*.

One should study the twelve collections of the Veda. Whatever one has studied on days unfit for study, whatever the teachers have been angered by, and whatever improper acts one has committed—one purifies oneself through these [recitations]. His sacred knowledge (brahman) becomes pure and sanctified.
From this point forward is the section on the accumulation [of provisions].
Having studied another twelve collections of Vedic hymns, one attains through them the world of Uśanas.
Having studied another twelve collections of Vedic hymns, one attains through them the world of Bṛhaspati.
Having studied another twelve collections of the Veda, one attains through them the world of Prajāpati.
Fasting, he should study the *Saṃhitā* one thousand times; having become Brahman, free from passion, he becomes Brahman.
One who subsists on alms for a year obtains divine vision.

For six months subsisting on barley-gruel, for four months subsisting on water and barley-meal, for two months subsisting on fruits, for one month subsisting on water, or for twelve nights fasting entirely, he quickly becomes invisible; he purifies his kinsmen—seven descendants and seven ancestors—and he purifies himself as the fifteenth, as well as the row [of diners].
This very [practice] they call the "divine support."
By this [sacrifice], indeed, the gods attained godhood and the seers attained seerhood.
Indeed, for this very sacrifice, there are exactly three times for its commencement: at the morning libation, at the midday libation, or during the latter part of the night in the sacred precinct.
Prajāpati taught this very [text] to the Seven Seers; the Seven Seers to Mahājajñu; and Mahājajñu to the Brāhmaṇas—yes, to the Brāhmaṇas.
The duties of the social classes and the duties of the stages of life have been declared.

Now, indeed, this person may act wrongly through a blameworthy deed: he either officiates at a sacrifice for one for whom it should not be performed, accepts what should not be accepted, eats the food of one whose food should not be eaten, or engages in what should not be practiced.
Regarding this, they deliberate whether one should perform an expiation or not.
"For action is never exhausted. (BDhS 3.10.4)
"One should simply perform [the rite]," so it is said.
It is known from scripture: "Having sacrificed with the *punastoma*, they return to the *savana*.
Furthermore, they also cite this: "He who sacrifices with the *aśvamedha* overcomes all evil; he overcomes even the murder of a Brahmin."
"One who is being falsely accused should perform the Agniṣṭut sacrifice," it is said.
Its means of expiation are: recitation, austerity, burnt offerings, fasting, and giving gifts.

The Upaniṣads, the beginnings of the Vedas, the Vedāntas, the Saṃhitās among all the Vedic meters, the Madhu-hymns, the Aghamarṣaṇa, the Atharvaśiras, the Rudras, the Puruṣasūkta, the Rājana and Rauhiṇa Sāmans, the Bṛhat and Rathantara, the Puruṣagati, the Mahānāmnīs, the Mahāvairāja, the Mahādivākīrtya, any one of the Jyeṣṭha-sāmans, the Bahiṣpavamāna, the Kūṣmāṇḍas, the Pāvamānī verses, and the Sāvitrī—these are the purifiers.

BDhS 3.10.11: According to the rule for approaching [the teacher], the following are pure: subsisting on milk, eating vegetables, eating fruits, eating roots, barley-gruel from a handful (*prasṛti-yāvaka*), consuming gold, consuming clarified butter, and drinking Soma.
All mountains, all flowing rivers, sacred lakes, holy fords, the dwellings of seers, cow-pens, fields, and threshing-floors—these are the [sacred] places.

Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, touching water at the three libations, service to the guru, celibacy, sleeping on the ground, wearing a single garment, and fasting—these are the austerities (tapas).
Gold, a cow, clothing, a horse, land, sesame seeds, clarified butter, and food—these are the things to be given.
The time periods are: one year, six months, four, three, two, or one month; twenty-four days, twelve days, six days, three days, a day and night, or a single day. BDhS 3.10.15.
These [rites] should be performed when there is no specific instruction.
In cases of heavy sins, the penances are heavy; in cases of light sins, they are light.
The Kṛcchra, the Atikṛcchra, and the Cāndrāyaṇa constitute the expiation for all [sins]. This is the expiation for all [sins].
We shall now declare the penances, which serve various purposes and are distinct from one another,
both heavy and light according to their respective offenses.
For whatever is appropriate in this context should indeed be specified right there;
likewise, in cases of increasingly grave offenses, the penances should be increasingly heavy, and in cases of minor ones, they should be correspondingly lighter.
One should perform breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures.
Whatever sin has been committed by the genitals, or whatever has been done by the feet,
by the arms, by the mind, by speech, or by the ear, skin, nose, and eyes— [all that is purified].
BDhS 4.1.4 Or else, in cases of transgression involving the eye, ear, skin, nose, or mind, one becomes pure by means of three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*).

BDhS 4.1.5 In the case of eating the food of a Śūdra, sexual intercourse with a woman, or eating [forbidden food], when these occur individually and separately, one should maintain seven breath-restraints for each, for a period of seven days.

In the case of consuming what is unfit to be eaten, what is unfit to be drunk, what is unfit to be sipped, or what is unfit to be tasted, as well as in the sale of forbidden goods—with the exception of honey, meat, clarified butter, oil, alkaline substances, salt, and the food of low-caste persons—one should perform twelve breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) for twelve days, twelve for each such offense; and this same rule applies to whatever else is of a similar nature.

In cases other than the major sins (pātaka), the sins causing loss of caste (patanīya), and the minor sins (upapātaka), as well as in other matters of a similar nature, one should perform twelve breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) each for half a month.

In cases other than those involving mortal sins (pātaka) or acts causing loss of caste (patanīya), and whatever else is of a similar nature, one should perform twelve breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) for each of twelve days.
In cases other than those involving mortal sins (pātaka), and for whatever else is similarly prescribed, one should perform twelve breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) for each of the twelve half-months.
Now, for [the commission of] mortal sins (pātaka), one should perform twelve breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) each day for one year.
He should give his daughter to a virtuous man who is a celibate student while she is still a *nagnikā* (pre-pubertal);
or else, he should give her even to one lacking in virtues, but he must not let her remain beyond the time when she reaches puberty.
He who does not give away a maiden who has reached puberty within three years undoubtedly incurs a guilt equal to that of killing an embryo.
If he does not beg, this shall be so; but if he begs, then for each individual season, Manu has declared a fault that constitutes a sin.
A woman who has reached puberty should wait for the command of her father for three years;
then, in the fourth year, she should find a suitable husband. If no suitable man is available, she may resort even to one deficient in good qualities.
If a maiden has been carried off by force, but not consecrated with the sacred mantras, she may be given to another according to the prescribed rule; for she remains just as a maiden.
If her husband should die after she has been given away in marriage, or even after the fire-oblation has been performed, she—
provided she remains a virgin and has returned [to him]—
is worthy of a second consecration according to the rite for remarriage (paunarbhava).
If a man does not approach his wife when she is in her season for three years,
he undoubtedly incurs a guilt equal to that of killing an embryo.
But he who does not approach his wife when she has bathed after her menses and is present near him—
his ancestors lie upon that menstrual blood for that entire month.

"He who does not approach his wife during her season, and he who approaches her outside her season—they both incur an equal fault, as does he who discharges semen in a place other than the womb. (BDhS 4.1.19)
If a wife, by staying in her husband's family home, causes her fertile season to pass in vain,
she shall be proclaimed as a destroyer of the embryo (bhrūṇaghnī) in the midst of the village and driven out from the house.
If he does not approach his wife when she has bathed after her menses— she being self-restrained and observing the dharma—
it is traditionally taught that for his transgression of this rule, he must perform one hundred *prāṇāyāmas*.
Seated with purifying grass in hand, one should practice the daily Veda-recitation, as well as breath-control exercises, the purifiers, the Vyāhṛtis, and the Praṇava.
Always disciplined, one should repeatedly perform breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma);
from the tips of the hair to the ends of the nails, one performs the highest austerity.
From suppression, wind is born; from wind, fire is born;
from heat, water is produced; thus, it is purified internally by these three.
Through yoga, knowledge is attained; yoga is the defining characteristic of dharma.
All virtues have their root in yoga; therefore, one should always be disciplined in yoga.
The three Vedas begin with the syllable *praṇava* and are established within the *praṇava*;
the *praṇava* and the *vyāhṛtis* are indeed the eternal, primeval Brahman.
For one who is constantly disciplined in the *praṇava*, in the seven *vyāhṛtis*,
and in the three-footed *gāyatrī*, no fear exists anywhere.
One should recite the Gāyatrī together with the Vyāhṛtis, the Praṇava, and the Śiras three times while restraining the breath;
that is called prāṇāyāma.

Sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), accompanied by the Vyāhṛtis and the Praṇava, performed daily for a month, purify even the slayer of a learned Brāhmaṇa. This is the foremost austerity; this is the defining characteristic of dharma.
For the purpose of destroying all defects, this very [penance] is distinguished as superior.
"This very [rule] is further specified."
We shall now declare the various expiations, each distinct from the other,
which are heavy or light according to their respective faults.
For if something were appropriate here, he would have specified it right there;
likewise, among the more serious [offenses] he mentions them repeatedly, while for the lighter ones he mentions fewer.
One should prescribe the penances according to the rule seen in the scriptures.
But when about to accept a gift, or having already accepted one,
he should recite four times the *taratsamandī* verses from the Rigveda.
BDhS 4.2.5ab: But for eating the food of any of those whose food should not be eaten, BDhS 4.2.5cd:
purification from sin is performed by sprinkling with water while reciting the *taratsamandī* verses of the Rigveda.
BDhS 4.2.6ab: There is, however, another rule regarding the killing of a learned Brahmin (*bhrūṇahatyā*); that I shall explain hereafter.
By which rule they are liberated from all sins whatsoever.

BDhS 4.2.7ab: One should likewise recite breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), purificatory formulas (*pavitra*), the *vyāhṛtis*, and the *praṇava*; BDhS 4.2.7cd: Or, subsisting on milk, one should recite the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn for twelve nights. BDhS 4.2.8ab: Or, for three nights, one may subsist on air alone, wearing wet clothes, or remaining immersed in water, being pure.
"Even after repeatedly practicing forbidden customs, one is released from all sins by performing worship with the Vāruṇī verses. Thus it is said.

Now, a student who has broken his vow of chastity (*avakīrṇin*), having kindled the fire at night on the new moon day and performed the ritual preparations for a wood-oblation (*dārvihomika*), offers two oblations of clarified butter: "O Kāma, I have been scattered; I have been scattered, O Kāma! To Kāma, svāhā! O Kāma, I have been violated; I have been violated, O Kāma! To Kāma, svāhā! [cf. BDhS 2.1.1.34]

Having offered the oblation, with hands joined in reverence, he should worship the fire from the side, saying: "May the Maruts pour into me; may Indra pour into me; may Bṛhaspati pour into me; may this Agni pour into me with life and with strength—make me long-lived! (BDhS 2.1.1.35). The Maruts bestow the vital breaths upon him; Indra bestows strength; Bṛhaspati bestows spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*); and Agni bestows everything else. Having become whole in body, he attains a full span of life.

He should consecrate [the water] three times; for it is known that "the gods are indeed true to the triad. He who might consider himself as if unpurified by minor offenses (upapātaka) is liberated from all sin by performing an oblation according to this rule.

Alternatively, having committed an act involving food that should not be eaten, drink that should not be drunk, or the consumption of forbidden food—whether intentionally or unintentionally—and having discharged semen into a Śūdra woman or into a non-vaginal opening, one becomes pure by touching water with the *ābliṅga* verses and the *vāruṇī* verses while remaining self-restrained.
Moreover, they cite this: "In the case of eating what is unfit to be eaten,
drinking what is unfit to be drunk, or consuming what is forbidden, and in performing actions contrary to dharma—
even when such acts are committed intentionally— one is purified from those sins that are equal to mortal transgressions, as well as from all other sins."
Or, fasting for three nights and entering the water three times a day,
restraining his vital breaths within himself, he should recite the *Aghamarṣaṇa* hymn three times;
Manu has declared that this is equivalent to the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of a horse sacrifice.
And it is known from scripture:
"The ancient, far-spreading, purifying foot—by which one who is purified overcomes evil deeds—with that pure, sanctifying foot, may we, being purified, cross over sin and enmity. Thus [it is said].
We shall declare the penances for those who are composed and disciplined, specifically regarding those not previously mentioned; how should it be in cases of negligence?
In all cases of sin, one should sip water while reciting the *vyāhṛtis* preceded by *oṃ* and including all of them.
That which he sips first, with that he gratifies the Ṛgveda; that which he sips second, with that the Yajurveda; that which he sips third, with that the Sāmaveda.
That which he wipes first, by that [he obtains] the Atharvaveda; that which he wipes second, by that [he obtains] Itihāsa and Purāṇa.

When he sprinkles his left hand, his feet, his head, his heart, his two nostrils, his two eyes, his two ears, and his navel, by that act he gratifies the plants, the trees, and all the deities. Therefore, through this very act of sipping water (ācamana), one is liberated from all evil.

Or he should offer eight fuel-sticks: "Thou art the expiation for the sin committed against the gods, svāhā! Thou art the expiation for the sin committed against men, svāhā! Thou art the expiation for the sin committed against the ancestors, svāhā! Thou art the expiation for the sin committed against oneself, svāhā! For whatever sin we have committed by day and by night, thou art its expiation, svāhā! For whatever sin we have committed while sleeping and while waking, thou art its expiation, svāhā!"
"Whatever sin we have committed, whether knowing or unknowing—you are the expiation for that, svāhā! You are the expiation for every sin, svāhā!"
Having offered these eight oblations, one is liberated from all evil.
Furthermore, they also cite:
"The *aghamarṣaṇa*, the *devakṛta*, the *śuddhavatīs*,
the *taratsamās*, the *kūśmāṇḍyas*, the *pāvamānyas*, the *virajas*, and the *mṛtyulāṅgala*."
The Durgā verses, the Vyāhṛtis, and the Rudras are the destroyers of great evils.
"These [mantras] are the destroyers of great evils."
We shall declare the penances, especially those that have not been specifically mentioned;
how [should it be] for those who are composed and self-controlled when they commit lapses?
"Ṛtaṃ ca satyaṃ ca"—by reciting this Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times while submerged in water, one is liberated from all sin.
Reciting this verse, "The spotted cow has come hither," three times while submerged in water, one is liberated from all evil.
Reciting three times this verse, "As if released from a post," while remaining within the water, one is liberated from all sin.
Reciting this verse, "The swan dwelling in purity," three times while submerged in water, one is liberated from all sin.
Alternatively, by reciting the Sāvitrī verse—first quarter by quarter, then half-verse by half-verse, and finally the whole verse—three times while submerged in water, one is liberated from all sin.
Alternatively, by reciting the Vyāhṛtis, both individually and collectively, three times while submerged in water, one is liberated from all sin.
Or alternatively, by reciting the syllable *praṇava* three times while submerged within the water, one is liberated from all evil.

BDhS 4.4.9 One should not give this treatise on Dharma to one who is not a son, nor to one who is not a disciple, nor to one who has not resided [as a student] for a year. [K: nor to one who is not devoted]. BDhS 4.4.10 A thousand [cows] with a bull as the eleventh is the sacrificial fee, or it may be the favor of the teacher; or it may be the favor of the teacher. BDhS 4.5.1ab Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the Sāman, Ṛg, Yajus, and Atharvan [Vedas].
By means of those actions, one quickly attains the desires that are in the mind.
Having purified one's own body through recitation, fire-offerings, sacrifices, yantras, and so forth, one should accomplish all rites; otherwise, one does not attain success.
A twice-born man, intending to perform recitations (japa), burnt offerings (homa), sacrifices (iṣṭi), or mechanical rites (yantra),
should first have his hair and beard shaved during the bright fortnight, on an auspicious day, and under favorable lunar mansions (nakṣatra).
He should bathe at the three periods of the day and protect himself from anger and falsehood;
as a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*) observing the vow of the sacrificial oblation (*havirvrata*), he should not converse with women or *śūdras*.
While sleeping during the day, he should pay homage to cows, Brahmins, ancestors, and gods;
remaining engaged in recitation, burnt offerings, sacrifices, and the use of mystical diagrams, he should stand during the day and sit at night.

The *prājāpatya* penance consists of eating only what is obtained by begging during the day for three days, and likewise at night for three days; then, for three days each, one subsists on food obtained by begging neither by day nor by night, and finally, for three days, one subsists on air alone, consuming it in this sequence over twelve days.
One day and likewise one night, or subsisting on air when it is unknown [to others],
this threefold reversal is called the *bāla-kṛcchra* (the child’s penance).
One should eat a single morsel for three days each according to the previously mentioned method;
for another three days, one should subsist on air alone—this is called the *atikṛcchra* penance.
For these three days he shall subsist on water, and after that, he shall subsist on air;
this third penance is known as the *Kṛcchrātikṛcchra*, which is exceedingly purifying.
For three days at a time, one should drink hot milk, clarified butter, and water boiled with *kuśa* grass;
for another three days, one should subsist on air alone—this is called the *taptakṛcchra*.
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with *kuśa* grass,
along with a fast for one night, is known as the *sāṃtapana* penance.

Taking cow urine with the *gāyatrī* mantra, cow dung with the verse beginning "gandhadvārā," milk with "āpyāyasva," curd with "dadhikrāvṇo," clarified butter with "śukram asi jyotiḥ," and *kuśa*-water with "devasya tvā."
One part of cow urine, half as much of dung, three parts of milk,
two parts of curd, one part of ghee, and one part of *kuśa* water—
this is the *sāṃtapana* penance, which purifies even a dog-eater.
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, and likewise clarified butter—
by consuming these five products of the cow for five nights as one's sole food, one is purified by the *pañcagavya*.
When one who is vigilant fasts for twelve days,
this penance called Parāka destroys all sins.
The exponents of the Veda declare that the Mahāsāṃtapana Kṛcchra consists of each of those [substances], beginning with cow’s urine, practiced twenty-one times.
"In the bright fortnight, one increases the morsels by one each day; in the dark fortnight, one decreases them by one from that number.
There are two fast days at the beginning of the two fortnights; this is indeed remembered as the Cāndrāyaṇa."
A Brahmin, composed in mind, should eat four morsels in the morning;
having eaten four when the sun has set, he should perform the *śiśu-cāndrāyaṇa*. Eight morsels each, at midday for one month, [he should eat].
With self-restraint, one should perform the *yaticāndrāyaṇa* penance using sacrificial food (*haviṣya*).
O twice-born one, by eating eighty-three morsels (*piṇḍas*) of sacrificial food in any manner whatsoever during a month, one attains the same world as the Moon.
Just as the rising moon destroys the world's fear of darkness,
so too does the twice-born man performing the Cāndrāyaṇa penance destroy the fear of sin. He may subsist on grains, oil-cakes, buttermilk, barley-water, or air, or likewise on water.
"Consisting of one, three, five, or seven [verses], this *tulāpuruṣa* rite is the destroyer of sin."
Barley gruel consumed for seven nights destroys the sins of embodied beings;
or alternatively, a fast for seven nights achieves this—this has been observed by the wise.
In the months of Pauṣa, Bhādrapada, and Jyeṣṭha, by taking refuge in the rain, the open air, and the sun respectively,
a twice-born man is freed from the three types of white sins, except for those that cause loss of caste.
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with *kuśa* grass; when combined with barley and *ācāma*, this is the extremely purifying *brahmakūrca*.
On the new moon day, fasting, and on the full moon day, eating sesame seeds;
by means of these seasonal festivals throughout the year, one is liberated from the sins committed during the bright and dark fortnights.
One who subsists on almsfood becomes purified in one month by [eating from] those who maintain the sacred fires;
[one becomes purified] in ten or five days by [eating from] those who follow the Yāyāvara mode of life or dwell in the forest.
One who possesses wealth from a single day is purified by one day's fast;
one who is devoted to the "pigeon-like" mode of subsistence (kāpotavṛtti) is purified by drinking water for three days.
Having recited the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, or *Sāma* Vedas, or any one of the Vedas,
three times through to completion while fasting, he becomes supremely purifying.
Now, if he hastens to perform it, he should subsist on air during the day;
standing in water at night until dawn, that is equal to the Prājāpatya penance. Having performed eight thousand recitations of the Gāyatrī when the sun has risen—
One is released from all sins, provided one has not been a slayer of an embryo.
He who gives food, speaks the truth, and abides in compassion toward all beings surpasses all those previously mentioned as purified by the *yantras*.
The Rudras with the *ucchandas* verses, the *gāyatrī* accompanied by the *praṇava*,
and the seven *vyāhṛtis* should be recited as they destroy sin.
The *mṛgāreṣṭi*, the *pavitreṣṭi*, the *trihavis*, and the *pāvamānī* hymns [should also be recited].
Sacrifices accompanied by the Vaiśvānara oblation are destroyers of sin.
And hear now this other secret being declared:
one is released from all sins, except for the greatest of transgressions.
Performing the purification with purifiers while reciting the Rudraikādaśinī,
offering oblations of clarified butter with purifiers, and bestowing gold, cows, and sesame seeds.
He who eats boiled barley-gruel mixed with cow urine,
dung-liquid, along with curd, milk, and clarified butter, is liberated from his sin in an instant.
He who has fathered a child upon a Śūdra woman, and he by whom an unapproachable woman has been violated—
both of them are liberated from that sin after seven nights by this rite.

In the case of consuming semen, urine, or feces; in eating the food of those whose food should not be eaten; in the re-consecration of the sacred fires; in performing a sacrifice for one who has already sacrificed; and in the case of a younger brother marrying before his elder—this [penance] is the remedy.
"Even after performing very many acts that do not cause loss of caste,
one is released from all sins"— this is the teaching of the virtuous.
The procedure proclaimed here is the authoritative standard for the path of mantra,
by means of which Bharadvāja and others attained identity with Brahman.
A Brahmin whose heart is serene through the performance of this rite—
He attains those various desires, whatever desires reside in his heart.
"Whatever desires reside in the heart," so it is said.
For that Brahmin who has desisted from evil deeds and is engaged in meritorious deeds,
his ritual acts succeed even without the use of mechanical devices.
Brāhmaṇas are upright; therefore, whatever they desire in their hearts, that very thing they quickly attain, being purified by their upright deeds.

Thus, a wise person should perform these restraints for as long as it takes until his body attains purity of the self. Then, having purified himself by means of these restraints, he should fast for three nights.
One should undertake that action by which one desires to attain prosperity.
The *kṣmāpavitra*, the *sahasrākṣa*, the *mṛgāra*, the two *aṃhomuc* groups, the *pāvamānya* verses, the *kūśmāṇḍya* verses, and those *ṛc*s dedicated to Vaiśvānara.
Offering oblations of rice cooked with ghee three times a day for seven days, observing a vow of silence, eating sacrificial food, and restraining the activities of the senses; BDhS 4.7.6cd.
Having looked into a vessel full of water at a crossroads while reciting "siṃhe me," one is released from all sins, even from a great heinous crime.
Whatever accumulation of sin has been committed in old age, youth, or childhood,
and even that which was done in previous births through ignorance— from all that one is liberated. Having fed the twice-born at the conclusion with milk-rice mixed with ghee.
And having bestowed cows, land, sesame seeds, and gold upon those who have already eaten.
The Brahmin becomes purified in soul, with the fuel of his sins consumed;
he thus becomes fit for optional rites as well as for rites such as the establishment of the sacred fires.
He who performs this rite out of excessive greed or through negligence—
Possessed by the sin of another, he perishes like one who has swallowed poison.
Performing this rite for his teacher, his father, his mother, and himself, the Brahmin shines like the sun; therefore, this rite must be performed for them.
Who, by means of this thousand-eyed purifier,
made Agni, Vāyu, Ravi, Soma, Yama, and the other lords of the gods pure?
Whatever is renowned here in the three worlds as meritorious,
that has been performed by the Brahmins and others through this purifying rite.
This secret *prājāpatya* [mantra], which destroys sin, was the first to arise;
after it, thousands of purifiers were subsequently produced.
He who offers these eight groups of oblations for a year, a half-year, a season, a fortnight, or a day,
purifies his own lineage— ten ancestors and ten descendants.
Even while remaining on earth, he is recognized by the immortals dwelling in heaven as a performer of meritorious deeds;
moreover, as a doer of merit, he rejoices like a god in the heavenly world. If a twice-born man is unable to offer these eight groups [of oblations], [he should perform the following].
Even if he offers only one [oblation] with that [mixture], his impurity (rajas) is thereby destroyed.
He whose sons or disciples offer these eight groups [of oblations] is also liberated from sin by means of those [offerings] performed for the sake of teaching.
Even by means of those purchased with wealth, one who desires to destroy his own sin must cause the fires to be maintained;
for he who is unable [to maintain them himself] should not cause the bearer of the body (the sacrificer) to despair.
The renunciation of wealth, even of well-performed deeds, is performed;
sometimes the liberation of a man from sin occurs when he is free from debt.
Released from the ocean of all sins by this rite,
he considers himself pure and capable of accomplishing ritual acts.
But when one whose self is liberated from the debt of all sins undertakes ritual actions,
those actions attain perfection without effort for that person of purified body.
This meritorious *prājāpatya* [text], proclaimed by the seer,
one should constantly teach, retain, or even listen to;
such a person is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
One who desires to master those mantras should mutter them for twelve days,

consuming once at night a portion of boiled rice with ghee, milk, and curd. Likewise, there should be ten oblations of clarified butter during each of the three daily pressings for the Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, Sāmaveda, and also the Atharvāṅgirasa.
This shall be the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) for these mantras in the accomplishment of rites.

Regarding the phrase "the accomplishment of rites through mantras": whether due to excessive greed or negligence, one who has desisted from sinful deeds—[with] the Rudras [accompanied] by the *chandasa* [verses] in a composed manner—now, therefore, I shall fully declare; we shall declare the expiations (*prāyaścitta*). We shall declare the expiations. We shall declare the expiations. We shall declare the expiations. Thus ends the fourth book (*praśna*).
Thus the *Baudhāyana-Dharmasūtra* is completed.
