Text based on the edition:
*Vasiṣṭhadharmaśāstra*, Bombay Sanskrit and Prakrit Series, 23, input by M. Fushimi, checked by F. Enomoto.
Now, therefore, follows the inquiry into dharma for the sake of the supreme good of man.
Having understood [the law], one who practices it is righteous.
He becomes most praiseworthy in this world, and after death, he attains the heavenly world.
Dharma is that which is prescribed by the Śruti and the Smṛti.
In the absence of that, the conduct of the learned (śiṣṭas) is the authority.
But a cultured man (śiṣṭa) is one whose nature is free from desire.
Dharma is that whose cause is not perceived.
Āryāvarta lies to the east of Ādarśa, to the west of Kālakavana, to the north of Pāriyātra, and to the south of the Himavat.
And [the region] to the north of the Vindhya mountains.
Whatever laws and whatever customs exist in that region, all of them are to be accepted everywhere.
But this does not apply to others who follow the duties of those born in the inverse order of castes.
Some [say] that it is also [the region] between the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā.
"Or as far as the black antelope roams, so far extends spiritual luster," say others.
Moreover, the Bhāllavins cite this verse in their Nidāna:
To the west is the Sindhu river, which holds [the world] back; to the east is the rising of the sun.
As far as the dark [horse] runs, so far indeed is the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*).
Whatever those who are learned in the three Vedas and knowers of dharma may declare to be dharma—both in its purifying and its cleansing aspects—that is indeed dharma; there is no doubt about this.
Manu declared that, because there is no revealed scripture (śruti) for them, one should follow the laws of countries, the laws of castes, and the laws of families.
One who is overtaken by the sun rising while he is still asleep, and one who is overtaken by the sun setting while he is still asleep;
they declare these five to be the great sins (mahāpātaka).
Violating the teacher's bed, drinking liquor, killing an embryo, stealing the gold of a Brāhmaṇa, and associating with outcasts.
Either through the *brāhma* [form of marriage] or through the *yauna* [form of marriage].
Moreover, they also cite this:
"By associating with an outcast for a year—through officiating at sacrifices, teaching, or marriage—one becomes an outcast; but not through sharing a vehicle, a seat, or gifts."
"Those who cast away the sacred fires, those who show hostility toward their teacher, atheists, those who live as atheists, and those who sell Soma—these are the minor offenses (upapātaka)."
A Brāhmaṇa may have three wives according to the order of the castes, a Rājanya two, and a Vaiśya and a Śūdra each one.
Some [teachers] say that even a Śūdra woman may be taken in this same manner, with the exception of the sacred formulas (mantras).
One should not act in that manner.
For from this results the certain ruin of the family and the loss of heaven after death.
There are six forms of marriage.
The Brāhma, Daiva, Ārṣa, Gāndharva, Kṣātra, and Mānuṣa [are the forms of marriage].
If she is given with water first by one who desires [to marry her], that is the Brāhma form.
When the sacrificial ritual has been spread out and the officiating priest is performing his duties, one should give a daughter, having adorned her; that they call "the divine" (daiva) marriage.
And the Ārṣa [form of marriage] is characterized by a pair of cattle.
If a man, desiring her, approaches a willing woman of equal birth, that is the Gāndharva marriage.
That which they carry off by force, having violently overpowered [the victim], is the Kṣatriya way.
That person who has been purchased with wealth after bargaining is a human being.
Therefore, it is understood here that the purchase [of Soma] consists in giving a hundred [cows] along with an extra chariot to one who has a daughter.
"She who, having been purchased by her husband, then behaves [unfaithfully] with others"—this is stated in the context of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"Knowledge that has been lost may be acquired again; but when a family line perishes, there is a total destruction here [in this world].
Even a mere horse is honored by the designation of its lineage; therefore, they marry a woman of noble birth."
The three social classes should conduct themselves according to the instruction of the Brāhmaṇa.
A Brāhmaṇa shall proclaim the duties.
And the king should issue commands.
But the king, governing by means of righteousness, shall take a sixth part of the wealth.
Except in the case of a Brāhmaṇa.
"But he partakes of a sixth share of his sacrifices and charitable works," so it is said.
The Brāhmaṇa makes the Veda wealthy; the Brāhmaṇa rescues one from calamity; therefore, the Brāhmaṇa is not to be eaten. "Soma is his king," so it is said.
"And it is known from tradition that there is prosperity after death; it is known from tradition."
There are four social classes: the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra.
The three castes, the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, and the Vaiśya, are the twice-born.
For them,
the first birth is from the mother, and the second at the tying of the girdle of Muñja grass;
here, his mother is said to be the Sāvitrī, and his father is the Ācārya.
Because he imparts the Veda, they call the teacher "father."

Moreover, they cite this: "A man has indeed two kinds of seed for a Brāhmaṇa: that which is above the navel and the other which is below the navel. That which is above the navel—by means of it he procreates offspring when he initiates Brāhmaṇas, when he teaches them, when he officiates at their sacrifices, and when he performs meritorious deeds. Now, that which is below the navel—by means of it his own biological offspring is produced here. Therefore, they do not say of a learned man who has studied the Vedas, 'You are childless.'"
Hārīta also cites:
"Indeed, no ritual act whatsoever exists for him prior to the tying of the girdle of muñja grass;
for he is equal to a Śūdra in his mode of livelihood until he is born into the Veda."
Except for water-rites, *svadhā* offerings, and those connected with the ancestors.
Knowledge indeed came to the Brahmin, saying: "Guard me; I am your treasure.
Do not speak of me to one who is censorious, dishonest, or lacking self-control, so that I may remain potent."
O Brahmin, teach me to that person who you know to be pure, vigilant, intelligent, endowed with celibacy, and who would never do you any harm in any way— that keeper of the treasure.
He who pierces one's ears with what is not false, causing no pain while bestowing immortality—him one should regard as both father and mother; one should not bear him malice for anything whatsoever.

Those Brahmins who, having been instructed, do not respect their teacher in word, thought, or deed— just as they are not worthy of being fed by the teacher, even so the sacred learning does not nourish them.
Just as fire burns dry grass, so does the Veda burn one who questions it without respect; one should not teach the Veda to such a person, for it is impossible to make him show due honor.
VaDhS 2.13: There are six duties for a Brāhmaṇa.
The study and teaching of the Veda, sacrifice and officiating at sacrifices, giving gifts and receiving gifts.
For a Kṣatriya, there are three [days].
Study, sacrifice, and giving are [the three duties].
And protecting the subjects with the sword is his own duty; he should live by that.
These same [rites] belong to the Vaiśya.
Agriculture, trade, cattle-rearing, and money-lending.
Service to them is the constant duty and livelihood of a Śūdra.
All [the mourners] must maintain their hair and dress according to the prescribed rule, or else all may have their hair loose except for the top-knot (*śikhā*).
If they cannot subsist by their own duty, they should adopt the next lower mode of livelihood.
But never [should he marry] one who is older.
Adopting the livelihood of a Vaiśya, for one who lives by trade, [the forbidden items are] stone, salt, gems, whetstones, silk, linen, and skins.
All woven cloth that is dyed red [is impure].
Cooked food, flowers, fruits, roots, perfumes, juices, water, the sap of medicinal plants, Soma, weapons, poison, meat, milk and its derivatives, iron, tin, lac, and lead.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"A Brahmin falls immediately from his caste by selling meat, lac, or salt; by selling milk, he becomes a Śūdra within three days."
Among village animals, those with solid hooves and those with manes [are unclean], as are all wild animals, birds, and fanged beasts.
Regarding grains, they say that sesame seeds [are the most significant].
Moreover, they also cite this:
"If one performs with sesame seeds any act other than eating, anointing, or giving,
he becomes a worm and sinks into the excrement of dogs along with his ancestors."
Or, if they so desire, they may themselves cultivate sesame seeds and sell them.
Therefore, from the two ploughs yoked to the cart until the morning meal, he should be a laborer.
In the summer, one should offer water.

"May the plough, sharp-pointed, very auspicious, with a handle for grasping, turn up the cow, the sheep, and the fat, swelling earth; may it turn up the chariot-stand along with the wagon. (VaDhS 2.34)

VaDhS 2.35: He throws away [the soma-stalk] from afar, for it is the *somapitsaru*; since *soma* reaches it, he sows that *sarū*. [He gives away] cows, sheep, goats, horses, mules, and camels; and a *prapharvī*, a plump, beautiful, auspicious, and youthful woman. VaDhS 2.36:
For how indeed could one plow with a ploughshare otherwise than by selling grain?
Flavors are to be exchanged for flavors, whether they are superior or inferior.
But one must never [use] salt with savory juices.
Through bartering, sesame, rice, cooked food, knowledge, and human beings may be acquired.
A Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya shall not practice usury.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"He who, having taken grain at a low price, gives it back at a high price,
is indeed called a usurer and is censured among those who discourse on the Veda."
He weighed the killing of a Brahmin against usury on a scale;
the killer of an embryo remained [lower] at the end, while the usurer trembled.
Or they may, at their will, give [the property] to one who has neglected his duties or to a wicked person.
Gold is doubled; grain is tripled.
By means of grain, liquids are likewise explained.
And flowers, roots, and fruits.
Gold weighed on a scale [is increased] eightfold.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"One may take interest of two, three, four, five,
and ten percent per month, according to the order of the social classes."
But a king, by means of his death, destroys the increase of wealth;
yet again, through royal consecration, the root of wealth increases.
Listen to the rate of interest proclaimed by the words of Vasiṣṭha regarding a moneylender:
"Five māṣas for twenty [paṇas]; thus the dharma is not violated."
"He does not fall away. Thus it is said.
Those who have not studied the Vedas, those who do not recite the Vedic texts, or those who maintain no sacred fires, become equal in status to Śūdras.
And regarding this, they cite a verse of Manu:
"The twice-born man who, without having studied the Veda, exerts himself in other matters,
quickly sinks to the status of a Śūdra while still living, along with his descendants."
A Brāhmaṇa does not become [unworthy] by failing to recite the Ṛgveda, nor by being a merchant, nor by being an actor;
nor by serving a Śūdra, nor by being a thief, nor by being a physician.
For the king should punish that village where twice-born men wander for alms without observing vows and without studying; for it provides sustenance to thieves.
Even if they have gathered by the thousands, those who lack vows, who lack sacred mantras, and who subsist merely by their birth— no assembly-status exists for them.
Whatever those fools, deluded by darkness and ignorant of dharma, proclaim—
that sin becomes a hundredfold and falls upon those who speak it.
Whether they be four or even three who have mastered the Vedas, whatever they declare should be known as Dharma; not so the declarations of thousands of others.
Sacrificial offerings to the gods and the ancestors should always be given to one learned in the Vedas;
for what is given to one who is not learned in the Vedas reaches neither the ancestors nor the deities.
Whether a fool resides in one’s own house or a man of great learning lives far away, the gift should be given to the man of great learning; there is no transgression in this.
There is no offense in bypassing a Brahmin who is devoid of Vedic knowledge;
for one does not offer oblations into ashes while setting aside a blazing fire.
An elephant made of wood, a deer made of leather,
and a Brahmin who has not studied the Veda— these three are merely bearers of names.
Those kingdoms in which the ignorant eat food that should be eaten by the learned meet with drought, or a great danger arises.
VaDhS 3.13: If [the property] is not recognized [as belonging to anyone], [it is considered ownerless].
VaDhS 3.14: If a Brāhmaṇa should find it while engaged in the six duties, the king shall not take it away.
VaDhS 3.15: Having slain an assailant, they say that there is no sin whatsoever for the one who takes the life.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"The incendiary, the poisoner, one with a weapon in hand, the robber of wealth,
and the seizer of land or wife— these six are *ātatāyin*s (assassins)."
One may strike down an assailant who comes with intent to kill, even if he is a master of the Vedāntas; by doing so, one does not become a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa.

If one kills an assailant who has come with intent to harm—a man born of a noble family and devoted to the study of the Vedas—he does not thereby become a killer of an embryo; for it is the fury of the attacker that meets his own fury.

One who has performed the Triṇāciketa sacrifice, one who maintains the five sacred fires, one who knows the Trisuparṇa, one who has performed the four Medha sacrifices, a follower of the Vājasaneyi school, one who knows the six Vedāṅgas, one who belongs to a lineage of those who have received the gift of the Veda from a Brahmin, a Chāndoga, a singer of the Jyeṣṭhasāman, and one who studies the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas—these, as well as he who studies the Dharma, and he whose maternal and paternal lineages extend ten generations back and are known to be learned Śrotriyas and Snātakas, are purifiers of the assembly (paṅktipāvanas).
One who is learned in the four Vedas, one who can deliberate on legal alternatives, one who knows the auxiliary sciences (aṅgas), and a reciter of the Dharma;
these three belonging to the [three] stages of life are the principal members of an assembly, which shall consist of at least ten such persons.
Having initiated him, he should teach him the entire Veda; such a person is an *ācārya*.
But he who teaches a single portion [of the Veda] is an upādhyāya.
And he who [studies] the Vedāṅgas.
In self-defense and when the social order is threatened, a Brāhmaṇa and a Vaiśya may take up arms.
But for a Kṣatriya, that [study] is indeed obligatory, because he has the duty of protection.
Having washed his feet and hands up to the wrists, and sitting facing either east or north, he should sip water three times silently using the *brāhma* tīrtha—the line above the root of the thumb.
He should wipe [the mouth] twice.
One should touch the cavities of the head with water.
He should pour water on the head and on the left hand.
One should not perform ācamana while walking, standing, lying down, or bowing.
A Brāhmaṇa [should sip] water that reaches the heart, which is free from bubbles and froth.
But a Kṣatriya [is purified] by [water] reaching the throat.
A Vaiśya [is purified] by sipping water.
And likewise after touching a woman or a Śūdra with water that has already been used for bathing.

Even from a wound, those [rays] which are capable of satisfying a cow [are acceptable]. (VaDhS 3.35) [One should not use water] that is corrupted by color, smell, or taste, nor that which comes from an impure source. (VaDhS 3.36)
Large drops do not cause impurity from food remnants, provided they do not touch the body.
Having slept, eaten, sneezed, drunk, wept, or bathed, and after sipping water internally, one should sip water again even after putting on a garment.
Having touched the two lips where they are hairless.
There is no defilement from what has adhered to the beard.
Regarding things stuck between the teeth, they are like the teeth themselves; and whatever may enter the mouth, one becomes pure by simply swallowing it.
Even for one who causes others to sip water, those drops that have fallen upon his feet do not cause him to become impure; they are considered equal to the ground.
If, while eating, he should touch something that is impure,
he should set that object down on the ground, perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and then proceed with his meal again.
Whatever may require examination, one should touch it with water.
Wild animals killed by dogs, fruit fallen by birds,
that which has been trodden upon by children, and that which has been handled by women.
And whatever merchandise is displayed for sale, as well as the faults found in the faces of women.
"One is not defiled by mosquitoes or flies that have settled upon it;
and those waters which rest upon the earth and which satisfy the thirst of cows— having enumerated all such [waters], Prajāpati declared them to be pure."
VaDhS 3.48: Purification for removing stains and odors consists of water and earth for that which is smeared with impure substances.
For objects made of metal, clay, wood, and woven cloth, the methods of purification are cleansing with ashes, burning, planing, and washing, respectively.
The purification of stones and gems is like that of gold.
The purification of conch shells and mother-of-pearl is like that of gems.
The treatment of bones is like that of wood.
The purification of ropes, split bamboo, and leather is like that of cloth.
For those made of fruit, [the purification is] with cow-hair.
For those made of linen, [purification is performed] with a paste of white mustard seeds.

The ground attains purity according to the specific nature of the defilement through sweeping, smearing with cow-dung, scraping, sprinkling, and by means of [other] purificatory rites as appropriate to the place.
Moreover, they cite this:
"By digging, by burning, by trampling, and also by the treading of cows..."
The ground is purified by four means, and by a fifth, by smearing it with cow dung.
A woman is purified by her menses; a river is purified by its current;
bell-metal is purified by ash; and an earthen vessel is purified by being fired again.
An earthen vessel that has come into contact with intoxicating liquors, urine, feces, phlegm, pus, tears,
or blood is not purified even by baking it again.
The limbs are purified by water; the mind is purified by truth;
the inner self (bhūtātman) is purified by knowledge and austerity; and the intellect is purified by wisdom.
Gold is purified by water alone.
Likewise, silver [is not to be used for a vessel].
Copper is purified by an acid.
The divine (daiva) sacred site is at the base of the little finger.
On the finger-joints, [the name] of the sages.
Human [beings] are on the tips of the fingers.
The center of the palm is sacred to Agni.
The ancestral [lineage] is between the forefinger and the thumb.
One should honor the evening and morning meals with the words, "It is pleasing."
"May it be well-savored," [one says] at a rite for the ancestors.
"In the rites for prosperity, [the word] 'it is prepared' is used at each rite for prosperity.
(VaDhS 3.71) "The fourfold caste system is distinguished by its origin and by specific sacramental rites. (VaDhS 4.1)
"The Brāhmaṇa was his mouth; the Rājanya was made from his arms;
that which was his thighs became the Vaiśya; from his feet the Śūdra was born. Thus also there is a Vedic verse (Nigama).

With the Gāyatrī he created the Brāhmaṇa, with the Triṣṭubh the Rājanya, and with the Jagatī the Vaiśya; [he created] the Śūdra with no metre at all—thus it is known that the Śūdra is not subject to the sacraments.
For all [these], truthfulness, freedom from anger, generosity, non-violence, and procreation [are essential].
"Even in the worship of the ancestors, the gods, and guests, one may indeed kill an animal"—this is the teaching of Manu.
"Manu has declared that one may kill an animal only on these occasions— the offering of honey-mixture (madhuparka), at a sacrifice, and in rites for the ancestors or deities— and not otherwise."
Meat is never produced without having caused injury to living beings; yet the killing of living beings does not lead to heaven. Therefore, in a sacrifice, killing is no killing at all.
Furthermore, if a Brāhmaṇa or a Rājanya has arrived as a guest, one should cook a large bull or a large goat, thinking, "In this way we shall perform hospitality for him."
The water-rites and the period of impurity begin from the second year [of age].
Some say [the period lasts] until the eruption of the teeth.
Having consigned the body to the fire, they enter the water without looking back.
They should perform the water-rites with both hands—the left and the right—facing south on odd-numbered days.
For the ancestors, that direction which is to the south is their quarter.
Having gone to their homes, they should sit upon a layer of grass for three days without eating.
In case of inability, they should subsist on what has been purchased or produced.
Impurity on account of a death is ordained for ten days among the sapinda relatives.
Sapiṇḍaship is understood to extend up to the seventh person.
And for women who have been given away in marriage, it is known that [the impurity lasts] for three generations.
The others [the sons] should perform [the rites] for those women who have been given away in marriage, and they [the women] should do so for them.
The same rule applies even at birth for those who desire complete purification.
Or [he may do so] for his mother and father.
"Because she is the cause of that [birth], some say it belongs to the mother."
Moreover, they also cite this:

"There is no impurity for a man during childbirth, provided he does not come into contact [with it]. In that case, it is the menstrual flow that should be known as impure, and that is not found in a man."
If that [impurity] occurs again within [the period], they shall be purified by the remainder [of the first period].
If it is the remainder of the night, [he should perform the rite] with two [verses].
At dawn, with three [verses].
A Brāhmaṇa [is purified] in ten nights.
A Kṣatriya [is purified] in fifteen nights.
A Vaiśya [is purified] in twenty nights.
A Śūdra becomes pure after one month.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"He who eats during the period of impurity of a Śūdra, or during his birth-impurity,
shall go to a terrible hell and be born among the animal species."
If a twice-born man eats meat from an animal that has died within ten days, at the command [of another],
he becomes a worm and, at the end of his body, consumes its own excrement.
It is known from tradition that one becomes purified by studying the Saṃhitā while fasting for twelve months or twelve half-months.
When a child less than two years old has died, or in the case of a miscarriage, the period of impurity for the sapinda relatives is three nights.
Gautama says that there is immediate purification.
If the deceased is in another country, one shall observe impurity for one night upon hearing of it after the ten days have passed.

If one who has maintained the sacred fires should die while traveling abroad, Gautama says that after performing the funeral rites again, the purification is to be conducted as in the case of a corpse.

Having touched a sacrificial post, a funeral pyre, a cemetery, a menstruating woman, a woman who has recently given birth, or anyone who is impure, one should enter the water for a bath including the head; indeed, one should enter the water.
A woman is not independent; she has man as her primary authority.
It is known from tradition that those who maintain no sacred fires and women who have not reached their fertile age are "immortal" (amṛta).
Moreover, they also cite this:
"The father protects her in childhood, the husband protects her in youth, and the son protects her in old age; a woman does not deserve independence."
Regarding her husband's practice of malevolent magic, the expiation has been stated in the secret [sections].
For month after month, their menstrual flow carries away their evil deeds.
A woman in her menses remains impure for three nights.

She shall not apply collyrium, nor anoint herself; she shall not bathe in water, she shall sleep on the ground, and she shall not sleep during the day; she shall not touch fire, nor let go of a rope, nor clean her teeth, nor eat meat, nor gaze at the planets, nor laugh, nor perform any such act; she shall not run, but drink from a vessel that is not small, or drink from her joined palms, or from a vessel of red metal.

For it is known from tradition: Indra, having slain the three-headed son of Tvaṣṭṛ, was seized by evil and thought of himself thus: "I am bound by great unrighteousness. All beings reviled him, crying out, "Foe of the embryo! Foe of the embryo! He ran to women, saying, "Accept a third part of this guilt of killing the embryo for me. They asked, "What shall be ours? He said, "Choose a boon."

They said, "Let us obtain offspring during the fertile season; let us unite according to our desire until the birth. "So be it," they agreed, and they accepted [the condition]. This very sin of foeticide manifests itself month after month; therefore, one should not eat the food of a woman in her courses, for she remains assuming the form of foeticide itself.

Regarding this, they say: "One must not accept from her even eye-ointment or ointment for the body, for that is the food of women. Therefore, people feel disgust toward her and toward that [act], thinking, "She has come here."
Those whose women remain in their courses, those who maintain no sacred fires,
and those families in which there are no Vedic scholars— all these follow the customs of Śūdras.
"All of them follow the dharma of Śūdras."
"Good conduct is the highest dharma for all; this is the settled conclusion.
One whose soul is overwhelmed by deficient conduct perishes both in this world and after death."
Neither austerities, nor sacred knowledge, nor the Agnihotra sacrifice,
nor sacrificial gifts can ever save one who has fallen away from this [dharma] due to deficient conduct.
The Vedas do not purify one who is devoid of right conduct, even if they have been studied together with the six auxiliary sciences;
at the time of death, the Vedic hymns abandon him, just as birds with grown wings leave their nest.
But for a Brāhmaṇa devoid of proper conduct, even the Vedas with their six auxiliary limbs and all the sacrifices—what pleasure can they produce? They are like beautiful wives to a blind man.
The Vedic meters do not rescue this man from evil who lives by deceit, practicing illusion.
But even these two syllables, when properly studied, purify that Brahman, just as rain-clouds purify the earth.
For a man of evil conduct becomes censured in the world;
he constantly shares in suffering, being diseased and short-lived.
From right conduct dharma bears fruit; from right conduct wealth bears fruit.
Through right conduct one attains prosperity; right conduct destroys inauspicious marks.
Even if he is devoid of all auspicious marks, the man who possesses good conduct,
is full of faith, and free from envy, lives for a hundred years.
One who knows the Dharma must perform the activities of eating, excreting, and moving about with great self-restraint;
likewise, speech, mental actions, austerity, as well as wealth and longevity, must be kept strictly guarded.
One should void both urine and feces facing north during the day;
at night, however, one should do so facing south, for in this way one's life-span is not diminished.
Facing the fire, facing the sun, facing a cow, facing a Brahmin,
facing Soma, water, or the twilight— wisdom perishes for one who urinates in these directions.
One should not urinate in a river, nor on a path, nor in ashes;
nor on cow dung, nor in a ploughed field, nor in a sown field, nor in the shade of trees that provide livelihood or are grassy meadows.
In shade or in darkness, by night or by day, a twice-born man may perform [the purification] facing any direction he finds comfortable, as well as when there is danger to his life.
One should perform one's duties with water that has been drawn up.
Bathing may be performed even with water that has not been drawn up [from a well or river].
A Brahmin should fetch clay from a riverbank that contains sand.
The five kinds of earth should not be taken: that from within water, from a temple, from an anthill, from a mouse-hole, or what remains after purification has been performed.
One application of clay is prescribed for the penis, three for the hands; thus two applications are traditionally taught.
Five applications are for the anus, ten for one hand, and seven applications of clay for both hands together.
This is the purification for householders; it is twofold for students, threefold for forest-dwellers, and fourfold for ascetics.
Eight mouthfuls are the meal for a sage (muni), sixteen for a forest-dweller (vānaprastha),
thirty-two for a householder (gṛhastha), and an unlimited amount for a student (brahmacārin).
The maintainer of the sacred fires, the draft-ox, and the student—these three achieve success only while eating; for them there is no success while fasting.
Regarding vows, observances, sacrifices, Vedic study, and religious duties.
Yoga, austerity, self-restraint, charity, truthfulness, purity, sacred learning, compassion, knowledge,
discernment, and faith— this is the defining characteristic of a Brāhmaṇa.
One should recognize long-standing enmity, envy, untruthfulness, reviling Brahmins,
backbiting, and cruelty as the characteristics of a Śūdra.

Those Brāhmaṇas who are peaceful and self-controlled, whose ears are filled with sacred learning, who have conquered their senses, who abstain from killing living beings, and whose hands are restrained from accepting gifts— they alone are capable of delivering [others] across [the ocean of saṃsāra].
One vessel consists of the Veda, and another vessel consists of austerity;
but among all vessels, that is the true vessel whose belly does not contain the food of a Śūdra.
If a twice-born man dies while the food of a Śūdra remains in his stomach,
he shall become a domestic pig or be born into that Śūdra’s family.
For one whose limbs are nourished by the food of a Śūdra, even if he constantly studies the Vedas,
performs sacrifices, or recites prayers, he does not attain the higher goal.
But he who engages in sexual intercourse after having eaten the food of a Śūdra—
his sons belong to the one whose food it was, and he himself shall not ascend to heaven.
One who has risen through Vedic study, who possesses a noble birth, who is tranquil, established in the sacrificial fires, fearful of sin, and possessed of great knowledge;
who is patient toward women, righteous, a refuge for cows, and exhausted by religious observances—they say such a person is a worthy recipient.
Just as milk, curd, ghee, or honey placed in an unbaked earthen vessel would perish due to the weakness of the vessel, yet neither the vessel nor those liquids [would be lost if it were strong].
In this way, an ignorant man who accepts cows, gold, clothing, a horse, land, or sesame seeds is reduced to ashes like a piece of wood.
One should not practice fingernail-clapping.
And one should not eat with the fingernails at the beginning of a meal.
And one should not drink water with cupped hands.
One should not strike water with the foot or with the hand.
Nor [should one touch] water with water.
One should not gather fruit with bricks.
One fruit is not [to be exchanged] for another fruit.
One should not be a schemer nor a deceiver.
One should not learn the language of the barbarians.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"One should not be fickle with hands or feet, nor fickle with the eyes; one should not be fickle with speech or limbs—this is the sphere of conduct for the disciplined."

Those Brāhmaṇas to whom the Veda, along with its supplements, has been transmitted through an unbroken lineage, are to be known as the learned (śiṣṭas), who are the direct authorities for the revealed scripture.
He whom no one knows— whether he exists or does not exist, whether he is unlearned or deeply learned, whether he is well-conducted or ill-conducted— that man is a Brāhmaṇa.
"He is a Brāhmaṇa. Thus [it is said].
VaDhS 7.1: There are four stages of life (āśramas).
The student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and the wandering mendicant.
Having studied one Veda, two Vedas, or all the Vedas among them, and having remained firm in his vow of celibacy, he may dwell with whomever he desires.
A student of sacred knowledge shall serve his teacher until the liberation of his body.
And when the teacher has died, he shall tend the sacred fire.
For it is known: "The teacher is indeed Agni for you."
Restraining his speech.
He should eat at the fourth, sixth, and eighth meal-times.
He should practice begging for alms.
He is dependent on his teacher.
He should wear matted hair, or have a single lock of matted hair on his head.
If the teacher is walking, he should follow him; if the teacher is standing, he should stand; and if the teacher is reclining, he should sit near him.
He shall study when summoned.
Having offered everything he has obtained, he should eat with their permission.
He shall avoid using a bedstead for sleeping, brushing his teeth, washing [his face], applying collyrium, anointing [his body with oil], and wearing shoes or a parasol.
He should stand during the day and remain seated at night.
Three times a day he should approach water, saying, "Water! Water! (VaDhS 7.17).

A householder, having subdued anger and joy, being permitted by his teacher, and having bathed, shall take a wife who is of the same lineage as himself, who has not had sexual intercourse, who is younger in age, and of equal status.
The fifth generation on the mother's side and the seventh generation on the father's side.
He should kindle the nuptial fire.
One should not turn away a guest who has arrived in the evening.
He should not stay in his house without eating.
If a Brahmin seeking lodging comes to one's house and does not eat,
he departs taking with him whatever merit that person has performed.
A Brāhmaṇa staying for even a single night is traditionally known as a guest (atithi);
because he stays for a non-permanent duration, he is therefore called a guest.

A Brahmin who is a resident of the same village or a mere acquaintance is not considered a guest; when he arrives, whether at the proper time or otherwise, he should not stay in the house without eating.
One who is faithful, free from covetousness, and capable of maintaining the sacred fires should not fail to establish those fires.
And [the soma] is sufficient for Soma; one who has not sacrificed with Soma is not [sufficient].
He should be devoted to Vedic study, sacrifice, and procreation.
One should honor a guest who has arrived at one's house by rising to meet him, offering a seat, speaking kind words, and being free from envy.
And one should satisfy all beings with food according to one's ability.
Only the householder performs sacrifice; the householder practices austerity. Indeed, among the four stages of life, the householder is distinguished as superior.
Just as all rivers and streams find their resting place in the ocean,
so do all those in the [other] stages of life find their support in the householder.
Just as all living beings live by depending on their mother,
so do all mendicants live by depending on the householder.

A Brāhmaṇa who constantly uses water for purification, constantly wears the sacred thread, constantly engages in Vedic study, avoids the food of outcasts, approaches his wife during her season, and offers oblations according to the rules, does not fall from the world of Brahman.
"From the world of Brahman," so it is said.
The forest-dweller (vānaprastha) has matted hair and wears garments of bark or skins.
And he shall not enter a village.
He should not stand upon ground that has been ploughed by a plow.
He should gather roots and fruits that have not been cultivated.
One whose vital energy is drawn upward;
one whose disposition is patient.
One should honor a guest who has arrived at the hermitage with alms consisting of roots and fruits.
One should indeed give, but one should not accept [such gifts].
He should touch water at the three times of day.
Having established the sacred fire according to the Śrāmaṇaka rite, he shall become one who maintains the consecrated fires.
Having his dwelling at the foot of a tree, after six months he shall be without fire and without a fixed abode.
He should give to the gods, the ancestors, and human beings; he shall go to eternal heaven—this is what is meant by "eternal."
The wandering mendicant, having given the gift of fearlessness to all beings, should depart.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"The sage who wanders about having granted fearlessness to all beings—
for him, too, there is never any fear from any beings."
But he who, having granted safety to all beings, turns back from his vow,
kills both those born and those unborn, as does one who accepts gifts for himself.
One should renounce all ritual acts, but one should not renounce the Veda alone;
by renouncing the Veda one becomes a Śūdra, therefore one should not renounce the Veda.
The single syllable is the supreme Brahman; breath control is the highest austerity;
begging is superior to fasting, and compassion excels giving.
Shaven-headed, free from the sense of "mine," and without possessions.
He should go for alms to seven houses that have not been previously designated.
When the smoke has subsided and the pestle is at rest.
He is clothed in a single garment.
Or, having covered his body with a deerskin or with grasses cut by cows.
He should sleep on the bare ground.
One should dwell in a transient residence.
At the edge of a village, in a temple, in an empty house, or at the foot of a tree.
One who studies knowledge with the mind.
He should be constantly dwelling in the forest.
One should not walk about when domestic animals are in sight.
For one who dwells constantly in the forest, whose senses are conquered, who has turned away from the gratification of all the senses,
whose mind is absorbed in reflection on the inner self, and who is equanimous— for such a person, there is indeed certain non-return [to saṃsāra].
He should have unmanifest signs and unmanifest conduct.
One who is not insane but wears the garb of an insane person.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"There is no liberation for one who is devoted to the science of grammar, nor for one who delights in grasping worldly affairs;
there is none for one intent on food and clothing, nor for one who is fond of beautiful dwellings."
He should never seek alms by means of portents or omens, nor by the science of astrology and bodily marks,
nor by teaching or by engaging in debate.
In the absence of gain he should not despair, nor should he rejoice upon obtaining it;
he should be content with only what is necessary for the maintenance of life, remaining free from attachment to material things.
He who has no attachment to a hut, nor to water, nor to clothing, nor to the three hollows (of the body),
nor to a house, nor to a seat, nor to food— he indeed is a knower of liberation.
In a Brāhmaṇa family, he should eat as much as he may obtain, both morning and evening, avoiding honey and meat.
And he should not be satiated.
Or he may live in a village.
One who is not crooked, not deceitful, not seeking refuge [in others], and not fickle.
And he should not engage in sexual intercourse with anyone.
He should be indifferent toward all living beings by avoiding both injury and favor.

The avoidance of slander, envy, pride, egoism, lack of faith, dishonesty, self-praise, disparagement of others, hypocrisy, greed, delusion, anger, and malice is held to be the duty of all stages of life.

A Brāhmaṇa who wears the sacred thread over the left shoulder, holds a water-pot in his hand, remains pure, and avoids the food of a Śūdra, does not fall from the world of Brahman—yes, from the world of Brahman.
There are six who are worthy of the guest-offering (argha).
The officiating priest, the father-in-law, the king, the paternal uncle, the *snātaka*, and the maternal uncle are those with whom one may marry.
Having prepared the Vaiśvadeva food, one should offer it into the domestic fire every morning and evening.
One should offer the bali-oblation to the household deities.
Having given the first portion to a learned Vedic scholar (śrotriya) or to a student observing the vow of celibacy (brahmacārin), he should thereafter offer it to the ancestors.
Then he should feed the guest, each more distinguished than the last, in successive order.
Among those belonging to one's own *gṛhya* tradition, [the duties apply to] maidens, children, the elderly, the young, and women who have recently given birth.
Then [he should study] the other domestic [texts].
One should cast [the food] on the ground for dogs, Cāṇḍālas, outcasts, and crows.
One should give the remains of one's food, or that which is not the remains, to a Śūdra woman.
The remaining [food] the husband and wife should eat together.
VaDhS 11.12: If a guest should arrive when the Vaiśvadeva offering has already been set aside, one should cook again using all available means and provide him with special food.
For it is known: "A Brāhmaṇa guest enters as Vaiśvānara; therefore they bring water and food from the rain-vessels, for people know this to be the propitiation."
Having fed him, he should attend upon him.
One should follow him as far as the boundary, or until one receives permission to depart.
During the dark fortnight, after the fourth day, one should offer [the śrāddha] to the ancestors.

On the day before [the ceremony], having assembled Brāhmaṇas—ascetics, householders, or virtuous men who are not of advanced age, who do not follow improper occupations, who are learned in the Vedas, and who are neither pupils nor resident disciples.
One should also feed disciples who possess good qualities.
One should exclude those who are naked, white-complexioned, eunuchs, blind, those with black teeth, those afflicted with leprosy, and those with deformed nails.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"If one who is learned in the mantras is afflicted by physical defects that defile the company, Yama has declared him to be undefiled; he is indeed a purifier of the company."
At a *śrāddha*, the remnants of the food should not be removed until the end of the day;
for streams of nectar drip from them, which those who have not yet performed their water-libations (*udaka*) drink.
One should not wipe away the remnants [of the food] until the sun has set;
then, streams of milk flow inexhaustibly for those who partake in the distribution of the remains.
Regarding those of one's own lineage who have died before their sacramental rites,
it is the established rule that Manu has declared both the leavings of food and the scrapings from the dish to be their share.
One should offer the remnants that have fallen on the ground, the scattered grains, and the water used for washing to those deceased who were childless and short-lived.
Food offered to the ancestors that is released from both hands—
during that interval, indeed, the evil-minded Asuras wait for it.
Therefore, one should approach food with hands that are not empty;
or, having touched it, one should stand until both [the giver and the recipient] have finished eating.
Two [should be invited] for the rite for the gods, three for the ancestral rite, or one for each of the two.
Even if he is very wealthy, he should feed [the guests] but should not be attached to abundance.
Hospitality, the proper time and place, purity, and the excellence of the Brahmins—these five things are destroyed by prolixity; therefore, one should avoid it.
Or alternatively, he should feed a single Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas,
who is endowed with learning and good character, and who is free from all inauspicious marks.
If one should feed only a single person at a śrāddha, how should the portion for the gods (daiva) be provided there?
Having set aside food from the entire prepared quantity into a vessel—
Having performed [the rite] in a temple of the deities, one should then proceed with the śrāddha;
one should either cast that food into the fire or give it to a celibate student (brahmacārin).
As long as the food remains warm, as long as they eat in silence,
and as long as the qualities of the sacrificial offering have not been described, for so long do the ancestors eat.
The qualities of the sacrificial offering should not be mentioned as long as the ancestors have not been satisfied;
once the ancestors have been satisfied, one may afterwards say that the offering is excellent.
But an ascetic who, being appointed, eats meat at a rite for the ancestors or for the gods,
falls into hell for as many years as there are hairs on that animal's body.
Three things are purifying at a *śrāddha*: a daughter’s son, a *kutapa* blanket, and sesame seeds.
Furthermore, three things they praise in this context: purity, freedom from anger, and lack of haste.
In the eighth part of the day, when the sun grows dim, that time is known as *kutapa*; what is given to the ancestors at that time becomes inexhaustible.
If one engages in sexual intercourse after having given or partaken of a *śrāddha* feast,
his ancestors become consumers of that semen for an entire month.
The offspring born from one who has given away or consumed his paternal inheritance does not attain sacred knowledge and is born with a diminished lifespan.
The father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather wait upon the son who is born,
just as birds wait upon the peepal tree.
"With honey, meat, vegetables, milk, and milk-rice—
this man will offer us the *śrāddha* during the rainy season and under the asterism Maghā."
The ancestors rejoice in a son who increases the lineage, who is diligent in the duties toward his father, and who is endowed with devotion to the gods and the Brahmins.
His ancestors rejoice, just as farmers do at well-plowed fields;
for when one staying at Gayā gives food, his ancestors consider themselves truly blessed with a son.
One should offer to the ancestors on the full moon days of Śrāvaṇa and Āgrahāyaṇī, and on the Anvaṣṭakā day.
When the necessary materials, the location, and a Brāhmaṇa are available, there is no restriction regarding time.
A Brahmin must necessarily establish the sacred fires.
He shall sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices, the Āgrayaṇa offering, the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, the animal sacrifice, and the Soma sacrifice.
For this is both a constant obligation and is described as a debt.

For it is known from scripture: "A Brāhmaṇa is born burdened with three debts: by sacrifice to the gods, by progeny to the ancestors, and by the life of a student (brahmacarya) to the seers. He indeed is free from debt who has performed sacrifices, who has a son, and who has lived as a student.
One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth year from conception;
a Rājanya in the eleventh year from conception.
A Vaiśya [should be initiated] in the twelfth year from conception.
The staff of a Brāhmaṇa should be made of Palāśa wood.
Or, for a Kṣatriya, [the staff] may be made of Nyagrodha wood.
Or the staff of a Vaiśya may be made of Udumbara wood.
The sacrificial cord of a Brāhmaṇa should reach up to his hair.
For a Kṣatriya, it should reach up to the forehead.
The nose-length [staff] is for the Vaiśya.
The girdle of a Brāhmaṇa should be made of Muñja grass.
The bowstring is the [sacrificial cord] for a Kṣatriya.
The garment of a Vaiśya should be made of hempen threads.
A black antelope skin is the upper garment for a Brāhmaṇa.
The Raurava [chant] is for a Kṣatriya.
For a Vaiśya, the skin of a cow or a goat [is prescribed].
The garment of a Brāhmaṇa shall be white and unwashed.
The garment of a Kṣatriya should be madder-red.
For a Vaiśya, [the garment] shall be yellow or made of silk.
Or, for all [of them], it may be woven cloth that is not dyed.
A Brāhmaṇa should beg for alms using a formula that begins with the word "bhavat" (sir).
A Kṣatriya [should address his teacher] as "bhavat" placed between [the vocative particle and his name].
In the case of a woman of the Bhavadantī class, a Vaiśya [is the husband].
For a Brāhmaṇa, the time [for initiation] does not expire until the sixteenth year.
For a Kṣatriya, [the period lasts] until the twenty-second year.
For a Vaiśya, [the period lasts] until the twenty-fourth year.
From this point onward, they become those whose Sāvitrī has been lost.
One should not initiate them, nor teach them, nor officiate sacrifices for them, nor should one have marriages performed with them.
One whose *sāvitrī* has been lost shall perform the *uddālakavrata*.

For two months he should subsist on barley-gruel, for one month on milk, for half a month on *āmikṣā* curd, for eight nights on clarified butter, for six nights on food obtained unasked, for three nights on water, and he should fast for a day and a night.
He should go to the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*).
Or he should perform the Vrātyastoma sacrifice; "he should sacrifice, or he should sacrifice," so it is said.
Now, therefore, follow the observances of a Snātaka.
He shall not beg from anyone except the king and his students.
But if overcome by hunger, he may beg for just a little—be it prepared or unprepared food, a field, a cow, a goat or sheep, or, at the very least, gold, grain, or cooked food.
"But a Snātaka must not let himself perish from hunger"—this is the instruction.
One should not live together with one who wears soiled garments.
Nor with a woman in her menses.
Nor with an unsuitable woman.
One should not be a *kulakula*.
One should not step over a stretched-out calf-rope.
One should not look at the sun when it is rising, nor when it is setting.
One should not void urine or excrement in water.
One should not spit.

Having wrapped his head and covered the ground with grass unfit for sacrifice, he shall void urine and feces facing north during the day; at night, facing south; and during the morning and evening twilights, he shall sit facing north. Moreover, they also cite this: "For those who have completed their Vedic studies (snātakas), there should always be an inner garment as well as an upper one."
Two sacred threads, a staff, and a water-pot with water.
"In water, in the hand, and on wood, [the vessel] is declared pure even when touched by fire;
therefore, one should wipe the water-pot with both hands and water."
For Manu Prajāpati has declared this to be the "circling with fire" (paryagnikaraṇa).
Having performed the necessary duties, one who is most intent on purity should sip water for ritual sipping (ācamana).
One should eat food facing the east.
He should swallow the entire morsel silently, including the thumb.
And one should not make a sound.
He should approach his own wife during her fertile period, avoiding the forbidden lunar days.
He should approach her without crossing over [her].
But he who performs sexual intercourse in the mouth of his wedded wife—
his ancestors become eaters of that semen for a month.
That pleasure which is pursued through irregular conduct is based on unrighteousness.
Moreover, it is known from the *Kaṭhaka*: "May those among us who are yet to be born tomorrow lie with their husbands"—this is the boon granted to women by Indra.
One should not climb a tree.
One should not descend into a well.
One should not blow on the fire with one's mouth.
One should not pass between the fire and a Brāhmaṇa.
Nor [should one study] while standing between two fires.
Nor [should one eat] from two Brāhmaṇas, even after having obtained their permission.
"One should not eat together with one's wife; for it is known in the Vājasaneyaka that [otherwise] the offspring will be lacking in vigor."
One should not point it out by the name "Indra’s bow."
One should say, "The jeweled bow."
One should avoid a seat made of *pālāśa* wood, sandals, and a tooth-stick made of *pālāśa*.
One should not eat from one's lap.
One should not eat on a couch.
He should carry a staff made of bamboo.
And [the theft of] gold earrings [is a minor offense].
One should not wear a garland outside [the body], except for one made of gold.
One should avoid assemblies and public gatherings.
Moreover, they also cite:
"The invalidation of the Vedas, the reviling of the seers,
and a lack of discipline in all matters— this is the destruction of the self."
One should not go to a sacrifice unrobed; if one should go, one should return again by circling to the right.
One should not set out on a journey when the sun is directly overhead the trees.
And one should not board a boat whose safety is doubtful.
One should not cross a river by swimming with one's arms.
Having risen during the latter part of the night and studied, he should not go back to sleep again.
During the *muhūrta* sacred to Prajāpati, a Brāhmaṇa should observe certain restrictive rules; he should observe them, indeed, he should observe them.
VaDhS 13.1: Now, therefore, follows the commencement of Vedic study (svādhyāyopākarma), on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa or of Prauṣṭhapada.
Having established the fire, he offers unbroken grains of parched barley.
"To the gods, to the seers, and to the meters."
Having caused the Brahmins to pronounce auspicious blessings and having consumed curds, they should then commence the study of the Vedas.
For four and a half months, or five and a half months.
From that time forward, he should study during the bright fortnights.
But one may study the Vedāṅgas at will.
His days of non-study are as follows.
[One should not study] during the twilight or when there is thunder.
At the twilights.
In cities where there is a corpse inside or which are designated as unfit for praise.
If one desires, [one may eat] on ground that has been soaked with cow dung or on ground that has been smeared.
At the edge of the cremation ground.
[The same applies] to one who is lying down.
[This applies] to one who performs a *śrāddha*.
Regarding this, they cite a verse from the *Mānava*:
"Having accepted fruits, water, sesame seeds, food, or whatever else may be offered at a *śrāddha*, there is no suspension of study; for Brāhmaṇas are said to have their hands as their mouths."
For one who runs, there is purification from foul odors and the like by means of a salt-flat.
[The same applies] to one who has climbed a tree.
Nor on a boat or in an army.
And [one should not study] after eating while the hands are still wet.
[One should not study] when there is the sound of an arrow.
On the fourteenth day, on the new moon day, on the eighth day, and on the Aṣṭakā days.
And [one should not eat] while resting with one's feet and genitals extended.
In the presence of the teacher.
In the case of a woman who has abstained from sexual intercourse.
[One becomes impure] by wearing a garment used for sexual intercourse that has not been washed.
At the edge of the village.
[The same penance applies] to one who has vomited.
For one who has urinated or evacuated [the bowels].
And [the same applies] when the sound of the Sāman occurs within the Ṛgveda or the Yajurveda.
When there is indigestion.
In the event of a thunderclap.
In the case of an earthquake, [one should perform the same].
During an eclipse of the moon or the sun.
In the case of the sounds of the quarters, mountains, or precipices, and during rains of stones, blood, or dust, the impurity lasts until the same time the next day.
In the event of the conjunction of a meteor and lightning, [the impurity lasts] for three nights.
A meteor and lightning are [inauspicious] as long as their light remains visible.
When it has not been purified, it is impure for the duration of the day and night.
When the teacher has died, [the impurity lasts] for three nights.
In the case of the teacher’s son, a pupil, or a wife, [the impurity lasts] for one day and night.
One should rise to greet and salute the officiating priest, the father-in-law, the paternal uncle, and the maternal uncle, provided they are not younger than oneself.
And those who are to be approached by the feet, as well as the wife of one's teacher.
And [he should honor] his mother and father.
He who knows how to greet [an elder] should approach him, saying, "I am so-and-so, sir."
And he who does not know [the sacred texts].

In the case of a return greeting when one has been addressed, the final vowel undergoes prolation; a non-pragṛhya diphthong likewise undergoes the state of becoming *āy*. For example: *bho bhāv* (O sir!).
A father who has fallen [from his caste] is to be abandoned, but a mother does not fall because of her son.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"Ten teachers are equal to one sub-teacher; a father exceeds a hundred teachers in dignity; a mother exceeds a thousand fathers in dignity."
A wife, sons, and disciples who have associated with those who commit sinful deeds should be reprimanded and then abandoned; he who abandons them otherwise [becomes] an outcast.
If one abandons a sacrificial priest or a teacher who fails to officiate at sacrifices or teach, one falls from his status, except in the case of actual abandonment due to a grave fault.
They say that one born from an outcast becomes an outcast, except in the case of a woman.
For she indeed goes to another.
He should approach her as one who does not inherit property.
When the teacher's own teacher is present, one's conduct toward him is required to be as toward the teacher;
according to the Vedic revelation, one should behave toward the teacher's son as toward the teacher himself.
A weapon, poison, and liquor are not to be accepted by a Brāhmaṇa.
Learning, wealth, age, relationship, and ritual action are grounds for respect.
Each preceding one is more serious than the following.
When meeting on a path, way should be yielded one after another to the elderly, the young, the sick, those burdened with loads, women, and those riding in vehicles.
When a king and a *snātaka* meet, way should be yielded by the king to the *snātaka*.
[The same applies] for all [the verses] when the bride is being led away.
Grass, ground, fire, water, kind speech, truthfulness, and freedom from envy—these are never lacking in the houses of the virtuous, never at any time.
VaDhS 14.1: Now, therefore, we shall describe what may and may not be eaten.
The food of a physician, a hunter, an unchaste woman, a staff-bearer, a thief, one accused of a crime, a eunuch, and an outcast is not to be eaten.
[The food] of a miser, one initiated for a sacrifice, a prisoner, a sick person, a seller of Soma, a carpenter, a washerman, a vintner, an informer, a usurer, and a leather-cutter [is forbidden].
And [the same applies] to a Śūdra.
And those who bear weapons.
And he who considers his paramour to be a paramour.
And he who burns houses.
And he who does not strike down those deserving of death.
Or that which has been proclaimed by word of mouth, [saying] "Who shall eat? (VaDhS 14.9).
The food of a group and the food of a courtesan—these [are forbidden].
Moreover, they also cite this:
"The gods do not eat the food of one who keeps a dog, nor of the husband of a *vṛṣalī*, nor of one conquered by his wife, nor of him in whose house lives a paramour."
One may accept these things: fuel, water, grass, *kuśa* grass, parched grain, that which is offered, a vehicle, a dwelling, *śapharī* fish, *priyaṅgu* seeds, garlands, perfumes, honey, and meat.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"One who wishes to support his wife for the sake of his teacher, or who intends to honor the deities and guests, may accept gifts from anyone; yet he himself should not find satisfaction therein."
The food of a hunter who roams with arrows is not to be avoided.

For it is known: "Agastya engaged in hunting during a thousand-year sacrificial session (*sattra*). For him, the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) consisted of the flesh of recommended wild animals and birds, prepared without a bed of grass.
Moreover, in this regard, they cite these verses concerning Prajāpati:
"A morsel of alms-food that is offered, brought forward, and not previously solicited—"
Prajāpati considered even those who have committed evil deeds to be fit for being fed.

One may eat the food of a person who has faith, even if he is a thief, especially so; but one must never eat the food of one who performs many sacrifices for hire, nor of one who initiates many pupils.
The ancestors do not eat his offerings for fifteen years,
nor does the fire carry his oblations, he who treats her with contempt.
The food of a physician, a hunter, a surgeon, a sinner, a eunuch,
and an unchaste woman, even if offered, is not to be accepted.
The food of one who is not a guru, if it is leavings, is not to be eaten.
One's own leavings, and that which has been defiled by the leavings of others.
And that which has been defiled by cloth, hair, or insects.
But if one so desires, having removed hair or insects, sprinkled it with water, or scattered ashes over it, one may use what has been declared pure by word.
For in this regard, they cite these verses concerning Prajāpati:
"The gods ordained three purifiers for Brahmins:
that which is unseen, that which is cleansed with water, and that which is praised by speech."
In a temple courtyard, at weddings, and during established sacrifices,
food touched by crows or dogs should not be discarded. Therefore, having removed that [contaminated] food, the remainder deserves purification.
For liquids, purification is by means of pouring [into water], while for solids, it is by sprinkling.
For that which has been touched by the mouth of a cat shall indeed remain pure.
Food that has stood overnight, food corrupted by its nature, food containing hair or insects, food cooked again after being set aside, and raw meat as well as cooked meat [should not be eaten].
But he may, at his pleasure, consume it when it has been sprinkled over with curd or ghee.
For on this matter they cite these verses concerning Prajāpati:
"If a Brahmin eats ghee or oil that has fallen onto his nails,
Yama declared that to be impure, equal to the eating of cow's flesh."
But those fats, salts, and condiments which are given with the hand do not reach the giver; the eater consumes only sin.
One should give [the gift], but never with one's hand nor with an iron vessel.

In the case of eating garlic, onions, leeks, scallions, the exudation of trees that cause phlegm, red exudations, things cut with a knife, things licked by dogs or crows, or the remnants of food left by a Śūdra, one must perform an *atikṛcchra* penance.
The milk of a cow in heat and the milk of a cow whose calf has not yet been born [are forbidden].
[The same applies] to cows, buffaloes, and goats within ten days of calving.
Water within a boat is [pure].
One should avoid cakes, fried grains, *karambha*, parched barley flour, *vaṭaka* balls, oil, milk-rice, vegetables, and anything that has turned sour.
And other products made from milk and barley flour.
Among five-toed animals, the porcupine, the hedgehog, the hare, the tortoise, and the monitor lizard are edible.
Among domestic animals, those with teeth only on one side and camels are not to be eaten.
Or among fish, the following are edible: the ceṭa, gavaya, śiśumāra, crocodile, and crab.
Those with deformed shapes and those with serpent-like heads [should be avoided].
The white cow, the gavaya, and the śarabha as well.
Likewise, those who have not been specifically designated [for the rite].
And [the meat of] cows and oxen whose teeth have not yet fallen out.
In the Vājasaneyaka, it is known that the cow and the ox are fit for consumption and are pure.
But regarding the rhinoceros and the non-domestic pig, there are conflicting opinions.

And among birds, those born in the equinox or on trees with hollow trunks, web-footed birds, sparrows, water-fowls, swans, ruddy geese, vultures, crows, pigeons, ospreys, saranga ducks, white doves, curlews, cranes, kanka herons, vultures, hawks, cranes, balaka herons, madgu water-hens, tiṭṭibhas, mandhala birds, night-prowlers, woodpeckers, cakravāka birds, elātakas, hārītas, khanjarīṭas, domestic cocks, parrots, mainas, cuckoos, and carnivorous birds, as well as those that frequent villages—these are [forbidden]. And those that frequent villages [are forbidden]. Thus it is said.
A person is born from the union of blood and semen, having the mother and father as its cause.
In the giving away, selling, or abandoning of that [son], the mother and father have authority.
But one should neither give away nor accept an only son.
For he [is appointed] for the sake of the continuity of his ancestors.
A woman shall neither give away nor accept a son, except with the permission of her husband.

One who intends to adopt a son shall summon his kinsmen and inform the king; then, having offered oblations with the *vyāhṛti* formulas in the middle of his house, he should adopt a boy whose kinsmen are not far away and who is closely related by blood.
And when a doubt arises, one should treat him as a distant relative or like a Śūdra.
For it is known from scripture that by means of one person, many are saved.
If, after he has been adopted, a son should be born to him from his own body, the *dattaka* shall be entitled to a fourth part of the inheritance.
If he should not be engaged in rites for prosperity (nābhyudayika).
A violator of the Vedas, a priest for Śūdras, and those who have fallen from the ranks of the highest varṇa—these are the ones from whose vessels [the water] is poured out.

To prevent the mixing of unworthy recipients, one should take up an incomplete vessel and pour out the full vessel for him, having spread out *darbha* grass with their tips pointing forward—or red flowers—with the left foot by a slave, the son of a woman of a different caste, a kinsman, or someone of a dissimilar class who is devoid of good qualities.
And his relatives, with their hair disheveled, should touch the one who leads him away.
Having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder, they may enter their homes at will.
From this point forward, they should not subject him to legal proceedings.
Those who possess his qualities and practice that dharma.
But for those who have fallen [from their caste], once they have performed the penance, there is restoration.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"He who takes [the food] first should go as if playing, as if laughing;
he who causes it to fall behind should go as if grieving, as if weeping."
For those who have killed their teacher, mother, or father, purification from these sins occurs through their favor or by being banished.

VaDhS 15.20: Having filled a golden vessel or one made of clay from a sacred pool or a flowing stream with water, they consecrate him with these waters while reciting the *apohiṣṭhā* verses. {cf. 9.1: *obhtūrjhātana | mahṇāya ce*} VaDhS 15.21: The entire ritual for the restoration of one who has been consecrated is explained by the [ceremony] on the birth of a son; it is explained. It is explained.
VaDhS 16.1 Now, the legal procedures.
The king or his minister shall conduct the affairs of the assembly.
When two parties are disputing, he should not take the side of one against the other.
As is the seat, so is the offense; indeed, the offense is determined by the end [of the meal].
He should be impartial toward all beings according to their rank; for offenses against the first two castes must be dealt with up to the point of knowledge.
And he should protect what has been acquired.
The property of a king and of a minor [belongs to the state].
[This applies] to those who have not attained legal capacity.
But when the time has arrived, that which [is prescribed] should be done.
VaDhS 16.10: Writing, witnesses, and possession are declared to be the three kinds of evidence;
by means of these, the owner of the wealth shall first recover his property.
In the case of paths and fields, there is likewise the right to abandon them or to exchange them;
in the case of young houses and other types of property, [the penalty is] three-quarters of a pāda.
In a dispute concerning a house or a field, the testimony of the neighbors is decisive.
In a dispute with neighbors, documentary evidence is the means of proof.
In case of a contradiction with a counter-document, the evidence of the elders and guilds of the village or city shall prevail.
Moreover, they also cite this: "That which is inherited from a father, that which is purchased, that which is received as a gift, that which is acquired through marriage,
that which is obtained from a sacrifice, that which comes from a sister, and likewise that which comes from a woman with smoke-crested hair— these are the eight kinds of property."
In that case, [the period of ownership] is ten years, whether the property has been enjoyed or not enjoyed [by others].
Moreover, they cite this as an example:
"A pledge, a boundary, the property of a minor, a deposit, a sealed deposit,
women, royal property, and the wealth of one learned in the Vedas are not lost through adverse possession."
Property that has been abandoned becomes the property of the king.
Therefore, in other matters, the king should carry out his affairs together with his ministers and the citizens.
Or, a king who is a performer of the Vedic sacrifice is better; he may have a retinue of vultures.
Or, surrounded by vultures, the king is better off.
One should be surrounded by vultures, but one should not be a vulture surrounded by vultures.
For indeed, faults arise from one's retinue.
And [the rite] for the destruction of theft and seizure.
Therefore, he should first ask about his family lineage.
