Witnesses should be those who are learned in the Vedas, handsome, virtuous, meritorious, and truthful.
In all [these cases], either all [the ancestors] or indeed every single one [may be invited].
One should appoint women as witnesses for women; for the twice-born, similar twice-born men; for Śūdras, virtuous Śūdras; and for those of the lowest castes, those born of the lowest wombs.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"A son is not liable for a gift made under pressure, a gift made in vain, what is due to gambling, what is due to a tavern, or the remainder of a fine or a tax."
"Speak, witness, according to the truth; your ancestors hang suspended, awaiting your word as they rise and fall."
Naked, shaven-headed, and carrying a skull-bowl, tormented by hunger and thirst,
he who gives false testimony shall go as a blind beggar to the house of his enemy.
By lying regarding a maiden, one kills five; by lying regarding a cow, one kills ten;
by lying regarding a horse, one kills a hundred; by lying regarding a human being, one kills a thousand.
When her husband has died during a legal dispute, this is the expiation for a woman of good family:
by those who bring false accusations against them, their previous distinctions are severed here.
At the time of marriage, during sexual intercourse, when life is at stake, or when all one's wealth is being seized—
if they speak untruth for the sake of a Brahmin, they say that these five kinds of falsehoods do not cause a fall from dharma.
If they speak regarding their own affairs, or for the sake of wealth, or out of partiality,
those men cause even their ancestors who reside in heaven to fall from the lineage of their family.
"They even cause [the fetus] to fall."
When a son is born, the father pays off his debt to the ancestors and attains immortality,
provided that he beholds the face of his living son.
Infinite are the worlds for those who have sons; there is no world for one who has no son.

"May those who devour [us] be childless"—this is a curse. There is also a Vedic verse: "O Agni, may I attain immortality through my offspring. "Through a son one conquers the worlds; through a grandson one attains infinity."
Now, through a grandson of a son, one attains the world of the sun, according to the verse: "He reaches the realm of the sun."
Regarding the son of a woman who has been given in marriage, they dispute whether he belongs to the owner of the field or to the biological father.
Regarding this, they cite both [traditions]:
"If a bull were to sire a hundred calves upon the cows of others, those calves belong only to the owners of the cows; the bull's seed was in vain."
"Vigilantly guard this lineage; let not others sow their seed in your field. In the world beyond, the son belongs to the progenitor; thus the sower makes his lineage fruitless.
(VaDhS 17.9) "If among many born of one [father], one man has a son, the sacred tradition (*śruti*) declares that they are all possessed of a son by virtue of that son. (VaDhS 17.10)
If among many wives of one husband, one has a son,
the sacred tradition (śruti) declares that they all become possessed of sons through that son.
There are exactly twelve sons seen in the ancient tradition.
The first [son] is one begotten by oneself on one's own wedded wife who has been consecrated.
In the absence of that, a son born of a wife duly appointed [to bear a child] is the second [type].
VaDhS 17.15: The third [type of son] is the appointed daughter (putrikā).
It is known from tradition: "A daughter who has no brother goes toward the ancestors of her father; she goes back to become his son."
Regarding this, there is a verse:
"I shall give you this sisterless maiden, adorned;
whatever son is born of her, let him be my son."
The fourth is the paunarbhava (the son of a remarried woman).

VaDhS 17.19: She who, having abandoned her husband from her youth and having lived with others, returns to his very household, she becomes a *punarbhū* (a remarried woman). VaDhS 17.20: And she who, having abandoned a husband who is impotent, fallen [from caste], or insane, takes another husband, or [does so] when he has died, she becomes a *punarbhū*. VaDhS 17.21: The son born of an unmarried girl (*kānīna*) is the fifth.
They say that a son whom a woman, not having been consecrated, bears in her father's house out of desire, becomes the son of her maternal grandfather.
Moreover, they also quote:

"If the unmarried daughter of one should obtain a son through a husband of equal status, by that son the maternal grandfather becomes a father of a son; he shall offer the funeral cake and inherit the wealth."
And the one secretly born in the house is the sixth.
"These are the heirs, kinsmen, and protectors from great danger," so they say. (VaDhS 17.25)
Now, among those who are neither heirs nor kinsmen, the son born of a pregnant bride (sahoḍha) alone is the first [in right of inheritance].
A woman who is married while pregnant gives birth to a son known as *sahoḍha*.
The second is the adopted son (dattaka).
That which the mother and father may give.
The third [son] is the one purchased.
This has been explained by Śunaḥśepa.
King Hariścandra indeed purchased the son of Ajīgarta Sauyavasi.
One who has come of his own accord is the fourth [type of pupil].
This has been explained by Śunaḥśepa.

Śunaḥśepa, having been bound to the sacrificial post, praised the deities. Thereupon the deities released his bonds. The officiating priests said to him, "Let this son belong to me alone. He did not agree to them. They then reached an agreement, saying, "Let him be the son of whomever he desires. Viśvāmitra was his *hotṛ* priest; thus he attained the status of his son.
The fifth is the *apaviddha* (abandoned).
One who might take in a child who has been abandoned by his mother and father.
"The son of a Śūdra woman alone is the sixth," so they say; these are the non-heirs and kinsmen.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"If among his six ancestors there should be no heir whatsoever, these [descendants] shall take his inheritance."
Now follows the division of the inheritance among brothers.
And for those who are childless, [the rule applies] until they obtain a son.
The eldest shall take two shares.
And for a cow or a horse, it is one-tenth less than that.
Goats, sheep, and the house belong to the youngest.
Vasiṣṭha Dharma Sūtra 17.45: Iron implements and tools belong to the middle [class].
The women shall divide the mother's dowry among themselves.
VaDhS 17.47: If a Brāhmaṇa should have sons by a Brāhmaṇī, a Kṣatriyā, or a Vaiśyā wife...
The son of a Brāhmaṇī woman shall take three shares.
The son of a Kṣatriya wife shall receive two shares.
The others shall divide [the estate] equally.
And whoever among them should have produced [an offspring] by himself, he shall take two shares.
But those who have entered other stages of life are not entitled to a share.
And those who are impotent, insane, or outcasts.
The maintenance of eunuchs and the insane [is the duty of their relatives].
The widow of a deceased husband shall observe a vow for six months, eating food that is neither pungent nor salty, and sleeping on the ground.

After six months have passed, having bathed and offered the *śrāddha* for her husband, and having assembled those related by learning, ritual action, teachers, or birth, the father or brother shall arrange for the *niyoga*.
He shall not, however, appoint one who is insane, lacking self-control, or diseased.
Even if she is older [in age].
Sixteen years.
Unless he should be afflicted by illness.
During the *muhūrta* sacred to Prajāpati, she should behave toward him as if he were her husband, except for laughing with him, harshness of speech, and physical violence.
In matters of food, clothing, bathing, and the application of unguents, she should take the initiative.
They say that a son born of a woman who has not been authorized belongs to the progenitor.
If there should be two appointed [officiants].
There is no authorization for appointment [to raise offspring] out of greed for inheritance.
Some say that one should appoint him after first instructing him in the expiation.
A maiden who has reached puberty shall wait for three years.
After three years, she should find a husband of equal status.
Moreover, they also cite this: "If,
through the negligence of the father, a girl here is given away after she has passed the proper age,
she destroys the giver while he looks on, like an excessive sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) given at the wrong time."
Out of fear that her daughter might reach puberty, the father should give away the maiden while she is still pre-pubescent;
for if she remains until she has reached menstruation, the fault falls upon the father.

As many menstrual periods as touch a maiden who, being of equal status and desirous [of marriage], is being solicited by [a suitor], so many embryos are slain by those two, the mother and the father; such is the declaration of the Dharma.
If the bridegroom should die first after she has been given by water and word,
but before she has been led away by the sacred mantras, the maiden remains the property of her father alone.
If a maiden has been forcibly abducted but not consecrated with the sacred mantras, she may be given to another according to the prescribed rule; for she remains just as a maiden.
If the husband dies while she is still a young girl and has been consecrated by the sacred formulas alone,
and if her virginity remains intact, she is entitled to undergo the marriage rite again.
A wife whose husband has gone abroad shall wait for five years.
After five years, she should go to her husband's presence.
If she is not willing to go abroad for the sake of dharma or wealth, she should be treated as if she were dead.

Thus, for a Brāhmaṇī, five [years] have passed since she gave birth and four if she has not given birth; for a Rājanyā, five have passed since she gave birth and three if she has not given birth; for a Vaiśyā, four have passed since she gave birth and two if she has not given birth; and for a Śūdrā, three have passed since she gave birth and one if she has not given birth.

From this point forward, among those who share the same purpose, birth, funeral rice-balls (*piṇḍa*), water-libations (*udaka*), and lineage (*gotra*), each preceding one is more venerable than the next.
But indeed, while a man of noble birth is available, she must not go to another.
If among his six ancestors there should be no heir whatsoever, his sapinda relatives or those who stand in the place of a son shall divide his wealth.
In the absence of these, the teacher and the pupil shall take [the property].
In the absence of those two, the king shall take it.
But the king shall not take the property of a Brāhmaṇa.
But the property of a Brahmin is terrible poison.
They say that poison is not truly poison; the property of a Brahmin is called poison.
Poison kills only a single person, but the property of a Brahmin destroys sons and grandsons.
He should bestow [the gift] upon those who are learned in the three Vedas and are virtuous; he should bestow it, indeed.
They say that one born to a Brāhmaṇa woman by a Śūdra becomes a Caṇḍāla.
From a Kṣatriya woman, a Vaiṇa is born.
From a Vaiśya woman, an Antyāvasāyin is born.
They say that one born of a Vaiśya father and a Brāhmaṇa mother is a Rāmaka.
From a woman of the Rājanya caste, a Pulkasa is born.
They say that one born of a Kṣatriya man and a Brāhmaṇa woman becomes a Sūta.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"Whosoever are born in secret and have resorted to the qualities of the inverse order (prātilomya),
one should recognize them by their actions, due to the lapse in their qualities and conduct."
Those born from women one, two, or three classes lower than the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, or Vaiśya fathers become Ambaṣṭhas, Ugras, and Niṣādas respectively.
Among Śūdras, the Pāraśava [is the son born of a wife of equal caste].
Regarding the Pāraśava, they say that he becomes a corpse even while still alive.
"Some say that those who are Śūdras are this cremation ground."
Therefore, one should not study in the vicinity of a Śūdra.
Moreover, they cite these verses sung by Yama:
"This cemetery is manifest before our eyes—those who are Śūdras are evildoers;
therefore, one must never study in the vicinity of a Śūdra."
One should not give counsel to a Śūdra, nor his leavings, nor what has been prepared for sacrifice;
nor should one teach him the Dharma, nor prescribe a vow for him.

"He who teaches him the Dharma and he who instructs him in his vow—both of them enter together with him into dense, terrible darkness. (VaDhS 18.15) "He in whose wound a worm should ever arise... (VaDhS 18.16)
One is purified by a Prājāpatya penance; the sacrificial fee consists of gold, a cow, or a garment.
Having piled the fire-altar, one should not approach a beautiful woman.
A woman who is black in complexion is for pleasure alone, not for dharma; she is for pleasure alone, not for dharma.
The specific duty of a king is the protection of living beings; his success comes from the performance of that duty.

The learned say that this sacrificial session (*sattra*), which lasts from old age until death, involves the abandonment of fear and compassion. Therefore, one should appoint a domestic priest for the obligatory rites of the householder's life.
It is known from scripture: "The kingdom prospers when the Brahmapurohita sacrifice is performed."
Because of the protection of both.
And because of incapacity.
Having thoroughly understood all these regional laws, as well as the laws of castes and families, the king shall establish the four social orders in their respective duties.
If they act improperly toward them, he shall inflict punishment.
But the punishment for injury and verbal abuse must be determined according to the specific circumstances of place, time, social status, age, learning, and occupation.
On account of scripture and of analogy.
One should not harm trees that bear flowers and fruit.
And he may kill [an animal] for the purpose of providing the means for cultivation.
And the measures and weights used for the requirements of the householder's life shall be protected.
There is no concealment of one's own interests by means of a pretext.
The value of the measure should not be taken for one's own personal use.
In the case of the two *mahāmahas*, the road should be taken from the place [of sacrifice].
In a journey, a carriage drawn by ten horses shall yield double the benefit.
There should be water-stalls at each [stage].
And he should cause men of at least one hundred years of age to be summoned.
Women should not be barren.
A hand’s fistful of gravel, a māṣa, water from the middle of a reed, and a quarter [of a measure] shall be equal to one kārṣāpaṇa.
A tree that has no water nearby should be stripped of its fruit.

A person who does not know the syllable *akāra*, a learned Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*), a king’s man, and those who are destitute, wandering mendicants, children, the elderly, the young, and women who have recently given birth.
Girls who have already been married and women whose husbands are maintained by others [are ineligible].
With his two arms, he should give a hundredfold more than that.
The burning of rivers, thickets, and forests, as well as the utilization of mountains, shall be free of taxes.
Or those who depend upon him for their livelihood shall give it.
But he should cause him to bring back the marriage-fee every month.
And when the king has died, one should give what is incidental.
By this, the proper conduct toward one's mother is explained.
The king shall maintain the paternal uncle and the maternal uncle of the queen.
And [he should address] his relatives and others as well.
The wives of the king shall receive food and clothing.
Or they may go forth [into the religious life] even if they are unwilling.
The king shall support those who are impotent or insane.
Because the inheritance goes to him.
Regarding the toll, they also cite this verse of Manu:
"There is no toll on a broken kārṣāpaṇa coin, nor on one engaged in a craft, nor on a child, nor on a messenger;
nor on what is obtained as alms, nor on what remains after being seized, nor on a Śrotriya, nor on a wandering ascetic, nor at a sacrifice."
A thief does not incur guilt if he enters [the house] unobserved.
One who bears arms, one who was seized while being carried away (sahoḍha), one who has received a wound, and one who has been designated [by another]—according to some authorities.
Upon releasing one who deserves punishment, the king shall fast for one night.
The domestic priest shall observe a fast for three nights.
The domestic priest incurs a *kṛcchra* penance for failing to punish one who deserves punishment.
For a king, it is three nights.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"The killer of an embryo transfers his guilt to the one who eats his food; an unfaithful wife to her husband;
a pupil and a sacrificer to their teacher; and a thief transfers his sin to the king."
But men who have committed sins and have been punished by kings go to heaven stainless, just like virtuous people who have performed meritorious deeds.
The sin overtakes the king who releases a guilty man; but if the king should have him executed, he destroys the evil deed through righteousness.
For kings, immediate purification is prescribed in matters of urgent necessity;
likewise, it is not so in non-urgent matters, for in these cases time alone is the determining factor.
Regarding this, they cite a verse sung by Yama:
"There is indeed no fault today for kings, nor for those observing vows, nor for those performing long sacrificial sessions;
for they are ever become Brahman, seated in the station of Indra."
"For they are indeed ever-present."
An expiation is prescribed for an offense committed unintentionally.
Some [hold that there is no offense] even when it is done intentionally.
The teacher is the instructor for those who possess self-control; the king is the instructor for the wicked;
and Yama, the son of Vivasvat, is the instructor for those whose sins are concealed.
And in that case, if he has been overtaken by the rising sun, he should remain standing during the day and mutter the Sāvitrī.
In this manner, one who has been dismissed by the sun shall remain seated during the night.
One with deformed nails or black teeth, however, shall perform the Kṛcchra penance for twelve nights.
A younger brother who marries before his elder brother shall perform the Kṛcchra penance for twelve nights, and then he may enter the household and marry that same woman.
Now, one who has superseded his elder brother, having performed the Kṛcchrātikṛcchra penances and having given [the property] to him, may marry again and take that same woman as his wife.
The husband of an *agredidhiṣū* shall perform the *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights, and having done so, he may enter into household life and marry her.
The husband of a *didhiṣū* (a woman whose elder sister has not yet been married) shall perform the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra* penances, give [the property] to her, and then marry again.
We shall explain the killer of a hero further on.
One who has forsaken the Veda shall perform the Kṛcchra penance for twelve nights and then receive the Veda again from a teacher.

One who has violated the bed of his guru shall cut off his penis together with the testicles, hold them in his joined palms, and walk facing south; wherever he meets with an obstacle, there he shall remain until his body perishes.
"Or, having been stripped of his clothes and smeared with ghee, he should embrace a red-hot iron image; it is known from tradition that he becomes purified through death."
The same applies to the wife of the teacher's son and to female disciples.

Having had sexual intercourse with a woman of a higher caste, a female friend, the wife of a teacher, one who has lost her caste, or an outcaste woman, one shall perform the Kṛcchra penance for one quarter of a year.
VaDhS 20.17: This same [penance] applies to eating the food of a Cāṇḍāla or an outcast; thereafter, however, there is a re-initiation, but with the exclusion of the shaving and other such rites.
Regarding this, they cite a verse from the *Mānava*:
"Shaving, the girdle, the staff, the practice of begging for alms, and the vows—
these are indeed discontinued upon the performance of the rite of re-consecration (*punaḥsaṃskāra*)."

If one intentionally drinks intoxicating liquor other than *asurā* or *surā*, or drinks them unknowingly, one must perform the *kṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra* penances respectively, consume clarified butter, and undergo the sacramental rite (*punaḥsaṃskāra*) again.
And likewise in the case of consuming urine, feces, or semen.
If any twice-born man should drink water that has stood in a vessel for liquor, he becomes pure by drinking water from the lotus, the *udumbara*, the *bilva*, and the *palāśa* trees for three nights.
But in the case of repeated consumption of *surā*, a twice-born man shall drink it while it is red-hot like fire; he becomes purified through death.
We shall now declare the penance for the slayer of a learned Brāhmaṇa (bhrūṇahan). One becomes a bhrūṇahan by killing a Brāhmaṇa, and also by killing an embryo whose sex is unknown.

"For embryos are indeed unknown as to whether they will be males; therefore, one offers oblations with rites intended for males. Having kindled the fire, the killer of an embryo (bhrūṇahan) should offer these [oblations].

"I offer the body hairs to Death; with the body hairs, I clothe Death"—this is the first [offering]. "I offer the skin to Death; with the skin, I clothe Death"—this is the second. "I offer the blood to Death; with the blood, I clothe Death"—this is the third. "I offer the flesh to Death; with the flesh, I clothe Death"—this is the fourth. "I offer the sinews to Death; with the sinews, I clothe Death"—this is the fifth.

"I offer fat to Death; with fat I clothe Death"—with this he offers the sixth oblation. "I offer bones to Death; with bones I clothe Death"—this is the seventh. "I offer marrow to Death; with marrow I clothe Death"—this is the eighth.
For the sake of the king or for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa, one should cause oneself to be slain facing the enemy in battle.
It is known from tradition that one who has failed three times, even if unconquered [by the sin], becomes purified.
"For when a sin is explained, it becomes less," so it is said.
Nevertheless, they cite this:
"If one says of an outcast, 'He is an outcast,' or of a thief, 'He is a thief,' he incurs an equal guilt by that statement; if it be false, he shall incur double the guilt."
In the same way, having killed a Kṣatriya woman, one should perform the penance for eight years.
A Vaiśya [should wait] for six [years].
For a Śūdra, three [years].
Having killed a Brāhmaṇa woman who is an Ātreyī, as well as a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya engaged in a Soma sacrifice.
We shall now discuss the *ātreyī*. They say that a woman who has bathed after her menstrual period is an *ātreyī*.
For in this case, it is said: "the offspring yet to come."
In the case of harming a Kṣatriya who is not an Ātreyī woman, [the penance is that of a Kṛcchra].
In the case of injury to a Vaiśya woman by a Kṣatriya.
In the case of injury to a Śūdra by a Vaiśya woman, [the same penance applies].
Having killed a Śūdra woman, [one must perform penance] for one year.

VaDhS 20.41: Upon stealing gold from a Brāhmaṇa, one should dishevel his hair, run toward the king, and say: "I am a thief, sir; may your majesty punish me. The king should give him an axe made of Udumbara wood; with that he should take his own life, for it is known from tradition that by death he becomes purified. VaDhS 20.42: Or, having removed all clothing and being smeared with clarified butter, he should burn himself with a fire of cow-dung starting from the feet; for it is known from tradition that by death he becomes purified.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"Listen to how the body becomes a limb for those who died long ago due to sin from various actions, once they have again obtained a physical form."

A thief becomes one with deformed nails; a killer of a Brahmin becomes one with white leprosy; a drinker of spirituous liquor has black teeth; and one who violates the teacher’s bed suffers from skin disease.

And in the case of association with outcasts—whether through Vedic study or through marriage—one must abandon those portions of the inheritance received from them, and one must not live together with them.
It is known from tradition that by going toward the northern direction and studying the Saṃhitā while fasting, one becomes purified.
Moreover, they cite this:
"By the mortification of the body, by austerity, and by Vedic study, the doer of evil is released from evil; and by means of giving, he is also liberated."
Thus it is known; thus it is known.

If a Śūdra should have sexual intercourse with a Brāhmaṇa woman, one should wrap the Śūdra in vīraṇa grass and cast him into the fire; having caused the Brāhmaṇa woman’s head to be shaved and having anointed her all over with clarified butter, she should be made naked, mounted upon a black donkey, and paraded along the high road; thus it is known that she becomes purified.

If a Vaiśya should have intercourse with a Brāhmaṇa woman, one should wrap the Vaiśya in red darbha grass and cast him into the fire; having caused the shaving of the Brāhmaṇa woman’s head and having anointed her all over with clarified butter, she should be led naked upon a bullock-cart along the high road. It is declared that she thus becomes purified.

If a Kṣatriya should have sexual intercourse with a Brāhmaṇa woman, one should wrap the Kṣatriya in reed-leaves, besmear him with clarified butter, cast him into the fire, place the woman naked upon a white donkey, and cause her to be led along the high road; thus she becomes purified—so it is known.
In this same manner, a Vaiśya [begets] on a Rājanyā woman.
And a Śūdra [is the son] of a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya woman.

VaDhS 21.6: In the case of a transgression against her husband committed through the mind, she should eat barley-gruel or milk-rice for three nights and sleep on the ground. After the three nights, while submerged in water, she should offer oblations with one hundred and eight repetitions of the Sāvitrī verse for each head [of rice]. It is declared that she becomes purified. VaDhS 21.7: In the case of a verbal transgression, having performed this same penance for one month, after the month, while submerged in water, she should offer oblations with four times one hundred and eight repetitions of the Sāvitrī verse for each head [of rice]. It is declared that she becomes purified.

But in the case of sexual intercourse, one should wear a cloth soaked in ghee for a year and sleep on a bed of kusha grass in a pit filled with cow dung; after a year has passed, one should offer oblations with the head [of the garment] while submerged in water, reciting the Sāvitrī verse one hundred and eight times; it is declared that she thus becomes purified.
But upon sexual intercourse or going on a pilgrimage, he turns away from his religious duties.
But four [wives] must be abandoned: one who has gone to a pupil, one who has gone to a teacher, one who especially kills her husband, and one who has approached a degraded man.
The gods do not lead that Brāhmaṇī woman who drinks liquor to the world of her husband; here on earth she wanders with exhausted merit, becoming a water-snail or a pearl-oyster shell.
The wives of Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas who have had intercourse with a Śūdra are purified by penance if they have not conceived; others are not.
If they should have intercourse in the reverse order, they must perform the Kṛcchra penance followed by the Cāndrāyaṇa.

For those women who are devoted to their husbands, who maintain the household, who are firm in truth, and who observe pure vows, their worlds are equal to those of their husbands; but for those who are unchaste, the worlds are like those of jackals.
Half of the body of that man falls [from grace] whose wife drinks liquor;
for one whose half-body has fallen, no expiation is prescribed.
If a Brāhmaṇa should intentionally approach the wife of a Brāhmaṇa, he must perform the Kṛcchra penance if she has not ceased her religious duties, and the Atikṛcchra penance if she has ceased them.
The same applies for a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya.
If he should kill a cow, he shall remain for six months wrapped in her fresh hide, performing either the Kṛcchra or the Taptakṛcchra penance.
The rule for those two is as follows.
He eats during the day for three days, and indeed eats at night for another three days;
he observes the vow of not asking for food for three days, and does not eat for three days—this is the Kṛcchra penance.
For three days he should drink warm water; for three days he should drink warm milk;
having drunk warm clarified butter for three days, he should subsist on air for the final three days.
Thus ends the *taptakṛcchra* penance according to the Vaikhānasa Dharmasūtra 21.21.
And one should give [an offering] upon the death of a bull or a cow.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"In ancient times there were only three diseases: envy, fasting, and old age.
Having killed a spotted goat, one may bring back ninety-eight [goats]."
Having killed a dog, a cat, a mongoose, a snake, a frog, or a rat, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance for twelve nights and give some small gift.
But having killed a heap of boneless creatures as large as a cow, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance for twelve nights and give some gift.
But for each single bone that possesses marrow, [one day of impurity is required].
He who casts away the sacred fires shall perform the Kṛcchra penance for twelve nights and then have the fires re-established.

If one has falsely accused or persistently pressured one's teacher, one should bathe with one's clothes on and propitiate the teacher; it is traditionally taught that through his favor, one becomes purified.
An atheist, having performed the Kṛcchra penance for twelve nights, shall desist from atheism.
But for one who lives as an atheist, the *atikṛcchra* penance is prescribed.
By this, the seller of Soma is explained.
A forest-dweller, having performed the Kṛcchra penance for twelve nights upon the breach of his initiation, should increase the growth of large grass in the wilderness.

Beggars (bhikṣukas) shall follow the rules of forest-dwellers (vānaprasthas) regarding the increase of the Soma during its growth, as well as the refinement according to their own scriptures; and the refinement according to their own scriptures.

Now, indeed, this man gives false testimony, or he officiates at a sacrifice for one who should not be sacrificed for, or he accepts what should not be accepted, or he eats what is not food, or he performs what should not be performed.
Regarding this, they deliberate whether one should perform an expiation or not.
"One should not do so," they say.
"For indeed, action is not exhausted."
Therefore, one should simply perform [the rite], because of the evidence shown in the Śruti.
"He who performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice overcomes all evil, he overcomes even the murder of a Brahmin" (VaDhS 22.6).
And one who is accused [of such a crime] should perform the Gosava and the Agniṣṭut sacrifices (VaDhS 22.7).
The means of expiation for that are recitation, austerity, burnt offerings, fasting, and giving gifts.

The Upaniṣads, the beginnings of the Vedas, the Vedāntas, all the Vedic meters, the Saṃhitās, the Madhu hymns, the Aghamarṣaṇa, the Atharvaśiras, the Rudras, the Puruṣasūkta, the Rājan and Rauhiṇa Sāmans, the Kūṣmāṇḍas, the Pāvamānī verses, and the Sāvitrī—these are the purifiers.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"By performing the Vaiśvānarī, the Vrātapatī, and likewise the Pavitreṣṭi sacrifice once during the season, one purifies ten generations of one's lineage."
According to the rule for fasting, the following are purifying: subsisting on milk, eating fruits, consuming a handful of barley-gruel, ingesting gold, and drinking soma.
All mountains, all rivers, sacred lakes, holy fords, dwellings of sages, cow-pens, and sacred enclosures—these are the [auspicious] places.
The periods of time are a year, a month, twenty-four days, twelve days, six days, three days, and a day and night.
In the absence of a specific injunction, these very [rites] may be performed optionally.
For heavy sins, the penances are heavy; for light sins, they are light.
The Kṛcchra, the Atikṛcchra, and the Cāndrāyaṇa constitute the universal expiation; this is the universal expiation.
If a student of sacred knowledge should have sexual intercourse with a woman, he shall sacrifice an ass dedicated to the Rākṣasas as the victim in a common fire at a crossroads in the forest.
Or he should offer a sacrificial pap (caru) to Nirṛti.
For him, he should offer oblations with: "To Desire, svāhā! To the one who desires desire, svāhā! To Nairṛtī, svāhā! To the deities of the Rākṣasas, svāhā!"
This same [penance applies] for the intentional emission of semen during the day in a dream, or during other vows, until the ceremony of returning home (samāvartana).
In the case of sexual intercourse with an animal, one should give a white bull as a gift.
Having approached a cow, the offense is explained as being equal to that of killing a Śūdra.
For a student who performs the funeral rites for a corpse, there is a cessation from his vows.
Except in the case of one's mother and father.
If he should fall ill, he may at will eat all the remnants of his teacher's food for the sake of medicine.
VaDhS 23.10: If one commissioned by his teacher should die, the teacher shall perform three *kṛcchra* penances.
VaDhS 23.11: If a student (*brahmacārī*) should eat meat or food that is the leavings of another, he shall perform a *kṛcchra* for twelve nights and then complete the remainder of his vow.
The same applies to eating at a *śrāddha* ceremony or during periods of ritual impurity (*sūtaka*).
In the Vājasaneyaka, it is known that honey obtained unintentionally does not cause defilement.
If one who has attempted suicide is accused [of a grave offense], the performance of the funeral rites for his sapinda relatives is interrupted.
He who destroys himself by means of wood, water, clods of earth, stones, weapons, poison, or ropes becomes a self-destroyer (ātmahā).
Moreover, they also cite this:
"If a twice-born man, out of affection, should perform the funeral rites for one who has committed suicide,
he shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow accompanied by the Taptakṛcchra penance."
We shall explain the Cāndrāyaṇa penance further on.
In the case of a resolve to commit suicide, [the penance lasts] for three nights.

VaDhS 23.19: One who abandons his life while still living shall perform the *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights; he shall fast for three nights, always wearing a smooth garment, and having restrained his vital breaths within himself, he shall recite the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn three times.
VaDhS 23.20: Or alternatively, he may recite the *gāyatrī* according to this same procedure.
Or alternatively, having kindled the fire, one should offer clarified butter with the Kūṣmāṇḍa verses.
"And whatever else besides the great sins (mahāpātaka), all that is purified by this."

Furthermore, having mentally contemplated evil, one should sip water while reciting, "May Agni and Manyu [purify me]," and then mutter the *vyāhṛtis* preceded by *oṃ* and ending with *satya*, or recite the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn.
Having touched a human bone that is still moist, there is impurity for three nights.
But if it is not oily, [the penance lasts] for one day and night.
And the same applies when following a corpse.
If one enters while others are studying, there shall be a fast for a day and a night.
For three nights there shall be ritual sprinkling and mutual separation from one another.
For a dog, a cat, a mongoose, or a swift-moving animal, the period of impurity lasts one day and night.

For eating the flesh of a dog, a cock, a village pig, a heron, a vulture, a bearded vulture, a pigeon, a human, a crow, or an owl, there shall be a fast for seven nights, becoming free of feces, consuming clarified butter, and undergoing the purificatory rite again.
But a Brāhmaṇa bitten by a dog, having gone to a river that flows into the ocean,
shall perform one hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) and, after consuming clarified butter, he becomes pure.
It is known from tradition that upon touching a dog, a *caṇḍāla*, or an outcaste, one becomes pure immediately by bathing with one's clothes on.
Upon hearing the cry of an outcaste or a Cāṇḍāla, they shall remain for three nights observing silence and fasting.
It is known from tradition that those who practice this up to ten thousand times become purified.

By this very same [rule], those who teach what is censurable and those who officiate as priests for such persons are explained; it is known from the tradition that they become pure by relinquishing their fees.
By this very same [rule], the accused person is explained.

In the case of killing an embryo, one should subsist on water for twelve nights and fast for twelve nights. Having falsely accused a Brāhmaṇa of a crime entailing loss of caste or of a lesser crime, one should subsist on water for a month and repeat the Śuddhavatī verses.
Or he should go to the final purificatory bath of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
By this very same [rule], sexual intercourse with a Caṇḍāla woman is explained.
Now follows another general rule for the performance of the Kṛcchra penance.

One day of eating in the morning, one day of eating at night, one day of eating food obtained unasked, one day of fasting (parāka)—this constitutes one ritual cycle; likewise, two further cycles of four days each.
For the sake of favoring the Brahmins, Manu, the best among the upholders of dharma,
prescribed the *śiśukṛcchra* penance in this manner for children, the elderly, and the sick.
Now follows the procedure for the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
At the beginning of the dark fortnight of the month, one should eat fourteen morsels;
increasing the number of morsels, one should complete the remainder of the fortnight.
For thus, at the beginning of the bright fortnight, one should eat a single morsel;
eating with a reduction of morsels, one should complete the remainder of the fortnight.
In this very situation, he should sing the Sāman hymns, or else he should mutter the Vyāhṛtis.
This is the Cāndrāyaṇa month, a purifier praised by the seers;
it is prescribed as the expiation for all unmentioned offenses.
"It is prescribed," so it is stated.
Now follows the Atikṛcchra penance.

Eating only in the morning for three days, likewise in the evening for three days, and eating only what is unasked for for three days—this is the *parāka* penance; this constitutes the *kṛcchra*. Eating only as much as one can take in a single mouthful, as described previously, is the *atikṛcchra*.
Subsisting on water for one day is a *kṛcchra*; that same practice [repeated] for three days is a *kṛchrātikṛcchra*.
These are the forms of the vows for *kṛcchra* penances.

He should have his beard and hair shaved, except for the eyebrows, the eyelashes, and the top-knot; having trimmed his nails, wearing a single garment, eating blameless food, [begging alms once from blameless people], bathing at the three periods of the day, carrying a staff and a water-pot, avoiding conversation with women and Śūdras, and habituated to standing and sitting, he should remain standing during the day and seated at night—thus said the venerable Vasiṣṭha.
He should not give this Dharmaśāstra to one who is not his son, nor to one who is not his pupil, nor to one who has not lived with him for a year.
The sacrificial fee is a thousand [cows] with a bull as the eleventh, or it is the favor of the teacher; indeed, it is the favor of the teacher.
I shall declare, without omission, the purification for great sins whose defects have not been publicly proclaimed, as well as for all minor offenses.
For one who has maintained the sacred fires, who is disciplined, aged, or learned, the penance prescribed in secret applies; for other people, that which was previously mentioned applies.
By means of breath-restraints, purificatory rites, gifts, burnt offerings, and likewise recitations, those who are constantly disciplined are liberated from sins; of this there is no doubt.
With purifying grass in hand, seated, one should practice the daily Veda— the breath-control exercises, the purifiers, the Vyāhṛtis, and likewise the Praṇava.
Constantly engaged and repeatedly performing breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*),
let him practice the highest austerity from the tips of his hair to the tips of his nails.
From cessation wind is born; from wind indeed fire is born;
from heat water is then born; thus it is purified within by these three.

Neither by intense austerity, nor by Vedic study, nor by sacrifice are the twice-born able to attain that state which they reach through yoga. Through yoga, knowledge is attained; yoga is the defining characteristic of dharma.
Yoga is the supreme austerity; therefore, one should always remain disciplined in it.
One should be constantly devoted to the *praṇava* and to the seven *vyāhṛtis*, as well as to the three-footed *gāyatrī*; for such a person, no fear exists anywhere.
The Vedas proceed from the syllable *praṇava* and are established within the *praṇava*;
the *praṇava* is everything that consists of speech. Therefore, one should practice the *praṇava*.
The single syllable is remembered as the supreme Brahman, the highest purifier.
When a mixture of all these sins has occurred,
the great purification is the repetition of the Sāvitrī ten thousand times.
One should recite the Gāyatrī together with the Vyāhṛtis, the Praṇava, and the Śiras three times while restraining the breath; that is called prāṇāyāma.
"He is called thus."
If one, unwearied, performs three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) according to the rule,
the sin committed during a day and night perishes at that very moment.
Whatever sin has been committed during the day by deed, thought, or word, one sitting during the evening twilight removes it by means of breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma).
Whatever sin has been committed during the night by deed, thought, or word,
one dispels it by means of breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) upon rising for the morning twilight devotion.
Sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), accompanied by the vyāhṛtis and the praṇava,
performed day after day, purify even the slayer of a learned Brahmin within a month.

Having recited the *Kautsa* hymn and this three-verse section of the *Vāsiṣṭha*—namely, "O Agni, drive away our sin with your light; shine forth wealth upon us" and "The wise Vasiṣṭhas, the first singers, have awakened the Dawn with their hymns and songs"—even a drinker of *surā* is purified by the *Māhitra* hymn and the *Śuddhavatī* verses.
By reciting the Asyavāmīya and the Śivasaṅkalpa even once,
one becomes stainless in an instant, even after having stolen gold.
Having recited the *haviṣyantīya* hymn and the three-verse hymn beginning with "na tam aṃhaḥ" (*Ṛgveda* 10.126.1–3),
and having muttered the *puruṣasūkta*, one who has violated the teacher’s bed is liberated from that sin.
Or else, while submerged in water, one should mutter the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times;
Manu has declared that this is equal to the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) at the end of a horse sacrifice.

The sacrifice of silent recitation (*japayajña*) is ten times superior to the sacrifice of material offerings (*ārambhayajña*). The whispered recitation (*upāṃśu*) is said to be a hundredfold more effective, and the mental recitation (*mānasa*) is a thousandfold.
Those four *pākayajñas* which are accompanied by the *vidhiyajñas*—
all of them are not worth even a sixteenth part of the *japayajña*.
A Brāhmaṇa shall attain perfection through recitation alone; there is no doubt about this.
He may perform other rites or he may not; one who is friendly toward all is called a Brāhmaṇa.

Sins do not dwell with those who recite prayers, those who perform fire-sacrifices, those who practice meditation, those who reside at sacred fords, nor with those who have performed ritual ablutions accompanied by head-vows.
Just as fire, fanned by the wind and fed with oblations, blazes up,
even so a Brahmin who is constantly devoted to the recitation of prayers shines forth intensely.
For those who constantly engage in the private recitation of the Veda, who are ever self-restrained,
and who likewise perform silent prayers and burnt offerings, no downfall is known to exist.
One who desires purification, even if situated amidst all sins, should employ the divine [Gāyatrī] mantra consisting of a thousand at most, a hundred in the middle, and ten as the minimum.
A Kṣatriya should overcome his own misfortune through the strength of his arms;
a Vaiśya and a Śūdra through wealth; but the best of the twice-born through silent recitations and burnt offerings.
Just as horses would be without a chariot, or a chariot without horses, so it is with these means.
Thus, austerity is for one who lacks knowledge, and knowledge is for one who lacks austerity.
Just as food mixed with honey, or honey mixed with food,
so too austerity and knowledge, when combined, constitute a great medicine.
Sin does not attach itself even to a Brāhmaṇa who is constantly engaged in sinful deeds, provided he is endowed with learning and austerity and is devoted to the silent recitation of sacred texts.
"No sin attaches [to him]," so it is said.
If even more than a hundred forbidden acts have been committed, yet the Veda is retained,
the fire of that person's Veda burns them all away, just as ordinary fire consumes fuel.
Just as a fire that has gained strength burns even moist trees,
so does the fire of Vedic knowledge burn away the defects of one's own actions.
Even having destroyed these worlds and consuming [their wealth] from here and there,
a Brahmin who retains the Ṛgveda incurs no sin whatsoever.
One should not take pleasure in sinful deeds by relying on the power of the Veda;
for it is only through ignorance and negligence that one is consumed by the consequences of action, and not otherwise.
The ascetic who performs penance in the forest, subsisting on roots and fruits,
and he who studies even a single verse of the Rigveda— these two are equal.
One should augment the Veda with the Itihāsas and Purāṇas;
for the Veda fears one of little learning, thinking, "He will strike me."
The daily study of the Vedas according to one's ability and the performance of the sequence of the great sacrifices quickly destroy even those sins born of the most heinous crimes (mahāpātaka).
One should constantly perform, without sloth, one's own duty as declared by the Veda;
for by performing that to the best of one's ability, one attains the supreme goal.
From officiating at sacrifices, from teaching, from matrimonial alliance, and likewise from accepting improper gifts—
no fault shall accrue to Brahmins, for they are equal to fire and the sun.
When a doubt has arisen regarding whether food is fit to be eaten or unfit to be eaten, I shall declare the purification of food; listen to me as I speak it.
A Brāhmaṇa should drink the astringent, salt-free, and dry *brāhmī* and *suvarcalā*,
as well as *śaṅkhapuṣpī*, together with milk for three nights.
Having boiled the leaves of the *palāśa* and *bilva*, as well as *kuśa* grass, lotuses, and *udumbara* fruits, one should drink the water; thus one becomes pure in three nights.
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with *kuśa* grass,
along with a one-night fast, would purify even a *śvapāka*.
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, and likewise ghee—
if one subsists on these for five nights, one is purified by the *pañcagavya*.
One who consumes barley according to the prescribed rule becomes purified by direct perception itself.
When there is purity of intention, they are pure; but when it is impure, they are stained with passion.
Three morning meals of sacrificial food (haviṣya), and likewise three evening meals, as well as three meals obtained without asking— this constitutes a three-day fast.
Now, if he hastens to perform [the penance], subsisting on air during the day and remaining awake at a reservoir of water at night, that is equal to the Prājāpatya penance.
But by reciting the Sāvitrī eight thousand times when the sun has risen,
one is released from all sins, provided one is not a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa.
Indeed, whether one is a thief, a drinker of liquor, a killer of an embryo, or one who violates the teacher’s bed,
by merely studying the Dharmaśāstra, he is liberated from all sins.
For misfortunes, ill-performed rites, and likewise for great sins,
the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* penances are the destroyers of all evil.
One should increase the morsel by one each day during the bright fortnight and decrease it during the dark fortnight;
on the new moon day one should not eat at all—this is the rule for the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Thus is the rule for the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
A woman is not defiled by an adulterer, nor a Brahmin by his Vedic rites;
water is not defiled by urine or excrement, nor fire by its act of burning.
Whether she has herself consented, or has been driven away,
or has been enjoyed by force, or has even fallen into the hands of thieves;
A woman who has been defiled must not be abandoned; her abandonment is not ordained. She should wait for her menses; she becomes pure through the period of her courses.
Women are an incomparable means of purification; they are never defiled.
For month after month, their menstrual flow carries away their evil deeds.
Formerly, women were enjoyed by the gods—by Soma, Gandharva, and Agni;
they come to men afterwards, yet they are not defiled according to dharma. Soma gave them purity, and Gandharva taught them speech.
And because fire makes everything pure, women are therefore free from blemish.
Those who know the Dharma recognize three sins for women in this world:
the murder of a husband, the destruction of an embryo, and the causing of an abortion of one's own fetus.
A calf is pure when causing milk to flow; a bird is pure when causing fruit to fall;
women are pure during sexual intercourse; and a dog is pure when catching game.
Goats and horses are pure in their mouths, but cows are pure in every part.
Henceforth, I shall declare the purifiers of all the Vedas, by the muttering of which and by the offering of oblations men are purified; of this there is no doubt.
The Aghamarṣaṇa, the Devakṛta, the Śuddhavatīs, the Taratsamandīs,
the Kūṣmāṇḍas, the Pāvamānīs, and the Durgā-sāvitrī.
The *atiṣaṅgas*, the *padastobhas*, the *sāmans*, and likewise the *vyāhṛtis*; the *bhāruṇḍa* *sāmans*, as well as the *gāyatra* and the *raivata*.
The *puruṣavrata*, the *bhāsa*, and likewise the *devavratas*; the *abliṅga*, the *bārhaspatya*, the *vāksūkta*, and the *madhvṛcas*.
The Śatarudriya, the Atharvaśiras, the Triṣuparṇa, the Mahāvrata, the Gosūkta,
the Aśvasūkta, and the two Sāmans, the Śuddha and the Aśuddhi.
The three Ājyadohas, the Rathantara, the Vrata of Agni, the Vāmadevya, and the Bṛhat—these, when recited, purify living beings; and if one so desires, one obtains the memory of former births.
Gold is the first offspring of Agni; the earth belongs to Viṣṇu, and cows are the daughters of the Sun.
He who gives gold, a cow, and land shall enjoy infinite fruit.
A cow, a horse, gold,
or land obstruct the donor when they see the hand of a Brahmin who is not learned in the Vedas and is devoid of sacred learning.
On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, however, one should [feed] seven or five Brāhmaṇas with black sesame seeds or others, mixed with honey.
"May the Lord of Dharma be pleased"—or whatever else may be in one's mind;
by this, the sin committed throughout one's life perishes at that very moment.
Having fashioned a black antelope with its hooves intact and a golden navel,
and having covered it with sesame seeds, listen to the fruit of the merit for him who should give it as a gift.
By him, the earth—with its gold mines, its mountains, forests, and groves, and its four faces—is as good as given; of this there is no doubt.
"Having placed sesame seeds, gold, honey, and clarified butter upon a black antelope skin,
he who gives them to a Brahmin overcomes all evil deeds."
"He overcomes all evil deeds. Thus it is said.
Through giving, one obtains all desires.
A celibate student shall be long-lived and handsome.
One who does not cause injury attains heaven.
By entering the fire, one attains the world of Brahmā.
From observing silence, one attains good fortune.
The lord of the *nāgas* [attains this] from dwelling in the water.
Free from disease and with his treasury exhausted.
The giver of water has all his desires fulfilled.
The giver of food becomes one with clear vision and a retentive memory.
One who is intelligent and a giver of fearlessness in all respects [is a worthy recipient].
In the case of a carriage drawn by oxen, one should perform ablutions at all sacred bathing places.
By the gift of a bed and a seat, one attains lordship over the inner apartments.
From the gift of an umbrella, one obtains a house.
One who provides a house attains a city.
The giver of shoes obtains a vehicle. Moreover, they also cite this:
"Whatever sin a man oppressed by his livelihood commits..."
One is purified even by the gift of land measuring only a *gocarma*.
One should give a full water-pot to a Brahmin for the purpose of sipping;
having attained supreme satisfaction after death, he is born again as a drinker of Soma.
The gift of thousands of oxen, fit for bearing burdens,
given according to the rules to a worthy recipient, is equal to the gift of a daughter in marriage.
They say there are three supreme gifts: cows, the earth, and Sarasvatī;
for among all gifts, the gift of knowledge is indeed superior to them.
He who, being free from malice and possessing knowledge, follows this code of conduct, attains the gift of the ultimate fruit— the liberation from the cycle of worldly existence.
One who is faithful, pure, and self-controlled should either uphold or even hear this;
having abandoned all sins, he is glorified in the highest heaven.
"He is honored on the back of the vault of heaven."
Practice dharma, not adharma; speak truth, not falsehood.
Look to the long-term, not the short-term; look to what is beyond, not what is near.
The Brāhmaṇa becomes Agni.
For there is a Vedic revelation stating, "The Brahmin is indeed Agni."
And how is that so?

In this regard, for a Brāhmaṇa, the sacrificial hall (*sadas*) is the body, the altar (*vedi*) is the will, the sacrifice is the intention, the victim is the self, the tethering rope is the intellect, the *sadas* is the mouth, the *āhavanīya* fire is the navel, the *gārhapatya* fire is the stomach, the *adhvaryu* priest is the out-breath (*prāṇa*), the *hotṛ* priest is the down-breath (*apāna*), the *brahmā* priest is the middle-breath (*vyāna*), the *udgātṛ* priest is the equalizing breath (*samāna*), the self and the senses are the sacrificial vessels. He who, knowing thus, offers the objects of the senses with the senses—this is also known in the *Kāṭhaka*.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"The giver protects and saves both himself and the recipient from sin,
when an oblation is poured into the fires that are the mouths of Brahmins, which are enriched by the fuel of the Vedas."
That which is offered into the mouth of a Brāhmaṇa is superior even to the Agnihotra; it does not spill over, it does not cause distress, and no one can surpass it.

Having performed the mental sacrifice— wherein meditation is the fire, truth is the piling of the altar, patience is the oblation, modesty is the sacrificial ladle, non-violence is the cake, contentment is the sacrificial post, and the granting of fearlessness to all beings is the priestly fee— the wise man reaches the end of his existence.
The hair of an aging man decays; the teeth of an aging man decay.
But the hope for life and the hope for wealth do not decay, even in one who is aging.
"That which is difficult for the wicked-minded to abandon, which does not decay even as one decays,
that thirst which is a disease ending only with life— for him who abandons it, there is happiness."
"Adoration be to Vasiṣṭha, the son of Urvaśī and of Mitra and Varuṇa, who has a hundred ways of life; to Vasiṣṭha! Thus [he says].
Vaikhānasa Dharmasūtra (i.e., Vaikhānasa Smārtasūtra 8–10)
