Now, regarding the duties of the social classes and stages of life (*varṇāśramadharma*):
the four classes (*varṇas*)— the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra— were born from the mouth, arms, thighs, and feet [of the Creator],
for the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) states, "The Brāhmaṇa was his mouth."
For the first three [classes], the purificatory rites beginning with the *niṣeka* (conception) are prescribed.
For those twice-born ones, there is the entitlement to the Vedas.
Therefore, for a Brāhmaṇa, there are six duties: studying and teaching [the Veda], sacrificing and officiating at sacrifices for others, and giving and receiving gifts.
For the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya, [the duties] are sacrificing, studying, and giving gifts.
For the Kṣatriya, [the specific duties] are protecting the subjects, punishing the wicked, and fighting. For the Vaiśya, [the specific duties] are cattle-rearing, money-lending, and trade.
For a Śūdra, service to the twice-born and agriculture are the duties.

For a Brāhmaṇa there are four stages of life (āśramas); for a Kṣatriya, the first three; and for a Vaiśya, only two. Those belonging to the stages of life are four: the student (brahmacārī), the householder (gṛhastha), the forest-dweller (vānaprastha), and the mendicant (bhikṣu).

Having been initiated, the religious student (*brahmacārī*), wearing a girdle, a sacrificial cord, a deerskin, and carrying a staff, shall bathe; he shall perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*), the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*), the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) both morning and evening, and the fire-oblation with fuel-sticks (*samiddhoma*). Having clasped the feet of his teacher and saluted him daily, he shall study the Veda according to his vow. While the teacher stands, he shall stand; when the teacher rises, he shall rise before him and follow him as he walks. When the teacher is seated or lying down, being so directed, he shall sit or lie down at a lower level.
He shall not perform any action that has not been prescribed.
Even though not specifically told, he should perform the study of the Vedas (*svādhyāya*) and his daily obligatory duties (*nityakarman*).

Having avoided bathing in hot water, cleaning the teeth, applying collyrium, ointments, perfumes, flowers, shoes, umbrellas, sleeping during the day, seminal discharge, looking at or touching women, sexual intercourse, and [the vices of] lust, anger, greed, delusion, pride, envy, violence, and so forth, he should always be intent on service and perform those actions which are pleasing and beneficial to his teacher.
Free from malice and agreeable in speech and mind, he speaks what is pleasant and true;
even when distressed, he shall not utter that which is untrue, unpleasant, or slanderous.

Avoiding the consumption of honey, meat, fish, broth, fermented acids, and other forbidden foods, he shall subsist on alms-food after having performed the practice of begging and being permitted by his teacher.
One should not utter the names of one's guru, elders, or those initiated for sacrifice (dīkṣita).
In the absence of the guru, one should perform the duties toward his son as one would toward the guru himself.
There are four types of religious students (brahmacārins): the gāyatra, the brāhma, the prājāpatya, and the naiṣṭhika.

After the initiation (*upanayana*), for three nights he shall eat food that is neither pungent nor salted; having studied the *Gāyatrī*, until the completion of the *Sāvitra-vrata*, he remains here observing his vows.

After the *Sāvitra-vrata*, he shall practice begging alms in the houses of householders who are neither accused of crimes nor fallen from their status, and he shall observe the Vedic vows. Having stayed in the teacher’s house for twelve or twenty years, and having completed the study of the Vedas—either all four, two, or one—along with the Sūtras, he may enter the life of a householder.

The Prājāpatya, having bathed, being devoted to his daily duties and the practice of celibacy, intent upon Nārāyaṇa, and having reflected upon the meaning of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, takes a wife. Regarding the Prājāpatya, the sages declare that one should not remain [without a wife] for more than three years.

The lifelong student (naiṣṭhika), having put on a saffron-colored garment, a raw-silk cloth, an antelope skin, or a bark garment; wearing matted hair or a top-knot, a girdle, and a staff; carrying the sacred thread and an antelope skin; remaining chaste, pure, and eating food that is not pungent or salty; shall stay in the teacher’s household until his own death, subsisting on alms-food offered after being announced.

Having taken a wife, the householder—observing the rules and conduct such as ritual bathing and always performing the *aupāsana* fire-sacrifice and the *pākayajña* offerings—should, at the conclusion of the *vaiśvadeva* oblation, rise to meet a teacher (*guru*) or a *snātaka* who has arrived at his home, salute them, and provide a seat, water for the feet (*pādya*), and water for sipping (*ācamana*). Having also offered the *madhuparka* mixed with clarified butter, curd, and milk, he should feed them with various foods according to his ability.

He should honor, according to their merit, mendicants, celibate students, guests who are knowers of the Veda and learned in the scriptures, paternal uncles, teachers, officiating priests, maternal uncles, fathers-in-law, and others who have arrived, as well as children, the elderly, the helpless, the afflicted, and those exhausted by travel.
Even if he is unable to provide much, he should eat only after giving the first portion or alms, along with water, to them.

Endowed with compassion, truthfulness, purity, and proper conduct, he should constantly worship the sages through Vedic study and libations; the gods with sacrifices, offerings, oblations, water, flowers, and the like; the ancestors with *śrāddha* rites and sons; and all beings with sacrificial food (*bali*), as well as men with gifts of food and other necessities.

Thus, liberated from the three debts, he becomes free from debt. Householders are of four types: those who subsist by agriculture and trade (*vārtāvṛtti*), those who live by the domestic mode (*śālīnavṛtti*), those who wander for alms (*yāyāvara*), and those who practice severe austerities (*ghorācārika*).
One who subsists by the *vārtā* way of life earns his livelihood through agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade.

One who follows the *śālīna* way of life is endowed with restrictive observances; having performed the *pākayajñas* and established the sacred fires, he performs the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices every fortnight, the *cāturmāsya* sacrifices every four months, the *paśubandha* sacrifice every six months, and the *soma* sacrifice every year.

The *yāyāvara* performs sacrifices with *havis*-offerings and *soma*-sacrifices; he officiates as a priest for others, studies and teaches the Vedas, gives gifts and accepts them; devoted to these six duties, he constantly attends to the sacred fires and provides food to guests who arrive.

The Ghorācārika, endowed with restrictive observances, sacrifices but does not officiate at sacrifices for others; he studies but does not teach; he gives but does not accept gifts; he subsists by the practice of gleaning. Devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa, having performed the morning and evening *agnihotra* oblations, he performs the *asidhārāvrata* during the months of Mārgaśīrṣa and Jyeṣṭha, tending the sacred fire with forest herbs.

A householder together with his wife, whether he maintains the five fires or the three fires (tretāgnis), when about to depart from the household for the forest hermitage, should—whether he is one who has consecrated the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) or one who has not—place the *aupāsana* fire upon the kindling woods (*araṇi*). Having churned it out at home and established it according to the rules for the *śrāmaṇaka* fire, and having offered the *āghāra* libation, he should take the *śrāmaṇaka* fire and proceed to the third stage of life. As before, he should perform the rites such as sprinkling and scraping the fire-chamber.

Having wiped the third altar as well, and having prepared a grass-bundle (*kūrca*) for strewing—measuring thirty-six finger-breadths, made like a cord by being tripled and knotted at the base with *darbha* grasses tied beneath the fire at a distance of six finger-breadths—he strews it upon the middle altar for the *Śrāmaṇaka* rite.

Having invoked the Śrāmaṇaka sacrifice with the formula ending in "yajñadaivaviśvān devān," and having set aside clarified butter, he should offer oblations ending with "svāhā to the Śrāmaṇaka," "svāhā to the Śrāmaṇaka sacrifice," and "svāhā to the Viśvedevas, the deities of the sacrifice. Having thus offered, he should sacrifice the *caru* offering; this is the specific characteristic of the supporting base (*ādhāra*).
Furthermore, the upper altar (*ūrdhvavedi*) of the Śrāmaṇaka fire is thirty-two finger-breadths in length, four finger-breadths in width, and four finger-breadths in height.
The middle [altar] is surrounded by that [first one], measuring five *aṅgulas* in width and four *aṅgulas* in height.
The third altar is situated below, with its width and elevation equal to those of the upper altar.

Having constructed a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) provided with three altars and having a depression of twelve *aṅgulas* in the center, the forest-dweller, having established the fire, should offer the morning and evening oblations daily as in the *aupāsana* rite, and then sacrifice into the *śrāmaṇaka* fire with the *mahāvyāhṛtis*.

One who has a wife may go to the forest with his wives, but without the sacred fires. Vānaprasthas are both those with their wives and those without their wives; those with their wives are of four kinds.

The Audumbara, the Vairiñca, the Vālakhilya, and the Phenapa—among these, the Audumbara subsists on uncultivated grains, cultivated plants, or roots and fruits; he avoids onions, asafoetida, garlic, honey, fish, meat, stale food, fermented grain-sour, contact with others, and food cooked by others; he worships the gods, sages, ancestors, and men; he lives in the forest, excluded from the village; and having performed the morning and evening *agnihotra*, he practices austerity while performing the *śrāmaṇaka-agnihoma* and the *vaiśvadeva-homa*.
Having established only the single *śrāmaṇaka* fire, he offers oblations; so say some.

Belonging to Vairiñca, he gazes toward the eastern direction; having gone to that direction, there, having nourished his own guests with whatever is obtained such as *priyaṅgu*, barley, *śyāmāka*, *nīvāra*, and other grains, he becomes devoted to Nārāyaṇa, intent on austerity, and habitually performs the *agnihotra*, the *śrāmaṇaka*, and the *vaiśvadeva* offerings.

The *vālakhilya*, wearing matted hair and clad in rags or bark, maintaining the fire of the sun, should abandon abundant food on the full moon day of Kārttika and thereafter subsist on the remainder for the other months while performing austerities. Regarding him, they declare that the sun itself becomes his fire.

The *phenapa* (one who drinks foam), the *uddaṇḍaka* (one with raised staff), the *unmattaka* (the madman), the *nirodhaka* (the one who restrains himself), and the one who eats only fallen and withered leaves, while practicing the *cāndrāyaṇa* vow, sleeping upon the earth and meditating on Nārāyaṇa, seeks only liberation.

There are many kinds of those who live without wives: the *kālāśikas*, the *uddaṇḍasaṃvṛttas*, the *aśmakuṭṭas*, the *udagraphalinas*, the *dantolūkhalikas*, those who subsist by gleaning (*uñchavṛttika*), those who subsist by visible gleanings (*saṃdarśanavṛttika*), those who subsist like pigeons (*kapotavṛttika*), those who wander like deer (*mṛgacārika*), those who take food directly from the hand (*hastādāyin*), those who eat from stones or wooden planks (*śailaphalakādin*), those who eat what is scorched by the sun (*arkadagdhāśin*), those who eat only bilva fruits (*bailvāśin*), those who eat flowers (*kusumāśin*), those who eat withered leaves (*pāṇḍupattrāśin*), those who eat at fixed intervals of time (*kālāntarabhojin*), those who eat once a day (*ekakālika*), those who eat four times a day (*catuṣkālika*), those who sleep on thorns (*kaṇṭakaśāyin*), those who sleep in the *vīrāsana* posture (*vīrāsanaśāyin*), those who sleep in the midst of five fires (*pañcāgnimadhyaśāyin*), those who inhale smoke (*dhūmāśin*), and those who sleep on stones (*pāṣāṇaśāyin*).

"It is known that they have various modes of conduct: those who plunge into water, those who dwell in water-jars, those who observe silence, those who keep their heads downward, those who face the sun, those with upraised arms, and those standing on one foot" (VaikhDS 1.9). Now, mendicants seeking liberation are of four kinds: the *kuṭīcaka*, the *bahūdaka*, the *haṃsa*, and the *paramahaṃsa*.

Among them, the *kuṭīcakas*—who know the truth of the path of yoga and subsist on eight morsels of food in the hermitages of Gautama, Bhāradvāja, Yājñavalkya, Hārīta, and others—seek only liberation. The *bahūdakas*, who carry the triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*), the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), and wear saffron-colored garments and the attire of those who accept [alms], seek only liberation by begging for alms at seven houses, while avoiding meat, salt, and stale food in the homes of Brahmanical sages and other people of virtuous conduct.

Those known as *haṃsas* dwell for one night in a village and five nights in a town; staying no longer than that, they subsist on cow urine and cow dung, or fast for a month, or observe the perpetual *cāndrāyaṇa* vow, always aspiring toward spiritual awakening alone. Those known as *paramahaṃsas* dwell at the foot of a single tree, in an empty house, or in a cremation ground; they may be clothed or naked.
For them, there is no duality such as merit and demerit, truth and falsehood, purity and impurity, and so forth.
Equal toward all, having realized the Self in all, and regarding a clod of earth and gold as the same, they practice the mendicant’s round among all social classes.

For Brāhmaṇas, the four stages of life (āśramas) are prescribed; for Kṣatriyas, three stages; and for Vaiśyas, two stages. Indeed, the fruit of that [practice] is twofold: with desire and without desire.

In this world, "with desire" (*sakāma*) refers to the longing for the attainment of a son and so forth, or the longing for other fruits such as heaven, once one has recognized the increase [of worldly life] within this *saṃsāra*.

"Without desire" (*niṣkāma*) refers to the performance of prescribed duties without longing for anything whatsoever. In that regard, the "without desire" [practice] is of two kinds: engagement (*pravṛtti*) and withdrawal (*nivṛtti*).

*Pravṛtti* (the path of worldly engagement) is the attainment of powers such as *aṇimā* by one who, disregarding *saṃsāra*, relies upon infinite knowledge and practices breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), posture (*āsana*), withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*), and concentration (*dhāraṇā*) to master the vital air (*vāyu*).
However, the supreme sages do not favor it, because it leads to rebirth once the merit of austerity is exhausted and because it involves an abundance of diseases.

Renunciation (*nivṛtti*) is known as follows: having realized the impermanence of the worlds and that nothing exists apart from the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), one disregards the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) and severs the bond consisting of a wife. Having become a master of the senses and abandoned the body, one effects the union (*yoga*) of the individual soul (*kṣetrajña*) and the Supreme Self. Thus it is understood as the entry into the supreme light—that which is beyond the senses, the seed of the entire universe, devoid of all particularity, eternal bliss, like drinking the essence of immortality, always providing satisfaction, and leading to liberation.

Indeed, due to differences in their conduct regarding withdrawal (*nivṛtti*), yogins are of three kinds: *sāraṅga*, *ekārthya*, and *visaraga*. The *sāraṅgas* are of four types: those who do not restrain [the breath], those who restrain it, those who follow the path, and those who follow the wrong path. The *ekārthyas* are of five types: those who go far, those who do not go far, those whose focus is between the eyebrows, those who are undivided, and those who are divided.
The *visaraga* (those who have gone forth) are not numbered.

Among them, the *sāraṅga*s—so called because they go toward the *sāra* (essence), which is the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field)—are those who move about having meditated, "I am Viṣṇu, the unobstructed. For them, there are no *prāṇāyāma*s and the like.
However, for those who are obstructive (*nirodhaka*s), there exist the sixteen *kalā*s, beginning with *prāṇāyāma*, *pratyāhāra*, and *dhāraṇā*.
For those who follow the right path, there are only six [limbs], beginning with *prāṇāyāma*.

For those who follow the wrong path, they conceive of eight limbs—*yama*, *niyama*, *āsana*, *prāṇāyāma*, *pratyāhāra*, *dhāraṇā*, *dhyāna*, and *samādhi*—and they also represent the object of meditation (*dhyeya*) differently. Now follows the section on single-mindedness (*ekārṣyā*).
Those for whom there is only one seer are the *ekarṣis*.
For those among them who travel by the distant path, this is the way:

through the *piṅgalā* channel they enter the solar orb and, having united with the Person residing there, they proceed to the lunar orb and unite with the Person residing there; from there they go to lightning and unite with the Person residing there; and from there, in due order, they attain union (*sāyujya*) with Vaikuṇṭha.
This is the duty for those who are not far [from the goal]:

having brought about the union of the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) and the supreme self (paramātman) by means of the knower of the field, and having meditated upon the total dissolution right there, they meditate: "I am existence alone, like space."

Those who have reached the middle of the eyebrows [perform] the union of the *kṣetrajña* and the *paramātman*; having led [the breath] to the middle of the eyebrows by means of the fire whose nature is *sattva*, they perform the withdrawal from the five locations beginning with the big toe, and then either the exit through the *piṅgalā* channel until the end of dissolution (*pralaya*), or until the end of the yoga of the *kṣetrajña*.
Those called "unmixed" (*asaṃbhakta*) perform meditation with the mind;
they hear the scripture that establishes that [truth] with their ears.
With the eye they perceive the form of the deity;
with the nose they experience fragrance;
with the hand they pay homage to the deity.

The one named Saṃbhakta is the Brāhmaṇa; because he pervades everything, whether appropriate or inappropriate, that Supreme Self remains pervading like space. Therefore, apart from that Brahman, one does not perceive a self anywhere else.
Even regarding that which resides between the eyebrows, it has been stated that doubt is indeed without foundation.
Therefore, nothing other than Brahman is logically tenable.
Because they wander in various ways, because they hold diverse views, and because they follow wrong paths, they are called *visaraga*.
In ancient times, Prajāpati perceived the faction of the *visaraga* for the purpose of concealing the true instruction.
Seeing him, even the sages fell into a state of delusion, let alone ordinary men.

For those who possess the ego-sense and are intent on the liberation of animals, there is no liberation in this life, but only in future births. Therefore, the path of animal-like behavior should not be practiced.

Some [attain liberation] through the renunciation of bodily exertion; some through the recitation of mantras; some through a particular form of meditation; some through a particular syllable; others through the conquest of the vital breath (*vāyu*). Still others, having united the individual soul (*kṣetrajña*) with the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), meditate upon that very union with the Supreme Self. Some assert that the Person resides only within the heart. Others, understanding that yoga is the performance of what has been prescribed without any specific meditation, desire liberation.

For those who follow the path of releasing animals (*visaraga-paśu*), there is no liberation in this life. Therefore, one who desires liberation in this very life should not practice the release of animals.

It is known from scripture that one should first fix the intellect upon Brahman with qualities (*saguṇa-brahman*) and subsequently apply effort by taking refuge in the quality-less Brahman (*nirguṇa-brahman*).
Now, regarding the rule for the *śrāmaṇaka* (forest-dweller) stage of life:

A householder who has performed the *soma* sacrifice, having seen his son and grandson and having established their sons and so forth in the household, should shave his head and perform the *prājāpatya* penance.
In the spring, during the bright fortnight, at a sacred site (*puṇyakṣetra*), he goes to the forest hermitage together with his wife.

On the preceding day, having bathed and made a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), he should drink water with *kuśa* grass and observe a fast. Having performed the *aupāsana* oblation, he should consign the fire into the two kindling woods (*araṇi*) with the mantra, "This is your source. Then, according to the procedure for the New and Full Moon sacrifices, having gathered *darbha* grass and other materials, he prepares the ritual bundles for strewing (*paristaraṇa-kūrca*), the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), the fuel sticks (*samidh*), and the bamboo staff, sacred thread (*upavīta*), water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), bark garment (*valkala*), and so forth, as previously described.
One should prepare the fire-pit according to the previously stated rule.

On the following day, having churned the fire with the Vaiśvānara-sūkta and kindled it, one should bring the fire down with the mantra "āgneyāhi | upāvaroha. Having placed the fire [in the pit], one performs the *āghāra* libation for the *śrāmaṇaka* fire as before.

Having bowed to the fire and sprinkled water around it, and having offered the five-fold expiatory oblation (*pañcaprāyaścitta*) with the mantra "O Agni, you are the expiation" (*agne prāyaścitte tvam*), he should sprinkle himself with the *āpo hi ṣṭhā* verses and then perform the principal offerings (*pradhāna*) ending with the *vyāhṛtis*, dedicated to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the five forms of Varuṇa.

To the west of the fire, having placed two *kuśa* blades with their tips pointing eastward and having set a stone upon them, he should step upon the stone with the tip of his right big toe while reciting, "That excellent splendor of Savitṛ... Having put on a bark garment, an antelope skin, or a tattered rag, while reciting "May [the waters] rich in luster...", he takes up the girdle and the other items as before—three sacred threads (*upavīta*), an upper garment, and a black antelope skin.
Having sipped water (ācamana), saying "O gods, may there be well-being," and having circumambulated the fire while bowing to it, he should sit down.

Having sprinkled water on his own head with the mantra "May the altars be auspicious to us," and having offered the *jaya*, *abhyātāna*, *rāṣṭrabhṛt*, and *vyāhṛti* oblations, he should consume the remainder of the clarified butter by means of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).

Having sipped water twice with the mantra "In every union," and reciting "A hundred autumns indeed," he should perform a prostration and circumambulate the sun with the mantras "With the guest" and "The two great ones have come together."
With the mantra, "Thou art the sustainer of the kingdom," he should take up a seat (*kūrca*) with its tip pointing upward.

Having recited the *Sāvitrī* verse—first part by part (*pacchaḥ*) as: "Oṃ bhūs tat savituḥ," "Oṃ bhuvo bhargo devasya," and "Oṃ suvar dhiyo yo naḥ"; then half-verse by half-verse (*ardharcaśaḥ*) as: "Oṃ bhūr bhuvas tat savituḥ" and "Oṃ suvar dhiyo yo naḥ"; and finally the whole verse (*samastā*) as: "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ suvas tat savituḥ"—and having entered the forest hermitage (*vanāśrama*), he should formally resolve (*saṃkalpayet*) upon the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya-vrata*).
And his wife shall likewise remain a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacāriṇī*).

Having himself circumambulated the fire from left to right, he offers clarified butter with the *prājāpatya* [verse], the *dhātṛ* and other [verses], the two *mindāhuti* oblations, the *vicchinna*, the *aindra*, the *vaiśvadeva*, the *vaiṣṇava*, the *bāhya*, the *viṣṇornuka* and others, the *prājāpatya-sūkta*, and the *tad-vrata-bandha*. Having again offered these principal oblations, he binds the *prājāpatya-vrata*.

Having stood [firm], he takes up the two-staff (*dvidaṇḍa*) belonging to Viṣṇu—provided with five, seven, or nine joints, reaching to the hairline, and not crooked—with the two mantras, "Devasya tvā" and "Yo me daṇḍaḥ.
He then takes up the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) and the staff for clearing away dust (*mṛdgrahiṇī*), as well as sandals and an umbrella, in the same manner as before, with the mantra "Yena devāḥ."

Having kindled the fires, beginning with the Gārhapatya, and having performed the Agnihotra sacrifice, he offers the Prājāpatya oblation and the Viṣṇu-sūkta into the Āhavanīya fire. Having offered everywhere with the formulas "Svāhā to Agni," "Svāhā to Soma," and "Svāhā to Viṣṇu," he consigns the fires into the two kindling woods (araṇis).
In a forest, on a mountain, or on a secluded riverbank, having prepared a forest hermitage, he should construct the sacrificial fire-pits as prescribed.
Taking the fires along with his wife and equipped with the vessels and other necessary implements, he enters the forest hermitage.
Having sprinkled water upon the site for the fire-altar, having dug it, and having drawn six lines, he should place a piece of gold and grains of rice and then establish the *śrāmaṇaka* fire.

He collects wild materials: earthen items, products of trees, *kulīra*, *udghāta*, *śaṇa*, old *kuśa* and *darbha* grasses, a tuft of wool, the tip of a *plakṣa* tree, fragrant reeds, *guggulu* resin, pieces of gold, and a sun-crystal (*sūryakānta*).

Having chosen forest-dwelling officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), having churned the fire, and having established the three sacred fires—namely the *Āhavanīya*, *Gārhapatya*, and *Dakṣiṇāgni*—or the five fires according to the procedure for the formal setting up of the fires (*agnyādheya*), he offers two oblations each time; thereafter, he constantly performs his offerings twice daily using only forest-grown materials.

The sage belonging to the forest hermitage (*vanāśramin*) practices these ten observances (*niyamas*): bathing, purity, Vedic study, austerity, charity, sacrifice, fasting, restraint of the sexual organ, vows, and silence; as well as these ten restraints (*yamas*): truthfulness, compassion, straightforwardness, forbearance, self-restraint, friendliness, clarity, gentleness, non-violence, and sweetness. He practices both of these sets.

Meditating upon Viṣṇu with devotion, he does not neglect the two daily offerings—the *agnihotra* and the *śrāmaṇaka-homa*. Having abandoned food grown in villages, he resolves to take his regular meal from wild herbs, fruits, roots, or vegetables. Having fetched [the materials] in the afternoon with the mantra "Tirodhā bhūḥ," he himself, or accompanied by his wife, cooks the sacrificial food (*haviṣya*).
At the conclusion of the *vaiśvadeva* offering, after having fed the guests who have arrived, he eats an unlimited amount.
At night, he shall not eat.
Having spread *darbha* grass, ordinary grass, or leaves below, the man of good vows should sleep alone with his wife of good vows;
she performs service for him, and he should not approach her. Free from desire, viewing her as a mother, he should remain chaste and have his senses subdued.
He should perform the New and Full Moon sacrifices, the Cāturmāsya, the Nakṣatreṣṭi, and the Āgrayaṇeṣṭi with wild herbs, according to the previous sequence.

Sustaining his life with roots, fruits, leaves, or flowers that have ripened in their respective seasons and fallen off naturally, he should practice an ever-increasing degree of austerity, distinguished by the excellence of the fruits and other such offerings.

Now, one who maintains the sacred fires (vaikhānasa), having consigned all his fires into the two kindling woods (araṇis) and having gathered together all the terrestrial and arboreal fires with all the *saṃvāpa* mantras, should produce fire by friction (*nirmathyā*) according to this procedure and the rules for the establishment of the fires (*agnyādheya*). With all the mantras, he should then establish the *śrāmaṇaka* fire in the hearth of the *sabhya* fire and maintain it.
They say that the *śrāmaṇaka* fire is a modification of the *sabhya* fire.

And one who is without a wife, having performed the fire-oblation like a mendicant, having discarded the vessels for forest-gathering and the like, having entrusted his wife to a son, and likewise having internalized the sacred fires within himself, should take up bark garments, a sacred thread, and so forth, as well as an alms-bowl; then, being without fire and without a wife, he should go and dwell in the forest.
This is the root of all ascetic practices (*tapas*); therefore, Vikhanas said that this rule and this fire are called "the Śramaṇaka."

Regarding the procedure for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*): when one is aged beyond seventy, childless, or incapacitated, and desiring *yoga* after reflecting upon birth, death, old age, and so forth, he should then—either having entrusted his wife to his son and fixed his mind upon the Supreme Self, or otherwise—go from the forest to renounce the world.

Having shaved his head according to the prescribed rule and bathed outside the village, he should perform the *prājāpatya* penance. In the forenoon, having gathered a triple staff, a sling, a saffron-colored garment, a water-pot, a water-strainer, a vessel for taking earth, and an alms-bowl, and having consumed the three-fold [mixture] and observed a fast, he should bathe again on the following morning and, after offering the *agnihotra* and the *vaiśvadeva* oblations, perform the *vaiśvānara* sacrifice with a cake on twelve potsherds.

Having prepared clarified butter (*ājya*) in the *gārhapatya* fire and having offered two full oblations (*pūrṇāhuti*) and the *Puruṣasūkta* in the *āhavanīya* fire, he offers with the formula: "To Agni, to Soma, to Dhruva, to the Maker of Stability, to the Supreme Self, to Nārāyaṇa, Svāhā! (VaikhDhS 02.06).
Having taken four portions into the large ladle (*sruc*) with the small spoon (*sruva*), he should offer them into all the fires with the formula: "Oṃ, Svāhā! (VaikhDhS 02.07).
He casts the *agnihotra-havaṇī* ladle into the *āhavanīya* fire, and all other vessels made of clay or stone into the *gārhapatya* fire. (VaikhDhS 02.07)

A householder who has not established the sacred fires, as well as a forest-dweller, having offered the oblation in the *aupāsana* fire or the *śrāmaṇaka* fire respectively, should cast away his ritual vessels. Having recited the *sāvitrī* verse foot by foot, half-verse by half-verse, part by part, and in its entirety, he enters the stage of mendicancy (*bhikṣāśrama*) with the thought, "I enter the stage of mendicancy. Standing within the sacrificial altar (*antarvedyām*), he should smell each of the fires, beginning with the *gārhapatya*, three times with the mantra, "O Agni, that which is yours worthy of sacrifice," and then consign them into himself with the mantra, "May you two be of one mind for us."

Having uttered the call "bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ, may it be renounced by me" three times, both in a low voice and aloud, and having drunk water once with the right hand and sipped it, and having spoken in the same manner again, he should release three handfuls of water.
He gives his girdle, four sacred threads or one sacred thread, a black antelope skin, and an upper garment as before.

With the three formulas, "Of the god thee," "That staff of mine," and "My friend may protect me," he should take up the triple-staff (*tridaṇḍa*); with "That which is beyond this region," the sling (*śikya*); with "By which means the gods [purify]," the water-strainer (*appavitra*); and with "By which means the gods [attain] light," the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) and the clay-receptacle (*mṛdgrahaṇī*). Having bathed, he should perform the *aghamarṣaṇa* rite with the *aghamarṣaṇa-sūkta*.

Having sipped water (ācamana) and performed sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), and having recited the Sāvitrī mantra a thousand or a hundred times, he takes up an alms-bowl made of gourd, wood, or clay.

Having offered libations of water to the gods with the seven vyāhṛtis, each preceded by the syllable Om (praṇava), saying "I satisfy [you]," he should then offer libations to the ancestors with the first four [vyāhṛtis], saying "Svadhā.
He should worship the sun with the verse, "ud vayaṃ tamasaḥ" (RV 7.89.2).
Having offered a handful of water, he should grant fearlessness to all beings.
The ascetic, delighting in the inner self, subsisting on alms, practicing the rules and restraints, with his senses controlled, perceives the Supreme Self through the yoga of meditation.
[He should follow] the righteous conduct of the virtuous.

Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (nivītin), having placed it around the right ear, sitting in the utkaṭika posture, facing north during the day and south at night, he should void urine and feces on ground covered with grass.

He should not do so in a river, a cow-pen, on a path, in the shade, on ashes, in water, on kuśa grass, or on darbhā grass. Without looking at a cow, a Brahmin, water, fire, wind, the sun, or the moon, he should perform these acts.

Having grasped the penis with the left hand and risen, sitting by the side of water, the student (*brahmacārī*) and likewise the householder (*gṛhastha*) should perform purification with water drawn up [from the source], applying earth twice to the penis, twice to the hands, and six times to the anus.
He should wash his left hand ten times and both hands likewise with earth and water. For the forest-dweller (*vanastha*) and the mendicant (*bhikṣu*), this is double.

At night, half of what has been prescribed [should be performed]. In the case of the emission of semen, purification should be performed as in the case of urine; some say that for semen, it should be done three times.

Wearing the sacred thread, facing either the east or the north, and having sat down elsewhere, he washes his feet and hands with earth and water as before, sips water, and performs the ritual sipping (*ācamana*) with the mantra.

A Brāhmaṇa should sip water that reaches the heart, a Kṣatriya water that reaches the throat, and a Vaiśya water that reaches the palate. Having sprinkled himself with water and released the water toward each sun, he should circumambulate the sun.

Restraining his breaths on the left side of either water or fire, he should recite the Gāyatrī three times—preceded by the seven Vyāhṛtis beginning with Oṃ and including the Śiras at the end. This is Prāṇāyāma; having performed three or one such Prāṇāyāmas, he becomes purified.
Having performed the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā) at evening and morning, by reciting the Sāvitrī one hundred, ten, or eight times, one wipes away the sin committed during the night and the day.
A twice-born man who is devoid of the performance of the twilight devotions becomes equal to a Śūdra.
A student (brahmacārī), having announced his own name, should offer a salutation with the words, "I, O venerable sir" (ahaṃ bho).

Having touched the ears and the feet of the teacher—grasping the right foot with his right hand and the left foot with his left hand, alternating them down to the toes—and bowing his head, he greets him.
"May you be long-lived, O gentle one," he should say to him;
one who does not utter such a blessing is not to be saluted.
Every day, one’s mother, father, teacher, and learned men are to be saluted.
Other relatives are to be saluted upon returning from a journey.

An elder brother, a paternal uncle, a maternal uncle, and a father-in-law are to be honored like a father; likewise, a paternal aunt, a maternal aunt, an elder sister-in-law, a sister, and an elder female cousin are to be honored like a mother.
For all [men], the mother is most excellent, and the teacher is even more excellent. When touching a young woman who is another's wife, one should salute her while remaining on the ground.
Through saluting those worthy of veneration, longevity, knowledge, strength, health, and auspiciousness arise.

One should not wear a sacred thread, girdle, deerskin, or staff that have been worn by another. Having performed the initiatory rite (*upākarma*), one should study the Veda beginning with the *praṇava*, remaining pure and free from laziness; however, one should not study on the new moon day, the full moon day, the fourteenth days of both fortnights, nor on the first and eighth days of the lunar fortnights.
There is no prohibition against study during the daily recitation (*japa*) or the fire-oblation (*homa*).

If a cat, mongoose, frog, dog, snake, donkey, pig, or other such animal passes between [the teacher and student], there shall be no study for a day and a night. During the impurity caused by birth (*sūtaka*) or death (*pretaka*), there shall be no study for that duration; likewise during the three *aṣṭakās* and when the teacher has died, there shall be no study for three nights. Upon the death of his wife or son, or upon the death of his own pupil, there shall be no study for one day. Furthermore, there shall be no study during a time of distress or illness, or when one is in a state of ritual impurity (*aprāyatya*).

One should not study at the following times: when mounted on a tree, a boat, or a vehicle; with the feet outstretched; upon the voiding of urine, feces, or semen; when there is a corpse within a village; when eating food that is unfit to be eaten; after vomiting; in a cremation ground; during the twilight hours; when there is thunder; during an earthquake; when there is a conflagration of the quarters; when lightning, thunderbolts, or meteors fall; when there is a rain of blood, stones, or dust; and during an eclipse of the sun or moon—at these respective times one must not study. The Veda brings about welfare both in this world and the next; therefore, it should be studied.
At the conclusion [of the lesson], having uttered the *praṇava*, he says: "I have finished."
Having offered two fuel-sticks (*samidh*) into the common fire (*laukikāgni*), he should, observing silence, eat pure alms-food that bestows intelligence.

In the month of Pauṣa or Māgha, outside the village at the edge of water, having offered the oblation for the conclusion of the vow (*vratavisargahoma*) as before, and having ceased his private study (*svādhyāya*), he should thoroughly study the Veda during the bright fortnight and the Vedāṅgas during the dark fortnight until their completion; then, having given a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the teacher, he shall perform the ceremony of returning home (*samāvartana*).

At midday, having washed his feet and hands with clay and water in pure water, having sipped water (ācamana) and purified his limbs, he should immerse himself in the water while reciting, "May the waters purify [me].

Having sipped water again and bowed to Viṣṇu with Vaiṣṇava mantras and to Varuṇa with the mantra beginning "Hiraṇyaśṛṅga," and having performed the *aghamarṣaṇa* rite with the *Aghamarṣaṇa-sūkta*, he should bathe while reciting, "O Waters, you are auspicious. The four orders of life (*āśramins*) perform the obligatory bath daily according to this previously mentioned rule, as well as the optional and occasional baths.

Having covered himself with a washed garment, having performed *ācamana* as before and sprinkled himself with water, while either seated or standing and having performed *prāṇāyāma*, he should recite the *Sāvitrī* and worship the Sun.

Having gratified the kings and others with water from the *brāhma* (thumb-base) *tīrtha* of the right hand; Nārāyaṇa and others with the *daiva* (forefinger-base) *tīrtha*; Viśvāmitra and others with the *ārṣa* (palm-base) *tīrtha*; and the ancestors and others with the *paitṛka* (middle-finger-base) *tīrtha*, he should, intending to perform the *brahmayajña*, recite as much of the *yajurveda-saṃhitā* as he desires—beginning with the words "To food thee! To strength thee!"—for the first three sections (*anuvākas*) as his private study (*svādhyāya*).
He may also recite occasional hymns such as "Truth and reality" (*ṛtaṃ ca satyaṃ ca*), or the opening mantras of the four Vedas.
The sacrifice to Brahman (brahmayajña) is the beginning of all sacrifices;
therefore, it must be performed by the twice-born starting from the very time of their initiation (upanayana).
One should perform one's bath in a river, at a sacred ford (tīrtha), in a natural pool dug by the gods, in a lake, or in a large reservoir.
In the water of another person, one should bathe after having extracted five lumps of earth;
at a well, one should sprinkle oneself three times with a jar on its bank.
One who is impure or naked should not bathe, nor should one sleep in such a state.
One who is afflicted by illness should not immerse himself in water.

When an afflicted person performs an occasional bath (*naimittika-snāna*), one who is not afflicted should immerse himself in the water ten or twelve times, sip water (*ācamana*), and then touch him; thereby he becomes purified.

Twice a day, at the conclusion of the fire-oblation (*homa*), having washed his feet and sipped water, he should stand facing either the east or the west upon a square, smeared mandala and place a clean vessel there.
Having placed food therein, he honors it.

Placing two feet or one foot upon the ground, he sprinkles water around it in the evening with the mantra, "I sprinkle thee, the gracious, with truth," and in the morning with, "I sprinkle thee, truth, with ṛta. Having drunk the rinsing water with the mantra, "Thou art the underlayer of immortality," and having offered the oblations to the vital breaths (*prāṇāhutis*) according to the rule, he eats the food without finding fault with it.
Having eaten, and having drunk water with the mantra "Thou art the covering of nectar" (*amṛtāpidhānam asi*), he should sip water and rinse his mouth.
Wearing only a single garment, while lying down, standing, not having bathed, not performing *japa* or *homa*, with feet dry, or facing north, he does not eat.
He shall not eat food from a broken vessel, nor food that is stale, nor food placed upon a bed, a seat, or one's lap.
One should not drink water with cupped hands (añjali).

One should not eat food that has been touched by those who are impure from remnants of food (ucchiṣṭa), those who are unclean (aśuci), those in a state of ritual impurity (āśaucin), outcasts (patita), or those who have performed funeral rites for a birth or death (sūtakapretaka). Sesame flour, curd, and parched grain (lāja) are not to be eaten at night.
Food that has stood overnight may be eaten if it is mixed with clarified butter or curd.
Food contaminated by worms, hair, or insects, smelled by a cow, or pecked at by birds, becomes pure when sprinkled with ashes and water.

When a large quantity of food is defiled by dogs, crows, or similar creatures, one should remove and discard only as much as would satisfy a single person; then, having sprinkled the remainder with ashes and water while reciting the verse "pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ," and having touched it with a firebrand of *darbha* grass, one may take it.

Within ten days of giving birth, the milk of cows, as well as the milk of animals with uncloven hooves, camels, and women, must be avoided; likewise, onions, mushrooms, garlic, *gṛñjana*, and *viḍja*—if not otherwise specified—as well as fish and meat, are to be shunned.
Meat that remains from a sacrifice may be eaten.
One should avoid food touched by a woman in her courses, food touched by those born of the *śūdra* castes through *anuloma* unions, and the food belonging to them.
Raw food may be accepted from *anuloma* Śūdras who follow their own specific duties when one is hungry;
however, even if hungry, one should not with effort accept either raw or cooked food from any *pratiloma*, *antarāla*, or *vrātya* castes.
One should also renounce food that has been cooked by others if it has come into contact with them or has been mixed with such food.
Constantly performing the duties prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti through the actions of mind, speech, and body, he gradually practices righteousness.

The householder of the domestic stage of life (gṛhasthāśramī) should carry two sacred threads (yajñopavīta), a bamboo staff (vaiṇava-daṇḍa), and a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu). Having bathed together with his wife, he should perform the domestic rites in the domestic fire (gṛhya-agni) and the Śrauta rites in the Śrauta fires.
In the evening, at the conclusion of the *homa*, having fed any guests who have arrived and having himself eaten a moderate amount, he should sleep with his wife.
With wet feet and with his head toward the west or the north, he does not sleep. During the nights of her fertile period (*ṛtu*), he should approach his own wife.
At the outset, for three nights, she who has reached her menses must avoid sexual intercourse, sitting together, and sleeping together.
She must not have sexual union with another's wife;
for from union with another's wife, one’s lifespan, prosperity, and spiritual luster perish.
He does not eat together with his wife; he should not look at her while she is eating, yawning, or naked;
he avoids speaking untruths.
There is no sin greater than untruth, and there is no virtue greater than truth.

One should live for the welfare of all living beings by means of non-violence alone; one should possess pure wealth and subsist on a granary of grain, a jar of grain, or have nothing for the morrow. A twice-born man should not touch those who are outcaste or of the lowest castes.
At sunrise and at sunset, one should not look at the sun.
One should pass by gods, teachers, Brahmins, clarified butter, milk, curds, water containing life, sacrificial fuel, *darbha* grass, fire, and trees, keeping them to one's right.
One should yield the way to a *snātaka*, a king, a teacher, an eminent person, a sick person, a burden-carrier, and a pregnant woman.
Roads are purified by the rays of the sun and the wind.
One should not use the seats or beds of another without they being given. If one uses things that have not been given, he loses a fourth part of his own merit.
One should not wear garments, garlands, sandals, or umbrellas that have been used by another.
One should not warm one's feet over the fire; one should not blow upon it with the mouth, nor touch it with the foot. One should not place anything beneath the fire.
One should not throw fire into fire, nor cast urine, feces, pus, blood, semen, phlegm, food remnants, or bodily excretions into a temple, into a fire, or into water.

One should not look at another man’s wife while she is naked, nor at feces or urine. While impure from eating, one should not look at the gods, the sun, the moon, the planets, the constellations, or the stars.
One should not step over the shadow of a deity, a teacher, a *snātaka*, one initiated for a sacrifice, a king, a cow, or a person of high standing.
One should not show a rainbow to another, nor speak of it;
one should not wake a sleeping person;
and one should not travel alone on a road.
One should not prevent a cow grazing in another's field nor a suckling calf; one should not report such an occurrence.
One should not wear worn-out or dirty clothes, and one should avoid playing with dice, the smoke from a funeral pyre, and warming oneself over a fire by a child.
One should not step upon hair, body hair, chaff, embers, potsherds, bones, feces, urine, pus, blood, semen, phlegm, or food remnants.
One should cleanse with earth and water any limb smeared with impurity until the smell of that impurity is gone and no mental suspicion remains.
One should not dwell together with outcasts, those of the lowest castes, fools, unrighteous persons, or enemies.
While impure or defiled by food remnants, one should not touch the gods, cows, Brahmins, or fires.

One should not treat with contempt the gods, the Vedas, the king, teachers, parents, or learned Brahmins; nor should one revile them. For he who treats them with contempt and he who reviles them shall perish.
One should not engage in reviling or striking any living being.

One should not carry out disputes with one's teacher, mother, or father; nor with their fathers and so forth, nor with brothers, paternal uncles, maternal uncles, preceptors, officiating priests, and others.
Among all forms of purification, for a person, the purification of wealth, the purification of women, and the purification of food are the most excellent.

Among articles of property, those made of gems, gold, or silver he purifies with water, or he touches them in fire. Copper, tin, lead, iron, and the like [he purifies] with acidic water; those made of wood or ivory by planing or washing; and sacrificial vessels by wiping or rinsing with the right hand. Articles made of leather, woven fabrics, and vegetables, roots, and fruits he should sprinkle with water; small quantities of these he should wash.
Having purified substances such as clarified butter and the like, one should examine them with a firebrand.

Silk and woolen garments [should be cleaned] with alkaline salt; fine cotton cloths with *śrīphala* fruits; conch-shells, mother-of-pearl, and cow-horns with mustard seeds mixed with water; earthenware with fire; a house by burning, sweeping, smearing, sprinkling, and scraping; and the ground by digging it up, filling it with fresh earth, letting cows graze upon it, and by sweeping and other such means. One should thus purify them.
Water that reaches the ground and satisfies the throat is free from defects and well-purified; water consecrated by speech, water cleansed by a cloth, and water not seen [to be defiled] are pure.
Likewise, the mouth of a woman and the hand of an artisan with goods spread out for sale are always pure.
Fruit left by a bird is not to be censured; likewise, that which is settled upon by mosquitoes, flies, or gnats, as well as their droplets, are not defiled.
Furthermore, anything touched by the wind, fire, or the rays of the sun is pure.

When one is ill, when dealing with a child, or in a kitchen, purity need not be scrutinized; it should be maintained according to one's ability. Water that is abundant is not defiled by feces or urine.

One who is performing the ritual sipping (ācamana) does not become impure by drops of water from another person’s sipping that fall to the ground and then rise up again, or by those touched by the feet.

A forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), constantly engaged in Vedic study, should gather *kuśa* grass, fuel, and the like for the sake of the sacred fires, as well as vegetables, roots, and fruits grown in a pure place for his own food.
He should avoid that which depends on others, that which has been discarded by others, that which grows in an impure place, and cow’s milk.
He should not accumulate grain or wealth.
He should not wear clothing.
When honey is mentioned, he takes water; when meat is mentioned, he takes food made of flour.

Compassionate toward all beings, impartial, patient, pure, free from envy, indifferent to pleasure, possessing auspicious speech, and avoiding malice and miserliness, he should renounce fish, biting insects, things grown in ploughed soil, bulbs, roots, fruits, vegetables, and the like. Wearing matted hair, beard, body hair, and nails, bathing three times a day, and dwelling on the ground, he should offer sacrificial oblations of cooked rice and cakes using only forest-grown products.
He avoids onions and the like, plant resins, white eggplant, *suniṣaṇṇaka*, *śleṣmātaka*, *vrajakali*, *citraka*, drumstick tree, *bhūs-tṛṇa*, *kovidāra*, and radish.
For a sage, all meat is equal to beef, and fermented grain-water (*dhānyāmla*) is equal to liquor (*surā*).
He discards previously stored food and his former garments in the month of Āśvayuja.

A practitioner of meditation (*dhyānayogin*) who has mastered the Vedas and Vedānta performs austerity (*tapas*). Being without a wife, without sacred fires, without a household, and without a fixed dwelling, he lives at the root of a tree or in the forest hermitages, or in the houses of householders; having begged for alms, he eats food sufficient merely for the maintenance of life on a clean leaf near water, like a mendicant. Withering his body, he should perform increasingly intense austerities.

The mendicant, having bathed daily, should satisfy himself with the *praṇava*; he should offer salutation with that very same [syllable]. Having performed at least six breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) and having recited the *Sāvitrī* at least one hundred times, he should perform the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyopāsana*).
He should sip water purified by straining it through a non-sacrificial filter (*apavitra*).
He should practice wearing saffron robes (*kāṣāya*), renouncing everything, abstaining from sexual intercourse, and avoiding theft and other such acts.

Without a companion, without a sacred fire, without a fixed dwelling, free from doubt, equal toward honor and dishonor, and avoiding dispute, anger, greed, delusion, and falsehood, he should dwell outside the village in a secluded hut, a temple, or at the foot of a tree.
Except during the four-month period [of the rainy season], he shall not dwell in a single place for more than one day.
During the rains, the autumn, and the four-month period, he may stay in one place alone.

Having fastened the triple staff, the ochre-colored garment, the strainer, and other implements, and holding them with his left hand around his neck, while holding the alms-bowl with his right hand, he should go for alms at one time to the houses of pure Brahmins at the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva offering.
Having looked at living beings on the ground, he should place his foot down while avoiding them;
standing with his face downward, he should seek alms.
Having stood for the duration of time it takes to milk a cow, or half of that, he should proceed.

Even when there is no gain or when he is treated with contempt, he should not be despondent; even upon obtaining honor, he should not be over-satisfied. He should not walk either too quickly or too slowly.
Except at the time for begging, he should not go to the house of another.
He should not go more than a *krośa* to beg for alms.

Having wandered for alms, he should wash his hands and feet by the water’s edge, perform the ritual sipping (*ācamana*), and offer the first portion of the alms to the Sun with the mantra "ud u tyam," to Viṣṇu with "ato devāḥ," and to Brahmā with "brahma jajñānam. Then, saying "to all beings," he should cast the *bali* offering.

Having resolved upon the sacrifice to the Self (*ātmayajña*) according to the procedure for the *agnihotra*, he should eat eight mouthfuls—just enough for the maintenance of life—or he may eat at his pleasure. Or he may not eat at all.
Having drunk water filtered through a cloth and performed the ritual sipping (ācamana), he sips water again.
He should not engage in censure or abuse. He should abandon his kinsmen and relatives.
He should not speak of his lineage, conduct, austerity, or learning.

Having abandoned attachment, practicing restraint and self-control, speaking what is pleasant and true, non-hostile toward all beings, equanimous, always devoted to the inner self, and a practitioner of yoga through meditation, he should maintain concentration while beholding Nārāyaṇa as the Supreme Brahman;
thus he attains the imperishable Brahman.
"The supreme Brahman is Nārāyaṇa"—thus says the Śruti.

When the body of a renunciant (saṃnyāsin) who has not maintained the sacred fires has died, his son or another person, having covered it with grass and having placed it near pure Brāhmaṇas, digs a pit in a river flowing toward the ocean or on a sandy bank, in such a way that it will not be touched by jackals or other scavengers.

Having bathed [the image] with the Gāyatrī, and having likewise caused it to be seated or laid down, he should place the triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*) in the right hand with Vaiṣṇava mantras; the water-strainer (*śikya*) and the *appavitra* in the left with the verse "yad asya pāre rajasaḥ"; the alms-bowl (*bhikṣāpātra*) on the belly with the Sāvitrī; the saffron robe (*kāṣāya*), the clay-receptacle, and the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) in the private part with the verse "bhūmir bhūmiṃ" and then cover them.
If jackals or other animals touch that [image], the one who made it becomes a sinner.

Having transferred the fires of the *āhitāgni* into his own self, [the officiant] bathes the deceased body of the renunciant with the *gāyatrī*, carries it as before, places it in a pure location, and having descended that fire into the common fire (*laukikāgni*) with the mantra "Descend into this fire" (*tadagnim upāvaroha*), he pours clarified butter and milk into the mouth with the mantra "Thou art a purifier" (*pavitraṃ te*). Having arranged the triple staff and other implements as before, he performs the cremation using the mantras of the *āhitāgni* and those fires, according to either the *brahmamedha* or the *pitṛmedha*. For these two [the renunciant and the *āhitāgni*], one should not perform the impurity rites, the water libations, the offering of funeral cakes, the *ekoddiṣṭa* rites, and so forth.
He who performs the *nārāyaṇabali*—
whether by digging up the remains for removal, by covering them, by cremating them, or by performing the *nārāyaṇabali* itself— shall obtain the fruit of a horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*).

Regarding the *Nārāyaṇabali*: "From Nārāyaṇa alone comes the accomplishment of all goals. One performs this for those killed by Brahmā or other [divine beings], for suicides, for those who died from ropes, weapons, water, lightning, fanged animals, beasts, serpents, and so forth; for those who died of all manner of sins and are otherwise unfit for cremation; for a mendicant after the eleventh day; and for the five types of great sinners (*mahāpātakin*) after twelve years have passed. It is performed on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight or on the *Śravaṇa* lunar mansion, at the place where the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* would otherwise take place, for the sake of the deceased.

On the previous day, one should invite twelve Brāhmaṇas. On the following day, having prepared a fire-sanctuary near the temple of Viṣṇu, by a riverbank, or in one's own house, one should perform the *āghāra* oblation. Having strewn grass around the fire and spread darbha grass to the northwest of the fire, one should place an image made of that [same] material or gold upon it. Meditating on the Puruṣa, one should invoke the god Nārāyaṇa, facing eastward, with the mantra "Oṃ bhūḥ puruṣam" and so forth, and offer him a seat, water for the feet (*pādya*), and water for sipping (*ācamana*).

Having bathed [the image] with the *Puruṣasūkta*, or with the eight-syllable mantra beginning with "nārāyaṇāya vidmahe," he worships it with a garment, an upper cloth, ornaments, water for the feet, water for sipping, flowers, perfumes, incense, lamps, unbroken grains (*akṣata*), and water for sipping.
He should offer libations of water with the twelve names beginning with Keśava.

Having sprinkled [the offering materials], he should sacrifice clarified butter and sacrificial porridge (*caru*) with the hymns beginning with "sahasraśīrṣā" and "viṣṇor nu kaṃ," and with the twelve names [of the Lord].

Having offered as an oblation milk-rice (pāyasa) mixed with molasses, clarified butter, and fruit to the Lord of Gods with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī, one should present water for the feet, water for sipping, and a mouth-cleanser.

Having worshipped, beginning from the south, upon *darbha* grass with tips pointing northward to the south of the fire, he offers an oblation of milk-rice (*pāyasa*) with the following mantras: "To Nārāyaṇa, the thousand-headed, the thousand-eyed, the thousand-footed, the Supreme Person, the Supreme Self, the Supreme Light, the Supreme Brahman, the Unmanifest, the Cause of All, the Lord of Sacrifice, the Soul of Sacrifice; to the Viśvedevas, to all the deities, to the Sādhyas. Having thus offered the oblation, he sacrifices clarified butter (*ājya*) with these same [mantras].

Having washed the feet of the Brahmins, given them new garments, upper cloths, and ornaments, and having honored them with flowers and other offerings, he should feed them white food accompanied by side dishes, clarified butter, molasses, curd, and fruit, while meditating upon the twelve forms [of Viṣṇu]. He gives gold as a sacrificial fee according to his capacity.

Having praised [Viṣṇu] with the hymns beginning with "sahasraśīrṣā" and with the twelve names, he should prostrate himself and perform the concluding oblation (*antahoma*). Having attained the supreme goal desired by him, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Regarding those born from the intermixture of the four castes—namely the *anulomas*, *pratilomas*, *antarālas*, and *vrātyas*—their origin, names, and occupations [shall be described].
A son born from a woman of lower birth by a man of higher birth is an *anuloma*;
one born from a woman of higher birth by a man of lower birth is a *pratiloma*.
From that, one born from a man of a higher class by a woman of a higher class is an *antarāla*;
one born from a man of a lower class by a woman of a lower class becomes a *vrātya*.
From the mouth of Brahmā arose the Brāhmaṇas and Brāhmaṇī women; the Brahman-sages became their wives.

Among them, one born from a limb-born man (gātrotpanna) upon a Brāhmaṇa woman of a different gotra who has been wed according to the prescribed rite with the recitation of mantras shall be a pure Brāhmaṇa. One born by an improper rite upon a woman who has previously belonged to another, or upon a Golakī, is a Kuṇḍa; these two types of Brāhmaṇas are censured.
Therefore, one born according to the rite from a Kṣatriya father and a Kṣatriya mother below the arms is a pure Kṣatriya.

Of these two, the one born in secret (*gūḍhotpanna*) who is not according to the rule is impure and is called *bhojaka*; he is not to be consecrated with the binding of the turban, yet he exercises the command of the king’s army.
In the absence of a pure [son], even one without the binding of the turban should protect the people;
his conduct should be like that of a king.

From a Vaiśya born below the thighs [of a Kṣatriya] with a Vaiśya woman, a Vaiśya is likewise pure, though he is excluded from the prescribed rites. A Maṇikāra is impure; he is one who pierces gems, pearls, and the like, and works with conch shells and bracelets. Now, from a Śūdra born from the feet [of a Brāhmaṇa] with a Śūdra woman, a Śūdra is pure according to the rule.
The *jāra*, the *mālavaka*, the censured *śūdra*, the horse-keeper, and the one who gathers grass for horses—
these belong to the four castes (*cāturvarṇika*).
All those born from their respective sacraments (*saṃskāra*) are the *anuloma* and other [mixed-caste] offspring.
One born from a Brāhmaṇa father and a Kṣatriya daughter is a Savarṇa; among the *anuloma* castes, he is the foremost.

His livelihood consists of the rites of the Atharvaveda, the driving of horses, elephants, and chariots, mounting [the throne], serving as a king’s general, and the practice of Ayurveda. One secretly born [to such a union] is known as an *Abhiniṣakta*.
If he becomes an anointed king, he should study the eight-limbed Āyurveda or the Bhūtatantra.
Following the conduct prescribed therein, endowed with compassion, and speaking the truth, he should act for the welfare of all living beings according to those injunctions;
or else, his additional occupation may consist of the calculation of the luminaries and so forth.
From a Brāhmaṇa and a Vaiśya woman is born an Ambaṣṭha; he is a kakṣyājīvī, an Āgneya, a dancer, a herald, and a surgeon.

From old age, he becomes a potter, subsisting by the craft of a potter, or a barber who shaves from the navel upwards. From a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya woman is born a Madgu; having attained preeminence, he is known as Mahānarma and follows the occupation of a Vaiśya, but does not perform the duties of a Kṣatriya.
From a hidden [union], the offspring of a horse-seller shall be a dealer in horses for purchase and sale.

From a Brāhmaṇa father and a Śūdra mother, a Pāraśava is born; his livelihood consists of the worship of Bhadrakālī, painting, knowledge of the limbs [of the body], sounding musical instruments, and massage.
Born from an adulterous union, a Niṣāda is one who commits violence against wild beasts and other animals.

From a Kṣatriya father on a Śūdra woman is born an Ugra, whose duty is to inflict severe punishment upon those who should not be punished; from a paramour on a Śūdra woman is born a Śūlika, whose duty is to subject criminals to tortures such as impalement on a stake;
from a Vaiśya father on a Śūdra woman is born a Cūcuka, whose trade is the buying and selling of betel nuts, betel leaves, sugar, and similar items.

From a *gūḍha* (secretly born) father, a *kaṭakāra* is born; and from a *kaṭakārī* mother, likewise. From that, one born in the direct order (*anuloma*) from an *anuloma* woman is an *anuloma*. He shall follow the livelihood of either his father or his mother.

A *sūta* is one born from a *kṣatriya* father and a *brāhmaṇa* maiden through the performance of mantras. Among those born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*), this is the foremost; though initiated with mantras, he is devoid of the duties of the twice-born (*dvija*).
His livelihood consists of instructing others in their duties and preparing food for the king.

A Rathakāra is born from a man of lower caste through a woman of higher caste without the performance of sacred mantras; he is excluded from the status of the twice-born and performs the work of a Śūdra, living by the service of horses, such as feeding and taming them.

From a Vaiśya father and a Brāhmaṇī mother is born a Māgadha. He is one whose food may not be eaten even by Śūdras, who is untouchable, and who is a servant to all; his livelihood consists of praising, proclaiming, singing, and executing errands.

From a Vaiśya by a Kṣatriya woman is born an Āyogava; he is a weaver, a maker of cloth, and he subsists by dealing in garments and bronze vessels. From a Vaiśya by a Śūdra woman is born a Puliṇda; he lives in the forest, subsisting by hunting wild animals and beasts of prey. From a Śūdra by a Vaiśya woman is born a Cakra; he is a seller of salt and oil. From a Śūdra by a Kṣatriya woman is born a Dhigvaṇa; he is a cartwright. From a Śūdra by a Brāhmaṇa woman is born a Pukkasa; he is a hunter of birds and deer. From a Brāhmaṇa by a Śūdra woman is born a Cāṇḍāla; he is a carrier of corpses and a public executioner. From a Kṣatriya by a Śūdra woman is born a Śvapāka; he is a dog-cooker. From a Vaiśya by a Śūdra woman is born a Vaiṇa; he is a basket-maker. From a Śūdra by a Vaiśya woman is born a Māgadha; he is a bard. From a Śūdra by a Kṣatriya woman is born a Sairandhra; he is a servant. From a Śūdra by a Brāhmaṇa woman is born a Kṣatta; he is a charioteer. From a Brāhmaṇa by a Kṣatriya woman is born a Sūta; he is a genealogist. From a Brāhmaṇa by a Vaiśya woman is born a Vaidehaka; he is a trader. From a Brāhmaṇa by a Śūdra woman is born an Ābhīra; he is a cowherd. From a Kṣatriya by a Vaiśya woman is born a Māhiṣya; he is a counselor. From a Kṣatriya by a Śūdra woman is born a Karaṇa; he is a scribe. From a Vaiśya by a Kṣatriya woman is born a Rathakāra; he is a carpenter. From a Vaiśya by a Brāhmaṇa woman is born a Bhr̥jjakaṇṭha; he is a fisherman. From a Śūdra by a Kṣatriya woman is born a Kukkuṭaka; he is a butcher. From a Śūdra by a Vaiśya woman is born a Vena; he is a sweeper. From a Śūdra by a Brāhmaṇa woman is born a Puṣkasaka; he is a scavenger. From a Brāhmaṇa by a Kṣatriya woman is born a Rājanya; he is a king. From a Brāhmaṇa by a Vaiśya woman is born a Vaiśya; he is a merchant. From a Brāhmaṇa by a Śūdra woman is born a Śūdra; he is a laborer. From a Kṣatriya by a Vaiśya woman is born a Māhiṣya; he is a counselor. From a Kṣatriya by a Śūdra woman is born a Karaṇa; he is a scribe. From a Vaiśya by a Kṣatriya woman is born a Rathakāra; he is a carpenter. From a Vaiśya by a Brāhmaṇa woman is born a Bhr̥jjakaṇṭha; he is a fisherman. From a Śūdra by a Kṣatriya woman is born a Kukkuṭaka; he is a butcher. From a Śūdra by a Vaiśya woman is born a Vena; he is a sweeper. From a Śūdra by a Brāhmaṇa woman is born a Puṣkasaka; he is a scavenger. From a Brāhmaṇa by a Kṣatriya woman is born a Rājanya; he is a king. From a Brāhmaṇa by a Vaiśya woman is born a Vaiśya; he is a merchant. From a Brāhmaṇa by a Śūdra woman is born a Śūdra; he is a laborer. From a Kṣatriya by a Vaiśya woman is born a Māhiṣya; he is a counselor. From a Kṣatriya by a Śūdra woman is born a Karaṇa; he is a scribe. From a Vaiśya by a Kṣatriya woman is born a Rathakāra; he is a carpenter. From a Vaiśya by a Brāhmaṇa woman is born a Bhr̥jjakaṇṭha; he is a fisherman. From a Śūdra by a Kṣatriya woman is born a Kukkuṭaka; he is a butcher. From a Śūdra by a Vaiśya woman is born a Vena; he is a sweeper. From a Śūdra by a Brāhmaṇa woman is born a Puṣkasaka; he is a scavenger. From a Brāhmaṇa by a Kṣatriya woman is born a Rājanya; he is a king. From a Brāhmaṇa by a Vaiśya woman is born a Vaiśya; he is a merchant. From a Brāhmaṇa by a Śūdra woman is born a Śūdra; he is a laborer. From a Kṣatriya by a Vaiśya woman is born a Māhiṣya; he is a counselor. From a Kṣatriya by a Śūdra woman is born a Karaṇa; he is a scribe. From a Vaiśya by a Kṣatriya woman is born a Rathakāra; he is a carpenter. From a Vaiśya by a Brāhmaṇa woman is born a Bhr̥jjakaṇṭha; he is a fisherman. From a Śūdra by a Kṣatriya woman is born a Kukkuṭaka; he is a butcher. From a Śūdra by a Vaiśya woman is born a Vena; he is a sweeper. From a Śūdra by a Brāhmaṇa woman is born a Puṣkasaka; he is a scavenger. From a Brāhmaṇa by a Kṣatriya woman is born a Rājanya; he is a king. From a Brāhmaṇa by a Vaiśya woman is born a Vaiśya; he is a merchant. From a Brāhmaṇa by a Śūdra woman is born a Śūdra; he is a laborer. From a Kṣatriya by a Vaiśya woman is born a Māhiṣya; he is a counselor. From a Kṣatriya by a Śūdra woman is born a Karaṇa; he is a scribe. From a Vaiśya by a Kṣatriya woman is born a Rathakāra; he is a carpenter. From a Vaiśya by a Brāhmaṇa woman is born a Bhr̥jjakaṇṭha; he is a fisherman. From a Śūdra by a Kṣatriya woman is born a Kukkuṭaka; he is a butcher. From a Śūdra by a Vaiśya woman is born a Vena; he is a sweeper. From a Śūdra by a Brāhmaṇa woman is born a Puṣkasaka; he is a scavenger. From a Brāhmaṇa by a Kṣatriya woman is born a Rājanya; he is a king. From a Brāhmaṇa by a Vaiśya woman is born a Vaiśya; he is a merchant. From a Brāhmaṇa by a Śūdra woman is born a Śūdra; he is a laborer. From a Kṣatriya by a Vaiśya woman is born a Māhiṣya; he is a counselor. From a Kṣatriya by a Śūdra woman is born a Karaṇa; he is a scribe. From a Vaiśya by a Kṣatriya woman is born a Rathakāra; he is a carpenter. From a Vaiśya by a Brāhmaṇa woman is born a Bhr̥jjakaṇṭha; he is a fisherman. From a Śūdra by a Kṣatriya woman is born

From a Śūdra father and a Kṣatriya mother is born a Pulkasa; having offered *surā* that is either artificial (*kṛtakā*) or made from the juice of the *arka* plant (*vāārkṣā*), he sells cooked food. From a Śūdra father and a Vaiśya mother is born a Vaidehaka; he is untouchable even by other Śūdras, his food is not to be eaten by them, and he subsists by gathering forest produce, tending goats and buffaloes, and selling their products.
From theft, one becomes a *cakrika*, living by means of salt, oil, and oil-cakes.

From a Śūdra father and a Brāhmaṇa mother, a Caṇḍāla is born; he wears ornaments of lead and iron, has his neck bound with leather, carries a rattle-topped staff (*kakṣerī*), wanders here and there excluded from all activities, and having removed impurities elsewhere, he casts them out outside the village or on the path in the forenoon.
He shall dwell far outside the village among those of his own kind.
After midday, he does not enter a village; if he should enter, he is to be executed by the king,
otherwise he incurs the guilt of killing an embryo.

And those who violate the intermediate vows: from a Brahmin woman, [the offspring of] a *cūcuka* is a *takṣaka*, who is untouchable; [the offspring of] a Kṣatriya woman is a *matsyabandhu* or *matsyabandhī*. [The offspring of a Vaiśya woman is] a woodworker, a goldsmith, a blacksmith, or a brazier. From a Śūdra woman, [the offspring of] a *cūcuka* is a *takṣaka*, who is untouchable; [the offspring of] a Kṣatriya woman is a *matsyabandhu* or *matsyabandhī*. [The offspring of a Vaiśya woman is] a woodworker, a goldsmith, a blacksmith, or a brazier. From a Śūdra woman, [the offspring of] a *cūcuka* is a *takṣaka*, who is untouchable; [the offspring of] a Kṣatriya woman is a fisherman or female fisherman. [The offspring of a Vaiśya woman is] a woodworker, a goldsmith, a blacksmith, or a brazier. From a Śūdra woman, [the offspring of] a *cūcuka* is a *takṣaka*, who is untouchable; [the offspring of] a Kṣatriya woman is a fisherman or female fisherman. [The offspring of a Vaiśya woman is] a woodworker, a goldsmith, a blacksmith, or a brazier. From a Vaiśya father and a Vaiśya mother, a Sāmudra is born; he lives by sea-trade and is a fisherman. From an Ambaṣṭha father and a Brāhmaṇa mother, a Nāvika is born; he lives by sea-trade and fishing, and he navigates a boat that crosses the ocean. From an Ambaṣṭha father and a Kṣatriya mother, an Adhonāpita is born; he shaves the hair below the navel.
From a Madgu with a Brāhmaṇa woman is born a Veṇuka, who plays the flute and the lute;
from a Kṣatriya woman, a Karmakara, who performs manual labor;
and from a Vaidehaka with a Brāhmaṇa woman, a Carmakāra, who lives by working with leather.
From an Āyogava father and a Brāhmaṇa mother is born a Sūcika, who performs the work of piercing with needles;
from an Āyogava father and a Kṣatriya mother is born a Tāmra, who lives by working in copper; and from an Āyogava father and a Vaiśya mother is born a Khanaka, who lives by digging.
From a *Nṛpa* man and a *Vaiśya* woman is born a *Udbandhaka*; from a *Śūdra* man and a *Vaiśya* woman is born a *Vastra-nirṇejaka*.
From a *Pulkasa* man and a *Brāhmaṇa* woman is born a *Rajaka*, a washer of clothes by removing their dirt.

From a *Caṇḍāla* man and a *Brāhmaṇa* woman is born a *Śvapaca*, who, like a *Caṇḍāla*, bears the prescribed marks, is eternally censurable, is excluded from all ritual acts, and serves as a remover of filth in cities and other places; dwelling in the cremation ground, he collects discarded vessels and shall release a deceased person who has no relatives.

Having killed those who deserve to be killed, he shall seize their clothes and other possessions, subsist on food dependent on others, eat from a broken vessel, consume dog meat, and engage in the trade of skins and armor.
When such a base son is born, the father becomes fallen and ruined, and goes to terrible hells.
A virtuous son is a savior from the hells; having purified his ancestors, he leads them to auspicious worlds.
"Therefore, Brāhmaṇas and the others should procreate a son according to the rule upon a wife of the same caste," so says Vikhanas.
